notes.title: OpenVLA: An Open-Source Vision-Language-Action Model
notes.tldr: OpenVLA fine-tunes the 7B Prismatic VLM (DINOv2 + SigLIP vision, Llama 2) on 970k Open X-Embodiment episodes, predicting 256-bin discretized actions as tokens; it beats the 55B RT-2-X and adapts cheaply via LoRA and 4-bit inference.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
- OpenVLA is basically a 7B vision-language-action model.
- They take the Prismatic VLM (DINO + SigLIP vision encoders, Llama 2) and fine-tune it on Open X-Embodiment, about 970k robot episodes.
- Actions are discretized into 256 bins per dimension and just predicted as tokens, which is super simple.
- Beats RT-2-X (55B) with way fewer parameters.
- They also show LoRA fine-tuning works on a consumer GPU.
- Question for me: does the token discretization hurt for dexterous tasks? Compare with π0's flow-matching action expert.

## Summary
OpenVLA is a 7B open-source VLA: a pretrained Prismatic-7B VLM fine-tuned end-to-end to map one camera image plus a language instruction to a 7-DoF end-effector action, emitted as discrete tokens. Trained on a curated 970k-trajectory subset of Open X-Embodiment, it outperforms the closed 55B RT-2-X by 16.5% absolute success over 29 tasks on WidowX and Google Robot. The paper also studies fine-tuning to new robots (full FT, LoRA, other PEFT variants) and quantized inference, and releases weights, data mixture and a training codebase.

## Problem
VLAs like RT-2 showed that Internet-pretrained VLMs give robot policies much better generalization, but those models are closed (architecture, data and training recipe hidden) and there were no best practices for adapting a VLA to a new robot or running one on commodity hardware. Open generalist policies such as Octo stitch pretrained parts to modules trained from scratch and generalize worse.

## Related work
- **RT-2 / RT-2-X**: the same "actions as language tokens" recipe on PaLI-scale VLMs (RT-2-X is 55B, trained on ~350k OpenX trajectories and co-fine-tuned with web data). OpenVLA is about 8× smaller, open, trained on more robot data, and fine-tuned on robot data only.
- **Octo, RT-1-X**: small transformer policies (93M, 35M) trained from scratch on OpenX. OpenVLA borrows Octo's data-mixture weights.
- **Prismatic VLMs** (Karamcheti et al.): the backbone. Its fused DINOv2+SigLIP encoder adds spatial features on top of SigLIP's semantics.
- **Diffusion Policy**: the strong from-scratch imitation-learning baseline in the fine-tuning experiments.

## Method
![Figure 2 from the paper: OpenVLA architecture: DINOv2 + SigLIP vision encoder, MLP projector, Llama 2 7B backbone predicting discretized action tokens](assets/openvla/fig1.png)

**Reused:**
- The Prismatic-7B VLM: a ~600M two-part vision encoder (SigLIP and DINOv2 run on the same patches, features concatenated channel-wise), a 2-layer MLP projector, and Llama 2 7B. Prismatic was trained on the LLaVA 1.5 mixture (~1M samples).
- RT-2's action tokenization: each action dimension is discretized separately into 256 bins. The 256 least-used Llama tokens (the last 256 in the vocabulary) are overwritten as action tokens, because Llama reserves only 100 special tokens.
- Standard next-token cross-entropy, computed on action tokens only.

**Changed or new:**
- Bin edges divide the 1st–99th quantile range of each action dimension uniformly, instead of RT-2's min–max range, so outliers don't waste resolution.
- Design findings from small-scale BridgeData V2 sweeps:
  - Prismatic beat LLaVA by about 10% absolute, and LLaVA beat IDEFICS-1 by 35% on language-grounding tasks.
  - 224 px input matched 384 px at a third of the training cost.
  - Unfreezing the vision encoder is crucial, contrary to VLM practice.
  - Many more epochs than usual for LLM/VLM training (27), training until action-token accuracy passes 95%.
  - Fixed LR of 2e-5 with no warmup.
- Policy interface: single image, no proprioception, no history, and one action per step (no chunking).

## Data
The base is Open X-Embodiment (70+ datasets, >2M trajectories). They keep only manipulation data with at least one third-person camera and single-arm end-effector control, then weight the datasets with Octo's mixture weights. The result is 970k trajectories. DROID was added at a 10% weight, but its action-token accuracy stayed low, so it was removed for the final third of training. They also cleaned the data, e.g. filtering all-zero actions from Bridge.

## Training
The model was trained on 64 A100s for 14 days (21,500 A100-hours) with batch size 2048. Inference in bf16 needs about 15 GB and runs at about 6 Hz on an RTX 4090 without speed-up tricks. Full fine-tuning on a new task took 8 A100s for 5–15 hours. LoRA fine-tuning takes 10–15 hours on a single A100.

## Results
- **Out of the box (WidowX/BridgeData V2: 17 tasks, 170 rollouts; Google Robot: 12 tasks, 60 rollouts):**
  - OpenVLA beats RT-2-X by 16.5% absolute averaged over the 29 tasks.
  - On Bridge it beats RT-2-X in every category except semantic generalization, where RT-2-X's web co-training helps.
  - On Google Robot it is comparable to RT-2-X. RT-1-X and Octo are much weaker on both.
- **Fine-tuning to Franka (7 tasks, 10–150 demos):**
  - OpenVLA has the highest average success rate. It is the only method at ≥50% on every task.
  - Diffusion Policy matches or beats it on narrow single-instruction tasks ("Put Carrot in Bowl", "Pour Corn into Pot") and produces smoother, more precise trajectories.
  - OpenVLA (scratch), meaning Prismatic fine-tuned without OpenX pretraining, does worse, which shows the value of robot pretraining.
- **PEFT** (Franka-Tabletop, 33 rollouts per method):

  | Method | Success | Trainable params | VRAM |
  |---|---|---|---|
  | Full FT | 69.7% | 7,188M | 163 GB |
  | LoRA r=32 | 68.2% | 97.6M (1.4%) | 59.7 GB |
  | Sandwich | 62.1% | 914M | 64.0 GB |
  | Frozen vision | 47.0% | 6,760M | 156 GB |
  | Last layer only | 30.3% | 465M | 51.4 GB |

  LoRA rank had negligible effect.
- **Quantization** (8 Bridge tasks):
  - bf16: 71.3%, 16.8 GB.
  - int8: 58.1%, 10.2 GB. The drop comes mostly from slow inference (1.2 Hz on an A5000), not from accuracy.
  - int4: 71.9%, 7.0 GB, at 3 Hz.
- **Consumer GPU caveat:** the paper's LoRA runs use a single A100 (~60 GB at batch 16). The consumer-GPU claim rests on LoRA plus quantization making that feasible. I did not find a LoRA fine-tuning run on an actual consumer card in v1 of the paper.

## Takeaways / questions
- The recipe is very simple: an off-the-shelf VLM, RT-2 tokenization and lots of epochs on curated OpenX data. Its gains over RT-2-X come from data size and cleaning plus the fused DINOv2+SigLIP encoder, not from model scale.
- **Does token discretization hurt dexterous tasks?** The paper partly concedes this:
  - Diffusion Policy is smoother and more precise on narrow dexterous tasks.
  - The limitations section names high-frequency control (ALOHA at 50 Hz) and bimanual dexterity as out of reach. The causes are single-step autoregressive decoding at ~6 Hz, no action chunking, and 256-bin resolution per dimension.
  - The paper doesn't separate the effect of bin resolution from the lack of chunking and history.
- **Comparison with π0:**
  - π0 keeps a VLM backbone but replaces token decoding with a flow-matching action expert that outputs continuous action chunks. This targets exactly these weaknesses (precision and high frequency).
  - Worth checking π0's reported comparisons to OpenVLA on dexterous tasks. See also [Robot Foundation Models](#/note/robot-foundation-models).
- Other limitations the paper lists:
  - Single image only, with no proprioception or history.
  - Success rates are usually below 90%.
  - Open questions: the effect of VLM size, co-training with web data (it might fix the semantic-generalization gap) and the best visual features.

notes.title: An Image is Worth 32 Tokens for Reconstruction and Generation
notes.tldr: TiTok is a ViT-based 1D image tokenizer: a few learnable latent tokens attend to image patches and are vector-quantized, so a 256×256 image becomes as few as 32 discrete tokens, enabling much faster generation with competitive or better FID.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Used as the simple discrete image tokenizer in an early Latent Sketchpad (discrete) variant of my COVA project. (Also the tokenizer behind my cat-latents side project.)

## Summary
TiTok (Transformer-based 1-Dimensional Tokenizer, ByteDance/TUM) asks whether image tokens need to sit on a 2D grid. Standard tokenizers like VQGAN map each latent position to a fixed image patch, so a 256×256 image always costs 256–4096 tokens even when large regions are redundant. TiTok instead appends a small set of learnable "latent tokens" to the ViT patch sequence; after encoding, only those latent tokens are kept and quantized, giving a 1D sequence with no fixed spatial correspondence. A 256×256 image fits in 32 tokens, and a MaskGIT generator on these tokens matches or beats far heavier models while sampling orders of magnitude faster.

## Problem
2D tokenizers waste tokens on redundant regions and tie the token count to a fixed downsampling factor ($f=16,8,4$ → 256, 1024, 4096 tokens at 256²). Fewer tokens would make every downstream generator or multimodal model cheaper, but it was unclear whether a compact 1D latent could still reconstruct well.

## Related work
- VQ-VAE — [1711.00937](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.00937) and VQGAN (Esser et al., 2021): the 2D quantized tokenizers TiTok departs from.
- MaskGIT (Chang et al., 2022): bidirectional masked-token generator used on top of TiTok, and its VQGAN supplies "proxy codes".
- ViT (Dosovitskiy et al.) — [2010.11929](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929): encoder and decoder backbone.
- Perceiver/Q-Former-style learnable queries: the general idea of summarizing inputs with a few latent tokens.
- DiT (Peebles & Xie): diffusion baseline at 512².

## Method
![Figure 3 from the paper: TiTok reconstruction (a), generation (b) and framework (c) — image patches plus a few latent tokens go through a ViT encoder, the latent tokens are vector-quantized, and the quantized tokens plus mask tokens go through a ViT decoder](assets/titok/fig1.png)

**Tokenize.** Split the image into patches (patch size 16 → 256 patches at 256²) and concatenate $K$ learnable latent tokens (e.g. $K=32$). A ViT encoder processes the joint sequence; only the $K$ latent-token outputs are kept.

**Quantize (reused VQ).** Each latent output is snapped to the nearest entry of a learned codebook ($N=4096$ in the final setting), giving $K$ integers.

**De-tokenize.** The quantized latent tokens are concatenated with a grid of mask tokens (one per output patch) and fed to a ViT decoder, which fills in the image patches. Since the decoder must reconstruct every patch from only $K$ global tokens, each token is free to encode whatever content is most useful, not a fixed location.

**Variants.** TiTok-S-128, TiTok-B-64 and TiTok-L-32: as the token count halves, the model size grows. At 512² they use TiTok-L-64 and TiTok-B-128.

**Generation.** A standard MaskGIT transformer (arccos masking schedule) is trained on TiTok token sequences; sampling uses only 8 steps over 32–128 tokens.

## Data
ImageNet-1K at 256×256 and 512×512, for both tokenizer and class-conditional generation.

## Training
Two-stage. *Warm-up*: rather than regressing pixels with perceptual and GAN losses, the 1D tokenizer is trained to predict the discrete **proxy codes** of an off-the-shelf MaskGIT-VQGAN, whose decoder then renders pixels; this sidesteps fragile GAN training while tuning the 1D design. *Decoder fine-tuning*: encoder and quantizer are frozen and the decoder is fine-tuned to output pixels directly (500k iterations). For one image: patches + 32 latent tokens → ViT encoder → quantize latents → ViT decoder with mask tokens → predicted codes (warm-up) or pixels (fine-tuning) → loss. Final tokenizers train for 1M iterations (200 epochs).

## Results
- ImageNet 256 (Table 1): TiTok-L-32 reconstructs with rFID 2.21 using 32 tokens (vs MaskGIT-VQGAN 2.28 with 256 tokens) and generates with gFID 2.77; TiTok-B-64: rFID 1.70, gFID 2.48; TiTok-S-128 with a MaskGIT-UViT-L generator: gFID 1.97, 4.21 better than the MaskGIT baseline.
- ImageNet 512: gFID 2.74 vs 3.04 for DiT-XL/2 with 64× fewer tokens and 410× faster generation; the best variant reaches gFID 2.13 while still 74× faster.

## Takeaways / questions
- The core insight — images are redundant, so a global 1D code can be far shorter than a patch grid — is directly relevant to latent visual reasoning: 32 tokens is a cheap "visual thought" for a VLM to emit. It is also why my cat-latents project could describe a cat in 32×12 numbers.
- Trade-off seen in practice: very compact tokens lose fine detail and text, which is why COVA later moved to WeTok for out-of-domain fidelity.
- Tokens have no fixed spatial meaning, which makes them harder to interpret or edit locally than grid tokens; what each of the 32 tokens encodes is an interesting open question.

notes.title: WeTok: Powerful Discrete Tokenization for High-Fidelity Visual Reconstruction
notes.tldr: WeTok is a discrete image tokenizer combining group-wise lookup-free quantization (scalable binary codebooks without the memory blow-up of LFQ) with a generative, noise-conditioned decoder; it reaches zero-shot rFID 0.12 on ImageNet, beating continuous VAEs like FLUX-VAE.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Picked as the new discrete tokenizer in my COVA project for out-of-domain performance: “high fidelity, also seems good at rendering text.”

## Summary
WeTok (Tencent WeChat Vision) is a discrete visual tokenizer that tries to break the usual trade-off between compression and reconstruction quality. Discrete tokenizers turn an image into a grid of integer codes for autoregressive or unified multimodal models, but historically reconstructed worse than continuous VAEs. WeTok closes that gap with two ideas: **group-wise lookup-free quantization (GQ)**, which makes very large implicit codebooks trainable without running out of memory, and a **generative decoder (GD)** that samples plausible detail from noise instead of averaging when a heavily compressed token is ambiguous. It reports reconstruction better than leading continuous tokenizers at the same compression and strong results at very high compression.

## Problem
Two issues with discrete tokenizers: (1) *codebook scalability* — larger codebooks reduce quantization error, and lookup-free quantization (LFQ) makes huge codebooks possible, but its entropy loss needs memory that grows with codebook size; BSQ fixes memory but introduces approximation error; (2) *deterministic decoders* — at high compression one token sequence corresponds to many possible images, and an MSE/LPIPS-trained decoder outputs their blurry average.

## Related work
- VQ-VAE — [1711.00937](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.00937) and VQGAN (Esser et al.): nearest-neighbor codebooks with perceptual and GAN losses.
- MAGVIT-v2 / LFQ (Yu et al., 2024) — [2310.05737](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.05737): lookup-free quantization with codebook $\{-1,1\}^d$ and entropy loss.
- Binary Spherical Quantization (Zhao et al., 2024): per-bit factorized entropy to save memory.
- Open-MAGVIT2, Cosmos tokenizer, FLUX-VAE, SD-VAE 3.5: the discrete and continuous baselines.
- TiTok — [2406.07550](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07550): a compact 1D alternative.

## Method
![Figure 2 from the paper: WeTok with group-wise lookup-free quantization and a generative decoder](assets/wetok/fig1.png)

**Backbone (reused).** A conv encoder $\mathcal{E}$ maps an image to latents $\mathcal{U}\in\mathbb{R}^{h\times w\times d}$; a decoder $\mathcal{G}$ maps quantized latents back to pixels; training uses reconstruction, LPIPS perceptual and GAN losses with straight-through gradients, as in VQGAN.

**LFQ recap.** Instead of a learned codebook, quantize each channel by its sign: $\mathcal{Q}[i,j,k]=\text{sign}(\mathcal{U}[i,j,k])$, i.e. an implicit codebook $\{-1,1\}^d$ with $2^d$ entries. To avoid codebook collapse, an entropy loss encourages each token to be confident (low per-token entropy) while the codebook as a whole is used evenly (high average entropy). Computing these entropies over $2^d$ codes is what blows up memory.

**Group-wise LFQ (new).** Split the $d$ channels into $g$ groups of $d'$ channels ($d=gd'$), each with its own small implicit codebook $\{-1,1\}^{d'}$. Assuming the groups factorize, both entropy terms become sums over groups:
$$H\big(q(\mathbf{c}\mid\mathcal{U}[i,j])\big)=\sum_{k=1}^{g}H\big(q_G(\mathbf{c}_k\mid\mathcal{U}_G[i,j,k])\big),$$
so memory scales with $2^{d'}$ instead of $2^{d}$. In their ablation (Table 1), LFQ runs out of memory at $d\ge24$ while GQ stays at ~10.6 GB up to $d=40$. GQ unifies LFQ ($g=1$) and BSQ ($d'=1$), and the authors argue its error is strictly smaller than BSQ's.

**Generative decoder (new).** Concatenate Gaussian noise $\mathbf{z}\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ with the quantized latents and train the decoder adversarially as a conditional generator, $\mathcal{L}_{\text{GAN}}=\mathbb{E}_{\mathbf{z}}[\log(1-\mathcal{D}(\mathcal{G}(\mathbf{z},\mathcal{U}_Q)))]$. The decoder now samples one sharp, plausible image (e.g. a specific fur texture) rather than the average, in a single step (cheaper than diffusion decoders).

## Data
Ablations and class-to-image generation on ImageNet; the released general models are pretrained on a 400M-image general-domain dataset across multiple compression ratios; zero-shot reconstruction evaluated on the ImageNet 50k validation set (plus other benchmarks).

## Training
Two stages. Stage 1: train encoder, GQ and decoder with reconstruction + perceptual + GAN + group-wise entropy losses (for one image: encode → sign-quantize each channel group → decode → compare). Stage 2: widen the decoder's input conv to accept $\mathbf{z}$, zero-initializing the new channels so it starts identical to stage 1, then train the generative decoder. A constant learning rate worked better than decay for large-scale tokenizer training.

## Results
- Zero-shot rFID **0.12** on ImageNet 50k val in the high-fidelity setting, vs FLUX-VAE 0.18 and SD-VAE 3.5 0.19 (continuous) — at what the paper calls a 400% compression ratio.
- High compression: rFID 3.49 at 768× compression, vs Cosmos 4.57 at half that compression ratio.
- Class-conditional ImageNet generation with an AR model on WeTok tokens: WeTok-AR-XL (1.5B) gFID 2.31 vs Open-MAGVIT2-AR-XL 2.33; WeTok-based AR models are slightly worse at small sizes but overtake as parameters grow.

## Takeaways / questions
- Why it fits COVA: a discrete tokenizer whose reconstructions are good enough that out-of-domain images (charts, text) survive tokenization — my own observation was that it renders text well, which the paper does not specifically benchmark.
- GQ is a clean answer to the codebook-collapse/memory problem I hit with VQ-VAEs at LBNL: no learned codebook to collapse, entropy terms that factorize.
- Open question: a generative decoder means reconstructions are *samples*, so fine details may be plausible but not faithful — a concern if downstream reasoning depends on exact visual content.

notes.title: CoVA-SFT: A Large-Scale Dataset for Chain of Visual Abstractions
notes.tldr: CoVA-SFT is a 51.9K-sample dataset (222K rendered visual steps, 17 tasks) teaching multimodal models to draw tables, graphs, boards and diagrams while reasoning about text-only problems, plus the 1,700-sample CoVA-Bench and a latent-visual-token baseline.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
My own paper (co-author; BAIR, with Tsung-Han Wu, Trevor Darrell, Joseph Gonzalez, David Chan). Accepted to EMNLP 2026 Findings. Saved in my *Relevant Links* doc as “COVA”.

## Summary
CoVA-SFT ("Chain of Visual Abstractions") is a dataset paper from UC Berkeley (authors Tsung-Han Wu, Heekyung Lee, Anya Ji, Haoming Chen, Trevor Darrell, Joseph E. Gonzalez, David M. Chan). Its premise: text-only chain-of-thought forces models to describe naturally visual intermediate states (a chessboard, a family tree, a constraint table) in clumsy prose, while humans would just sketch them. Existing interleaved reasoning data mostly grounds reasoning in images given in the input. CoVA-SFT instead targets **text-only problems** where the model must construct its own visual workspace from scratch, render it, check it, and keep updating it across many steps. It comes with a held-out benchmark (CoVA-Bench) and a baseline model that reasons with latent visual tokens.

## Problem
Interleaved text-and-image reasoning is promising, but the community lacked a large, multi-step, self-corrected dataset that teaches models *how* to build and maintain internal visual workspaces when solving purely textual reasoning problems.

## Related work
- Visual Sketchpad, Whiteboard-of-Thought, CodePlot-CoT — external drawing or code-rendered scratchpads for reasoning.
- Zebra-CoT and Math-VR — interleaved reasoning datasets, but grounded in given images or math-specific plots.
- Mirage (Machine Mental Imagery) and CoVT (Chain-of-Visual-Thought) — latent visual tokens inside the reasoning trace, aligned to features of input images.
- MathCanvas, Thinking with Generated Images (TwGI) — unified/agentic models that generate intermediate images.
- Qwen3-VL — the base model fine-tuned for the baseline.

## Method
**Data generation pipeline** (Claude 4.5 Sonnet as an agentic generator, three stages):
1. **Rationale and QA formulation:** the model explains *why* a visual workspace helps for this task, what to render, and writes the question–answer pair.
2. **Agentic rendering:** the interleaved trace is produced step by step; each visual workspace is drawn with Matplotlib (or networkx etc.) tool calls, and the rendered image is fed back as context before reasoning continues.
3. **Verification and self-correction:** the model checks each rendered image for structural consistency with the problem and redraws it if wrong.

**Baseline model.** Qwen3-VL-8B-Thinking is fine-tuned to produce both the textual reasoning and the intermediate *latent* visual trajectory, with each interleaved image represented by a fixed budget of 128 visual tokens. Loss: standard cross-entropy on text plus a cosine-similarity loss aligning each predicted (normalized) latent visual token $e_i$ with its target embedding $\hat{e}_i$:
$$\mathcal{L}_{\text{visual}} = \frac{1}{N}\sum_{i=1}^{N} \ell_{\cos}(e_i, \hat{e}_i), \qquad \mathcal{L}_{\text{SFT}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{visual}} + \gamma\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{text}}$$

## Data
- **CoVA-SFT:** 51,904 trajectories with 222,046 visual abstraction steps across 17 tasks in five layout families: **Table** (ACP, logic puzzles, scheduling), **Graph** (CLUTRR kinship, graph coloring, GraphInstruct, ProsQA), **Layout** (bin packing, seating arrangement, SpatialEval), **Game** (ARC-AGI, chess, maze, Sudoku) and **Math** (Math-VR, MathNet, 3D cube). Problems are either generated programmatically or taken from open datasets; Math-VR is the largest source (32.4%).
- **CoVA-Bench:** 1,700 held-out test samples (100 per task), verified to need multi-step reasoning and maintained visual state. Answers are graded with Gemini-2.5-flash as judge.

## Training
A sample is a text-only problem (say, a kinship puzzle) followed by an interleaved solution: reasoning text, then a rendered family-tree image, more text, an updated image, and the final answer. During SFT, text tokens get next-token cross-entropy, and at each image position the model must output 128 latent tokens whose cosine similarity to the target image embedding is maximized. Setup: 2 epochs on 51.9K samples, AdamW, LR $5\times10^{-5}$ with cosine schedule and 50 warm-up steps, global batch 16, max response length 32,768, visual encoder unfrozen, 8 H200 GPUs with FSDP2 in bf16.

## Results
CoVA-Bench accuracy (%), Table / Layout / Graph / Game / Math / average:
- Qwen3-Think (text-only LLM): 67.3 / 69.3 / 44.5 / 19.3 / 25.0 / 45.1
- Qwen3-VL-Thinking (text-only mode): 80.3 / 76.3 / 46.5 / 25.5 / 27.3 / 51.2
- Best interleaved baseline, MathCanvas: average 16.8 (CodePlot-CoT 12.9, Zebra-CoT 11.2, TwGI 0.9)
- **CoVA-SFT baseline (latent tokens): 47.2 / 53.4 / 62.0 / 20.0 / 8.5 / 38.2**

So the fine-tuned model beats every interleaved CoT baseline by more than 2× on average and beats all text-only models on Graph reasoning (62.0 vs 57.0), but still trails strong text-only CoT overall, with the largest gap on Math (8.5 vs 27.3), where symbolic text is already a good representation. External-rendering baselines suffer because rendering errors propagate with little chance to recover.

## Takeaways / questions
- The dataset is the contribution; the baseline shows it is learnable but leaves a clear open problem: interleaved latent visual reasoning does not yet beat text-only thinking models except on relational (graph) tasks.
- Limitations stated in the paper: dependence on the upstream generator (subtle hallucinations can leak in), visual abstractions limited to static schematic formats (tables, graphs, grids, plots), and the extra compute of joint text + latent-token training.
- Follow-up in my COVA progress deck: evaluated Latent Sketchpad, Monet and BAGEL on COVA; trained and evaluated Latent Sketchpad (SFT with 3 stages, RL with GRPO, RL with VLPO), Monet SFT, and Latent Sketchpad with a latent codebook (marked "Winner!"). The deck's overall status notes improved image dependency and out-of-domain performance over earlier attempts, but still behind the thinking baseline out of domain.

notes.title: Imagine while Reasoning in Space: Multimodal Visualization-of-Thought
notes.tldr: MVoT fine-tunes an autoregressive text+image model (Anole-7B, from Chameleon) to interleave generated images of intermediate states with verbal reasoning steps, adding a token discrepancy loss that improves image fidelity; robust gains on grid-based spatial tasks.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
"Actually generates intermediate images interleaved with textual reasoning in an autoregressive multimodal model. It sits between external whiteboard methods and fully latent visual reasoning because the visual thoughts are still explicitly rendered."

## Summary
Multimodal Visualization-of-Thought (MVoT) trains a multimodal-native model to "imagine" while it reasons: after each verbal reasoning step it generates an actual image (as discrete image tokens) showing the updated state, then conditions the next verbal step on all previous text and images. It is, per the authors, the first method where visual thoughts are natively generated as part of the reasoning trace, and it is the explicit-image predecessor of Latent Sketchpad (same group).

## Problem
CoT degrades on dynamic spatial reasoning, where the model has to track how a grid world changes as actions are applied. Earlier fixes either caption the image into text first (losing detail, introducing caption errors) or call external tools in a ReAct loop, so the model never itself reasons in the visual modality. Visualization-of-Thought (VoT) used text "drawings" as proxies, which are too simplistic.

## Related work
- Chameleon ([arXiv 2405.09818](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.09818)) and Anole: unified early-fusion models with a VQ image tokenizer, the backbone here.
- Visualization-of-Thought (VoT): text-based "mental images" for spatial reasoning.
- ReAct-style tool pipelines and [Whiteboard-of-Thought](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.14562): external visual tools.
- LoRA ([arXiv 2106.09685](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685)) for the fine-tuning.

## Method
Reused: Anole-7B (Chameleon tuned for interleaved image generation), its frozen VQ image tokenizer and text tokenizer, and LoRA. New: the interleaved reasoning formulation and the token discrepancy loss.

The trace is $z_1, v_1, z_2, v_2, \dots$, with verbal steps $z_i$ and visual thoughts $v_i$:
$$\hat v_i \sim P_\theta(v_i \mid \hat z_1, \hat v_1, \dots, \hat v_{i-1}, \hat z_i),\qquad \hat z_{i+1} \sim P_\theta(z_{i+1} \mid x, \hat z_1, \hat v_1, \dots, \hat z_i, \hat v_i).$$

**Token discrepancy loss.** Plain cross-entropy over image tokens treats every wrong codebook index as equally wrong. Because the transformer and the image tokenizer were trained separately, this hurts image quality. For each target image token $t_{\text{vis}_i}$ they compute its MSE distance to every codebook embedding, giving a row $S_{t_{\text{vis}_i}} \in \mathbb{R}^{1\times N}$, and penalize probability mass on visually distant tokens:
$$\mathcal{L}_D = \sum_{i=1}^{n} S_{t_{\text{vis}_i}} \cdot P(t_i),\qquad \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_C + \mathcal{L}_D.$$

![Figure 3 from the paper: MVoT training with the token discrepancy loss on image tokens alongside cross-entropy on text and image tokens](assets/mvot/fig1.png)

## Data
Three grid-based dynamic spatial tasks with newly collected interleaved datasets: Maze (predict the final location A–D after an action sequence; 5007 train / 1255 test), MiniBehavior InstallingAPrinter (6400 / 1604), and FrozenLake (fine-grained visual patterns, holes; 6846 / 1664). Each training example is an interleaved text–image trace with an image of the state after each action.

## Training
One Maze example: input = maze image + action list. Target = "Step 1: move up" → image tokens of the maze with the agent moved → "Step 2: move left" → image → … → "the answer is B". The transformer is trained with next-token cross-entropy on both text and image tokens plus $\mathcal{L}_D$ on the image tokens; tokenizers are frozen; only LoRA parameters are tuned, for 40 epochs on MI300X. The "Interleaved" baseline trains on the same traces but with loss on text only.

## Results
MVoT reaches 92.95% on Maze, 95.14% on MiniBehavior and 85.60% on FrozenLake. Direct answering sits around 70%; GPT-4o (zero-shot, CoT) does worse. Text CoT with explicit coordinates and layout captions beats 95% on Maze and MiniBehavior but falls below Direct on FrozenLake: 90.80% of its FrozenLake errors are wrong coordinates for holes, and its accuracy drops from 0.9401 on 3×3 to 0.3911 on 6×6 grids, while MVoT stays above 83% as grids grow. The token discrepancy loss visibly improves visualization quality.

## Takeaways / questions
- Visual thoughts mainly buy robustness and interpretability rather than raw accuracy over a well-captioned text CoT. Generating full images is expensive and much harder than the reasoning needs, which is the motivation for latent approaches.
- Mirage later found fine-tuned MVoT weak on VSP planning with only 1k samples, so this approach seems data-hungry.
- Tasks are small synthetic grids where the visual state is fully determined by the actions; whether this scales to natural images is open.

notes.title: What's Holding Back Latent Visual Reasoning?
notes.tldr: Analysis paper: replacing latent visual tokens in LVR, Monet, ILVR and LanteRn with dummy tokens barely changes accuracy (latent bypass), because oracle latents add little beyond the input image; and generated latents collapse to a narrow region far from the oracles.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
A recent paper, "What Is Holding Back Latent Visual Reasoning?", makes this issue concrete. The authors replace meaningful latent visual tokens in existing systems with uninformative dummy tokens and find that accuracy often barely changes. They call this latent bypass. They then study why it happens and show that many oracle intermediate visual representations provide limited information beyond what the original image already contains. When they instead construct a diagnostic task where the intermediate state genuinely simplifies or enables the final prediction, the model can learn to causally depend on that state. They identify a second problem as well: at inference time, predicted visual latents can collapse into a narrow region of representation space rather than reproducing the diversity of the oracle visual states. So to me there are really two separate failures: bypass means the dataset gives the model no reason to use the latent; collapse means that even when the latent would be useful, the model has trouble generating a sufficiently informative one.

## Summary
A careful diagnostic study of the latent visual reasoning line (Mirage-style continuous "visual thoughts"). Using causal interventions on four off-the-shelf models, the authors show the latents have little to no effect on answers, trace this to training data whose intermediate images are mostly crops of the input, show on two controlled setups that models *do* rely on latents when the intermediate carries new information, and then show a second failure: the latents a model generates at test time collapse and don't match the oracle latents. The conclusion is that progress needs both informative intermediate data and better latent prediction.

## Problem
Latent visual reasoning papers report accuracy gains, but nobody had checked whether the latents causally matter or what they encode. If the model can answer from the image alone, the gains might come from extra fine-tuning or extra compute rather than from "visual imagination".

## Related work
- LVR — [Latent Visual Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24251): ROI-token reconstruction.
- Monet — [Reasoning in Latent Visual Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2511.21395): distillation SFT + VLPO, trained free-running.
- ILVR: multiple latent blocks with an EMA momentum teacher; trained on CoMT and VSP.
- LanteRn: encodes intermediate images independently; the testbed for their retraining experiments.
- Pause tokens ([Goyal et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.02226)): the compute-matched control.
- VisCoT: bounding-box intermediate data used by LVR, LanteRn and Monet.

## Method
**Common framework.** All four models emit `latent_start`, generate a fixed block of $K$ latents from hidden states (6–12 steps), then resume text. Training combines NTP with a latent alignment loss to oracle latents $z^*$ (MSE or cosine) derived from intermediate images, usually followed by RL with text-only supervision:
$$\mathcal{L} = -\tfrac{1}{T}\sum_t \log P_\theta(y_t\mid y_{<t}, z, x) + \gamma\,\tfrac{1}{K}\sum_k \ell(\hat z_k, z^*_k).$$

**Causal interventions.** Decode from $P_\theta(y \mid do(z = z'), x)$ with $z'$ = latents from a random subregion of an unrelated image (in-distribution but irrelevant), zeros, Gaussian noise, or skipping latents entirely; compare with standard inference and with oracle latents. Benchmarks: BLINK (localization and spatial tasks), V*, and held-out VisCoT.

**Why bypass happens.** Retrain LanteRn three ways: (a) a *pause-token* baseline with placeholder tokens instead of oracle latents (same compute, no intermediate info); (b) *masked training*, where the relevant region is blacked out in the input but kept in the intermediate image, so the info is only in the latents; (c) a new *Tetris-like rotation* task: given polyominoes A and B (B is a rotation of A), apply the same rotation to C and pick among four candidates; the intermediate image shows the rotation, which is not trivially recoverable from the input.

**Collapse analysis.** On 300 held-out VisCoT samples, rank all oracle latents by cosine similarity to each generated latent and measure retrieval@1/5/10; USP (how often a generated latent is closer to an unrelated generated latent than to its own oracle); and mean pairwise similarity within predicted vs within oracle latents.

![Figure 2 from the paper: oracle latent tokens are computed from intermediate visual representations, and training extends next-token prediction into continuous latent space with teacher forcing on the oracle latents](assets/whats-holding-back-lvr/fig1.png)

## Data
BLINK, V* and VisCoT for the interventions; LanteRn's VisCoT-based training data (filtered to remove text-solvable samples) for pause/masked experiments; the new Tetris-like dataset with over 8k synthetic combinations, 4k training and 400 evaluation instances, color removed from intermediate images.

## Results
- **Bypass.** For every model and benchmark there is at least one uninformative intervention that keeps accuracy within 2 points of standard inference, sometimes slightly higher, both after SFT and after RL. Feeding *oracle* latents also gives no consistent improvement.
- **Pause tokens match latents.** On filtered VisCoT, LanteRn with oracle latents and the pause-token baseline both reach 79%.
- **Masked training creates reliance.** Oracle latents 75% vs 59–61% under random subregion, noise or zeros, and 59% for pause tokens.
- **Tetris.** Oracle latents 0.86 accuracy; random intermediate image 0.30, noise 0.26, zeros 0.25, pause tokens 0.34, so the latents matter. But standard inference (model-generated latents) gives only 0.33.
- **Collapse.** Retrieval@10 is at most 10% for all models; USP is 99–100%; predicted latents have pairwise similarity 0.82–0.98, while oracle latents are more diverse (e.g. 0.22 for LVR, 0.33 for ILVR). Monet is an exception, with high similarity in both predicted and oracle latents. Consecutive latent positions also become increasingly similar over time.

## Takeaways / questions
- This is the critical sanity check for my area: any latent-reasoning result should report dummy, zero, noise, shuffled and pause-token controls at matched compute.
- Bypass is a *data* problem (crops add nothing beyond the input), so it argues for intermediate states that transform the input: rotations, state prediction, planning. This motivates scaling COVA-style data beyond crops.
- Collapse is a *modeling* problem: even when the latent would help (Tetris: 0.86 with oracle), the model can't generate it (0.33). Better latent prediction (codebooks/VQ, diffusion heads, better targets) is an open direction. My COVA finding that a VQ-codebook Latent Sketchpad variant worked best is at least consistent with this.
- Open question: does RL on latents (VLPO) help with collapse, or just move the collapsed point?

notes.title: Training Large Language Models to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space
notes.tldr: Coconut feeds the LM's last hidden state back as the next input embedding instead of decoding a token, trained with a curriculum that replaces CoT steps by continuous thoughts; on GPT-2 it beats CoT on search-heavy logic (ProsQA 97.0% vs. 77.5%) with far fewer tokens.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
“Not visual, but introduces the key continuous-reasoning concept: feed the LM's final hidden state back as the next input instead of decoding every reasoning step into language. It's an important conceptual precursor to Mirage-style continuous thinking.”

## Summary
Coconut (Chain of Continuous Thought), from FAIR at Meta and UC San Diego, asks whether a language model has to think in words. In “latent mode” it skips the vocabulary entirely: the final hidden state at one position becomes the input embedding at the next. A staged curriculum teaches this using ordinary chain-of-thought data. The surprising emergent behaviour is that one continuous thought can hold *several* candidate next steps at once, so the model effectively does breadth-first search instead of committing to a single path as CoT does. It is the reference point for latent-reasoning work, including the latent *visual* reasoning (Mirage, Monet) in my xAI prep notes.

## Problem
In CoT, every reasoning step is a sequence of word tokens. Most of those tokens serve fluency rather than reasoning, while a few critical tokens require hard planning; and committing to one sampled token at each step forces early decisions. Is unconstrained latent space a better medium for reasoning?

## Related work
- Chain-of-thought prompting ([arXiv:2201.11903](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903)) — the language-space baseline.
- Deng et al., iCoT, *From Explicit CoT to Implicit CoT* ([arXiv:2405.14838](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.14838)) — gradually removing CoT tokens; Coconut borrows its multi-stage curriculum.
- Goyal et al., pause tokens ([arXiv:2310.02226](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.02226)) — extra compute via dummy tokens, a baseline.

## Method
A standard LM computes $H_t = \text{Transformer}(E_t)$ and $p(x_{t+1}\mid x_{\le t}) = \text{softmax}(W h_t)$. Coconut adds special tokens `<bot>` / `<eot>` around a latent segment. Inside it, the input sequence becomes
$$E_t = [e(x_1), \dots, e(x_i), h_i, h_{i+1}, \dots, h_{t-1}]$$
— the previous position's last hidden state (already through the final layer norm) is used directly as the next input. After `<eot>`, normal token embeddings resume. No new modules are added: the base model (pretrained **GPT-2**) is reused, and only the use of its hidden states changes.

![Figure 1 from the paper: chain-of-thought decodes each step into word tokens, while Coconut feeds the last hidden state back as the next input embedding](assets/coconut/fig1.png)

**Curriculum (the essential ingredient).** Stage 0 trains on normal CoT. At stage $k$, the first $k$ language reasoning steps are replaced by $k \times c$ continuous thoughts ($c$ thoughts per step), and the optimizer state is reset between stages. The loss is ordinary next-token NLL on the *remaining* text, masked on the question and latent positions — so continuous thoughts are not trained to reconstruct the removed words, only to help predict what comes next.

**Training cost.** With $n$ latent thoughts, training needs $n+1$ sequential forward passes (each thought depends on the previous one), which limits parallelism.

**Inference.** Same as decoding, except in latent mode; the number of thoughts is fixed to match the final training stage.

## Data
GSM8K (math; synthetic augmented training data from the iCoT authors, $c = 2$), ProntoQA (logical reasoning, $c = 1$), and a new **ProsQA** dataset — proof questions over randomly generated DAGs of fictional concepts with many distracting branches, which require real planning/search.

## Training
For a ProsQA example at stage 3: the question is embedded normally, then `<bot>`, then three continuous thoughts generated by three forward passes (each pass's last hidden state appended as the next input), then `<eot>`, then the remaining language steps and the answer. One more forward pass computes cross-entropy on those remaining tokens only; gradients flow back through all the continuous thoughts. GPT-2, learning rate $1\times10^{-4}$, effective batch 128, 5 epochs per stage, up to 50 epochs.

## Results
| Method | GSM8K acc. (tokens) | ProntoQA | ProsQA |
|---|---|---|---|
| CoT | 42.9 (25.0) | 98.8 (92.5) | 77.5 (49.4) |
| No-CoT | 16.5 | 93.8 | 76.7 |
| iCoT | 30.0 | 99.8 | 98.2 |
| Pause token | 16.4 | 77.7 | 75.9 |
| **Coconut** | 34.1 (8.2) | 99.8 (9.0) | 97.0 (14.2) |
| Coconut w/o curriculum | 14.4 | 52.4 | 76.1 |

- Continuous thoughts beat No-CoT by a large margin on GSM8K but stay below full CoT there; on search-heavy ProsQA they beat CoT while generating far fewer tokens.
- Without the curriculum, Coconut collapses — learning latent reasoning from question–answer pairs alone fails.
- More thoughts per step ($c$) improves GSM8K steadily (“chaining” continuous thoughts acts like test-time scaling).
- **Latent BFS:** probing $\text{softmax}(W h_t)$ shows a continuous thought assigns probability to multiple frontier nodes; the model keeps options open and prunes them over later thoughts. Nodes with lower “height” (closer to leaves) get sharper, more accurate value estimates. CoT, by contrast, sometimes hallucinates edges after reaching dead ends.

## Takeaways / questions
- The cleanest statement of the continuous-thought idea; Mirage applies the same “feed $h_t$ back instead of a token” move but anchors those hidden states to visual embeddings.
- It does not beat CoT on math with GPT-2, and the sequential training passes are expensive — scaling to large models is open.
- Continuous thoughts have no likelihood, so RL (GRPO) can't directly optimise them; that's exactly the problem Monet's VLPO tries to solve for latent visual tokens.
- Interpretability bonus: decoding $h_t$ through the LM head gives a cheap probe of what a latent thought “contains”.

notes.title: Latent Sketchpad: Sketching Visual Thoughts to Elicit Multimodal Reasoning in MLLMs
notes.tldr: Adds a Context-Aware Vision Head to a frozen MLLM so it can autoregressively generate vision-encoder-space latents between text steps, plus a separately pretrained Sketch Decoder that renders those latents as sketches; evaluated on a new MazePlanning dataset.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Main architecture in my COVA project; in the COVA deck, Latent Sketchpad with a latent (VQ) codebook was the winning variant.

Latent Sketchpad explores one architectural answer to this. Instead of simply reusing the standard language-model hidden state like Mirage, it introduces a Context-Aware Vision Head that autoregressively generates visual representations and a separately pretrained Sketch Decoder that can render those latents into human-interpretable sketches. I like this because it separates the question of "what representation is useful for the model?" from "can we inspect what information that representation contains?" But decodability alone still isn't enough: if I can decode a beautiful maze from a latent but replacing that latent with noise doesn't change the answer, then I haven't shown the model actually reasons through it. I would want both representational probes and causal interventions.

## Summary
Latent Sketchpad gives a pretrained MLLM (Gemma3-12B, Qwen2.5-VL-7B) an "internal visual scratchpad". After a `<start_of_image>` token the model generates a full image's worth of visual latents, one token at a time, in the *vision encoder's* feature space, using a small new Vision Head on top of the backbone's hidden states. Those latents are projected back into the LM input stream so reasoning continues with them in context, and a standalone Sketch Decoder can turn them into sketch images so a human can see what the model "drew". It comes from the same group as MVoT and is the latent-space successor to it.

## Problem
Explicit visual thinking either relies on external tools (detectors, code) or on unified generators (MVoT on Chameleon/Anole) whose objectives favor pixel realism, not reasoning-friendly abstractions. Meanwhile strong perception-oriented MLLMs like Qwen2.5-VL and Gemma3 cannot generate visual content at all. The question: can their pretrained visual features be repurposed as a generative sketchpad without damaging their reasoning?

## Related work
- MVoT — [Multimodal Visualization-of-Thought](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.07542): interleaves real generated images with text; direct predecessor.
- Visual Sketchpad and code-based tools such as [Whiteboard-of-Thought](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.14562): external drawing.
- Mirage — [Machine Mental Imagery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17218): reuses the LM hidden state directly as the latent.
- SDXL-VAE (frozen decoder) and AlignerNet (used inside the Sketch Decoder); Quick, Draw! dataset for sketch pretraining.

## Method
Reused: the whole MLLM backbone and its ViT encoder + connector (kept **frozen**), and a frozen SDXL-VAE decoder. New: the Context-Aware Vision Head, the Sketch Decoder (AlignerNet), and the MazePlanning dataset.

![Figure 2 from the paper: architecture of the Context-Aware Vision Head (hidden states to visual latents) and the standalone Sketch Decoder](assets/latent-sketchpad/fig1.png)

**Context-Aware Vision Head.** When generating the $t$-th visual token of image $X_k$, the head takes the backbone's last-layer hidden states for all previous images (global context) and for the tokens of the current image generated so far (local context), projects them into the vision-encoder latent space, then applies causal cross-attention (local attends to everything preceding) and causal self-attention within the current image. The output latent $l^*_{X_k,t}$ is passed through the existing connector back into the LM embedding space as the next input. After a fixed $n_v$ tokens, `<end_of_image>` is emitted and text resumes. The head is trained with a latent regression loss against the real encoder features of the target image:
$$\mathcal{L}_\text{reg} = \mathcal{D}(l^*_{X_k}, l_{X_k})$$
with $\mathcal{D}$ e.g. cosine or L1. Only the head is trained; the MLLM is frozen, which is what makes it "plug-and-play" and preserves the backbone's reasoning.

**Sketch Decoder.** A transformer encoder–decoder (AlignerNet) maps ViT tokens to a Gaussian over SDXL-VAE latents; the frozen VAE decoder renders the image. Loss = focal pixel reconstruction (foreground-weighted) + Gaussian NLL against the VAE encoder's posterior + MSE on patch embeddings. Pretrained on Quick, Draw! (50M sketches, 345 categories) and works zero-shot across OpenCLIP, Qwen2.5-VL and Gemma3 encoders. It is only a visualizer; it plays no role in the reasoning loop.

## Data
MazePlanning: 47.8K training mazes from 3×5 to 5×5, each with an interleaved text-and-image reasoning trace (the images show the maze state as the path progresses); 500 test mazes split into easy (< 4×5) and hard (4×5, 5×5).

## Training
One maze example: input maze image + "give the action sequence". The target trace alternates text steps ("move right to (1,2)…") with images of the updated maze. The backbone is fine-tuned on the text parts (a unified scheme supporting both text-only and multimodal CoT modes); at each image slot the Vision Head, reading the frozen backbone's hidden states, predicts the image's visual tokens one by one and is regressed onto the encoder's real tokens for that image. At test time its own latents replace the real image tokens, and the answer is read from `<actions>…</actions>`. Metrics: success rate (whole action sequence correct) and progress rate (fraction of consecutive correct actions before the first mistake).

## Results
Proprietary models struggle: o4-mini 19.60% SR, o3-pro (with tools) 18.40%, o1 15.20%, GPT-4o 8.60%. Fine-tuned text-only Gemma3 reaches 70.00% SR / 87.57% PR and Qwen2.5-VL 52.60% / 81.35%. Adding Latent Sketchpad gives small gains: +2.20 SR for Gemma3 and +0.40 for Qwen2.5-VL. The largest gain is the GPT-4o + Latent Sketchpad setting (Vision Head trained on a frozen Qwen2.5-VL): +3.80 SR and +9.06 PR, which the authors say surpasses o1 on progress rate. The Sketch Decoder gets consistently high SSIM across three encoders; the rendered sketches are blurry in details (arrows, digits) but structurally stable.

## Takeaways / questions
- The main claim is "no harm + interpretable traces", not big accuracy gains: on fine-tuned backbones the improvements are a fraction of a point to ~2 points.
- Supervising toward raw ViT features ties the latent to a perception space; whether that is the right space for reasoning is exactly the architectural question I care about (ViLex-style or VQ-codebook latents as alternatives).
- Decodability is not causality: a nice sketch doesn't prove the answer depends on it. Dummy/noise-latent interventions (as in *What's Holding Back Latent Visual Reasoning?*) are needed.
- In COVA, adding a latent VQ codebook on top of this architecture was the best-performing variant.

notes.title: Latent Implicit Visual Reasoning
notes.tldr: LIVR appends K learnable latent tokens to the prompt and, in a first stage, masks attention so the answer and prompt can only see the image through those tokens, forcing them to learn task-useful visual abstractions with no intermediate supervision.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
"Moves away from hand-designed helper images and directly learns task-dependent visual reasoning representations from the original image. Important because it questions whether specifying exactly what the intermediate visual thought should look like is itself limiting."

## Summary
Latent Implicit Visual Reasoning (LIVR) is a minimal, task-agnostic way to give an LMM extra visual computation space. It adds $K$ new special tokens to the vocabulary, appends them to every prompt, and trains with a *visual bottleneck*: an attention mask under which the answer (and the prompt text) cannot attend to the image tokens, only to the latent tokens, which themselves can attend to the image. The only loss is on the answer, so the latents are forced to carry whatever visual information the task needs. No helper images, boxes, crops, depth maps or CoT annotations are needed.

## Problem
Mirage, LVR, Aurora and MVoT all specify what the intermediate visual thought should be (a helper image, a crop, a depth map, a future frame). That costs annotation, bakes in human assumptions, and may be impossible for abstract tasks (what is the right intermediate for "which image is most visually similar?"). Simply appending latent tokens doesn't work either, because the model can bypass them and read the image directly.

## Related work
- Mirage — [Machine Mental Imagery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17218) and LVR — [Latent Visual Reasoning](https://arxiv.org/abs/2509.24251): latents supervised by helper images or crops.
- MVoT — [Multimodal Visualization-of-Thought](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.07542): explicit generated images.
- Aurora: discrete perception tokens for depth maps and boxes.
- Coconut ([arXiv 2412.06769](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.06769)) and pause tokens ("Think before you speak", [arXiv 2310.02226](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.02226)): extra latent compute in LLMs.
- BLINK ([arXiv 2404.12390](https://arxiv.org/abs/2404.12390)): source of the perception-heavy tasks.

## Method
Reused: Qwen2.5-VL-3B, Qwen3-VL-4B, LLaVA-OneVision-1.5-4B (vision encoder and projector frozen), LoRA on attention and MLP blocks. New: the latent tokens (only their $K$ embedding rows are unfrozen) and the two-stage bottleneck schedule.

![Figure 2 from the paper: latent tokens are appended to the prompt and the loss is on the answer; under bottleneck attention masking, answer and prompt tokens cannot attend to image tokens](assets/livr/fig1.png)

**Latent tokens.** Prompt $Q' = Q + L$ with $L = \{l_1..l_K\}$, randomly initialized. Unlike Mirage/Monet/LVR, the latents are *not generated* autoregressively from hidden states; they are fixed input slots whose processing (their hidden states through the layers) becomes task-adaptive. They act like learned queries that re-encode the image.

**Stage 1 (bottleneck).** Attention mask: answer tokens see $Q$ and $L$ but not $I$; $Q$ also cannot see $I$ (to avoid leakage); $L$ can see $I$. Loss is standard NLL on answer tokens only.

**Stage 2 (standard mask).** Restore normal attention so the answer can use both the image and the now-informative latents; same loss.

## Data
Nine perception-heavy tasks adapted from BLINK: counting (PixMo-Count), jigsaw and localization (COCO), visual correspondence (HPatches), art style (ArtBench-10), semantic correspondence (SPair-71k), functional correspondence (FunKPoint), relative reflectance (MID), visual similarity (DreamSim). Training data is plain question–answer pairs; 1k examples per task for single-task, 6k for multi-task. Tested on BLINK validation splits (or held-out splits for the two small correspondence datasets), de-duplicated against train.

## Training
Example (visual similarity): reference image + two candidate images + "which is more similar?" + 16 latent tokens. In stage 1 the answer token "B" can only get information about the images through the 16 latents, which attend to all image patches; the NLL on "B" backpropagates into LoRA weights and the latent embeddings, shaping what the latents extract. In stage 2 the mask is removed and training continues. Schedule: 4 epochs stage 1 + 6 epochs stage 2 with $K=16$, vs 10 epochs for the Direct SFT baseline on identical data; checkpoints chosen by validation accuracy.

## Results
Data-matched single-task means (Direct SFT → LIVR): Qwen2.5-VL-3B 61.61 → 67.85 (+6.24), with +12.00 on Jigsaw and +13.02 on functional correspondence; Qwen3-VL-4B 74.12 → 77.55 (+3.43); LLaVA-OneVision-1.5-4B 63.70 → 69.30 (+5.60), including +27.40 on functional correspondence. Multi-task on Qwen3-VL-4B (six tasks): 69.60 → 72.37. The paper also reports it is competitive with or better than text-CoT and explicit-intermediate methods on their own benchmarks (I did not copy those tables). Latent-to-image attention maps show the tokens focus on task-relevant structure.

## Takeaways / questions
- Cleanly addresses the bypass problem by construction: in stage 1 there is no path from image to answer except through the latents. This is a useful tool for my own experiments.
- These are not really "reasoning steps": the latents are a fixed number of appended queries processed in one forward pass, closer to a learned Q-Former/pooler inside the LM than to an iterative visual thought. There is no sequential, generated visual state.
- Gains are on 1k-example single-task fine-tunes of BLINK-style perception, so it is unclear how this interacts with long reasoning chains or RL.
- The interpretability cost: nothing anchors the latents to a visual space, so we can only inspect them through attention maps.

notes.title: Latent Visual Reasoning
notes.tldr: LVR trains Qwen2.5-VL to generate last-hidden-state latents that reconstruct (MSE) the visual tokens of the query-relevant region, interleaved with text, then applies GRPO_latent which replays rollout latents; gains on V* and MMVP.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
"Trains latent states to reconstruct query-relevant visual tokens in a joint semantic space and interleaves those states with text generation. It also introduces RL adaptation for the latent/text reasoning process."

## Summary
Latent Visual Reasoning (LVR) proposes that since an MLLM already embeds image tokens and text tokens in one shared space, it should also *reason* in both. Between `<|lvr_start|>` and `<|lvr_end|>` the model feeds back its last hidden states (Coconut-style) and, during SFT, those hidden states are trained to reproduce the visual tokens of the image region that matters for the question. It is a latent replacement for "think with images" crop/zoom tools, aimed at fine-grained perception rather than spatial planning, and it needs no auxiliary images, only bounding boxes.

## Problem
"Thinking about images" (text CoT) can let text dominate the context and weaken perception; "thinking with images" (cropping/editing tools) depends on fixed tool sets, multi-turn calls, and models often ignore the injected sub-images. Earlier latent approaches (e.g. Mirage) need separately made auxiliary images. LVR asks for a cheap, tool-free way for the LM to re-attend to and re-express the visual evidence it needs.

## Related work
- Coconut — [Training LLMs to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.06769): last hidden state as next input.
- Visual CoT (Shao et al., 2024): 438K VQA pairs with bounding boxes of the critical region; the SFT data.
- PixelReasoner, Argus, DeepEyes: tool-based "think with images" baselines.
- Vision-R1 and PAPO: RL text-CoT ("think about images") baselines.
- Mirage — [Machine Mental Imagery](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.17218): latent tokens supervised by auxiliary images.

## Method
Reused: Qwen2.5-VL 3B/7B; the vision encoder and projector are **frozen**, only the LLM is trained. New: the LVR mode, ROI-token reconstruction loss, GRPO_latent and the decoding strategies.

![Figure 2 from the paper: LVR training and inference; bounding boxes select query-relevant visual tokens that supervise the last hidden states via MSE during SFT, and GRPO_latent supervises only the text during RL](assets/lvr/fig1.png)

**SFT.** For an image–question pair with an ROI bounding box, the patch indices inside the box select a subset of the image's own visual embeddings $v_1..v_{T_v}$ (from the frozen encoder + projector). The target sequence becomes: question → `<|lvr_start|>` → $T_v$ latent steps → `<|lvr_end|>` → answer. At each latent step the model's last hidden state $h_t$ is fed forward as the next input and regressed to $v_t$:
$$\mathcal{L}_\text{LVR} = \frac{1}{T_v}\sum_t \lVert h_t - v_t\rVert_2^2,\qquad \mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_\text{NTP} + \lambda_\text{LVR}\,\mathcal{L}_\text{LVR}.$$

**GRPO_latent.** Rewards are accuracy (1/0) and a format reward for including both LVR tokens. Latents have no token distribution, so the policy loss is only over text tokens; the trick is that the rollout's latent hidden states are recorded and *patched back in* during the teacher-forced log-prob passes for $\pi_\theta$ and $\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}$, so the text ratios are computed in the exact same context. No ROI boxes are needed in this stage.

**Decoding.** It is hard to know when to exit latent mode. They try a fixed step budget, a learned "latent end" vector, and a BCE mode-switching loss; the fixed budget works best and mode-switching fails.

## Data
SFT: Visual CoT, 438K question–answer pairs with bounding boxes for the critical region. RL: ViRL data. Evaluation: V* (detail search and relative position), MMVP, and BLINK subsets (Counting, IQ-Test, JigSaw, Relative Reflectance, Spatial Relation), via LMMs-Eval.

## Training
Example: a large street photo, "what is written on the small sign?", with a box around the sign. The patches inside the box give, say, 40 visual tokens. The model reads the question, emits `<|lvr_start|>`, then for 40 steps its hidden state is pushed (MSE) toward each of those 40 sign tokens in turn while being fed back as input; after `<|lvr_end|>` the answer text is scored with cross-entropy, conditioned on the latents. SFT: learning rate 1e-5, adaptive multimodal packing (~3.2 instances per device), 2,500 steps in ~40 h on 4× AMD MI250 for 7B. RL (3B only): 8 responses per input, LR 1e-5, temperature 0.9, KL 0.04, 1,500 steps.

## Results
Qwen2.5-VL-7B base vs LVR (fixed 4/8/16 steps): V* 78.5 vs 81.2 / 81.7 / 80.6; MMVP 66.7 vs 72.0 / 71.7 / 71.7 (the abstract quotes 71.67 vs 66.67). It also beats an SFT baseline on the same data (V* 79.1, MMVP 65.7) and the tool-based PixelReasoner (V* 80.1, MMVP 67.0). Text-CoT RL methods hurt V* (PAPO 36.1, Vision-R1 70.2). LVR does not win on Relative Reflectance, which is multi-image while training was single-image. On 3B, GRPO_latent lifts V* from 65.5 to 67.0 (8 steps) and MMVP up to 58.0; removing the LVR-token format reward destabilizes training into pure-text responses.

## Takeaways / questions
- The latent target is literally a subset of the input's own visual tokens. That is the clearest case of the "intermediate state carries little information beyond the input" issue flagged by *What's Holding Back Latent Visual Reasoning?*, though for perception tasks re-attending to the right region may be exactly the point.
- GRPO_latent still never optimizes the latents directly; it only makes text ratios consistent. Monet's VLPO is the follow-up that adds a latent likelihood.
- The format reward that pays for using LVR is a hack that may encourage indiscriminate latent use; Monet explicitly avoids rewarding latent use.

notes.title: Machine Mental Imagery: Empower Multimodal Reasoning with Latent Visual Tokens
notes.tldr: Mirage lets a VLM 'think visually' by feeding its own last-layer hidden states back as continuous latent visual tokens between text tokens, grounded first on pooled helper-image embeddings, then relaxed to text-only supervision, then GRPO.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
One of the main baselines for my COVA project (compared against Latent Sketchpad-style training in the COVA deck).

Mirage is probably the cleanest example of this idea. Mechanically, its visual latents have the same dimensionality needed to enter the language model's autoregressive stream, but that dimensionality alone does not make them visual. The important part is how they're trained. Mirage uses helper images during training and obtains visual embeddings from those images. During its first supervised stage, the model is trained both with normal text next-token prediction and with an objective that anchors selected hidden states toward those visual representations. What I find especially elegant is that Mirage doesn't require a separate image generator: when it enters visual-thinking mode, it takes the transformer's own final hidden states and recasts them as the next continuous input tokens.

The second stage of Mirage is just as important conceptually. Once the model has learned approximately what the visual latent space should look like, Mirage removes the direct visual target and continues training using downstream textual supervision. Because the generated continuous latent remains inside the differentiable computation graph, the loss on later text tokens can backpropagate through that latent. So I think about the first stage as saying, "put your thought somewhere around a meaningful visual manifold," while the second stage says, "now don't reproduce the teacher image perfectly; change that latent in whatever way actually helps solve the problem." Mirage then adds a brief reinforcement-learning stage, but there's an important subtlety there: ordinary GRPO has a probability for sampled text tokens, but a deterministic continuous hidden vector has no natural categorical likelihood. Mirage therefore applies the policy objective directly to textual probabilities while gradients can still flow indirectly through the latent computation. It is not really doing a normal GRPO policy ratio over each continuous visual latent.

## Summary
Mirage ("Machine Mental Imagery") is a decoding scheme plus training recipe that lets a vision-language model interleave a few continuous "latent visual tokens" into its chain of thought, without ever generating pixels. When the model emits a special token, it stops projecting to the vocabulary and instead appends its own last-layer hidden state as the next input embedding, for $k$ steps. The paper's framing is human mental imagery: we picture a rough, task-relevant sketch, not a photorealistic image. It is one of the first clean demonstrations that interleaved text + continuous visual latents beat text-only CoT on spatial reasoning benchmarks.

## Problem
VLMs see the image once through the encoder, but their reasoning trajectory is pure text. Spatial tasks (mazes, jigsaws, geometry) need the model to manipulate a visual state, and verbalizing that state is lossy. Unified models that generate real images (Chameleon/Anole, MVoT) pay for heavy pixel-level supervision and decoding, and the paper argues that asking one model to both synthesize pixels and reason tends to hurt reasoning.

## Related work
- Coconut — [Training LLMs to Reason in a Continuous Latent Space](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.06769): feeds the last hidden state back as the next input; Mirage's visual analogue.
- MVoT — [Multimodal Visualization-of-Thought](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.07542): generates explicit intermediate images; used as a baseline.
- Anole / Chameleon: unified token-based text+image models; baseline.
- ICoT and Visual CoT: interleave image crops or bounding boxes into rationales.
- GRPO ([DeepSeekMath](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300)) and LMM-R1 reward design for the RL stage.

## Method
Reused: the whole base VLM, Qwen2.5-VL 7B (also 3B), with its own vision encoder. New: the latent decoding mode, the helper-image data pipeline, and the two-stage SFT recipe. There is no extra image decoder or vision head.

**Data.** For each question–answer pair they build a task-specific *helper image* $I$ (e.g. the maze start map with the ground-truth path drawn in red arrows; the reference image with a candidate jigsaw piece concatenated; a CogVideoX-5B rendering of the described scene for SAT). Qwen2.5-VL-32B is then prompted with the input, the answer and the helper image to write a step-by-step rationale that "uses" the helper image, giving a trace $o = o_\text{pre} \oplus I \oplus o_\text{post}$.

**Stage 1: joint supervision (latent grounding).** The helper image is passed through the VLM's own encoder to get patch features $e_1..e_n$, which are compressed to $k$ vectors by simple average pooling. The model is trained to produce $o_\text{pre}$ with cross-entropy, then at the $k$ latent positions its last-layer hidden states are pulled toward the pooled targets with a cosine loss, and $o_\text{post}$ is predicted with cross-entropy while attending to the ground-truth latents:
$$\mathcal{L}_1 = \mathcal{L}_\text{visual} + \gamma\,\mathcal{L}_\text{text},\qquad \mathcal{L}_\text{visual}=\ell_{\cos}\big(\hat e_j,\, g_\theta(o_\text{pre}, \hat e_{1:j-1})\big).$$

**Stage 2: text-only supervision with latent relaxation.** The cosine loss is dropped. The model now generates its *own* latents autoregressively ($e_j = f_\theta(x, o_\text{pre}, e_{<j})$) and these replace the pooled targets. Because they are continuous, the cross-entropy on $o_\text{post}$ backpropagates through them, so the latents drift to whatever is useful for the answer while starting from the visual subspace.

**Stage 3: GRPO.** Accuracy reward (1/0) plus a 0.1 format reward (`<think>` tags, `\boxed{}`). The policy ratio is computed only over text tokens; gradients flow through the latents indirectly.

![Figure 1 from the paper: Mirage interleaves compact latent visual tokens with text tokens to solve spatial reasoning tasks without pixel-level image generation](assets/mirage/fig1.png)

## Data
Four spatial benchmarks: VSP (maze spatial reasoning and spatial planning, levels 3–6), BLINK-Jigsaw, SAT (synthetic and real), and the geometry subset of CoMT (which already provides interleaved trajectories). Per task, 1k training instances for SFT and 2k for RL; three rationale variants per helper image.

## Training
Walk-through on a VSP planning example: input = maze image + "what action sequence reaches the goal?". The model writes $o_\text{pre}$ ("Let me picture the path…"), emits the latent-start token, and then for $k=4$ steps feeds back its hidden states. In stage 1 each of those 4 hidden states gets a cosine loss against the average-pooled Qwen2.5-VL features of the red-arrow helper map; in stage 2 there is no target and only the later text ("…so the moves are down, down, right") is scored with cross-entropy, with gradients reaching the latents. Hyperparameters: batch size 8, cosine LR schedule from 1e-5 for both stages, $k=4$, $\gamma=0.1$, RL with the Verl framework.

## Results
On VSP (Qwen2.5-VL 7B), Mirage (CoT) + GRPO reaches 0.89 average on spatial reasoning and 0.60 on spatial planning, vs 0.85 / 0.51 for CoT SFT + GRPO; Mirage trained on direct answers gets 0.76 planning vs 0.72 for direct SFT. Fine-tuned MVoT and Anole get only 0.61 / 0.11 and 0.52 / 0.01. On the other benchmarks Mirage scores 0.77 CoMT, 0.88 Jigsaw, 0.98 SAT-synthetic avg, 0.72 SAT-real, each at or above the best text-only baseline. Ablations on VSP planning: full 0.58, without stage 1 0.52, without stage 2 0.21, so both stages matter, and unlike Coconut, ungrounded latents do not help much. $k$ from 2 to 6 is robust but $k=8$ drops by about 13 points. A t-SNE shows the latent tokens cluster near but just outside the image-embedding region.

## Takeaways / questions
- The key insight is the training signal, not the shape: a $d_\text{model}$ vector becomes "visual" because stage 1 anchors it to image features. Stage 2 then trades grounding for usefulness.
- RL only optimizes text likelihoods, so the latents are never directly treated as actions; Monet's VLPO is one answer to this gap.
- The helper images are often simple transforms of the input (crop, path drawn on the map), which is exactly the "latent bypass" risk raised in *What's Holding Back Latent Visual Reasoning?*. I would want dummy/shuffled-latent controls.
- Gains are on narrow synthetic task families with ~1k examples each; cross-task transfer is untested, which is the data bottleneck my COVA work targets.
