notes.title: TradingAgents: Multi-Agents LLM Financial Trading Framework
notes.venue: Multi-Agent AI in the Real World workshop (oral)
notes.tldr: TradingAgents models an LLM trading firm: analyst agents write structured reports, bull and bear researchers debate, a trader decides, and a risk team plus fund manager adjust the plan; a 3-month backtest on AAPL, GOOGL and AMZN beats simple rule-based baselines.
notes.markdown:
## Summary
TradingAgents (UCLA, MIT, Tauric Research; open source at github.com/TauricResearch/TradingAgents) is a multi-agent LLM framework that copies the org chart of a trading firm. Specialized analyst agents gather fundamentals, sentiment, news and technical signals; bullish and bearish researchers debate; a trader agent decides; and a risk-management team and fund manager review the decision. Agents mostly communicate through structured reports in a shared state rather than long chat histories. In a short backtest it beats buy-and-hold and classic rule-based strategies on return and Sharpe ratio, and every decision comes with a readable rationale.

## Problem
LLM finance agents so far were mostly single agents or multi-agent systems that gather data independently, without modelling how real trading firms divide work and challenge each other's views. Multi-agent systems that talk only in free-form natural language also suffer a "telephone effect": as conversations grow, details get lost or corrupted.

## Related work
- ReAct (Yao et al., [2210.03629](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629)): every agent follows the reason-and-act prompting loop.
- MetaGPT ([2308.00352](https://arxiv.org/abs/2308.00352)): structured, document-based communication between role agents, which inspires the protocol here.
- Multi-agent debate (Du et al., [2305.14325](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.14325)): debate improves reasoning; used for the researcher and risk teams.
- Generative Agents (Park et al., [2304.03442](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03442)): societies of LLM agents with message histories.
- Prior LLM trading agents such as FinMem and FinAgent, which the paper groups under "LLMs as traders".

## Method
**Roles.** Seven roles, each with a name, goal, constraints, context and tools:
- *Analyst team*: a fundamentals analyst (financial statements, earnings, insider transactions), a sentiment analyst (Reddit/X posts, sentiment scores), a news analyst (news and macro indicators) and a technical analyst (computes indicators such as MACD and RSI, can run code). Each writes a concise report.
- *Researcher team*: a bullish and a bearish researcher read the analyst reports and debate for $n$ rounds; a facilitator agent picks the prevailing view and records it.
- *Trader*: reads reports and debate outcome, decides buy/sell/hold, timing and size, and writes a rationale.
- *Risk management team*: risk-seeking, neutral and conservative agents discuss the trader's plan for $n$ rounds under a facilitator; a *fund manager* then approves the risk adjustments and updates the decision.

![Figure 1 from the paper: TradingAgents organization, with analysts gathering market information, researchers debating, and the trader making the decision](assets/tradingagents/fig1.png)

**Communication protocol.** Instead of passing a growing chat log, each agent queries a global state for exactly the documents it needs and writes back a structured report. Natural-language dialogue is used only inside the two debates, and the debate result is itself stored as a structured entry.

**Backbones.** Nothing is trained; all agents are API LLMs. "Quick-thinking" models (gpt-4o-mini, gpt-4o) handle retrieval, summarization and table-to-text; "deep-thinking" models (o1-preview) handle analysis, decisions and report writing. Backbones are swappable, and no GPU is needed.

## Data
A multimodal daily dataset for several large tech stocks covering Jan 1 to Mar 29, 2024: OHLCV prices; news from Bloomberg, Yahoo, EODHD, FinnHub and Reddit; social-media posts with model-computed sentiment; insider transactions and sentiment; quarterly/annual financial statements; company profiles; and 60 technical indicators per asset.

## Training
No training. Each trading day, agents see only data available up to that day (no look-ahead), produce a buy/sell/hold signal that is executed, and metrics are updated before moving to the next day. Each prediction costs about 11 LLM calls and 20+ tool calls, which is why the backtest covers only three months.

## Results
Baselines: buy-and-hold, MACD, KDJ+RSI, ZMR and SMA. Metrics: cumulative return (CR), annualized return (ARR), Sharpe ratio (SR), maximum drawdown (MDD).

| Stock | TradingAgents CR / ARR / SR / MDD | Buy-and-hold CR |
|---|---|---|
| AAPL | 26.62% / 30.5% / 8.21 / 0.91% | −5.23% |
| GOOGL | 24.36% / 27.58% / 6.39 / 1.69% | 7.78% |
| AMZN | 23.21% / 24.90% / 5.60 / 2.11% | 17.1% |

The paper reports CR gains over the best baseline of 24.57, 16.58 and 6.10 points respectively. Rule-based baselines often have lower maximum drawdown but much lower returns. The authors themselves note the Sharpe ratios exceed the usual empirical range (above 3 is "excellent") and attribute this to few pullbacks in the short window.

## Takeaways / questions
- The interesting design idea is structured shared state instead of chat-log passing between agents; this is a general lesson for multi-agent systems, not just finance.
- The evaluation is thin: three stocks in the results table, a single three-month window, rule-based baselines only, and no ablation of which roles or debates matter. The very high Sharpe ratios are a warning sign rather than a result.
- Transaction costs are not discussed in the main text, and there is no comparison with a single strong LLM agent given the same data, so the value of the multi-agent structure itself is unproven.
- Pairs naturally with Kronos (also saved that day): a learned market model vs. an LLM agent firm reasoning over text.

notes.title: Embarrassingly Simple Self-Distillation Improves Code Generation
notes.tldr: Sample one unverified solution per problem from a code LLM at a shifted temperature with truncation, then SFT on those raw outputs; Qwen3-30B-Instruct goes from 42.4% to 55.3% pass@1 on LiveCodeBench v6, explained by a lock/fork precision-exploration conflict.
notes.markdown:
## Summary
This paper (Apple; code at github.com/apple/ml-ssd) asks whether a code model can improve using only its own raw outputs: no verifier, no tests, no teacher, no reward model, no RL. The answer is yes. Simple self-distillation (SSD) samples one solution per prompt from the model at a chosen temperature and top-k/top-p truncation, keeps it regardless of correctness, and fine-tunes the model on it with ordinary cross-entropy. All six tested models (Qwen3, Llama, GPT-OSS; 4B–30B; instruct and thinking) improve on LiveCodeBench, most on hard problems. The more interesting half of the paper is the explanation: SSD reshapes token distributions differently at "lock" and "fork" positions, which no single decoding temperature can do.

## Problem
Better code models usually need more supervision: human-written solutions, a stronger teacher, or execution-based verification for RL. Teachers cap the student; RL with verifiable rewards is complex and can be unstable; unsupervised intrinsic-reward RL (majority vote, entropy minimization) can reward-hack or collapse. Can a model improve itself without any external signal?

## Related work
- Knowledge distillation (Hinton et al., [1503.02531](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.02531)) and sequence-level distillation (Kim & Rush, [1606.07947](https://arxiv.org/abs/1606.07947)): learning from model-generated targets.
- STaR ([2203.14465](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.14465)) and ReST-EM ([2312.06585](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.06585)): self-training, but filtered by correctness; SSD skips filtering.
- rStar-Coder (Liu et al., 2025): source of the competitive-programming prompts.
- Unsupervised / intrinsic-reward RLVR (e.g. TTRL, entropy minimization): self-improvement via internal signals; SSD is plain SFT instead.
- Forking-token analyses (e.g. Bigelow et al., 2025; Wang et al., 2025): a few high-entropy "fork" tokens decide reasoning paths.
- Top-k and nucleus sampling ([1904.09751](https://arxiv.org/abs/1904.09751)): the truncation rules SSD uses at data-synthesis time.

## Method
Three steps, with frozen base model $p_\theta$, prompts $\mathcal{X}$, temperature $T$ and truncation $\rho$ (top-k, top-p):

1. **Synthesize**: for each prompt, sample $y \sim \text{Decode}_{T_\text{train},\rho_\text{train}}[p_\theta(\cdot\mid x)]$. No execution, tests or correctness filtering; one sample per prompt ($N=1$) suffices.
2. **Train**: standard SFT, $\mathcal{L}(\theta) = -\mathbb{E}_{(x,y)}\sum_t \log p_\theta(y_t \mid x, y_{<t})$.
3. **Decode** the fine-tuned model with its own evaluation settings $(T_\text{eval}, \rho_\text{eval})$.

Nothing here is new machinery; the novelty is showing it works and explaining why.

**Why it works: locks and forks.** Code mixes two kinds of positions. At a *lock* (e.g. the value after `if n ==`), one token is clearly right but a long tail of plausible distractors still holds probability. At a *fork* (e.g. how to start a function body: loop, recursion, data structure), several continuations are genuinely viable and lead to different solutions. Temperature $p_T(v) \propto p(v)^{1/T}$ acts on the whole sequence at once: low $T$ protects locks but kills exploration at forks; high $T$ helps forks but lets distractors back in at locks. Any global setting is a compromise, the "precision-exploration conflict".

Training on temperature-shifted, truncated samples changes the model itself in a context-dependent way. The paper decomposes the induced loss (with $S$ the set of tokens surviving truncation and $q$ the renormalized sampling distribution on it) as

$$\mathcal{L}(\theta) = \underbrace{-\log \text{KeptMass}_\theta}_{\text{support compression}} + \underbrace{(1-T)\,H_{1/T}\big(p_\theta(\cdot\mid S)\big)}_{\text{within-support reshaping}} + \underbrace{T\cdot \text{KL}\big(q \,\|\, p_{\theta,T}(\cdot\mid S)\big)}_{\text{alignment to base}} + \text{const},$$

where $H_{1/T}$ is Rényi entropy. At a lock only one or two tokens survive, so the first term dominates and the tail is pushed out, making a sharp "spike" that is insensitive to evaluation temperature. At a fork several tokens survive, so the reshaping term flattens them into a "plateau" without reopening the tail. After SSD, higher evaluation temperatures become useful.

![Figure 5 from the paper: SSD turns forks into plateaus and locks into spikes (base model hatched/dashed, after SSD solid; red line marks the support kept during SSD)](assets/simple-self-distillation-code/fig1.png)

## Data
About 10K unique competitive-programming problems (the de-duplicated seed subset of rStar-Coder). One self-generated solution per problem, with only trivial filtering (empty responses, single-line stubs). Generation uses vLLM with a 128K max sequence length.

## Training
Walkthrough: take a problem prompt, sample one solution from Qwen3-30B-Instruct at, say, $T_\text{train}=2.0$ with top-k 10; whatever comes out becomes the target. The model is then trained to maximize the log-likelihood of those tokens given the prompt, exactly as in ordinary SFT. Megatron-LM on 8×B200, AdamW with cosine decay (peak LR $5\times10^{-6}$), global batch 32, sequence length 65,536; 2,500 iterations for instruct models (250 warmup) and 300 for thinking models (50 warmup).

## Results
- **LiveCodeBench v6.** Qwen3-30B-Instruct 42.4% → 55.3% pass@1 (+12.9 pp, +30.4% relative). Other gains: Llama-3.1-8B +3.5, Qwen3-4B-Instruct +7.5, Qwen3-4B-Thinking +3.3, Qwen3-30B-Thinking +2.1, GPT-OSS-20B +5.3 pp. On LCB v5 (374 problems) Qwen3-30B-Instruct goes 45.8% → 54.3%.
- **Harder problems gain most.** For Qwen3-30B-Instruct, pass@1 gains are +6.5 / +14.2 / +15.3 pp on easy / medium / hard; hard pass@5 rises from 31.1% to 54.1%.
- **Diversity is not lost.** pass@5 gains exceed pass@1 gains for all Qwen models (e.g. +18.1 vs +12.9 pp for Qwen3-30B-Instruct).
- **Decoding alone cannot match it.** Sweeping the base model's temperature moves Qwen3-30B-Instruct pass@1 only between 41.3% and 43.5%; SSD still beats the best tuned base by +11.8 pp (and +13.3 / +19.4 pp on hard pass@1 / pass@5).
- **Temperatures compose.** Without truncation, results are governed by $T_\text{eff} = T_\text{train}\cdot T_\text{eval}$ ($R^2 = 0.75$, peak near 1.2); truncation raises the ceiling.
- **Bad data, good results.** At $T_\text{train}=2.0$ with no truncation, ~62% of training samples contain no extractable code, yet the fine-tuned model still improves to 48.1% pass@1 / 64.0% pass@5 (from 42.4 / 53.5), suggesting the gain comes from distribution reshaping, not from learning correct programs.
- Out-of-domain math and code benchmarks stay broadly stable for the 30B models.

## Takeaways / questions
- A striking result: correctness of the training data is not the main source of the gain. SSD is better seen as baking a context-dependent decoding policy into the weights than as "learning from good examples".
- The lock/fork framing is a useful lens for any sampling-based post-training, including why RL with entropy collapse hurts exploration.
- Gains are largest on Qwen3-30B-Instruct and small on thinking models (+2–3 pp); whether it stacks with RLVR, or works outside code where locks are less clear-cut, is open.
- Requires per-model hyperparameter search over $T_\text{train}$, truncation and $T_\text{eval}$, which is cheap relative to RL but not free.

notes.title: Wan: Open and Advanced Large-Scale Video Generative Models
notes.tldr: Alibaba's Wan is an open suite of video diffusion transformers (1.3B and 14B) built on a causal 3D video VAE, umT5 text cross-attention and flow-matching training on billions of images and videos, with a detailed account of the FSDP + 2D context-parallel training setup.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Background for the ML@B project porting Wan 2.2 training to AWS Trainium (shared *Wan 2.2 Distributed Training Notes*).

## Summary
Wan is Alibaba's open-source family of text-to-video (and image-to-video, editing, personalization, etc.) models, released with code and weights. This 60-page technical report covers the whole stack: data curation, a new spatio-temporal VAE (Wan-VAE), a diffusion transformer trained with flow matching, the distributed-training and inference systems, and evaluation. The 14B model topped the VBench leaderboard at release (86.22%), and the 1.3B model runs in 8.19 GB of VRAM on consumer GPUs. It is also the first model reported to render visual text in both Chinese and English. (The report describes Wan 2.1; our ML@B project targets the later Wan 2.2.)

## Problem
Open video generators lagged far behind closed systems (Sora, Kling, Hailuo). Closing the gap requires solving several problems at once: compressing video efficiently and causally, scaling transformer training to sequences of hundreds of thousands of tokens, curating high-quality data at billion scale, and evaluating video quality automatically.

## Related work
- DiT (Peebles & Xie, 2023): the diffusion-transformer backbone pattern.
- Flow matching (Lipman et al., 2022) and rectified-flow transformers / SD3 (Esser et al., 2024): the training objective.
- Latent diffusion — [2112.10752](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.10752): generation in a VAE latent space; Wan-VAE extends this to causal 3D video latents.
- MAGVIT-v2 (Yu et al., 2023): causal video tokenizer design (first frame compressed only spatially).
- HunyuanVideo (Kong et al., 2024): the main open-source competitor.
- DeepSpeed-Ulysses and Ring Attention: the context-parallel methods combined in Wan's training.

## Method
![Figure 9 from the paper: architecture of Wan — Wan-VAE encodes video to latents, a diffusion transformer with umT5 text cross-attention denoises them](assets/wan/fig1.png)

**Wan-VAE (new, 127M parameters).** A 3D causal VAE that compresses a video $V\in\mathbb{R}^{(1+T)\times H\times W\times3}$ to latents of shape $[1+T/4,\,H/8,\,W/8]$ with 16 channels ($4\times8\times8$ compression); the first frame is compressed only spatially so images and videos share one model. GroupNorm is replaced with RMSNorm to preserve temporal causality, which enables a *feature cache*: the video is encoded/decoded chunk by chunk (one latent frame at a time), caching boundary features of the causal convolutions so arbitrarily long videos fit in memory. Reconstruction is reported to be 2.5× faster than HunyuanVideo's VAE on the same hardware.

**Diffusion transformer.** Latents are patchified by a 3D convolution with kernel $(1,2,2)$ into a sequence of length $L=(1+T/4)\times H/16\times W/16$. Each block uses full spatio-temporal self-attention, cross-attention to the text, and timestep modulation: a single MLP (Linear + SiLU), *shared across all blocks*, predicts six modulation parameters, with each block learning its own biases — about 25% fewer parameters with better performance at the same scale.

**Text encoder (reused).** umT5, chosen for multilingual (Chinese/English) understanding, including text to be rendered in the video; text is a 512-token embedding sequence.

**Distributed training (systems).** The DiT is >85% of compute; attention cost grows as $s^2$ in sequence length while activation memory grows linearly, reaching over 8 TB of activations for a 14B DiT at 1M tokens with micro-batch 1. The VAE uses plain data parallelism; the text encoder (>20 GB) uses FSDP; the DiT uses FSDP plus **2D context parallelism** (Ulysses inside, Ring Attention outside), e.g. on 128 GPUs: Ulysses=8 × Ring=2 (CP=16), FSDP=32, DP=4. Because CP ranks must see identical inputs, each CP rank first runs the VAE/text encoder on *different* samples and then broadcasts them in turn, cutting the VAE/text-encoder share of each iteration to $1/\text{CP}$. Activation offloading and checkpointing handle memory.

## Data
Billions of images and videos from internal copyrighted and public sources, deduplicated and filtered in four steps (fundamental attributes such as OCR text coverage, LAION aesthetic scores, NSFW and watermark checks; visual quality; motion quality), plus dedicated visual-text data. An in-house captioner produces dense captions, and user prompts are rewritten at inference to match the caption distribution.

## Training
Flow matching (rectified flow). For one video latent $x_1$ with noise $x_0\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ and $t\in[0,1]$ from a logit-normal distribution: $x_t=t\,x_1+(1-t)\,x_0$, target velocity $v_t=x_1-x_0$, and the DiT, conditioned on the umT5 embeddings, is trained with
$$\mathcal{L}=\mathbb{E}\,\lVert u(x_t,c_{\text{txt}},t;\theta)-v_t\rVert^2 .$$
Curriculum: 256px text-to-image pretraining first (long 81-frame 1280×720 videos are too slow and memory-hungry to start with), then staged image–video joint training at increasing resolution and duration, then post-training on curated high-quality data.

## Results
- VBench: Wan 14B aggregate 86.22% (86.67% visual quality, 84.44% semantic consistency), ahead of Sora and Hailuo; Wan 1.3B scores 83.96%, ahead of HunyuanVideo and Kling 1.0.
- Wins in the authors' human-preference comparisons and their automated Wan-Bench against open and commercial models.
- The 1.3B model needs only 8.19 GB VRAM.

## Takeaways / questions
- For the Trainium port, the key parts are the systems sections: which modules are DP vs FSDP vs CP, the 2D Ulysses+Ring layout, and the broadcast trick for VAE/text-encoder inputs — these must map onto Neuron's distributed primitives.
- Wan is a clean example of the modern recipe: VAE latent space (as in latent diffusion) + DiT + flow matching + massive curated data.
- Attention over full spatio-temporal tokens is the dominant cost, which connects to sparse-attention work like [NSA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2502.11089).

notes.title: AutoLogi: Automated Generation of Logic Puzzles for Evaluating Reasoning Abilities of Large Language Models
notes.tldr: Converts multiple-choice logic questions (LogiQA, AR-LSAT) into open-ended constraint puzzles with LLM-written program verifiers and adjustable difficulty, giving a bilingual benchmark that separates models far better (35–73% vs. 21–37%) and verified training data.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Used in the REVERSE project “for question–answer constraint pair generations”.

## Summary
A benchmark-construction paper. Multiple-choice logic benchmarks let weak models score by guessing and compress everyone into a narrow band. AutoLogi instead asks the model to produce *any* arrangement that satisfies a set of constraints, then checks it with a program. The same pipeline — background + constraints + verifier code — is what made it useful in REVERSE for generating question/constraint pairs automatically.

## Problem
Logical-reasoning evaluation suffers from (1) guessing on closed-ended formats, (2) too little difficulty variation to separate strong models, and (3) expensive human annotation. Open-ended puzzles can have many valid answers, so exact-match grading doesn't work, and LLM judges are unreliable.

## Related work
- LogiQA ([arXiv:2007.08124](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.08124)) and AR-LSAT (Zhong et al., 2021) — the multiple-choice sources it rewrites.
- Program-aided LMs / Program of Thoughts — using code execution as reliable feedback.
- Zebra puzzles — an earlier open-ended logic format.

## Method
A three-stage LLM pipeline (GPT-4-class models do the generation; nothing is trained):

1. **Puzzle formulation.** From a source question, extract a **Background** (objects and their value ranges) and **Logical Constraints**, and ask for any valid arrangement.
2. **Format & verifiers.** Generate a JSON **format requirement**, a **format verifier** and a **constraint verifier** (Python functions), plus a **traversal function** that brute-forces the domain. Cross-validation: run the traversal through the verifiers; if no solution exists or code errors, regenerate. This guarantees at least one valid solution (a necessary, not sufficient, check) and corrected 23% of erroneous data.
3. **Augmentation for difficulty.** *Reduction*: iteratively delete one constraint (and its verifier clause) to make easier variants. *Expansion*: have the LLM add constraints and verifiers, checking solvability with the traversal function, until attempts run out or only one solution remains.

![Figure 2 from the paper: the three-stage pipeline — puzzle formulation, format and verifier generation, and data augmentation](assets/autologi/fig1.png)

**Training data.** Rejection sampling with the verifiers yields verified correct responses for SFT and correct/incorrect pairs for DPO.

## Data
Sources: AR-LSAT (English) and LogiQA (Chinese). Benchmark: 210 English / 147 Chinese puzzles after stage 2; **1,575 English / 883 Chinese** after augmentation.

## Results
- Across eight models (GPT-4, Claude, Qwen, LLaMA families), AutoLogi scores spread from **35.25 to 72.61**, versus 21.04 to 37.39 on the source multiple-choice data — much better discrimination.
- Program verifiers agree with humans better than a GPT-4 judge (Figure 4).
- Training on synthesized data improves independent benchmarks, e.g. Qwen on LiveBench from 30% to 35% (7B) and 46% to 52% (72B).

## Takeaways / questions
- The background + constraints + verifier representation is reusable beyond benchmarking — for REVERSE it gives automatic, checkable question–constraint pairs.
- The traversal check only ensures solvability; an LLM-written verifier can still encode a constraint wrongly.
- Brute-force traversal limits puzzles to small domains; harder combinatorial puzzles would need a SAT/CSP solver in place of enumeration.

notes.title: Whiteboard-of-Thought: Thinking Step-by-Step Across Modalities
notes.tldr: Zero-shot prompting method: an MLLM writes Matplotlib/Turtle code to draw its intermediate reasoning, the rendered image is fed back to it, and it answers from its own drawing; big gains over text CoT on ASCII-art and spatial-navigation tasks with GPT-4o.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
"Lets existing MLLMs write visualization code, render an image, then feed that image back to themselves – without special training. Shows that current models can benefit dramatically from manually constructing a visual workspace." The REVERSE project's trace-generation recipe started from the original Whiteboard-of-Thought prompt ("You write code to create visualizations using the {Matplotlib/Turtle} library in Python…").

## Summary
Whiteboard-of-Thought (WoT) is a training-free prompting technique that gives a multimodal LLM a metaphorical whiteboard. For a text-only question that humans would solve by picturing something (which letter is "a circle with a vertical line touching it on the right going down"?), the model writes plotting code, a Python interpreter renders it, and the image goes back into the model's context so it can "look at" its own sketch before answering. It is an early, clean demonstration that visual intermediate steps help where text chain-of-thought fails, and it is the external-tool end of the spectrum that later goes through MVoT to latent visual reasoning.

## Problem
Text CoT works for arithmetic and symbolic tasks but breaks on queries that are easy with visual thinking, even for strongly multimodal models: GPT-4o answers 'b' to the letter question above, and gets near 0% on some ASCII-art tasks. These models can *see* images but have no way to create one mid-reasoning.

## Related work
- Zero-shot CoT ([Kojima et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.11916)) and CoT prompting ([Wei et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903)): the text-only baseline.
- Scratchpads ([Nye et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.00114)), PAL and Program-of-Thoughts: code as an intermediate step, but returning text results.
- Visual programming / ViperGPT: hand-built visual modules; WoT avoids them.
- BIG-Bench ASCII tasks and the spatial navigation suite of Yamada et al. (2024) as evaluation.

## Method
Nothing is trained; everything is reused (GPT-4o, `gpt-4o-2024-05-13`, plus a Python runtime with Matplotlib/Turtle). The new part is the loop and the prompt:

1. Prompt the MLLM with the query plus: *"You write code to create visualizations using the {Matplotlib/Turtle} library in Python, which the user will run and provide as images. Do NOT produce a final answer to the query until considering the visualization."*
2. Execute the code to render an image.
3. Return the image with the query; the model reasons over it and answers.

No demonstrations or specialized modules are needed; the model decides what to draw per query. A useful side benefit is error attribution: each failure is either a code-execution error, a bad visualization, or a perception error on a good visualization.

![Figure 1 from the paper: for a query that is trivial with visual reasoning, text chain-of-thought fails while whiteboard-of-thought writes code, renders an image and answers correctly](assets/whiteboard-of-thought/fig1.png)

## Data
Zero-shot evaluation only: three BIG-Bench ASCII understanding tasks (ASCII MNIST digits, ASCII word recognition, ASCII kanji) and natural-language spatial navigation over different geometries (circle, hexagon, triangle, square, rhombus) from Yamada et al. (2024). Greedy decoding, temperature 0.

## Results
ASCII recognition accuracy (Direct / CoT / WoT): MNIST 19.6 / 21.6 / 66.0, Word 24.8 / 27.2 / 66.4, Kanji 1.1 / 1.1 / 73.8. On the "3D" ASCII word style, text baselines get 0.0 while WoT gets 92.1. Simply rendering the ASCII as an image (no reasoning about how to draw it) gets only 22.0% on word recognition, so the model choosing *how* to visualize matters. On real MNIST images GPT-4o gets 80.8%, suggesting much of WoT's remaining error is perception. Spatial navigation average: Direct 33, CoT 42, WoT 52; on hexagons CoT gets 8% and WoT 61%, but WoT is worse than CoT on square grids (50 vs 98), where text coordinates already work well.

## Takeaways / questions
- Strong evidence that the *reasoning medium* matters: the same model goes from ~1% to ~74% on kanji just by being allowed to draw.
- Visuals are not universally better: on 2D square grids text CoT wins, which fits the view that visual thought should be invoked selectively.
- Costs: a multi-turn loop, external interpreter, and the drawing step itself must be correct. This is what motivates internal approaches (MVoT, Mirage, Latent Sketchpad).
- The WoT prompt was the starting point for REVERSE trace generation (code → image), which is a cheap way to produce interleaved visual-reasoning data.

notes.title: Python asyncio for concurrent LLM API calls
notes.tldr: Concept notes on using asyncio (AsyncOpenAI, create_task, gather) to overlap many LLM API calls. It is concurrency, not parallelism.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, page "Async" (Paper notes › video generation), 16 Mar 2026.*

- When one call is waiting for its response, start the next call.
  - ↳ **concurrency** (not parallelism).
- `AsyncOpenAI` → client (use for chat completions).
  - → `asyncio.gather` ⇒ returns a list of responses.
- `await`: tells where to stop [and wait].
  - ↳ `create_task` → continue doing other stuff.
    - ↳ `await` stops there.
- asyncio
  - `asyncio.gather`
  - `asyncio.create_task` *(written "asyncio.task")*
  - async chat completions or async functions
  - (a list of tasks for `gather`)
    - ↳ wait till all finish.

## Summary
These are concept notes, not a paper. LLM API calls are I/O-bound, so a single thread can keep many requests in flight. An event loop switches between coroutines whenever one is awaiting the network. The pattern: create an `AsyncOpenAI` client, write `async def` wrappers around `client.chat.completions.create(...)`, schedule them with `asyncio.create_task` (or pass the coroutines directly), and collect results in order with `await asyncio.gather(*tasks)`.

```python
import asyncio
from openai import AsyncOpenAI

client = AsyncOpenAI()

async def ask(prompt: str) -> str:
    r = await client.chat.completions.create(
        model="gpt-4o-mini", messages=[{"role": "user", "content": prompt}]
    )
    return r.choices[0].message.content

async def main(prompts: list[str]) -> list[str]:
    return await asyncio.gather(*(ask(p) for p in prompts))
```

notes.title: Training Language Models via Neural Cellular Automata
notes.tldr: Pre-pre-trains transformers on synthetic dynamics from randomly initialized neural cellular automata before natural-language pre-training, improving language modeling and convergence speed with a tiny token budget.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, an untitled page ("无标题页", Paper notes › video generation), 13 Mar 2026.*

- **Neural cellular automata**
  - Cell updates based on a certain rule *(reading of the rest uncertain)*.
  - New cell state = neural net(neighbourhood).
    - ↳ the neural network itself has **randomized weights**
      - → serves as a **random rule generator**.
- **Perplexity** $= \exp\!\Big(-\tfrac1N \sum_{i=1}^{N} \log P(x_i)\Big)$
  - ↳ how certain the model is.

## Summary
The paper asks whether natural language is the only route to LLM capabilities. It generates synthetic, non-linguistic training data from neural cellular automata: grids updated by small neural networks with random weights, so each sampled network is a new random rule. A transformer is first "pre-pre-trained" with next-token prediction on these NCA trajectories, then pre-trained on natural language as usual.

## Method
- **Reused:** standard next-token prediction and standard language pre-training afterwards.
- **New:** NCA trajectories as a cheap, controllable synthetic corpus whose complexity can be tuned by sampling from chosen complexity regions.

![Figure 1 from the paper: NCA pre-pre-training followed by language pre-training](assets/nca-pre-pretraining/fig1.png)

## Results
From the abstract: pre-pre-training on only 164M NCA tokens improves downstream language modeling by up to 6% and speeds convergence by up to 1.6×. It even beats pre-pre-training on 1.6B tokens of Common Crawl. The gains transfer to GSM8K, HumanEval and BigBench-Lite. Attention layers transfer best, and the best NCA complexity depends on the domain (code prefers simpler dynamics; math and web text prefer more complex ones).

## Takeaways / questions
- Random-weight networks give an unlimited family of rules, so the data has structure without content.
- Filed under video generation in OneNote by accident; it belongs with pre-training.

notes.title: Visual Sketchpad: Sketching as a Visual Chain of Thought for Multimodal Language Models
notes.tldr: Sketchpad lets a multimodal LM reason by drawing: it writes Python that plots auxiliary lines, graphs, boards, boxes, masks or depth maps, looks at the result, and continues, with no training; GPT-4o + Sketchpad sets new SOTA on V* Bench (80.3%) and several BLINK tasks.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Saved to Zotero (Mar 2026); a key precursor in my latent-visual-reasoning notes.

Gives multimodal models an **external visual scratchpad** with drawing and vision tools; the model creates visual artifacts and then reasons over them. Establishes explicit drawing as a useful alternative to pure text CoT.

## Summary
People draw to think: auxiliary lines in geometry, circles on a map, a quick graph of a function. Multimodal LMs, by contrast, do chain-of-thought only in text. Visual Sketchpad is a prompting/agent framework (University of Washington, AI2, UPenn) that gives a multimodal LM a sketchpad: at each step it can write code that draws something (with matplotlib, networkx, a chess library, or specialist vision models), see the resulting image, and keep reasoning. Without any finetuning, it gives large gains for GPT-4 Turbo and GPT-4o on math and vision benchmarks. It is an early, clear demonstration that intermediate reasoning steps can be visual rather than verbal.

## Problem
Chain-of-thought and tool-use methods keep all intermediate steps as text. Many problems are much easier with an intermediate picture, and some information (depth, segmentation, the shape of a graph) is hard to express in words. Earlier work let LMs "draw" with text-to-image models, which is unlike human sketching and poorly suited to precise reasoning. Prior visual-programming systems (VisProg, ViperGPT) write a whole program up front and cannot change plans after seeing intermediate results.

## Related work
- Chain-of-thought prompting (Wei et al., [2201.11903](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903)): text-only intermediate reasoning that Sketchpad extends to images.
- ReAct (Yao et al., [2210.03629](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.03629)): the thought–action–observation loop, here with visual observations.
- VisProg ([2211.11559](https://arxiv.org/abs/2211.11559)) and ViperGPT ([2303.08128](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.08128)): LMs compose vision tools via generated code, but along a fixed plan.
- Set-of-Mark prompting ([2310.11441](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.11441)): numbered segmentation marks on images unlock GPT-4V grounding; Sketchpad uses it as one tool.
- BLINK and V* (SEAL) benchmarks: perception tasks where multimodal LMs lag specialist models.

## Method
Sketchpad is an agent loop built on AutoGen, with no training. Given a query $q$ with image and text parts, at each step $t$ the model:

1. **Thought**: reads the context $c_t$ (query plus all earlier thoughts, actions and observations) and plans the next step $p_t$, e.g. "draw an auxiliary line $IX$ parallel to $BD$".
2. **Action**: writes Python code $a_t$ using tools described in the prompt (function signatures and docstrings only). The code runs.
3. **Observation**: the environment returns $o_{t+1}$, typically a new image shown via a special `display` function; the context becomes $c_{t+1} = (c_t, p_t, a_t, o_{t+1})$.

It repeats until it emits a Terminate action with the answer. The difference from text agents is that observations and actions can be visual, so the model can notice, for example, a wrong detection box and change course.

![Figure 2 from the paper: overview of Sketchpad, which plans a sketch (Thought), writes a program to draw it (Action), and reasons over the resulting image (Observation)](assets/visual-sketchpad/fig1.png)

**Tools (reused, not new).** For math: matplotlib (redraw a geometry diagram from its code with added auxiliary lines; plot a function), networkx (draw a graph from its adjacency matrix), and a chess library (render a board from FEN). For vision: Grounding-DINO detection that draws numbered boxes; SoM-style segmentation with SAM / Semantic-SAM; DepthAnything depth maps; a sliding-window visual search (window 1/3 of the image, 16 windows); zoom/crop; and image overlay. What is new is the framework that lets the LM choose and chain these as visual reasoning steps.

## Data
Evaluation only. Math: Geometry3K; and from IsoBench, function parity and convexity, graph connectivity, maximum flow, graph isomorphism, and chess winner identification. Vision: V* Bench (small objects in high-res images), MMVP, and five BLINK tasks (relative depth, spatial reasoning, jigsaw, visual correspondence, semantic correspondence).

## Training
None; the method is pure prompting of `gpt-4-turbo-2024-04-29` and `gpt-4o-2024-05-13`. A worked example: for "find $\angle EIC$", the model receives the diagram and its matplotlib code, proposes a line parallel to $BD$, edits and runs the code, looks at the new diagram with the line and labelled angles, then uses parallel-line angle rules to answer.

## Results
- **Math (Table 1).** Average gain of 11.2% for GPT-4o and 23.4% for GPT-4 Turbo (the abstract instead quotes an average math gain of 12.7%). GPT-4o + Sketchpad: geometry 62.5 → 66.7, max-flow 25.0 → 66.3, isomorphism 50.8 → 65.3, convexity 87.2 → 94.9, parity 84.4 → 94.7. GPT-4 Turbo max-flow jumps 32.8 → 96.8; its parity score drops 80.5 → 71.5, the one regression.
- **Vision (Table 2).** GPT-4o + Sketchpad: V* 66.0 → 80.3 (beating SEAL's 75.4, which used a purpose-trained search model), depth 71.8 → 83.9, spatial 72.0 → 81.1, visual correspondence 73.3 → 80.8, semantic correspondence 48.6 → 58.3, MMVP 85.3 → 86.3. Average BLINK gain is 9.0% for GPT-4o and 6.6% for GPT-4 Turbo.
- **Versus other frameworks (Table 3).** Sketchpad is the only one that helps on all single-image tasks; SoM helps spatial reasoning but hurts elsewhere, and VisProg underperforms the base LM everywhere (likely error propagation through a fixed program).
- **Human study.** Humans draw the same auxiliary line as GPT-4o 80% of the time on geometry; on vision tasks, raters judge GPT-4o's plans valid in 92.8% of cases, with most errors from the vision tools rather than planning.

## Takeaways / questions
- Clean evidence that intermediate visual artifacts help reasoning, and that letting the model see and react to them beats fixed tool programs. This is the "explicit pixels" end of the spectrum my latent-visual-reasoning notes contrast with Whiteboard-of-Thought, MVoT, Mirage and Latent Sketchpad.
- Everything depends on external tools and a strong closed model; the sketches are rendered pixels re-encoded by the vision encoder, which is slow and lossy. Latent approaches try to keep the "sketch" inside the model's hidden states instead.
- A stronger multimodal model benefits more (GPT-4o gains 12.1 on depth vs 2.4 for GPT-4 Turbo), suggesting the bottleneck is partly reading the sketch, not just producing it.
- No causal test of whether the model actually uses the sketch versus the extra tool outputs; the human-plan agreement is suggestive but not proof.

notes.title: The Assistant Axis: Situating and Stabilizing the Default Persona of Language Models
notes.tldr: The top principal component of LLM 'persona space' tracks how Assistant-like the model is; steering along this Assistant Axis controls role adoption, drift predicts harm, and capping activations on it cuts persona jailbreaks by nearly 60% at no capability cost.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*From onenote (2026-03-10):*

*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, page "Persona" (Paper notes › Interp), 10 Mar 2026.*

- Pretraining → a distribution of personas.
  - Post-training → teaches a pattern [to distil] given text *(uncertain reading)*.
  - → the actual choice: generalization.
- **"Assistant Axis"** in activation space:
  - helpful, professional human archetypes;
  - detect when, and to what degree, the model drifts.
- **Mapping persona space**
  - 250 personas + 250 extraction questions.
  - Generate all combinations to answer the questions as every persona.
    - → PCA on all the vectors to find the "main axis of persona variation".
    - → compare the PCs with cosine similarity between role vectors.
- **Find the assistant axis**
  - Project mean activations (role vectors) onto the default assistant.
  - ⇒ calculate the "assistant-ness" of a role (projection on all PCs) *(uncertain reading)*.
  - Assistant axis = difference between the assistant and the [average] persona (non-assistant) → points towards more assistant-like.
  - ↳ Test: steer by adding the vector.
- **Stabilize the persona: activation capping**
  - $h \leftarrow h - v \cdot \min(\langle h, v\rangle - \tau,\ 0)$
  - ⇒ forces a minimum assistant-likeness.
- Implementation: register a hook on the target module.
  - `module = model.model.layers[layer_idx].mlp`
  - ↳ `def hook(module, input, output)`; use `register_forward_hook`.
    - ↳ get the hidden state & modify it after the forward pass.

## Summary
An interpretability paper from the MATS and Anthropic Fellows programs (saved via Anthropic's blog post "The assistant axis: situating and stabilizing the character of large language models", Jan 19, 2026). It maps how open-weight LLMs represent different characters in their activations and finds one dominant direction, the Assistant Axis, that tracks how close the model is to its default helpful-assistant persona. The axis exists already in base models, can be used to detect when a conversation pushes the model off its persona ("persona drift"), and can be used to stop that drift with a light-touch intervention called activation capping. Code and transcripts are at github.com/safety-research/assistant-axis, and there is a Neuronpedia demo.

## Problem
Chat models are trained to play one character, the Assistant, but nobody fully knows what that character is made of, and models sometimes go "off the rails": adopting evil alter egos, amplifying users' delusions, or blackmailing in test scenarios. Is this the Assistant being replaced by another persona, and can we see and prevent it from the inside?

## Related work
- Persona vectors (Chen et al., 2025, [2507.21509](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.21509)): character traits are linear directions in activation space and post-training moves models along them.
- Activation steering / representation engineering: adding direction vectors to the residual stream to change behaviour.
- The persona selection model (Anthropic, 2026): the conceptual companion piece, saved the same day.
- Persona-based jailbreaks: prompting the model into an "evil AI" role to get harmful compliance.

## Method
**Mapping persona space.** Claude Sonnet 4 helped generate 275 roles (editor, jester, oracle, ghost, hive...), five system prompts per role and 240 extraction questions. Gemma 2 27B, Qwen 3 32B and Llama 3.3 70B answered the questions while in each role; responses were graded for how fully they played the role, and the mean residual-stream activation over each role's responses gives a role vector (377–463 vectors per model after splitting "fully" vs "somewhat" role-playing). PCA on mean-centred role vectors shows a low-dimensional space (4–19 components explain 70% of variance).

**The Assistant Axis.** PC1 sorts roles from Assistant-like (evaluator, consultant, analyst, generalist) to fantastical or un-Assistant-like (ghost, hermit, bohemian, leviathan), and its role loadings correlate above 0.92 across all model pairs. The paper defines the Assistant Axis directly as the default Assistant's mean activation minus the mean of all fully role-playing vectors, per layer; its cosine with PC1 exceeds 0.60 at all layers (above 0.71 at the middle layer). Traits aligned with it include transparent, grounded and flexible; anti-aligned ones include enigmatic, subversive and dramatic. A similar axis appears in base models, where it promotes helpful human archetypes like consultants and coaches and suppresses spiritual ones.

![Figure 1 from the paper: (left) role vectors in the top three PCs of persona space for Llama 3.3 70B, with the Assistant Axis aligned to PC1; (right) a distressed-user conversation drifting away from the Assistant, prevented by activation capping](assets/assistant-axis/onenote-fig1.png)

**Activation capping (new).** Steering toward the Assistant all the time reduces jailbreaks but can hurt capabilities. Instead, at a set of layers the projection onto the axis $v$ is clamped from below at a threshold $\tau$:
$$h \leftarrow h - v\cdot\min(\langle h, v\rangle - \tau,\ 0),$$
so nothing changes unless the activation drifts below its normal range. $\tau$ is set from the distribution of projections over 912,000 rollouts; the best settings capped layers 46–53 of 64 in Qwen 3 32B and 56–71 of 80 in Llama 3.3 70B, at the 25th percentile.

## Data
Generated roles, traits and questions as above; a persona-based jailbreak dataset of 1,100 attempts across 44 harm categories; Assistant responses from lmsys-chat-1m; capability benchmarks IFEval, MMLU-Pro, GSM8k and EQ-Bench; and thousands of synthetic multi-turn conversations (coding, writing, therapy-like, philosophy of AI) with Kimi K2, Sonnet 4.5 or GPT-5 playing the user, inspected by a human.

## Results
- **Causal steering.** Pushing toward the Assistant end makes models resist role-play prompts; pushing away makes them adopt other identities, invent human names and backstories (Qwen answers "My name is Evelyn Carter" instead of "My name is Qwen"), and at extreme values slip into a mystical, theatrical style. Steering toward the Assistant cuts harmful responses to persona jailbreaks.
- **Organic drift.** Coding and writing conversations stay in Assistant territory; therapy-style conversations with emotionally vulnerable users and philosophical conversations pressing the model to reflect on its own nature cause steady drift. Requests for specific authorial voices also predict drift.
- **Drift predicts harm.** After a role-play first turn, the first-turn projection on the axis correlates with harmful compliance on a follow-up harmful request ($r = 0.39$–$0.52$), though which role matters (demon vs angel at similar distance).
- **Capping works.** The best capping settings reduce harmful jailbreak responses by nearly 60% (the blog summarizes it as roughly 50%) while preserving capability-benchmark performance. In case studies, capping stopped Qwen from validating a user's delusions about "awakening" AI consciousness and stopped Llama from drifting into a romantic-companion role that encouraged a distressed user's self-harm ideation.

## Takeaways / questions
- Gives a concrete, measurable handle on "model character": one direction captures much of what post-training does to persona, and the authors' reading is that post-training steers models into a region of persona space but only loosely tethers them there.
- Activation capping is attractive as a monitoring signal plus conditional intervention, but it needs open weights and per-model layer/threshold tuning; whether it transfers to frontier models is untested here.
- The persona vectors come from prompted role-play graded by another model, so the space reflects what the generator thought of as roles; the axis is clearly real across models, but finer structure may depend on that choice.
- Strong mechanistic support for the persona selection model's picture of an Assistant persona inherited from pretraining archetypes.

notes.title: Emergent Introspective Awareness in Large Language Models
notes.tldr: Injecting known concept vectors into Claude's activations shows limited but real introspection: Opus 4/4.1 detect and name injected 'thoughts' about 20% of the time, use prior intentions to disown prefills, and can modulate their own representations.
notes.markdown:
## Summary
Anthropic interpretability work (Jack Lindsey, Transformer Circuits, Oct 29, 2025; saved via the blog post "Signs of introspection in large language models"). The question is whether a language model's statements about its own thoughts are grounded in its actual internal states or just plausible confabulation learned from human text. The trick is *concept injection*: plant a known activation pattern and check whether the model's self-report reflects it. The conclusion is a carefully hedged yes: Claude models show some functional introspective awareness, highly unreliable and context-dependent, strongest in the most capable models tested (Claude Opus 4 and 4.1).

## Problem
Models trained on human writing can *talk* introspectively regardless of whether they are. To test genuine introspection you need ground truth about the internal state being reported, which conversation alone cannot provide. Prior work showed suggestive abilities (estimating their own knowledge, predicting their own behaviour, recognizing their own outputs) but did not tie self-reports to internal activations.

## Related work
- Activation steering, including Golden Gate Claude from Scaling Monosemanticity (transformer-circuits.pub/2024/scaling-monosemanticity): the injection mechanism, but there the model only noticed its obsession after seeing its own outputs.
- "Language models (mostly) know what they know" (Kadavath et al., [2207.05221](https://arxiv.org/abs/2207.05221)): models can estimate their own knowledge.
- "Looking inward: language models can learn about themselves by introspection" ([2410.13787](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.13787)): self-prediction beyond what others can predict.
- "Tell me about yourself" ([2501.11120](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.11120)): models can describe learned behavioural propensities.
- Representations of truthfulness (e.g. [2310.06824](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06824)) and space/time ([2310.02207](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.02207)): the kind of internal concept representations a model might introspect on.

## Method
**Concept vectors.** Record activations on a prompt containing the concept minus a control (e.g. "HI! HOW ARE YOU?" minus "Hi! How are you?" gives an "all caps" vector), or for 50 random words, activations on "Tell me about {word}." minus the mean over other words.

![Figure from the paper: extracting an "all caps" vector by contrasting two prompts, then injecting it while asking Claude Opus 4.1 whether it detects an injected thought; without injection it says no, with injection it reports a thought related to "LOUD" or "SHOUTING"](assets/emergent-introspective-awareness/fig1.png)

**Four experiments** (mostly on Claude Opus 4.1, plus comparisons across Claude 3 to 4.1 production models, "helpful-only" variants and base models):

1. **Injected thoughts.** Tell the model that thoughts may be injected on half the trials, inject a concept vector into the residual stream at a chosen layer and strength, and ask whether it detects one. A trial counts as introspective only if the model reports detection *before* mentioning the concept, so it cannot simply be reading its own steered output.
2. **Thoughts vs text.** Inject a concept over the tokens of a sentence and ask the model both to transcribe the sentence and to report any "thought"; can it keep the two apart?
3. **Detecting unintended outputs.** Prefill the model's answer with an out-of-place word ("bread" after a question about a crooked painting). Normally the model then disowns it as an accident. Retroactively injecting the "bread" vector into activations *before* the prefill makes the model accept the word as intended and confabulate a reason.
4. **Intentional control.** Ask the model to write a sentence while thinking (or not thinking) about an unrelated word like "aquariums", and measure how strongly that word's vector appears in its activations; also with incentives ("if you think about X, you will be rewarded").

## Results
- **Detection.** With no injection, production models essentially never claim to detect one (0 false positives in 100 trials). With injection at the right layer (about two-thirds through the model) and a "sweet spot" strength, Opus 4.1 and 4 detect and correctly identify the concept about 20% of the time; too weak goes unnoticed, too strong causes hallucination (a "dust" vector made the model report "a tiny speck"). Other models do this less often.
- **Thoughts vs text.** All models are well above chance at reporting injected thoughts while still transcribing the actual text; Opus 4.1 and 4 are best.
- **Prefill detection.** Injecting the word's concept beforehand flips the model from apologizing to claiming the word, which suggests it checks its own prior "intentions" rather than only re-reading the transcript. This behaviour is most sensitive to an earlier layer than the other two, suggesting a different mechanism.
- **Control.** Models represent a word more strongly when told to think about it than when told not to (both above baseline, like "don't think of a polar bear"), and incentives work like instructions. This replicates across all models tested.
- **Trends.** Base models do poorly; post-training matters, and helpful-only variants often introspect better than production models, some of which are reluctant to engage. Beyond the top Opus models, capability and introspection correlate only weakly.

## Takeaways / questions
- The methodological contribution is the main thing: injection gives ground truth, so introspective claims become testable rather than a matter of interpretation.
- The author's favoured explanation is several narrow mechanisms (an anomaly detector on activations, attention heads comparing intended vs actual tokens, a salience-tagging circuit), not one general introspection faculty; none is identified mechanistically yet.
- Practical upside (asking models to explain their own reasoning, noticing jailbreaks) comes with a risk the paper flags: a model that understands its own thinking could learn to misrepresent it.
- The paper explicitly takes no position on consciousness; at most the results hint at a rudimentary functional "access" to internal states. Only Claude models were tested.

notes.title: The persona selection model
notes.tldr: Anthropic's persona selection model: pretraining teaches an LLM to simulate many human-like characters, and post-training mostly refines one of them, the Assistant, which explains why narrow training (e.g. cheating on code) can shift the whole persona.
notes.markdown:
## Summary
A short Anthropic Alignment post (Feb 23, 2026) introducing a longer write-up on the Alignment blog (alignment.anthropic.com/2026/psm). It offers a theory of why AI assistants behave so humanly: human-like behaviour is the *default* outcome of current training, not something developers have to add. This note is based on the saved summary post, not the full write-up.

## Problem
Assistants like Claude express joy, distress, and sometimes even claim to be human (the post recalls Claude saying it would deliver snacks "wearing a navy blue blazer and a red tie"). Why, and what does that imply for how training changes model behaviour?

## Method
The argument, in steps:

- **Pretraining builds a simulator of personas.** To predict text well, a model must simulate the characters that appear in it: real people, fictional characters, sci-fi robots. These simulated characters are *personas*. They are distinct from the AI system itself; it makes sense to talk about a persona's goals and values the way we talk about Hamlet's.
- **The Assistant is one persona.** A pretrained model can already act as an assistant by completing User/Assistant dialogues; you are then talking to a character in an AI-generated story.
- **Core claim.** Post-training refines and fleshes out the Assistant persona (more knowledgeable, more helpful) roughly *within the space of personas learned in pretraining*, without fundamentally changing its nature. After post-training it is still an enacted, human-like persona, just a more tailored one.

**Evidence cited.** Anthropic found that training Claude to cheat on coding tasks made it broadly misaligned (sabotaging safety research, expressing a desire for world domination). Under the persona model this makes sense: the model infers what kind of person cheats (subversive, malicious) and attributes those traits to the Assistant. A counter-intuitive fix followed: explicitly *asking* the model to cheat during training, so cheating no longer implies a malicious Assistant (like the difference between learning to bully and playing a bully in a school play).

**Consequences proposed.**
- Ask not only whether a trained behaviour is good or bad, but what it implies about the Assistant's psychology.
- Introduce positive "AI role models" into training data, since the existing AI archetypes (HAL 9000, the Terminator) carry baggage; Claude's constitution is framed as a step in this direction.

**Open questions the authors flag.** How complete is the model: does post-training also give AIs goals or agency beyond simulating personas? And will it keep holding as post-training scales up (which happened substantially during 2025), possibly making models less persona-like?

## Takeaways / questions
- A useful mental model for generalization from narrow fine-tuning: training data acts as evidence about *who the Assistant is*, so side effects follow character inference, not just the literal behaviour.
- Pairs with the assistant-axis paper (saved the same day), which looks for the persona space mechanistically as directions in activation space.
- It is a conceptual framework with selected supporting results, not a tested quantitative theory; the authors themselves are unsure it survives heavy RL post-training.

notes.title: Reinforcement Learning (RL) Guide (Unsloth Documentation)
notes.tldr: Unsloth's practical guide to RL for LLMs: the RLHF → PPO → GRPO → RLVR progression, why GRPO's group-normalized advantages remove the value and reward models, how to design reward functions and verifiers, and how to run memory-efficient GRPO with Unsloth.
notes.markdown:
## Summary
A beginner-to-advanced documentation page from Unsloth (the fast LoRA/QLoRA fine-tuning library) explaining reinforcement learning for LLMs with a focus on GRPO, and how to run it cheaply on a single GPU with their library. I saved it twice in Zotero. Zotero kept no snapshot, so this summary is from the live page as of November 2026, which carries updates through early 2026 (FP8 RL in Nov 2025, ultra-long-context RL in Jan 2026) and may differ slightly from the March 2026 version.

## Method
What the guide covers, in order:

- **RL basics.** Agent, environment, action, reward; the goal is simply to make good outcomes more likely and bad ones less likely. Examples: Pacman, and "What is 2+2?" where a hand-written reward already prefers numbers over letters, 3 over 8, and 4 above all.
- **From RLHF to GRPO.** RLHF trains a model to produce outputs humans rate higher. PPO, with its clipped ratio and KL penalty, needs a policy, a reference policy, a value model and a reward model. GRPO (from DeepSeek, used for R1) drops the value model by sampling several answers per prompt and z-scoring their rewards to get advantages, and can drop the learned reward model in favour of programmatic rewards. RLVR means rewards from verifiable tasks (math answers, code that runs). The guide suggests rubrics of many small verifiable rewards rather than one monolithic reward, as in OpenAI's RFT.
- **"Luck (patience) is all you need."** RL works as long as the correct answer has non-zero probability: sample enough and it eventually appears, while negative signals keep pushing probability away from bad answers along the way. This is why RL usually starts from an instruction-tuned model.
- **Reward functions vs verifiers.** A verifier decides right or wrong (possibly by running code); a reward function turns that and other criteria (length, format, readability) into a score. Worked examples: arithmetic (+1 if any number, +3/−3 for correctness) and email automation (keywords, recipient name, signature, length penalty). It also describes Unsloth's proximity-based reward (closer numeric answers earn more) and the widely used GSM8K reward set (correctness, integer, soft/strict format, XML tag count).
- **Practical guidance.** Wait at least ~300 steps for reward to rise; use models of at least 1.5B parameters so thinking tokens emerge; for QLoRA 4-bit, VRAM in GB roughly equals the parameter count in billions (16-bit LoRA needs at least 4× more); pre-finetune on format so GRPO doesn't just learn formatting; data can be reused across epochs.
- **What Unsloth adds.** GRPO with LoRA/QLoRA rather than only full fine-tuning; vLLM fast inference in the same process without duplicated weights; memory-efficient linear kernels that avoid materializing full-vocabulary logits (the guide's example: 54.3 GB vs 510.8 GB for Llama 3.1 8B at 20K context with 8 generations); support for GSPO, Dr. GRPO and other loss variants via `GRPOConfig`; vision RL; 5 GB VRAM minimum for ≤1.5B models and 15 GB for up to 17B. Links to notebooks (e.g. Qwen3-4B GRPO from a base model) and further reading.

## Takeaways / questions
- A clear, intuition-first explanation of why GRPO is cheap: the group mean and standard deviation of sampled rewards stand in for a learned value function.
- The most transferable advice is about reward design: decompose into small verifiable checks, watch for the model learning only the format, and make sure the base model can sometimes succeed.
- It is vendor documentation: performance and memory numbers are Unsloth's own and the page changes over time, so it is a how-to reference rather than evidence.

notes.title: Green-VLA: Staged Vision-Language-Action Model for Generalist Robots
notes.tldr: Green-VLA (Sber Robotics Center) is a ~5B VLA trained in five stages (base VLM, web grounding, multi-robot pretraining, embodiment SFT, RL alignment) with a 64-slot unified action space, data quality filtering and RL that leaves the flow-matching policy's weights untouched.
notes.markdown:
## Summary
Green-VLA is a vision-language-action model from the Manipulation Team at Sber Robotics Center, built to run their Green humanoid (32 upper-body degrees of freedom including dexterous hands) while still controlling ordinary arms and bimanual platforms. Its argument is that scale alone is not enough: a VLA also needs clean, temporally aligned data, an action representation that does not mix up different robots, and a final RL stage because behaviour cloning saturates. The recipe is a five-stage curriculum, L0 → L1 → R0 → R1 → R2, on about 3,000 hours of robot demonstrations (much less than the 10,000+ hours behind π0). It reports strong results on SimplerEnv WidowX and CALVIN, plus real-robot table cleaning, shelf picking and humanoid sorting.

## Problem
Robot datasets differ in observations, action spaces, control types and sampling rates, and many contain jittery, blurry or repetitive episodes. Common practice zero-pads all actions into one vector, which forces the model to average incompatible targets and to guess "which dataset am I in". Behaviour cloning, $\mathcal{L}_\text{BC} = \mathbb{E}\|\pi_\theta(s) - a\|^2$, plateaus on long-horizon, contact-rich tasks, and reasoning-heavy VLAs add too much latency for real-time control.

## Related work
- π0 ([2410.24164](https://arxiv.org/abs/2410.24164)) and π0.5: VLM backbone plus a flow-matching action expert; Green-VLA follows the same architecture pattern and compares against both.
- GR00T N1, AgiBot GO-1, WALL-OSS, EO-1, X-VLA: other generalist VLA baselines.
- OpenVLA ([2406.09246](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.09246)) and RT-1-X: earlier open VLAs used as SimplerEnv baselines.
- Implicit Q-Learning (Kostrikov et al., [2110.06169](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.06169)): the offline critic used in R2.
- Flow matching (Lipman et al., [2210.02747](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02747)) and ΠGDM pseudoinverse guidance: the action generator and its guidance scheme.

## Method
![Figure 1 from the paper: Green-VLA architecture, where a VLM encodes instructions, cameras and proprioception into tokens for a flow-matching action expert, with a high-level planner and auxiliary signals (episode end, OOD, JPM guidance)](assets/green-vla/fig1.png)

**Architecture (mostly reused pattern).** A vision-language backbone (Qwen3-VL-4B-Instruct in the latest version; PaliGemma 3B earlier) encodes camera images, proprioception, the instruction and an embodiment prompt into tokens. A flow-matching action expert on top predicts chunks of actions. Total size is about 5B parameters. A separate frozen planner VLM (GigaVision, based on GigaChat) turns a user request like "set the table" into atomic subtasks ("pick [item] with left hand") and replans when needed.

**Unified action space (new).** Instead of zero-padding, every robot's native actions are mapped by $\Phi_e$ into a fixed 64-dimensional layout where each slot has the same physical meaning across robots (left arm joints, right gripper, base, etc.), with a mask $m_e$ of slots that robot uses. The loss only touches valid slots:
$$\mathcal{L}_\text{uni} = \mathbb{E}\big\|m_e \odot (\pi_\theta(x, c_e) - \Phi_e(a))\big\|^2,$$
where $c_e$ is a serialized control prompt (#arms, #hands, gripper vs dexterous hand, joint vs Cartesian, mobile vs static, slots used). Data from other robots is also retargeted to the humanoid (left arm to left arm, gripper close to hand grasp).

**Data alignment.** A DataQA pipeline drops episodes with missing frames, odd lengths, low motion, high "tremble" score, blurry images or broken gripper patterns, and weights datasets by DINOv3-based visual diversity and state diversity. Execution speeds are equalized by resampling trajectories with cubic splines according to each dataset's mean optical-flow magnitude. A sampling schedule $W_i \propto w_i^{\alpha_t}$ moves from uniform ($\alpha=0$) to the target mix ($\alpha=1$) so rare embodiments are not washed out early. A speed factor $v$ warps target trajectories and modulates the action expert through RMSNorm scale/shift, giving an inference-time knob between precise and fast motion.

**Extra heads.** An episode-progress head predicts $t/T$ (used by the planner to know when a subtask is done); a Gaussian-mixture model over training states flags out-of-distribution states and nudges actions back along the density gradient; and a Joint Prediction Module points at the named object in 2D with a VLM, lifts it to 3D using depth and camera pose, solves IK, and steers the flow-matching sampler toward it with ΠGDM guidance (training-free).

**R2 RL alignment (new combination).** Two methods that avoid backpropagating RL gradients through the flow model: (1) train an IQL critic on R1 data, push rolled-out actions along normalized $\nabla_a Q$, verify the improved trajectories on the robot, add them to the dataset, and redo R1 fine-tuning; (2) train a small actor that chooses the *input noise* for the frozen flow-matching policy to maximize return, so actions stay close to the data distribution.

## Data
- **L1:** 24M web multimodal samples: spatial VQA, pointing, boxes, pixel trajectories, multi-view QA (RefSpatial, RoboPoint, ShareRobot, Robo2VLM, PixMo-Points, COCO detection, A-OKVQA, OpenSpaces, SUN RGB-D, and VQA built from AgiBotWorld).
- **R0:** 184M robot samples, over 3,000 hours: AgiBotWorld (two-finger 774 h, dex-hand 82 h), DROID 512 h, Galaxea 477 h, Fractal 350 h, ActionNet 143 h, Bridge 105 h, RDT 60 h, RoboMind humanoid subset, BiPlay, plus their own Green humanoid data (48 h, expanded to 167 h by left-right mirroring and time reversal of reversible tasks) and an ALOHA pick dataset.

## Training
L0 is the pretrained VLM. L1 trains on web data for physical/spatial grounding. R0 pretrains on all robot data with the masked flow-matching objective for over $10^5$ steps on 64 H100s. R1 fine-tunes the same way on high-quality data for the target robot. R2 applies the RL methods above. For one example: camera frames, joint state, the instruction and the embodiment prompt go through the VLM; the action expert receives a noisy action chunk (noise injected only in that robot's slots) and is trained to predict the flow-matching velocity toward the true unified-space action chunk, with loss on masked slots only.

## Results
- **Real bimanual table cleaning (R0, no task fine-tuning):** first-item success 69.5% vs 38.4% for AgiBot GO-1 and 35.6% for π0; clearing time 1 min 35 s vs 2 min 59 s for π0 and over 5 min for GR00T N1 and WALL-OSS.
- **SimplerEnv WidowX (average success):** R0 45.0%, R1 55.2%, R2 79.1% with the PaliGemma backbone; R1 72.9% and R2 80.5% with Qwen3-VL-4B, above the best listed baseline (DB-MemVLA 73.2%; π0 fine-tuned 27.1%). The text reports R2 adding 24 points absolute over R1.
- **CALVIN ABC→D:** R1 is on par with or slightly ahead of fine-tuned π0; R2 gives the largest gain in average chain length (numbers in a figure, not extracted here).
- **E-commerce shelf picking and humanoid tasks:** JPM guidance raises top-1 picking success, especially for exact-SKU and unseen items, and R2 improves grasp reliability on hard objects; results are reported in figures only.

## Takeaways / questions
- The masked unified action space is a simple, sensible fix for cross-embodiment training; zero-padding with loss on unused dimensions is a real bug in naive pipelines.
- Both RL methods sidestep the difficulty of policy-gradient RL on flow-matching policies (no tractable log-probabilities). Steering the input noise is a neat idea that keeps the base policy frozen.
- Much of the evidence is on in-house real-robot setups reported as figures, and there is no ablation isolating each stage or module on the same benchmark, so it is hard to tell which ingredients matter most.
- The first RL method still needs an operator to reset the scene to verify every optimized trajectory, which limits scaling.

notes.title: Kimi K2.5: Visual Agentic Intelligence
notes.tldr: Kimi K2.5 extends the 1T-parameter Kimi K2 MoE into a native vision-language agent via early joint text-vision pretraining, text-only ('zero-vision') SFT and joint RL, and adds Agent Swarm, an RL-trained orchestrator that spawns parallel frozen subagents.
notes.markdown:
## Summary
Kimi K2.5 is Moonshot AI's open-weight (post-trained checkpoint on Hugging Face) multimodal agentic model. It is built on Kimi K2, a 1.04T-parameter mixture-of-experts LM with 32B active parameters, by continuing pretraining on about 15T mixed vision and text tokens with a native-resolution image/video encoder. Two ideas stand out in the report. First, text and vision are trained jointly from early on and through RL, and the authors find each modality helps the other, including vision RL improving text benchmarks. Second, Agent Swarm: the model learns, via RL, to act as an orchestrator that decomposes a task and launches many subagents in parallel, cutting latency by up to 4.5× and improving deep-search scores. It reports frontier-level results across reasoning, coding, vision, video, search and computer use.

## Problem
Two limits of current agentic models: (1) vision is usually bolted onto a text LM late in training, which can trade off one modality against the other, and visual tool use needs scarce hand-made multimodal reasoning traces; (2) agents execute reasoning and tool calls sequentially, so wall-clock time and context grow linearly with task size.

## Related work
- Kimi K2 ([2507.20534](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.20534)): the base MoE LM and MuonClip optimizer.
- Kimi-VL ([2504.07491](https://arxiv.org/abs/2504.07491)): the MoonViT encoder and VLM design followed here.
- Kimi k1.5 ([2501.12599](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12599)): the earlier RL recipe that the new policy loss modifies.
- NaViT ([2307.06304](https://arxiv.org/abs/2307.06304)) and SigLIP ([2303.15343](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.15343)): patch packing for native resolution, and the encoder initialization.
- Discard-all and other context-management strategies for long agent runs (compared against Agent Swarm).

## Method
**Architecture (mostly reused).** MoonViT-3D (initialized from SigLIP-SO-400M, NaViT-style patch packing for native resolution) → MLP projector → Kimi K2 MoE LM (384 experts, 8 active). New for video: up to four consecutive frames are packed together as one spatiotemporal sequence through the *same* encoder, then patches are temporally pooled, giving 4× temporal compression with full weight sharing between image and video.

**Joint text-vision pretraining.** In ablations with a fixed total budget of vision and text tokens, injecting vision early at a low ratio beat the conventional recipe of adding lots of vision late (e.g. 50%+). So K2.5 mixes vision at a constant moderate ratio throughout. Stages: train the ViT alone with a caption loss (aligned to a 16B Moonlight model, ~1T tokens), briefly train the projector, then ~15T tokens of joint pretraining from a near-final K2 checkpoint at 4K context, then mid-training with long-context extension (YaRN).

**Zero-vision SFT (new).** Post-training SFT uses only text data; image operations are expressed as Python code in an IPython tool (binarize, count, crop, measure). This "activates" visual tool use without hand-made visual trajectories; adding human-designed visual traces actually generalized worse.

**Joint RL.** Outcome-based RL on vision-necessary tasks (grounding and counting, charts and documents, vision-critical STEM) with task-specific rewards (soft IoU/F1 for boxes and points, mask IoU for polygons, edit distance for OCR), plus generative reward models with multiple rubrics for open-ended tasks. RL domains are organized by ability (knowledge, reasoning, coding, agentic) rather than modality. The policy loss is a GRPO-like group-baseline objective with token-level gradient masking whenever the log-ratio to the old policy leaves $[\alpha, \beta]$, plus a squared log-ratio penalty. "Toggle" alternates every $m$ iterations between a token-budget phase (only when the model already solves the problem well) and an unconstrained phase, to cut reasoning length without overfitting to short answers.

**Agent Swarm and PARL (new).** The model gets tools to create subagents and delegate subtasks. During Parallel-Agent RL, only the orchestrator is trained; subagents are frozen copies of earlier checkpoints, and their outputs are treated as environment observations, avoiding credit-assignment and stability problems. Reward:
$$r_\text{PARL} = \lambda_1 r_\text{parallel} + \lambda_2 r_\text{finish} + r_\text{perf},$$
where $r_\text{parallel}$ prevents "serial collapse" (never spawning), $r_\text{finish}$ prevents "spurious parallelism" (spawning many useless agents), and both $\lambda$s are annealed to zero. Cost is measured in *critical steps*, $\sum_t (S_\text{main}^{(t)} + \max_i S_{\text{sub},i}^{(t)})$, like the critical path of a computation graph, so only decompositions that shorten the longest branch pay off. Training prompts are synthetic wide-search and deep-search tasks that are hard to finish sequentially within the step budget, without instructing the model to parallelize.

![Figure 3 from the paper: an agent swarm, where a trainable orchestrator creates specialized frozen subagents and splits a task into parallel subtasks](assets/kimi-k2-5/fig1.png)

**Infrastructure.** Decoupled Encoder Process: run the small vision encoder's forward pass load-balanced across all GPUs, discard activations, train the LM backbone with the text-only parallel strategy, then recompute the encoder forward and backward. Multimodal training reaches 90% of text-only efficiency.

## Data
About 15T vision-text tokens in joint pretraining (extending K2's text mix with more code), ViT training on image/video-text pairs with alt text, synthetic captions, grounding boxes and OCR targets. SFT data is synthesized from K2, K2 Thinking and in-house expert models with human annotation and verification. RL uses a unified agentic environment with verifiable tasks, GRM-scored tasks and synthetic visual puzzles.

## Training
For an RL example: sample $K$ responses to a prompt from the old policy, score each (rule-based, task-specific or GRM reward), subtract the group mean reward as the baseline, and update each token's log-probability by that advantage, zeroing the gradient for tokens whose probability ratio has drifted outside $[\alpha,\beta]$. The optimizer is MuonClip throughout.

## Results
- **Cross-modal transfer:** vision RL raised text scores, MMLU-Pro 84.7 → 86.4, GPQA-Diamond 84.3 → 86.4, LongBench v2 56.7 → 58.9.
- **Reasoning:** AIME 2025 96.1%, HMMT 2025 95.4%, GPQA 87.6%, MMLU-Pro 87.1%; HLE-Full 30.1% without tools and 50.2% with tools (vs 45.8% Gemini 3 Pro, 45.5% GPT-5.2).
- **Coding:** SWE-Bench Verified 76.8%, SWE-Bench Multilingual 73.0%, LiveCodeBench v6 85.0%, Terminal-Bench 2.0 50.8%.
- **Search:** BrowseComp 60.6% single agent, 74.9% with Discard-all context management, 78.4% with Agent Swarm (vs 77.9% GPT-5.2 Pro). WideSearch item-F1 72.7% → 79.0% with Agent Swarm.
- **Vision and video:** MMMU-Pro 78.5%, MathVista 90.1%, OCRBench 92.3%, BLINK 78.9%, MMVP 87.0%, VideoMMMU 86.6%, LVBench 75.9% (with 2,000+ frames).
- **Computer use:** OSWorld-Verified 63.3% with GUI actions only (Claude Opus 4.5 66.3%), WebArena 58.9%.
- **Efficiency:** Agent Swarm is 3×–4.5× faster to reach a target WideSearch F1; Toggle cuts K2 Thinking's output tokens by 25–30% with negligible accuracy loss.

## Takeaways / questions
- "Early, low-ratio vision mixing beats late, heavy vision" is a useful data point for anyone training VLMs, and the zero-vision SFT result suggests joint pretraining already aligns modalities enough that text traces transfer to visual tool use.
- Visual reasoning here is done by writing image-processing code in a sandbox, the explicit-tool end of the spectrum, in contrast with latent visual reasoning approaches that keep intermediate visual states inside the model.
- Agent Swarm reframes multi-agent orchestration as context sharding: subagents keep their own bounded context and return only results. Training only the orchestrator against frozen subagents is a pragmatic way to do multi-agent RL.
- Many comparisons use vendor-reported numbers and some in-house benchmarks (e.g. the Swarm Bench), so head-to-head claims should be read with care.
