notes.title: OPUS: Towards Efficient and Principled Data Selection in Large Language Model Pre-training in Every Iteration
notes.tldr: OPUS selects pretraining data every step by scoring each candidate's optimizer-preconditioned update (AdamW or Muon) against a benchmark-aligned proxy gradient, with ghost gradients, CountSketch and Boltzmann sampling at 4.7% overhead.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*From onenote (2026-02-27):*

*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, page "OPUS" (Paper notes › SAE), 27 Feb 2026.*

- Era of unconstrained data scaling → era of **efficiency & quality data**.
- Previous "raw gradient methods" → follow the [validation] performance.
  - → don't work well with modern **momentum-based optimizers**.
- Now: select data based on its **direct optimizer influence** → the direction is now aligned.

## Summary
OPUS (Optimizer-induced Projected Utility Selection; SJTU EPIC Lab, Qwen Team at Alibaba, UW–Madison, UIUC, Mila) is a dynamic data-selection method for LLM pretraining. At every optimizer step it looks at a buffer of candidate sequences and keeps the half whose *actual* update, after AdamW's or Muon's preconditioning, would most reduce loss on a target "proxy" distribution, while penalizing redundancy among the chosen samples. The key point is that earlier gradient-based selectors score raw gradients, as if training used plain SGD; modern optimizers reshape updates heavily, so the score should be computed in the optimizer's geometry. With cheap approximations the overhead is 4.7%, and it improves GPT-2 Large/XL pretraining and Qwen3-8B continued pretraining at matched compute.

## Problem
High-quality public text is running out (the "data wall"), so pretraining needs better tokens rather than more. Static filters (FineWeb-Edu classifier, DCLM classifier, QuRating) score each document once and ignore that a sample's usefulness changes as the model trains. Dynamic selectors (e.g. GREATS) adapt during training but measure utility with raw gradients, which mismatches how AdamW and Muon actually move parameters, and naive per-sample scoring is too expensive.

## Related work
- GREATS (Wang et al., 2024): online batch selection via a Taylor approximation of validation-loss reduction plus the ghost-gradient trick; OPUS's direct starting point.
- FineWeb / FineWeb-Edu (Penedo et al., [2406.17557](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.17557)) and DCLM ([2406.11794](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.11794)): static quality filtering baselines.
- QuRating ([2402.09739](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.09739)) and DSIR ([2302.03169](https://arxiv.org/abs/2302.03169)): learned quality ratings and importance resampling.
- MATES / Group-MATES: learned influence models for dynamic selection.
- Influence functions (Koh & Liang, [1703.04730](https://arxiv.org/abs/1703.04730)): the conceptual root of "how much does this sample help validation loss".
- Muon (Jordan et al., 2024) and AdamW ([1711.05101](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.05101)): the optimizers whose geometry OPUS models.

## Method
**Utility in the optimizer's geometry (new).** For a candidate $z$ at step $t$, the optimizer turns its gradient into an effective update $\mathbf{u}_z = \mathbf{P}_t \nabla\mathcal{L}(z;\theta_t)$, where $\mathbf{P}_t$ is the preconditioner implied by the optimizer state (diagonal for AdamW; a non-linear matrix operation, Newton–Schulz orthogonalization, for Muon; the paper derives closed-form approximations for both). A first-order Taylor expansion of the proxy loss gives the marginal utility of adding $z$ to the already selected set:
$$U_z \approx \underbrace{\eta_t\langle \mathbf{u}_z, \mathbf{g}_\text{proxy}\rangle}_{\text{alignment}} - \underbrace{\eta_t^2\langle \mathbf{u}_z, \mathbf{G}\rangle}_{\text{redundancy}},$$
where $\mathbf{g}_\text{proxy}$ is the gradient of the proxy loss and $\mathbf{G} = \sum_{j \in \text{selected}} \mathbf{u}_{z_j}$ (the Hessian in the second-order term is approximated by the identity, following GREATS). So a sample is good if its update points where the proxy wants to go and does not duplicate what is already in the batch.

**Bench-Proxy (new).** Using raw benchmark examples as the proxy is off-distribution and noisy. Instead, a frozen embedder (Arctic-Embed-L v2) scores every pretraining document by its maximum cosine similarity to any benchmark validation example, and the top documents up to 30M tokens form the proxy pool. This keeps the proxy inside the pretraining distribution but aimed at the target tasks.

**Making it cheap (reused tricks, combined).** Per-sample gradients of a linear layer factorize as an outer product $\mathbf{a}_r \otimes \mathbf{b}_r$ of input activation and output gradient (the "ghost" technique), so they never need to be materialized. Preconditioned updates are projected to $m = 8192$ dimensions with CountSketch, and inner products are computed there. For AdamW's diagonal preconditioner this costs $O(d_\text{in} + d_\text{out})$ per layer; Muon's dense preconditioner costs $O(d_\text{in} d_\text{out})$.

**Boltzmann sampling.** Rather than greedy top-$K$, samples are drawn one at a time with probability $\propto \exp(U_z/\tau)$ ($\tau = 0.9$), updating the redundancy term after each pick. This guards against overfitting to a noisy proxy batch.

![Figure 3 from the paper: overview of the OPUS pipeline, from Bench-Proxy construction to optimizer-aware scoring and sampling](assets/opus-data-selection/onenote-fig1.png)

## Data
From-scratch pretraining on FineWeb and FineWeb-Edu (30B update tokens). In the FineWeb-Edu experiments OPUS selects only from the mid-quality subset (educational score 3) while baselines get the higher-quality partitions (scores 4–5). Continued pretraining uses SciencePedia, evaluated on SciAssess and OlympicArena. The proxy pool is 30M tokens retrieved from the corpus itself.

## Training
One step: read a buffer of $N = 32$ candidate sequences (64 in the tuned setting) plus a proxy mini-batch of 8; run a forward/backward pass on the first 512 tokens of each to collect activations and output gradients; form sketched, preconditioned update features for each candidate and the sketched proxy direction; sample $K = \rho N$ with $\rho = 0.5$ by Boltzmann sampling with the redundancy update; then do the real forward/backward on the full-length selected sequences and step the optimizer (AdamW, or Muon for matrices plus AdamW for the rest). Models: GPT-2 Large (774M) and XL (1.5B) from scratch, Qwen3-8B-Base for continued pretraining; gradient clipping at 1.0; all methods compute-matched on update tokens.

## Results
- **FineWeb.** OPUS has the best compute-matched average across model sizes and both optimizers. GPT-2 XL with Muon: 41.75 vs 40.29 for random selection; Figure 1 reports +2.2% average accuracy over random across 10 benchmarks and an 8× compute reduction. It often matches random training on twice the tokens (60B), and the abstract says it beats full 200B-token training.
- **FineWeb-Edu.** Selecting from lower-quality score-3 data, OPUS still matches or beats baselines trained on score-4/5 data; GPT-2 XL with Muon reaches the best average, 44.99.
- **Continued pretraining.** On Qwen3-8B-Base with SciencePedia, OPUS at 0.5B tokens beats random CPT at 3B tokens (a 6× data-efficiency gain).
- **Ablations (Table 7, FineWeb averages; random is 40.29).** Greedy top-$K$ 40.49 vs Boltzmann 41.75; standard proxy 41.03 vs Bench-Proxy 41.75.
- **Cost.** A naive online implementation is over 3.5× slower than random sampling; with ghost gradients and CountSketch the overhead is 4.7%.

## Takeaways / questions
- The core idea is simple and convincing: if you score data by its effect on the model, score the update the optimizer will actually apply, not the raw gradient.
- Bench-Proxy explicitly steers pretraining toward the evaluation benchmarks' distribution, which raises a fairness question when comparing against benchmark-agnostic filters; the gains over the non-benchmark proxy (41.03 vs 40.29 random) are the cleaner signal.
- Experiments are at GPT-2 scale for from-scratch training (≤1.5B, 30B tokens); whether the margin holds at frontier scale, and with Muon's more expensive projection, is open.
- Absolute averages differ by around 1–1.5 points, so variance across seeds would be useful to see.

notes.title: RiddleBench: A New Generative Reasoning Benchmark for LLMs
notes.tldr: 1,737 English logic puzzles from Indian competitive-exam mock papers (sequencing, seating arrangements, blood relations, coding-decoding); the best model reaches 69.3%, seating puzzles are hardest, and models rarely catch their own or others' reasoning errors.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Saved in my *Useful datasets* doc; its results table (RiddleBench, 1,737 puzzles) appears in my REVERSE deck.

## Summary
A short benchmark paper from AI4Bharat-affiliated authors. Many reasoning benchmarks test structured, quantitative skills; RiddleBench targets the mixed logical + spatial + constraint-satisfaction reasoning of classic exam riddles. Besides accuracy it probes *reliability*: can models verify other models' reasoning, correct themselves, and stay stable when constraints are reordered or a distractor is added? The answers are mostly no. The dataset is on Hugging Face (`ai4bharat/RiddleBench`) under CC0.

## Problem
Existing benchmarks under-measure flexible, compositional reasoning — keeping a consistent mental model of an arrangement while satisfying many textual constraints — and rarely test whether the reasoning process itself is robust.

## Related work
- GSM8K and MATH — structured quantitative reasoning.
- LogiQA ([arXiv:2007.08124](https://arxiv.org/abs/2007.08124)) and RuleTaker — formal rule-based deduction.
- BIG-Bench Hard ([arXiv:2210.09261](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.09261)) — complex reasoning as a persistent weakness.
- Zheng et al. (2023), LLM-as-a-judge — the evaluator paradigm whose reliability it questions.

## Results
Overall accuracy (Table 2): GPT-oss-120B **69.26%**, o3 63.37%, Claude 4 Sonnet 63.16%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 60.30%, DeepSeek-V3 58.28%, QwQ-32B 50.86%, DeepSeek-R1 50.56%, Mistral Small 24B 42.67%, Llama 3.3 70B 27.48%, Gemma 3 27B 25.04%.
- **Seating arrangements are hardest** (o3 25.93%, Gemini 2.5 Pro 24.31%, best 51.99%): models place the first few people correctly and then violate an earlier constraint.
- **Hallucination cascade:** given DeepSeek-R1's flawed reasoning, QwQ-32B correctly flags it only 44.1% of the time and validates it as sound in 45.2%; asked to re-check, it reverses only 4.4%. In forced-choice answer verification it ran out of thinking budget 55% of the time.
- **Self-correction is worse than peer review:** QwQ-32B catches its *own* flawed reasoning only 17.3% of the time (fails 67.7%) — a self-confirmation bias.
- **Fragility:** shuffling constraint order drops QwQ-32B by 6.70 points on blood relations and 3.69 on seating; one irrelevant sentence lowers most categories (oddly +2.74 on blood relations).

## Takeaways / questions
- Useful as a hard, cheap-to-grade puzzle set with a clear spatial-reasoning weak spot, which is why its table went into the REVERSE deck.
- Seating arrangements are a natural test case for “visual” or latent-state reasoning: the failure is exactly losing track of a spatial layout.
- Reliability experiments use a single generator/evaluator pair, so the cascade numbers are suggestive rather than general; mock-exam puzzles may also be in pretraining data.

## Contents
**Dataset.** Puzzles from publicly archived mock exams for Indian government services, digitised with Gemini 2.5 Flash OCR (questions, answers and official reasoning), structured, then manually verified by the authors. Composition: Sequential Reasoning 60%, Seating Arrangements 25%, Blood Relations 8%, Coding-Decoding 7%.

![Figure 2 from the paper: how RiddleBench was built — OCR extraction, structuring, and human verification](assets/riddlebench/fig1.png)

**Evaluation.** Zero-shot, temperature 0.7, thinking budget 8,192 tokens. Reliability experiments use DeepSeek-R1 as the “generator” and Qwen QwQ-32B as the “evaluator”.

notes.title: LLM inference and serving strategies: vLLM, paged attention, parallelism (concept notes)
notes.tldr: Concept notes on serving LLMs: vLLM servers with paged attention, batching, KV and prompt caching, tensor vs pipeline parallelism, and speculative decoding.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, VLMs › Inference: "VLLM" and "Common strats", 24 Feb 2026. Sections "World modeling" and "System design" (page "AI system design") were empty.*

### vLLM
- Faster inference: vLLM, which supports paged attention.
- → run a vLLM server on the GPU → send [async] HTTP POSTs to get JSON responses.
  - → model parallelism if the model is small *(as written)* → round-robin load balancing across vLLM instances on each GPU.
- **Pipeline parallelism** → sustains high GPU usage → memory/model split across GPUs.

### Common strategies
- **Batching** → balance weight loading & computation.
- **KV cache** → cache keys & values.
- **Paged attention**: the KV cache takes a lot of memory → partition it into "pages", allocated and accessed via a lookup table + scheduling.
- **Tensor parallelism** → split weights across GPUs. **Pipeline parallelism** → split transformer layers across GPUs.
- **Prompt caching** → the system prompt is cached → session-aware routing to maximize the prompt-cache hit rate.
- **Speculative decoding**: predict tokens ahead of time and verify/cancel → uses more FLOPs, not memory.

## Summary
These are concept notes. Decoding is memory-bandwidth-bound, so serving systems batch requests to amortize weight loading. vLLM's **PagedAttention** stores the KV cache in fixed-size blocks with a block table, removing fragmentation and allowing continuous batching. Large models are sharded with tensor parallelism (within a layer) or pipeline parallelism (across layers). Prefix/prompt caching reuses KV for shared system prompts, which works best with cache-aware routing. Speculative decoding drafts several tokens cheaply and verifies them in one pass of the big model, trading spare compute for latency.

notes.title: Consistently Simulating Human Personas with Multi-Turn Reinforcement Learning
notes.tldr: Defines three LLM-judged persona-consistency metrics (prompt-to-line, line-to-line, Q&A) for LLMs that simulate users — patients, students, chat partners — and uses them as rewards for multi-turn PPO, cutting inconsistency by over 55%.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
“While conducting my own experiments on AI safety, I stumbled upon your paper on persona simulation and deception, which aligns closely with my interests.” (cold email to Sergey Levine's lab, Feb 2026)

## Summary
From Berkeley (Levine) and the University of Washington (Althoff, Jaques). LLMs are increasingly used as stand-ins for humans — simulated therapy patients, tutoring students, study participants, and user simulators that RL agents train against. But they drift: a “depressed” patient is cheerful after one turn, a “high-school student” starts sounding like a postdoc. The paper flips the usual RL setup — instead of training the task agent against a fixed user simulator, it *trains the user simulator* to stay in character, using automatic consistency metrics as rewards.

## Problem
Off-the-shelf instruction-tuned LLMs drift from assigned personas, contradict earlier statements, and revert to RLHF's helpful, upbeat default, which makes simulations unrealistic and corrupts the signal for anything trained or evaluated on them. Existing consistency work uses narrow definitions or costly human contradiction labels.

## Related work
- Park et al., *Generative Agents* ([arXiv:2304.03442](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.03442)) — LLM agents simulating people.
- Zheng et al., *Judging LLM-as-a-Judge* ([arXiv:2306.05685](https://arxiv.org/abs/2306.05685)) — the judging approach used for the metrics.
- PPO (Schulman et al., [arXiv:1707.06347](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347)) and KTO ([arXiv:2402.01306](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.01306)) — online vs. offline fine-tuning compared.

## Method
Two LLM agents talk: a **user simulator** $\mathcal{U}_\text{sim}$ (given a task prompt plus a persona/strategy background) and a **task agent**. An LLM judge $J_\text{LLM}(x, y) \in \{0,1\}$ says whether utterance $y$ is consistent with reference $x$. Three metrics over the simulator's utterances $R = [r_1, \dots, r_T]$ with persona prompt $P$:
- **Prompt-to-line:** $C = \frac{1}{T}\sum_t J_\text{LLM}(P, r_t)$ — does each line fit the persona?
- **Line-to-line:** $C = \frac{1}{T-1}\sum_{t\ge2} \min_{i<t} J_\text{LLM}(r_i, r_t)$ — does any line contradict an earlier one?
- **Q&A:** generate diagnostic questions about the persona; answer them from the dialogue so far and compare to answers from $P$ — are the simulator's implied beliefs stable over time?

![Figure 1 from the paper: generate persona-conditioned dialogues, score them with three consistency metrics, then fine-tune with multi-turn RL](assets/consistent-persona-simulation/fig1.png)

**Fine-tuning.** Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct is trained as the user simulator with the prompt-to-line score as reward, comparing SFT, KTO (offline RL) and PPO (online, multi-turn RL).

## Data
Three roles: open-ended chit-chat partner, student (education), and patient seeking mental-health counselling. Dialogues of 10, 20, 40 and 60 turns from Llama-8B-Instruct, Gemma-2B-IT and Mistral-7B-Instruct, about 800 per task — roughly 39K dialogue lines in total. Evaluation: 40 new conversations over 10 personas, plus human ratings.

## Results
- The LLM judge agrees with human raters 80.03% of the time on average (Fleiss' κ 0.552), higher than humans agree with each other (pairwise ~71–75%, κ ~0.21–0.26).
- **PPO beats** the base model, SFT and KTO on prompt-to-line consistency: +58.5% (open-ended), +20.6% (education), +37.6% (mental health) over the base model; overall inconsistency drops by more than 55%. Consistency stays high as dialogues get longer.
- Human evaluation of PPO conversations corroborates the gains.

## Takeaways / questions
- Safety relevance: realistic user simulators are needed to red-team and train agents (e.g. therapy bots), and a simulator that is “too nice” hides failure modes.
- My email framed it as “persona simulation and deception”; the paper itself is about consistency (staying in persona) rather than deception per se, though persona drift and strategic role-play are close cousins.
- The authors note a real tension: humans legitimately change their minds, so maximising static consistency can penalise realistic evolution.
- Reward is an LLM judge, so the simulator could learn to satisfy the judge rather than to be realistic — a reward-hacking risk to probe.

notes.title: AlphaOne: Reasoning Models Thinking Slow and Fast at Test Time
notes.tldr: A training-free decoding scheme for reasoning models — insert “wait” after paragraph breaks with a linearly decaying probability until an “α moment” (α × the usual thinking length), then turn every “wait” into </think> — that improves accuracy while using fewer tokens.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
“Your recent research on AlphaOne, especially the use of moments to motivate reasoning transitions, [is] very exciting.”

## Summary
From UIUC with Berkeley co-authors (including Jitendra Malik). Large reasoning models (o1-style, DeepSeek-R1 distills, QwQ) decide on their own when to “slow down” (write “wait”, reconsider) and when to stop thinking — and they often overthink or underthink. Prior test-time tricks only push monotonically in one direction: s1 appends “wait” to force more thinking; Chain of Draft forces terse thinking. AlphaOne (α1) instead *schedules* the slow-to-fast transition: lots of slow thinking early, tapering off, then a hard switch to fast answering at a controllable point, the **α moment**.

## Problem
How to modulate a reasoning model's progress at test time — both how long it thinks and *when* it transitions between slow, reflective thinking and fast thinking — in a universal way that subsumes existing budget-forcing methods.

## Related work
- s1 / budget forcing (Muennighoff et al., [arXiv:2501.19393](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.19393)) — append “wait” when the model tries to stop; a special case of α1.
- Chain of Draft (Xu et al., 2025) — prompt for minimal, fast thinking.
- DeepSeek-R1 ([arXiv:2501.12948](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948)) — the RL-trained slow-thinking models being controlled.
- Kahneman, *Thinking, Fast and Slow* — the framing.

## Method
Entirely training-free; the base models are reused as-is (DeepSeek-R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B and 7B, QwQ-32B). Only decoding is changed.

1. **α moment.** Estimate the model's average thinking length $\overline{N}_\text{think}$ (from 10 sample questions). The α moment is the token position $T_m = \alpha \overline{N}_\text{think}$, with $\alpha > 1$ scaling the thinking budget.
2. **Pre-α: stochastic slow thinking.** Each time the model emits the paragraph delimiter `\n\n`, append “wait” with probability $p_\text{wait} = \mathcal{S}(t)$, a user-chosen schedule over $t = 0, \dots, T_m$. Insertions form a Bernoulli process. Linear annealing (high probability early, decaying to 0) works best, i.e. *slow first, then fast*.
3. **Post-α: deterministic termination.** After heavy slow thinking, models show “slow-thinking inertia” and rarely emit `</think>` on their own. So after the α moment, every generated “wait” is replaced by `</think>`, forcing the transition to the answer.

α1 reduces to s1 when $p_\text{wait}$ is simply 1 or 0 at the end, but supports dense, continuous modulation.

![Figure 2 from the paper: overview of AlphaOne — scheduled slow thinking before the α moment and forced fast thinking after it](assets/alphaone/fig1.png)

## Data
Evaluation only: AIME 2024, AMC23, Minerva-Math, MATH500 (math), LiveCodeBench (code), OlympiadBench (science); average Pass@1 and generated tokens.

## Results
Average Pass@1 gain over the base model across six benchmarks (Table 1):
| Model | s1 | Chain of Draft | **α1** |
|---|---|---|---|
| R1-Distill-Qwen-1.5B | +0.15 | +2.95 | **+6.15** |
| R1-Distill-Qwen-7B | +1.48 | +1.73 | **+4.65** |
| QwQ-32B | +0.63 | +2.10 | **+5.33** |

- Examples: 1.5B on AMC23 57.5 → 70.0 with fewer tokens (5339 → 4952); QwQ-32B on AIME24 40.0 → 53.3 (4058 → 3141 tokens) and LiveCodeBench 67.0 → 75.8.
- **Slow first, then fast** beats other schedules (constant, linear increase, exponential anneal) — the opposite of the human “fast first, slow when stuck” pattern.
- Slow thinking can make reasoning *shorter overall*: more informative progress means fewer total tokens.
- Frequent transitions help: α1 inserts “wait” over 2× more than s1 and does better.
- Larger α isn't always better — there is an optimal α moment under an 8,192-token budget.

## Takeaways / questions
- The “α moment” is a neat control knob: a single parameter that sets the thinking budget and where the slow-to-fast switch happens.
- It relies on o1-style models responding to “wait”; models trained with different transition behaviour may not be controllable this way (the authors note this).
- Connects to my interest in reasoning at multiple timescales (HRM): α1 imposes a slow-then-fast schedule from the outside, whereas HRM builds two timescales into the architecture.

notes.title: CLIPScore: A Reference-free Evaluation Metric for Image Captioning
notes.tldr: CLIPScore rates an image caption by the (rescaled) cosine similarity between CLIP's image and caption embeddings, needing no human reference captions, and correlates with human judgments better than reference-based metrics like CIDEr and SPICE.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
I recreated my own version of CLIPScore from scratch (mentioned in a Feb 2026 cold email).

## Summary
CLIPScore (Allen Institute for AI and University of Washington) is a simple idea that turned out to work very well: to judge how good a caption is for an image, just ask CLIP how well they match. Traditional captioning metrics (BLEU, CIDEr, SPICE) compare a candidate caption against human-written reference captions by word overlap, which unfairly punishes good captions that use different words and requires collecting references. CLIPScore needs no references at all, the way a human would judge a caption by looking at the image. A reference-augmented variant, RefCLIPScore, combines both signals and correlates with humans even better. It became a standard metric for captioning and for text-to-image generation.

## Problem
Reference-based caption metrics depend on n-gram or embedding overlap with human references, so they disfavor correct captions that use novel words and favor captions that reuse common reference words, and they cannot be used without references. Humans, in contrast, evaluate captions against the image.

## Related work
- CLIP ([2103.00020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020)) — supplies the image and text encoders (ViT-B/32).
- BLEU, METEOR, ROUGE, CIDEr, SPICE — reference-based n-gram and scene-graph metrics.
- BERTScore, ViLBERTScore, TIGEr — embedding-based reference metrics.
- FOIL (Shekhar et al. 2017) — captions with one swapped noun, used to test hallucination sensitivity.

## Method
![Figure 1 from the paper: CLIPScore uses CLIP to assess image-caption compatibility without references, avoiding n-gram metrics' biases against novel wording](assets/clipscore/fig1.png)

For a candidate caption $\mathbf{c}$ and image $\mathbf{v}$, with CLIP embeddings (the caption prefixed with "A photo depicts", which slightly improved correlations):
$$\text{CLIP-S}(\mathbf{c}, \mathbf{v}) = w \cdot \max(\cos(\mathbf{c}, \mathbf{v}), 0), \qquad w = 2.5$$
The rescaling by $w=2.5$ stretches the scores, since observed cosine similarities range from roughly 0 to 0.4, toward $[0,1]$.

**RefCLIPScore** adds references $R$ (embedded with CLIP's text encoder) by taking the harmonic mean of CLIP-S and the best caption–reference similarity:
$$\text{RefCLIP-S}(\mathbf{c}, R, \mathbf{v}) = \text{H-Mean}\big(\text{CLIP-S}(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{v}),\ \max(\max_{\mathbf{r}\in R}\cos(\mathbf{c},\mathbf{r}), 0)\big)$$

Nothing is trained: CLIP is used off the shelf. What is new is the evaluation recipe and the extensive study of where it works. More elaborate CLIP setups (region- or token-level matching) did not do better.

## Data
- Caption-level human judgments: Flickr8K-Expert (17K expert ratings over 5,664 images), Flickr8K-CF (crowdsourced), and Composite (12K judgments over COCO, Flickr8k and Flickr30k images).
- Pairwise preferences: Pascal-50S (4K caption pairs, 48 human judgments each).
- Hallucination sensitivity: FOIL (COCO captions with one plausible-but-wrong noun phrase swapped in).
- Case studies: Twitter alt-text ratings, Abstract-50S clip-art, and other non-literal domains such as news captions.

## Training
No training. To score one example: encode the image with CLIP's ViT-B/32, encode "A photo depicts" + caption with CLIP's text encoder, take the cosine similarity, clip negatives to zero and multiply by 2.5. For RefCLIPScore, also embed each reference caption, take the best cosine with the candidate, and combine with CLIP-S by harmonic mean. Runtime is fast: roughly 4K image–caption pairs per minute on a single consumer GPU.

## Results
- Flickr8K-Expert (Kendall $\tau_c$ correlation with humans): CLIP-S with **no references 51.2**, higher than every reference-based metric (e.g. SPICE 44.9, CIDEr 43.9, ViLBERTScore-F 50.1); RefCLIP-S reaches **53.0**.
- Across the caption-level corpora, CLIP-S without references beats reference-based metrics, and RefCLIP-S improves further in all cases.
- FOIL hallucination detection (pairwise accuracy): CLIP-S 87.2 with no references; RefCLIP-S 91.0 / 92.6 with one / four references, the best overall.
- Case studies: strong on Twitter alt-text quality and clip-art, weaker than reference-based metrics on news captions that need contextual knowledge not visible in the image.

## Takeaways / questions
- A one-line metric that made reference-free evaluation practical; "CLIP score" is now ubiquitous in text-to-image evaluation as well.
- It inherits CLIP's blind spots: weak on counting, spatial relations and fine detail, and biased toward whatever CLIP learned from web captions. ALOHa's object-level matching is one response to its lack of localization.
- I re-implemented it from scratch; that is how I came across the ALOHa paper, which I mentioned in my Feb 2026 cold email to David Chan.

notes.title: Robotic foundation models: from end-to-end control to VLAs
notes.tldr: Concept notes on robot foundation models. Covers the end-to-end hypothesis, the pretrain/post-train recipe, VLA generations (RT-2 to π0 with flow matching), embodied chain-of-thought test-time compute, and RL fine-tuning.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, page "Robotic foundation models" (Paper notes › video generation), 11 Feb 2026.*

- **End-to-end hypothesis**
  - Abstractions are hard to place in the real world.
    - ↳ directly learn from observation to controls.
  - Combining control & perception increases error tolerance.
- **Foundation-model training**
  - Pretraining → large amounts of internet-scale data *(uncertain reading)*.
  - Post-training / alignment → instruction fine-tuning; automated RL improvement *(uncertain reading)*.
- **VLA (vision-language-action)**
  - 1st gen (**RT-2**): take image, output "actions" (takes advantage of the vision-language backbone).
  - 2nd gen (**π0**): add a diffusion/flow transformer to produce actions with **flow matching**.
- **Test-time compute** ("thinking/reasoning mode", intermediate generation)
  - ↳ synthetically related robot data.
  - **Embodied chain of thought**
    - foundation model much better than individual [specialist models] *(uncertain reading)*;
    - output of plan + subtask + action on a "good strategy" (includes sub-tasks) *(partly illegible)*.
- **RL** → initially used for generalist policies *(uncertain reading)*.
  - ↳ fine-tune the foundation model with RL (strategies).

## Summary
This is a lecture-style overview, not a single paper. Robot foundation models bet on end-to-end learning from pixels to motor commands, trained like LLMs: pretrain broadly, then post-train. Vision-language-action models went from RT-2 (Google DeepMind), which fine-tunes a VLM to emit discretized action tokens, to π0 (Physical Intelligence), which adds a flow-matching action expert for continuous, high-frequency control. Newer work adds test-time reasoning (embodied chain-of-thought that predicts plans and subtasks before actions) and RL fine-tuning on top of the pretrained policy.

## Takeaways / questions
- The analogy to LLMs holds stage by stage: pretraining, instruction tuning, CoT and RL.
- I filed this page under the video generation section in OneNote. World models connect the two topics.

notes.title: Open-Sora: Democratizing Efficient Video Production for All
notes.tldr: Open-Sora is a fully open reproduction of the Sora recipe: a 3D autoencoder stacked on a pretrained 2D VAE, a spatial-temporal diffusion transformer (STDiT) adapted from PixArt, and staged rectified-flow training, generating up to 16 s, 720p video for about 35k H100 hours.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*From onenote (2026-02-10):*

*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, page "Open SORA" (Paper notes › video generation), 10 Feb 2026.*

- **Dataset**
  - Text–video pairs: video–caption pairs, public datasets *(uncertain reading)*.
    - ↳ for pure videos, use a few-shot language model to generate captions.
  - To filter for high-quality videos:
    - **Aesthetic score** (sample frames & pass through an aesthetic predictor).
    - **Optical-flow score** (UniMatch: predicts pixel displacement across frames).
    - **OCR score** (for contained text).
- **Architecture**
  - Video → video autoencoder; text → text encoder; both feed the **DiT** transformer.
  - Video autoencoder (3D):
    - compress video spatially + extract frames;
    - cascading: first compress spatially, then temporally;
    - ↳ additive encoders *(uncertain reading)*.
- **Training process**
  - Stage 1: 8 GPUs + 2D VAE frozen; reconstruct the 2D-VAE-compressed latents (from the 3D VAE).
  - Stage 2: identity loss removed.
  - Stage 3: reconstruction of 2D VAE *(uncertain reading)*.
- **Video latent dims** $\mathbb{R}^{T\times H\times W\times C}$ ($T$ = number of frames). Attention is applied along one of the dimensions at a time:
  - Spatial attention: $T \times (H\!\cdot\!W\!\cdot\!C)$, self-attention.
  - Temporal attention: $H \times (T\!\cdot\!W\!\cdot\!C)$, self-attention.
  - Cross-attention: $(T\!\cdot\!H\!\cdot\!W\!\cdot\!C) \leftrightarrow$ text tokens.
  - These alternate.

## Summary
Open-Sora (HPC-AI Tech) is one of the earliest open-source attempts to reproduce OpenAI's Sora. The paper is a technical report for version 1.2 (June 2024) that also summarizes 1.0 and 1.1. Everything is released: data-processing pipeline, training code and weights. The model does text-to-image, text-to-video and image-to-video, producing clips up to about 16 seconds, up to 720p, at arbitrary aspect ratios. Its value is less a new idea than a complete, reproducible recipe showing how to turn a pretrained image diffusion transformer into a video model on a modest budget.

## Problem
Sora showed that scaled diffusion transformers can generate long, high-fidelity video, but OpenAI released neither the model nor the details. Video models are also very expensive to train because a video has many more tokens than an image. The goal is an open, efficient pipeline that the community can reproduce and extend.

## Related work
- Sora report ("Video generation models as world simulators", OpenAI 2024): the architecture template (video compressor + text encoder + DiT).
- DiT (Peebles & Xie, [2212.09748](https://arxiv.org/abs/2212.09748)): diffusion with a Transformer backbone.
- PixArt-α / PixArt-Σ ([2310.00426](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.00426)): the T5-conditioned image DiT that Open-Sora is initialized from.
- Latte ([2401.03048](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.03048)): factorized spatial/temporal attention for video diffusion.
- Stable Video Diffusion ([2311.15127](https://arxiv.org/abs/2311.15127)): the data-filtering recipe they mostly follow.
- MAGVIT-v2 ([2310.05737](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.05737)): the 3D VAE architecture they adopt.
- Rectified flow / SD3 ([2403.03206](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.03206)) and flow matching ([2210.02747](https://arxiv.org/abs/2210.02747)): the training objective and stability tricks.

## Method
The pipeline follows the Sora report: compress the video into latents, encode the text, and run a diffusion transformer over the video latents conditioned on the text.

**Video compressor (3D autoencoder).** Versions 1.0/1.1 used Stability's 2D image VAE (8×8 spatial compression) and simply kept one of every three frames, which hurt smoothness. Version 1.2 stacks two autoencoders: first a pretrained 2D VAE (from SDXL, reused) compresses each frame 8×8 spatially, then a new 3D VAE (MAGVIT-v2 architecture, ~300M parameters, causal convolutions) compresses 4× in time. The insight is that after the 2D VAE, neighbouring frames' features are still highly correlated, so a second network can squeeze time cheaply instead of training a full 3D VAE from scratch. Total 384M parameters.

**Diffusion backbone (STDiT).** The denoiser is PixArt's image DiT with T5 text encoding and cross-attention from video tokens to text (reused). New: each block gets a temporal attention layer, so attention is factorized: spatial self-attention within each frame, then temporal attention across frames at the same spatial location. This is much cheaper than full attention over every token of every frame. The temporal layers' output projections are zero-initialized, so at the start the model behaves exactly like the image model. Adding them grows the model from 580M to 1.1B parameters. Other changes: RoPE for temporal attention, and QK-normalization (from SD3) with a tiny epsilon to avoid training spikes in half precision.

![Figure 6 from the paper: the Open-Sora spatial-temporal diffusion transformer (STDiT) architecture](assets/open-sora/onenote-fig1.png)

**Conditioning by masking.** To support image-to-video, video extension and similar tasks, some frames are "unmasked": they are given diffusion timestep 0 (treated as clean) while the rest are noised. Inspired by UL2, training randomly unmasks patterns such as the first frame, first k frames, last k frames, first-and-last, or random frames. Applying this to 50% of samples taught conditioning within 10k steps with little cost to text-to-video; 30% worked worse. Captions are also extended with scores, e.g. "aesthetic score: 5.5, motion score: 10, camera motion: pan left", which can be changed at inference to steer the output.

**Variable sizes by bucketing.** Instead of NaViT-style packing or padding, samples are grouped into buckets of (resolution, number of frames, aspect ratio); each batch has one fixed shape. Each bucket also has a keep-probability (to downsample some high-res videos) and its own batch size to balance GPU load.

## Data
About 30M clips of 2–16 s, ~80k hours in total, all from open sources: WebVid-10M, a 20M high-quality subset of Panda-70M, HD-VG-130M, MiraData, Vript, Inter4K, plus free-licensed videos from Pexels, Pixabay and Mixkit. About 3M images are mixed in (a LAION subset with aesthetic score > 6.5, and Unsplash-lite). Processing: PySceneCut splits scenes into clips; filters remove clips with low aesthetic score (LAION scorer), low motion (UniMatch optical flow) or too much on-screen text (DBNet++ OCR). Captions come from GPT-4V or PLLaVA-13B (4 frames per clip), and camera motion detected by optical flow is appended because captioners rarely describe it.

## Training
One training example: a video clip is encoded to latents by the stacked VAE, its caption (with appended scores) by T5. Some frames may be unmasked as conditions. Noise is added to the other frames' latents at a sampled time, and STDiT is trained with a rectified-flow (flow-matching) objective to predict the velocity that moves the noisy latents back toward the clean ones; learning rate $5\times10^{-5}$.

The model is built by staged adaptation of the PixArt-Σ 2K checkpoint on 8 H100s: multi-resolution image training, adding QK-norm, switching from DDPM to rectified flow (cutting video sampling from 100 to 30 steps), logit-normal and resolution-aware timestep sampling, a smaller AdamW epsilon, swapping in the new VAE with FPS conditioning, then adding temporal blocks. Video training is in three stages by data quality on 12×8 GPUs over about two weeks (~70k steps): WebVid-10M at 240p/360p (30k steps), the filtered Panda-70M subset at 360p/480p (23k steps), and ~2M curated high-quality clips (5k hours) at 720p/1080p with 25% masking (15k steps). The report quotes about 35,000 H100 GPU hours overall. The 3D VAE is trained separately for 1.2M steps in three stages (first matching the 2D VAE's features with an identity loss, finally reconstructing raw video with mixed lengths).

## Results
On VBench, Open-Sora 1.2 scores 79.76% total (81.35% quality, 73.39% semantic), above the other open models in their table, e.g. Show-1 78.93%, Latte 77.29%, LaVie 77.08%, Open-Sora-Plan v1.1 78.00%, and its own earlier versions 1.0 (75.91%) and 1.1 (75.66%). The 3D VAE reaches PSNR 30.59 / SSIM 0.880 on a Pixabay validation set, versus 29.89 / 0.882 for Open-Sora-Plan 1.1's VAE.

## Takeaways / questions
- The cheap path to a video model is "start from a strong image DiT and add zero-initialized temporal attention"; the same trick (zero-init new layers so the pretrained model is unchanged at step 0) appears all over adapter work.
- The stacked 2D+3D VAE is a pragmatic tokenizer design: reuse a frozen-quality image compressor and only learn the temporal part. Relevant to my interest in visual tokenizers.
- The report is light on ablations and compares only to open models on VBench, so it says little about how far it is from Sora itself.
- Factorized spatial/temporal attention saves compute but may limit motion coherence compared with full 3D attention, which later open models moved toward.

notes.title: Towards Monosemanticity: Decomposing Language Models With Dictionary Learning
notes.tldr: Anthropic trains sparse autoencoders on the 512-neuron MLP of a one-layer transformer and recovers thousands of far more interpretable “features” than the neurons themselves — the paper that launched SAEs as the main tool of mechanistic interpretability.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
First entry in my paper list, under “Sparse Autoencoders”.

*From onenote (2026-02-09):*

*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, page "Monotonicity" (Paper notes › SAE), 9 Feb 2026. The page title is my shorthand for Monosemanticity.*

- **Polysemanticity** → hard to reason about models.
  - ↳ caused by **superposition**: each feature gets its own linear combination of neurons (when there are more features than neurons).
- Weak dictionary learning algorithm (generates learned features from trained models).
- **Problem setup**
  - Large dimensionality → try to decompose the MLP activations with a **sparse autoencoder**.
  - $x^j \approx \sum_i f_i(x^j)\, d_i + b$, where $x^j$ is the activation vector for datapoint $j$, $f_i(x^j)$ the feature activation and $d_i$ the direction of feature $i$.
  - $f_i(x) = \mathrm{ReLU}\big(W_e (x - b_d) + b_e\big)_i$
  - Sparse autoencoder contents: weights ≈ activations, parameterizable ($d \times k$), $W, b$.
  - ↳ basically trying to build a lower-dimensional projection of the hyperspace *(last word uncertain)*.
- Right column:
  - Simply forcing sparsity doesn't work in LMs.
  - A neuron (even with 1-hot encoding) can learn to fire ambiguously:
    - $A, B, (C, D)$ → fire when $A \& B$: $\approx \tfrac12 \ln 2$
    - $A, B, C, D$ → fire when $A$: $\tfrac34 \ln 2$, which is a lower loss!
- **SAE training** (highlighted)
  1. Trained language model: input $N \times T \times C$ → MLP ($N\times T\times C \to N\times T\times h \to N\times T\times C$); $\mathrm{ReLU}(N\times T\times h)$ = activations ⇒ $(N\!\cdot\!D,\ h)$ = training dataset for the SAE.
  2. $(N\!\cdot\!D, h) \Rightarrow \mathrm{Linear}(h, k) \to \mathrm{ReLU}$ with $k \gg h$. Encoder = linear expansion into more features.
     - L1 sparsity → minimize active features; or **TopK sparsity**: $\mathrm{TopK}(z, k)$ masks the other features to exactly zero (sparsity enforcement: only $k$ non-zero features).
     - ⇒ Decoder (features back to activations) ⇒ L2 / MSE loss against the activations.
  3. Frozen SAE + LM → get many activations, $n \times k$ for $n$ tokens.
     - ↳ pick one $k$ (that's a feature) → take the $n \times 1$ vector and study the **top-activating tokens** → now interpret.

## Summary
Published October 4, 2023 on the Transformer Circuits Thread. Individual neurons are usually *polysemantic* — in this paper's model one neuron fires on academic citations, English dialogue, HTTP requests and Korean text — so they are bad units for understanding a network. The proposed fix is to learn a new, larger basis of directions (“features”) with a sparse autoencoder, such that each activation is a sparse combination of features. On a deliberately tiny model, the authors show in great depth that these features are mostly monosemantic, causally used by the model, partly universal across models, and organised in families that split as the dictionary grows. *Scaling Monosemanticity* (2024) then applied the method to Claude 3 Sonnet.

## Problem
How to undo **superposition** — the hypothesis (from *Toy Models of Superposition*) that a network represents more sparse features than it has neurons by giving each feature its own linear combination of neurons — so that a model can be decomposed into human-understandable units. The authors had found that building models without superposition (sparse architectures) didn't remove polysemanticity, and that standard dictionary learning overfit.

## Related work
- Elhage et al., *Toy Models of Superposition* ([arXiv:2209.10652](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.10652)) — the theory this paper tests on a real model.
- Cunningham et al., *Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models* ([arXiv:2309.08600](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.08600)) — independent concurrent SAE work.
- Olah et al., *Zoom In* / Circuits thread (2020) — polysemantic neurons in vision models (cat faces and car fronts in Inception v1).

## Method
**The model studied (trained for this purpose):** a one-layer transformer with residual stream dimension 128 and a single 512-neuron ReLU MLP, trained on 100B tokens of the Pile (public data for reproducibility).

**The sparse autoencoder (new):** one hidden layer, wider than the 512-dim input. It subtracts a learned bias, applies a linear encoder + ReLU to get feature activations $f(\mathbf{x})$, and a linear decoder to reconstruct; trained with
$$\mathcal{L} = \|\mathbf{x} - \hat{\mathbf{x}}\|_2^2 + \lambda \|f(\mathbf{x})\|_1$$
The L1 term pushes most features to zero on each token, so each token is explained by a few active features; each decoder column is a feature's direction in neuron space.

Practical lessons that later became standard:
- **Scale of data matters** — 8 billion MLP activation vectors (from 40M Pile contexts, sampled without replacement), 1M steps, batch 8192; more data gives “sharper” features.
- **Resampling dead features** — periodically re-initialise features that never fire toward inputs the SAE reconstructs poorly.
- No single metric for “is it working”: they combine manual inspection, feature density, reconstruction loss and loss when the MLP is replaced by its reconstruction.

Dictionaries range from 1× (512 features) to 256× (131,072); most analysis is on run **A/1** with 4,096 features.

**Evaluation of interpretability:** detailed case studies (Arabic script, DNA, base64, Hebrew), a blinded human rater scoring samples across the *whole* activation range (not just top examples), and automated interpretability on activations and on logit effects — all applied to features and neurons alike.

## Data
The Pile, both for training the transformer and for collecting activations.

## Results
- **Features are much more interpretable than neurons** by human and automated scores. Example: the Arabic-script feature A/1/3450 — Arabic script is only 0.13% of training tokens but 81% of the tokens where the feature fires, 98% when its activation is above 5. Some features (e.g. Hebrew) are effectively invisible in the neuron basis.
- **Causal:** pinning the base64 feature on makes the model generate base64; the Arabic feature produces Arabic text.
- **How much is explained:** replacing the MLP with A/1's reconstruction recovers **79%** of the MLP's loss reduction; the largest dictionary (131,072 features) recovers 94.5%.
- **Feature splitting:** as the dictionary grows, one base64 feature splits into three more specific ones — different sizes give different “resolutions”.
- **Universality:** SAEs on different transformers learn mostly similar features — more similar to each other than to their own model's neurons.
- **512 neurons can represent tens of thousands of features**, and features combine into finite-state-automaton-like systems (e.g. producing valid HTML).

## Takeaways / questions
- The core recipe (overcomplete dictionary + L1 + lots of activations + dead-feature resampling) is simple enough to replicate on a laptop-scale model — a good first SAE project.
- A one-layer model with a 512-neuron MLP is an extreme toy; the open question it left — does this scale? — was answered by *Scaling Monosemanticity*.
- SAE features are a property of the dictionary as much as the model (they split with size), which complicates any claim that there is one “true” feature set.

notes.title: Training and evaluating a sparse autoencoder (codebase notes)
notes.tldr: My implementation notes for an SAE pipeline. Hook a frozen LM's layer to collect activations, train the SAE on reconstruction, then track L0, MSE and explained variance, with a side note on Kaiming init.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, page "Codebase" (Paper notes › SAE), 9 Feb 2026.*

- SAE trained on 10k Pile text data.
- **Evaluate sparsity & effectiveness**
  - Analyze **L0** (number of features that activate per token position); small = sparse.
  - Use SAE activations as "explanations" to see how closely they follow [the model] *(uncertain reading)*.
- **Evaluate visually** → feature dashboards.
  - Collect activations.
  - Aggregate feature-specific stats.
- Pipeline
  1. Train the LM on a dataset → freeze.
     - ↳ pass new data through, register a hook on the target layer → get activations.
  2. Batch the activations to train the SAE on reconstruction.
- Side note: **Kaiming initialization**
  - $w \sim \mathcal{N}\!\left(0, \sqrt{2/n}\right)$, with $n$ = number of inputs.
  - $Y = wx + b$, so $Y_i = \sum_j w_{ij} x_j + b_i$.
  - $\mathrm{Var}(Y_i) = n \cdot \mathrm{Var}(w_{ij} x_j)$, applied for each layer.
- **Track:** MSE, explained variance, L0 (non-zero), dead / alive features *(uncertain reading)*.
  - Explained variance $= 1 - \dfrac{\mathrm{Var}(x - \hat x)}{\mathrm{Var}(x)}$ → what fraction of the activation is captured by the SAE.

## Summary
These are concept notes, not a paper: the practical loop for training a sparse autoencoder on LM activations, in the style of [Towards Monosemanticity](#/note/towards-monosemanticity). Freeze the LM, attach a forward hook at the target layer, stream activations into an SAE, then judge it on sparsity (L0) and faithfulness (MSE, explained variance), plus qualitative feature dashboards. Kaiming initialization ($\mathrm{std}=\sqrt{2/n}$) keeps activation variance roughly constant across ReLU layers.

notes.title: AdaEvolve: Adaptive LLM Driven Zeroth-Order Optimization
notes.tldr: Replaces the static schedules of LLM-driven evolutionary search with hierarchical adaptation (per-population exploration, bandit budget routing across populations, and meta-guidance when progress stalls).
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*From the "Alpha evolve" OneNote page (Paper notes › Evolution coding LLM), 5 Feb 2026. This paper got only one line there.*

- AdaEvolve: **design better evolution strategies**.

## Summary
AdaEvolve treats LLM-driven evolution (AlphaEvolve/OpenEvolve style) as a hierarchical adaptive optimization problem. One "accumulated improvement signal" drives decisions at three levels. Local adaptation sets exploration intensity within a population. Global adaptation routes the compute budget across populations with a bandit scheduler. Meta-guidance has the LLM generate new solution tactics when progress stalls.

## Problem
Existing evolutionary coding systems run on fixed schedules. They keep spending compute on stagnating populations and under-explore promising ones.

## Method
- **Reused:** the LLM-as-mutation-operator evolutionary loop and island-style populations.
- **New:** the improvement-signal-driven controller at the three levels above.

![Figure 1 from the paper: AdaEvolve overview, from static search policies to hierarchical adaptivity](assets/adaevolve/fig1.png)

## Results
The abstract reports that AdaEvolve consistently beats open-source baselines on 185 open-ended optimization problems (combinatorial, systems optimization, algorithm design). It gives no single headline number.

notes.title: AlphaEvolve: A coding agent for scientific and algorithmic discovery
notes.tldr: An evolutionary coding agent where LLMs propose code diffs to marked blocks of a program, automated evaluators score them, and a MAP-Elites/island program database balances exploration and exploitation.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, page "Alpha evolve" (Paper notes › Evolution coding LLM), 5 Feb 2026.*

- Provide the evolution **start/end block** and an **evaluate function**.
  - Send to the LLM an ensemble of prompts *(reading uncertain: "an ensembled prompt")*.
  - LLM output = mutation.
- Continue to generate solutions with an evaluation score.
  - Balance exploration & exploitation (**MAP-Elites** algorithm).
  - Use a database of candidates (algorithm 存储 a set of user-provided [illegible]).
- **Island**: independent population of candidate solutions.
  - Own competition & evolution.
  - Migrate the top 10% solutions to a nearby island at an interval.
- **Evolve** loop:
  1. Pick a random solution on the island (not the best → exploration); pick $k$ best + $N$ random solutions for inspiration.
     - ↳ exploit the current solution.
  2. Let the LLM generate a mutation given the prompt.
  3. Evaluate & score.
  4. Kill solutions that are too identical.
- GEPA → refine/combine solutions using the Pareto curve (see [GEPA](#/note/gepa)).
- AdaEvolve: design better evolution strategies (see [AdaEvolve](#/note/adaevolve)).
- Side note on the same page: image as a function $\mathbb{R}^2 \to \mathbb{R}^3$, i.e. represent it as $F(u,v)$; a steeper change of brightness/colour → sharpness *(reading of the last word uncertain)*.

Follow-up page "Gila" (same section, 5 Feb 2026, 16:03):
- Problem of AlphaEvolve = little feedback from logs.

## Summary
AlphaEvolve is Google DeepMind's evolutionary coding agent. The user supplies an initial program with the regions to evolve marked, plus evaluation code. An LLM ensemble proposes code changes, automated evaluators score the resulting programs, and a program database keeps the population and decides which programs to show the LLM next. The paper applies it to Google infrastructure: data-center scheduling, simplifying a hardware-accelerator circuit, and speeding up training of the LLM behind AlphaEvolve itself. It also applies it to open maths and CS problems.

## Problem
Earlier LLM-guided search (FunSearch) evolved single short functions. AlphaEvolve aims to evolve whole codebases and to work on any problem that has a machine-checkable evaluator.

## Method
- **Reused:** evolutionary search with LLMs as mutation operators (FunSearch lineage). The database combines MAP-Elites with island models.
- **New / scaled up:** the LLM rewrites full files through diffs, uses an ensemble of models (a fast model for breadth, a stronger one for depth), has rich prompt sampling (past programs, scores, meta-prompts), and can score programs on several evaluation metrics at once.

![Figure 2 from the paper: expanded view of the AlphaEvolve discovery loop (prompt sampler, LLM ensemble, evaluators, program database)](assets/alphaevolve/fig1.png)

## Results
- Found a procedure to multiply two $4\times4$ complex-valued matrices with 48 scalar multiplications. Per the abstract, this is the first improvement over Strassen's algorithm in this setting in 56 years.
- Infrastructure wins at Google: a better data-center scheduling heuristic, a simplification of an accelerator circuit design, and faster training kernels for its own underlying LLM.

## Takeaways / questions
- My notes pick out the exploration machinery: random parent selection, islands with migration, and pruning near-duplicates.
- Open question from my follow-up page: the evaluator returns little signal (a score and some logs). GEPA's reflective feedback and AdaEvolve's adaptive scheduling are both answers to that.

notes.title: GEPA: Reflective Prompt Evolution Can Outperform Reinforcement Learning
notes.tldr: A prompt optimizer that reflects on full execution traces in natural language to mutate prompts, and keeps a Pareto frontier of candidates to merge complementary lessons, beating GRPO with far fewer rollouts.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*From the "Alpha evolve" OneNote page (Paper notes › Evolution coding LLM), 5 Feb 2026. This paper got only one line there.*

- GEPA → refine/combine solutions using the **Pareto curve**.

## Summary
GEPA (Genetic-Pareto) optimizes the prompts of a compound LLM system. It samples trajectories (reasoning, tool calls, tool outputs) and has an LLM reflect on them in natural language to diagnose failures and propose prompt updates. It keeps a Pareto frontier of candidates, so prompts that win on different instances survive and can be merged.

## Problem
RL methods such as GRPO learn from sparse scalar rewards and need thousands of rollouts. Language traces carry much richer feedback, and that is the signal GEPA tries to use.

## Method
- **Reflective prompt mutation:** an LLM reads traces plus evaluator feedback and rewrites a module's prompt.
- **Pareto-based candidate selection:** candidates are sampled from the per-instance Pareto front instead of taking only the single best, which preserves diversity.
- **System-aware merge:** combines modules from different lineages.

![Figure 3 from the paper: GEPA's optimization loop](assets/gepa/fig1.png)

## Results
From the abstract: across six tasks GEPA beats GRPO by 6% on average and by up to 20%, while using up to 35× fewer rollouts. It beats MIPROv2 by over 10%, for example +12% accuracy on AIME-2025. It also shows promise as an inference-time search strategy for code optimization.

## Takeaways / questions
- Relevant to the AlphaEvolve feedback problem I noted ("little feedback from logs"). GEPA makes the logs themselves the learning signal.

notes.title: LLMs for simulating particle collision experiments (Astron 84 write-up)
notes.tldr: Short essay: collider experiments are expensive, so simulation matters; treating hits/particles as tokens and events as sentences lets language models act as fast simulators and particle-physics foundation models.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
### Google Doc *Astron 84 Final Writeup* (Dec 1 2025)

#### Abstract

This is a short writeup on one problem I am interested in – simulation of particle collision experiments with the help of large language models, which I believe is one of the most direct applications AI have in physics research.
This writeup briefly goes over the current status quo of these experiments, their importance, the need of simulation, and finally the application of large language models in quantum physics simulations and some exciting results.

#### Background

Currently, our best guess on what makes up the whole world comes down to the standard model – families of quarks, leptons, and bosons. These particles, through complex interactions and processes with each other, seem to explain many of the fundamental physical forces and processes. However, this model is still obviously unfinished since it didn’t explain many important phenomenons like gravity (the hypothesized graviton), dark matter, and dark energy.
Human’s best bet in improving the standard model is running huge particle collision experiments, using powerful accelerators, we can speed up particles to give them immense energy. This means that the collisions simulated the universe in their much earlier, more energetic state, and can use that to answer fundamental questions. For example, the electroweak force (electro magnetic and weak force) are united in the early ages of the universe, and thus by releasing enough energy to return to that state, researchers can observe electroweak interactions that will be impossible in the current days, and learn about their carrier particles (W and Z bosons).

#### Need of Simulation

Bigger the energy, more likely it can reveal interesting things. The electroweak interaction was revealed with about 100 Gev (electrovolts), if we raise the scale to 7 Tev (done by the LHC), then it can reveal information about the higgs boson – the particle that gives many interactions/substances mass.
However, running these energetic experiments is obviously expensive. The LHC is the single most expensive science project ever built, costing over 7 billion dollars. Moreover, it is nearly impossible to achieve the energy scale required to uncover some interesting questions. For example, to ‘backup’ the universe enough to observe the possible gravitons, we need to reach the plank scale, which is thousands of times more than the current standards.
All of these call for the need of simulations – ways we can simulate these complex experiments so it is feasible to start endeavors into finding dark matter or gravitons. There are already many efforts in these fields through the last decade, but the recent development of large language models shined new light on the simulation of particle physics experiments.

#### Large Language Models and Sequences

Most colliders use strips and pixel detectors (chips) to catch the particle jets flying out of a collision, this form complex hit clouds which can be reconstructed into tracks. The tracks look something like the image below.

After some processing, much useful information can be extracted from this, ranging from a list of particles or a list of hits. These things follow sequence structure and make up an ‘event’ for a physical process.
Many traditional statistical methods are used for this problem, but the rise of large language models brought unprecedented excitement to the field. All large language models are sequence to sequence, taking in a list of tokens (words) and doing the next token prediction for generation. If we think about each particle or each hit as a word, each jet/event as a sentence, and each physical process as a language, we seem to be able to directly apply the power of a large language model on this task. This means fast simulation that saves a lot of cost and very efficient downstream processing like classification of events.

#### Current Applications

There are already many exciting applications of machine learning models in particle physics (not necessarily large language models). With custom neural network layers (‘heads') these models can be used to extract track given hit points (for example, Tracking with Machine Learning in ATLAS: Graph Neural Networks for Track Reconstruction, arXiv:2012.08515) or the other way around, convert track parameters into Geant 4 hit clouds (for example, GEANT4-Inspired Fast Simulation Using Generative Adversarial Networks, arXiv:1705.02355, and Calorimeter Shower Simulation with Conditional Generative Models, arXiv:2105.00047) (given a few parameters, generate many ‘hit tokens’).
What large language models shine the most is their ability to be a ‘foundation model. These are particle physics models trained on multiple datasets and learning methods. The task is more challenging because the model needs to also distinguish between different classes of input signals it is trained on (kind of similar to different languages). They kind of learn the whole idea of ‘particle physics’ as a whole, so we will no longer need to train custom models for separate experiments. Examples include OmniJet-α, arXiv:2403.05618, Particle Twins, arXiv:2402.10239, JetCLR: Unsupervised Contrastive Learning for Jets, arXiv:2103.09429, and the HEPTrinity foundation model, arXiv:2407.07995. Built under a Transformer framework, these models used techniques such as latent codes and contrastive learning to understand the foundation framework of these experiments, and thus can be able to generalize to many downstream tasks.

## Summary
Haoming's Dec 2025 course write-up on why LLM-style sequence models fit particle physics: the Standard Model's gaps, why higher-energy collisions need simulation, the 'particles as words, events as sentences, processes as languages' framing, existing ML work (GNN tracking, GAN calorimeter simulation) and the promise of foundation models. Preserved in full (figures omitted).

notes.title: Interpretable Machine Learning in Physics: A Review
notes.tldr: A broad review of interpretable ML in physics: a taxonomy of kinds of interpretation, philosophical perspectives, standard methods (attribution, latent representations, symbolic regression), and applications from quantum matter to HEP and cosmology.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Discussed at the Nov 21, 2025 LLM-for-HEP meeting (Xiangyang Ju, Arihant Kaul, me).

## Summary
A long survey (Perimeter Institute, MIT/IAIFI and others) arguing that interpretability should be a core research goal when ML is used for science, because the point of science is human understanding, not just accurate prediction. As AI starts to make discoveries humans could not make alone, interpretation is the bridge that turns machine-found patterns into concepts humans can verify and build on. The review organizes the field conceptually, then walks through methods and physics subfields with many short paper summaries.

![Figure 2 from the paper: interpretation bridges AI-discoverable knowledge and human-verifiable understanding, unlocking concepts beyond what humans alone can discover](assets/interpretable-ml-physics-review/fig1.png)

## Problem
"Interpretable" and "explainable" ML mean different things to different people, and some critics argue the concepts are too vague to be useful. Physicists using ML need a shared vocabulary for which kind of interpretation they want and which methods deliver it.

## Takeaways / questions
- Useful taxonomy for our LLM-for-HEP discussions: most HEP interpretability work is post-hoc, local feature attribution; the more ambitious goal is global, discovering interpretations (symbolic formulas, new observables).
- Natural next question for our tokenizer/foundation-model line: what do learned particle tokens or codebook entries correspond to physically, and can they be mapped to known observables the way Faucett et al. map classifiers to energy flow polynomials?

## Contents
**Notions of interpretation (Sec. II).** The authors categorize interpretations along several axes: mechanistic vs functional (how internal operations compute vs what input–output function is learned), local vs global, verifying a hypothesized concept vs discovering a new one, low- vs high-level features, intrinsic (e.g. linear regression, PCA) vs post-hoc, and — importantly — interpreting the algorithm vs actually gaining scientific understanding of the phenomenon.

**Philosophy (Sec. III)** on what understanding and explanation mean in science, and **ML algorithms (Sec. IV)** compared on the interpretability–performance trade-off.

**Existing methods (Sec. V).** Feature importance (permutation importance, layer-wise relevance propagation, SHAP, attention weights), latent-representation approaches (InfoGAN, β-VAE disentanglement), Hessian-based analysis, and more.

**Symbolic regression (Sec. VI)** — e.g. PySR's genetic programming and neural approaches — as a route to explicit formulas.

**Applications by field (Secs. VII–XIV).** Quantum systems, classical condensed matter, high energy physics, astrophysics and cosmology, complex systems (including attention as relational strength), general physics (extracting symbolic expressions, autoencoders that discover physical parameters, RL, RBMs), conserved quantities and symmetry invariants, and phase diagrams.

**HEP section highlights.** Theory: networks reduced in capacity until only a few correlations remain, from which order parameters (e.g. Ising magnetization, SU(2) Polyakov loop) are extracted; symbolic regression rediscovering the Gell-Mann–Okubo mass formula. Experiment: mapping black-box jet classifiers onto human-readable observables (Faucett, Thaler & Whiteson — [2010.11998](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11998)), interpretable anomaly detectors, Shapley values and LRP for jet taggers and ML particle-flow, and VAE latent spaces of W jets with meaningful directions.

notes.title: Mapping Machine-Learned Physics into a Human-Readable Space
notes.tldr: Translates a black-box jet classifier (a CNN on jet images) into a few interpretable energy flow polynomials by iteratively picking observables that best match the network's pairwise decision ordering (ADO) on the inputs the current observables misorder.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Discussed at the Nov 21, 2025 LLM-for-HEP meeting (Phys. Rev. D 103, 036020).

## Summary
Neural networks trained on low-level detector data often beat physicists' hand-designed observables, but nobody knows what they learned. Faucett, Thaler and Whiteson propose a way to *read off* a black-box classifier in physics terms: search a huge, physically meaningful space of candidate observables for the small set whose combination makes the same decisions as the network. The key tool is a metric of decision similarity (average decision ordering, ADO) and an iterative "black-box guided" search that focuses on the examples where the current observables still disagree with the network. On boosted W-boson vs QCD jet tagging, it finds a seventh observable that closes the gap between six classic substructure variables and a CNN, and that observable has an interesting, previously overlooked physical interpretation.

## Problem
How do we interpret what a high-performing network learned, validate that it relies on real physics (not simulation artifacts), and possibly learn new physics from it? Comparing performance with/without features or projecting decision surfaces gives limited insight; we want an explicit, compact, human-readable equivalent of the network.

## Related work
- Baldi et al. (2016), "Jet Substructure Classification in High-Energy Physics with Deep Neural Networks" — [1603.09349](https://arxiv.org/abs/1603.09349): the benchmark where a jet-image network beat six high-level observables, whose dataset and observables are reused.
- Energy flow polynomials (Komiske, Metodiev, Thaler) — [1712.07124](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.07124): the (over)complete basis of IRC-safe observables searched over.
- Kendall's rank correlation: ADO is closely related.

## Method
**Decision ordering.** A classifier's AUC is the probability that a random signal/background pair $(x,x')$ is ordered correctly. For two classifiers $f,g$, the decision ordering $\text{DO}[f,g](x,x')$ is 1 if they order the pair the same way and 0 otherwise; averaging over signal/background pairs gives
$$\text{ADO}[f,g]=\int dx\,dx'\,p_{\text{sig}}(x)\,p_{\text{bkg}}(x')\,\text{DO}[f,g](x,x').$$
ADO = 1 means identical decision surfaces (monotonically related outputs), regardless of whether the decisions are correct.

**Candidate observables.** Energy flow polynomials: graph-indexed sums over particles of momentum fractions $z_a^{(\kappa)}=(p_{T,a}/\sum_b p_{T,b})^\kappa$ and angular distances $\theta_{ab}^{(\beta)}=(\Delta\eta_{ab}^2+\Delta\phi_{ab}^2)^{\beta/2}$. $\kappa=1$ gives IRC-safe observables; the authors add IRC-unsafe variants ($\kappa\ne1$) and different angular exponents $\beta$.

**Black-box guided search (new).** Start from a set of high-level observables combined by a small network (the "HLN"). Find the signal/background pairs that the HLN orders differently from the black-box network; among all candidates, pick the observable with the highest ADO to the black box *on that subset*; add it to the HLN, retrain, repeat.

![Figure 1 from the paper: the black-box guided search — pairs ordered differently by the black-box network and the high-level-observable network define a subset, and the candidate observable with highest ADO on it is added each iteration](assets/mapping-ml-physics-human-readable/fig1.png)

## Data
Simulated boosted $W^+W^-$ (2-prong signal) vs QCD dijet (1-prong background) jets, generated with MadGraph/Pythia and Delphes, anti-$k_t$ $R=1.2$; $5\times10^6$ events split equally between signal and background. The black box is a CNN on calorimeter jet images.

## Results
- Baseline (Table 1): six classic observables (jet mass, $C_2$, $D_2$, $\tau_2$ variants) combined reach AUC 0.9504 vs CNN 0.9531; all 488 EFPs together reach 0.9535.
- One black-box guided step finds an IRC-unsafe EFP with $\kappa=2,\beta=\tfrac12$ (AUC only 0.8031 alone); adding it as a seventh observable gives AUC 0.9528, essentially closing the gap with the CNN — though ADO with the CNN is 0.971, so the two still disagree on ~3% of pairs.
- Many top-ranked candidates share $\kappa=2$ and $\beta=\tfrac12$, pointing to IRC-unsafe, small-angle information the CNN exploits; constituent multiplicity also ranks highly. The best IRC-safe ($\kappa=1$) observable ranks 5531st.
- Starting from only jet mass and $p_T$, the guided search beats a label-guided search and matches brute-force search at much lower cost.

## Takeaways / questions
- A concrete recipe for "interpretation as translation into known physics", the theme of the Nov 2025 group discussion alongside the [interpretable ML in physics review](https://arxiv.org/abs/2503.23616).
- ADO compares *decisions*, not accuracy, which makes it a nice general tool for checking whether two models learned the same function — could apply to comparing tokenizer-based and continuous-input jet models.
- Limitation: the result is only as good as the candidate space; information outside EFPs (the residual 3% disagreement) stays unexplained.

notes.title: Scaling models on accelerators: rooflines, arithmetic intensity and TPUs (study notes)
notes.tldr: Study notes: step time is bounded by max(T_math, T_comms); arithmetic intensity (FLOPs/byte) decides compute- vs bandwidth-bound; matmul intensity; TPU anatomy (MXU, VPU, VMEM, HBM) and ICI/PCIe/DCN networking.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, "ML Infra" notebook: Basics › "Scaling" (28 Sep 2025), TPUs › "TPUs intro" (28 Sep 2025) and "Sharding" (1 Oct 2025, one line).*

### ML Infra / Basics / Scaling — Sunday, September 28, 2025 20:35
```text
TLDR: more chips (parallelism) = faster computation = more communication burden
  -> can't achieve a proportional linear increase in throughput (strong scaling)
Model speed = a bunch of floating point operations (FLOPs) -> mostly matrix multiplications
  T_math = computation FLOPs / accelerator FLOPs/s -> directly correlated to chip ability
Communication
  -> within chip: transfer data under HBM bandwidth   } T_comms = communication bytes / network bandwidth
  -> in between chips: transfer in between chips      }
Total speed: -> lower-bounded by max(T_math, T_comms); upper-bounded by sum of the two
Arithmetic intensity: FLOPs / bytes
  ↑ high intensity = compute bound; ↓ low intensity = communication bound
  [roofline sketch: FLOPs/s vs arithmetic intensity; at the ridge, fully utilize all FLOPs/s]
[B, D] (matmul) [D, F] = [B, F]
  Memory (highlighted): 2BD + 2DF + 2BF  ↳ precision (bf16)
  each operation = D multiply + (D-1) add = 2D for each vector multiply
  Computation (highlighted): B·F such vectors -> 2BDF
  intensity = 2BDF / (2BD + 2DF + 2BF)
```

### ML Infra / TPUs / TPUs intro — Sunday, September 28, 2025 21:33
```text
[Diagram] Scalar -> handles instructions [unsure] -> VPU (performs elementwise operations) -> matmul (MXU: systolic [array] that does matrix multiplications)
          VPU <-> VMEM <- higher bandwidth than HBM interconnect;  HBM (stores weights, activations, input data, etc.)
Bandwidth (memory): how fast to move data in/out (read/write)
Compute: ability to perform math operations (FLOPs) (systolic arrays)
Memory: how much can store (DRAM chips)
TPU networking (highlighted) (how they are connected)
  -> TPUs connected in ICI network (~2D torus)
     chip matrices interconnected by links -> reduces maximum distance [between chips] [unsure]
  Limitations (bandwidth):
    HBM: internal connection
    ICI: inter-chip (closest-neighbour communication)
    PCIe bandwidth: BW between CPU & TPU (load data)
    DCN: BW between multiple [pods/slices] [unsure]
```

### ML Infra / TPUs / Sharding — Wednesday, October 1, 2025 17:01
```text
Sharding = splitting data to fit in multiple [chips]
```

## Summary
These are concept notes that follow the "How to Scale Your Model" style of roofline analysis. A step takes at least $\max(T_\text{math}, T_\text{comms})$ and at most their sum, where $T_\text{math} = \text{FLOPs}/\text{FLOPs/s}$ and $T_\text{comms} = \text{bytes}/\text{bandwidth}$. Arithmetic intensity (FLOPs per byte moved) compared with the hardware's ratio decides whether a kernel is compute-bound or bandwidth-bound. For a bf16 matmul $[B,D]\times[D,F]$, the cost is $2BDF$ FLOPs over $2BD + 2DF + 2BF$ bytes. A TPU chip has a scalar unit, a vector unit (VPU), systolic matrix units (MXU), fast on-chip VMEM and HBM. Chips connect over the ICI (a 2D/3D torus with nearest-neighbour links), hosts over PCIe, and pods over the slower DCN. Sharding splits arrays across chips so they fit, at the cost of communication.
