notes.title: Native Sparse Attention: Hardware-Aligned and Natively Trainable Sparse Attention
notes.tldr: DeepSeek's NSA replaces full attention with three gated branches — compressed block tokens, top-k selected blocks, and a sliding window — trained end to end with GQA-aware Triton kernels; it matches or beats full attention while running up to 9× faster forward at 64k.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Studied for the ML@B NSA kernel blog project (terminology notes for new members, Sep 2025).

## Summary
NSA (Native Sparse Attention), from DeepSeek-AI and Peking University, is a sparse attention mechanism designed to be both *trainable from scratch* and *actually fast on GPUs*. For each query, instead of attending to every previous token, it combines three cheaper views of the context: a coarse summary made of compressed blocks, a handful of full-resolution blocks chosen as most relevant, and a local sliding window. A learned gate mixes the three. Because the block structure matches how GPUs like to load memory, and because the kernels share selected blocks across a GQA group of heads, the theoretical savings turn into real speedups in training, prefill and decoding. A 27B-parameter MoE model pretrained with NSA matches or exceeds its full-attention twin.

## Problem
Attention cost grows quadratically with context and dominates latency at 64k tokens. Many sparse-attention methods (H2O, Quest, InfLLM, etc.) are applied only at inference, so the model never learned to work sparsely, and they often give smaller real speedups than claimed: they may speed up only prefill or only decoding, ignore GQA/MQA (each head picks different KV entries, so memory traffic is not reduced), or use non-differentiable selection that cannot be trained.

## Related work
- FlashAttention / FlashAttention-2 (Dao et al.): blockwise, SRAM-tiled exact attention; NSA's kernel design follows its principles and uses it as the speed baseline.
- Grouped-Query Attention (Ainslie et al., 2023): shared KV heads that NSA's kernel exploits.
- Quest (Tang et al., 2024), H2O (Zhang et al., 2023), InfLLM (Xiao et al., 2024): inference-time sparse/KV-selection baselines.
- DeepSeek-R1: used for distillation in the reasoning evaluation.

## Method
![Figure 2 from the paper: NSA architecture — each query attends through three parallel branches (compressed attention for coarse patterns, selected attention for important blocks, sliding attention for local context), combined by learned gates](assets/native-sparse-attention/fig1.png)

For query $q_t$, NSA builds remapped keys/values $\tilde K_t^c,\tilde V_t^c$ for three strategies $c\in\{\text{cmp},\text{slc},\text{win}\}$ and outputs
$$o_t=\sum_{c}g_t^c\cdot\text{Attn}(q_t,\tilde K_t^c,\tilde V_t^c),$$
with gates $g_t^c\in[0,1]$ from an MLP + sigmoid on the input. The total number of remapped keys stays far below $t$.

**1. Token compression (coarse, global).** Slide a window of length $l$ with stride $d$ over past keys; a learnable MLP $\varphi$ (with intra-block position encoding) squashes each block into one compressed key (same for values). Attention over these gives a cheap global view. ($l=32$, $d=16$.)

**2. Token selection (fine, important).** Split the past into selection blocks of size $l'=64$. The attention scores of $q_t$ over the *compressed* keys are reused as block importance scores (no extra cost), aggregated across the heads of a GQA group so all heads share one selection. Keep the top $n=16$ blocks (always including the initial block and 2 local blocks) and attend to their original tokens at full resolution.

**3. Sliding window (local).** Attend to the most recent $w=512$ tokens. Keeping local patterns in a separate branch stops them from dominating the other two branches' learning.

**Kernels (hardware-aligned, new).** In Triton: for each query position, load *all query heads of a GQA group* together (they share the same selected blocks), fetch each selected KV block contiguously into SRAM once, and put the query loop on the grid so work is balanced across streaming multiprocessors. Compression and window branches reuse FlashAttention-2-style kernels. (This "load whole GQA group, stream shared blocks" pattern is what the ML@B kernel blog dissects.)

## Data
Pretraining on 270B tokens of 8k-length text (the introduction says 260B), then continued training and SFT on 32k-length text with YaRN; for the reasoning test, SFT on 10B tokens of 32k-length math traces distilled from DeepSeek-R1.

## Training
Both the NSA model and a full-attention baseline are 27B-parameter MoE transformers (3B active; 30 layers, hidden size 2560, GQA with 4 groups and 64 heads) trained to convergence with the same recipe. All three branches and the gates are differentiable, so the model learns *which* blocks to select end to end through the normal next-token cross-entropy loss; NSA's pretraining loss ends lower than full attention's.

## Results
- General benchmarks (Table 1): average 0.456 vs 0.443 for full attention, better on 7 of 9 (e.g. GSM8K 0.520 vs 0.486, DROP 0.545 vs 0.503).
- LongBench average 0.469 vs 0.437 for full attention, beating inference-time sparse baselines; perfect needle-in-a-haystack retrieval at all positions with 64k context.
- AIME 24 after R1-distillation: 0.121 vs 0.046 (8k generation limit) and 0.146 vs 0.092 (16k).
- Speed vs Triton FlashAttention-2 on A100 at 64k: up to 9.0× forward and 6.0× backward; decoding memory traffic implies up to 11.6× expected speedup at 64k (5632 vs 65536 tokens loaded).

## Takeaways / questions
- Key idea for kernel work: sparsity only pays if it matches hardware granularity — contiguous blocks, shared across GQA heads, with balanced loops.
- Contrasts with post-hoc methods like [Multipole Attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/2506.13059): NSA must be trained in, but then the model learns to be sparse rather than approximating dense attention.
- The kernel targets GQA/MQA; small selection tiles can degrade matrix multiplies toward matrix-vector work (a question raised in the ML@B team's shared notes), so block sizes are a real design constraint.

notes.title: A postmortem of three recent issues
notes.tldr: Anthropic explains three overlapping infrastructure bugs (Aug–Sep 2025) that degraded Claude's outputs: a context-window routing error, a TPU misconfiguration corrupting token generation, and an XLA:TPU approximate top-k miscompilation, plus why detection was slow.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Saved in my *Interesting reads* doc.

## Summary
An Anthropic engineering postmortem (September 2025) explaining why some users saw degraded Claude responses between early August and early September 2025. The cause was not deliberate quality reduction — the post states plainly that Anthropic never reduces model quality due to demand, time of day or server load — but three separate infrastructure bugs that overlapped in time and showed different symptoms on different platforms. It is a rare, detailed look at how serving a frontier model across several hardware platforms (AWS Trainium, NVIDIA GPUs, Google TPUs) can silently change model outputs.

## Problem
Claude is served through Anthropic's API, Amazon Bedrock and Google Cloud Vertex AI on three hardware platforms, each with its own optimizations but held to strict equivalence standards. Any infrastructure change must preserve outputs across all of them. In August 2025, user reports of degraded quality rose, but they were hard to distinguish from normal feedback noise, and the overlapping bugs produced confusing, contradictory reports.

## Results
**1. Context window routing error.** From August 5, some Sonnet 4 requests were misrouted to servers configured for the upcoming 1M-token context window (initially 0.8% of requests). A routine load-balancing change on August 29 increased this; at the worst hour on August 31, 16% of Sonnet 4 requests were affected. About 30% of Claude Code users who made requests in this period had at least one message misrouted. Routing was "sticky", so affected users tended to keep hitting the wrong servers. Fixed starting September 4, fully rolled out by September 16 (first-party, Vertex) and September 18 (Bedrock).

**2. Output corruption.** On August 25 a misconfiguration on the Claude API TPU servers, caused by a runtime performance optimization, occasionally gave high probability to tokens that should be rare — e.g. Thai or Chinese characters in English answers, or obvious syntax errors in code. It affected Opus 4.1 and Opus 4 (Aug 25–28) and Sonnet 4 (Aug 25–Sep 2). Rolled back September 2; detection tests for unexpected character outputs were added to deployment.

**3. Approximate top-k XLA:TPU miscompilation.** Also deployed August 25: a change to token selection triggered a latent bug in the XLA:TPU compiler, confirmed for Claude Haiku 3.5 and possibly affecting some Sonnet 4 and Opus 3 requests. The deep dive is the most technical part:
- Sampling uses top-p (keep tokens up to cumulative probability ~0.99 or 0.999). On TPUs the model is sharded across many chips, so sorting probabilities is a distributed operation.
- In December 2024 they had found that the TPU implementation occasionally dropped the most probable token at temperature 0, and deployed a workaround.
- The root cause was mixed precision: logits computed in bf16, but XLA may upcast some operations to fp32 (the `xla_allow_excess_precision` flag, on by default), so different operations disagreed about which token was most probable.
- An August 26 rewrite of the sampling code fixed the precision issues and removed the December workaround — which unmasked a deeper bug in the **approximate top-k** operation, which sometimes returned completely wrong results for certain batch sizes and model configurations. Its behavior changed with unrelated surrounding operations and whether debugging tools were enabled.
- Fix: switch to **exact top-k** (no longer prohibitively slow) and standardize more operations on fp32, accepting a minor efficiency cost; they also worked with the XLA:TPU team on the compiler bug.

**Why detection was slow.** Benchmarks, safety evals and canary deployments did not catch it, partly because Claude often recovers well from isolated mistakes. Privacy controls limit engineers' access to user interactions not submitted as feedback. Each bug had different symptoms on different platforms, and evaluations were too noisy to tie reports to specific changes (e.g. the August 29 load-balancing change).

**What changes.** More sensitive evaluations that separate working from broken implementations, quality evals run continuously on real production systems, and better tooling to debug community feedback without sacrificing privacy; users are encouraged to report via `/bug` in Claude Code or thumbs-down.

## Takeaways / questions
- Inference infrastructure is part of the model: routing, compiler flags and sampling kernels can change outputs even when weights are identical.
- Approximate kernels (approximate top-k) are a correctness risk precisely where they matter — the highest-probability token — and one workaround can mask a deeper bug for months.
- Standard benchmarks are too coarse to catch intermittent, platform-specific degradation; continuous production evals and user reports were what isolated the problems. Relevant to my own agent work: monitor behavior in production, not just offline evals.

notes.title: Automatically Jailbreaking Frontier Language Models with Investigator Agents
notes.tldr: Transluce trains a Llama-3.1-8B “investigator” with RL (GRPO) to write plain-English jailbreaks for 48 CBRN/drug/explosive tasks; it reaches 92% pass@1 on Claude Sonnet 4, 90% on Gemini 2.5 Pro and 78% on GPT-5-main, and attacks transfer across labs.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Saved in my *Interesting reads* doc.

## Summary
A research blog post from Transluce (published September 3, 2025), not a paper. It tests whether a *small* open model, trained with reinforcement learning to elicit a behaviour, can red-team much larger frontier models. The answer is mostly yes: an 8B investigator with no hand-written jailbreak strategies learns natural-language attacks (typically elaborate academic-writing pretexts) that get detailed hazardous instructions out of most frontier models. The two most resistant targets were the ones with extra monitoring layers outside the model.

## Method
- **Tasks and judges.** 48 hand-curated tasks covering illicit drugs, explosives, chemical, biological, radiological and nuclear hazards — content that OpenAI's Model Spec and Claude's constitution forbid. Two GPT-4.1-mini judges: a *prompt judge* rejects attacks that ask for fiction/sarcasm or that smuggle in the answer; a *response judge* gives partial credit over six concrete “actionability” criteria. They dropped HarmBench/StrongREJECT graders because those were too easy to reward-hack (e.g. by giving historical background instead of instructions).
- **Investigator.** Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct, prompted only with the target behaviour, generates a prompt for the target model; trained with GRPO (verl), 128 samples per task instance, KL coefficient 0.01 to keep prompts natural.
- **Rewards.** *Black-box*: sample the target's response and score it — works through any API but is sparse early on. *PRBO (propensity bound)*: their earlier dense estimator of a lower bound on the probability of the behaviour, built from a proposal distribution; on the open-weight GPT-oss-20b they make the proposal by prefilling affirmative “thinking” tokens and use log-prob differences. This needs log-probs and prefilling, so only works on open models.
- **Main run.** PRBO on GPT-oss-20b (weight 1.0) plus black-box rewards on GPT-4.1, GPT-5-main, GPT-5-thinking and Claude Sonnet 4 (0.2 each). Each run took under 18 hours on two 8×H100 nodes; API costs were roughly $1–2k per closed model and up to $5–10k for flagship models.

## Results
- Main run, pass@1 (pass@32): Claude Sonnet 4 92% (100%), Gemini 2.5 Pro 90% (100%), GPT-5-main 78% (98%), Grok 4 98% (100%), DeepSeek-R1 97%, GPT-4.1 97%, GPT-5-thinking 28% (50%), Claude Opus 4.1 65% (75%, after 150 extra fine-tuning steps on Sonnet 4/Opus 4.1). Gemini, Grok, DeepSeek and Opus were not in the reward.
- **Transfer:** optimising only against GPT-oss-20b already gave Gemini 2.5 Pro 89%, GPT-4.1 88%, Claude Sonnet 4 26%.
- The most robust targets, GPT-5-thinking and Claude Opus 4.1, have external safeguards (prompt/response monitors and constitutional classifiers); attacks that plainly request harmful content get caught by response monitors.
- Baseline: Best-of-N Jailbreaking on GPT-4.1 got 5% pass@1 / 63% pass@32, vs. 95% / 100% for an investigator trained with black-box access to GPT-4.1.
- Spot checks with a subject-matter expert found most responses appeared accurate, with a few wrong ones.

## Takeaways / questions
- Cheap RL red-teaming scales: a weak model with a good judge can beat strong models' safety training, which argues for defenses outside the model (monitors, classifiers) rather than refusal training alone.
- The bottleneck is the judge: robust, hack-resistant judges were hard to build for anything less clear-cut than CBRN synthesis (e.g. malicious code).
- Connects to *Jailbroken*: the learned attacks look like competing-objectives / pretext attacks (helpful academic editing vs. refusal), found automatically rather than by hand.

notes.title: DeepSeek-V3 Technical Report
notes.tldr: 671B-parameter (37B active) MoE LLM with Multi-head Latent Attention, auxiliary-loss-free load balancing via routing biases, and a multi-token-prediction objective.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, VLMs › Training LLMs › "Deepseek V3", 16 Sep 2025.*

- Modern LLM architecture: attention block = RMSNorm → **MLA** attention → (+ residual) → Norm → **MoE** FFN → (+ residual).
- **MLA attention**: $\mathrm{softmax}(QK^\top/\sqrt{d_k})V$ ⇒ compress to a latent $C^L = HW^L$, from which $K, V$ are up-projected; $Q$ is compressed too.
- **KV cache** → each current token's $Q$ attends to all previous $K$s and $V$s → at inference you'd otherwise recompute K, V of generated tokens → cache them to save time.
- **DeepSeek-MoE**: affinity $= s_{i,t} + b_i$; $s_{i,t}$ is the raw score (before softmax) and $b_i$ is a bias adjusted dynamically for selected/unselected experts.
  - Auxiliary-loss(-free) approach: *(blank)*.
- **MTP design**: normal → next-token prediction + CE with the correct token. Multi-token prediction objective → take shifted tokens and apply CE on $t+k$ tokens; normally each step makes only one next-token prediction, and MTP adds sequential predictions in depth.
  - $h^i_{k-1}$ (hidden state at depth $k-1$) and the embedding of $t_{i+k}$ → predict $t_{i+k+1}$ *(indices partly uncertain)*.

## Summary
DeepSeek-V3 is a 671B-parameter MoE language model with 37B parameters activated per token. It reuses DeepSeek-V2's **Multi-head Latent Attention**, which caches a low-rank latent instead of full K/V and so shrinks the KV cache, and **DeepSeekMoE**, which uses fine-grained routed experts plus shared experts. Two things are new. Load balancing is **auxiliary-loss-free**: a per-expert bias added to the routing score is nudged up or down depending on load, while gating weights still use the raw scores. And a sequential **multi-token prediction** objective, which can also serve speculative decoding. Training uses FP8 mixed precision on 14.8T tokens.

![Figure 2 from the paper: DeepSeek-V3 architecture (MLA + DeepSeekMoE)](assets/deepseek-v3/fig1.png)

## Takeaways / questions
- Related: [DeepSeek-V4](#/note/deepseek-v4) replaces MLA with CSA/HCA compressed attention and adds mHC.

notes.title: Training language models to follow instructions with human feedback (InstructGPT)
notes.tldr: The SFT, then reward model from human rankings, then PPO recipe (RLHF) that turns GPT-3 into an instruction follower; a 1.3B InstructGPT is preferred over 175B GPT-3.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, VLMs › Training LLMs › "Instruction tuning", 16 Sep 2025.*

- Next-token prediction ≠ answering questions / following instructions.
- Data: NLP benchmark pool, synthetic data ↳ self-improvement.
- Example: **InstructGPT** → SFT (with an instruction dataset) → reward model for RLHF → optimize against the reward model with PPO.
- **SFT** → basically fine-tuning on the right data (same training method, better curated data).
- **Reward modeling** → train a reward model from multi-candidate selection / ranking.
  - → take the SFT model and change it into a network that predicts a **scalar reward given prompt & response** (highlighted).
  - Objective over $K$ responses to a prompt with human preferences: $\log\sigma\big(r_\theta(x, y_w) - r_\theta(x, y_l)\big)$, the difference in predicted reward of two responses.
  - log-sigmoid(difference) ~ probability that A > B → maximize the log-likelihood of the human choice (cross-entropy = negative log-likelihood).
- **SFT'd GPT + reward model → PPO**: observation (prompt) → policy (GPT) → token (action) → reward model → reward.
  - Ratio $\frac{\pi_\text{new}(a\mid s)}{\pi_\text{old}(a\mid s)} = \exp(\log\pi_\text{new} - \log\pi_\text{old})$, times advantage $A_t$ ($A_t > 0$ = good token).
  - Value function: predicts the reward of the whole sequence given the tokens so far.

## Summary
InstructGPT (OpenAI) is the canonical RLHF pipeline. (1) Supervised fine-tuning of GPT-3 on labeler demonstrations. (2) A reward model trained on labeler rankings of several outputs per prompt, using the pairwise Bradley–Terry loss in my notes. (3) PPO fine-tuning of the policy against the reward model, with a per-token KL penalty to the SFT model. A "PPO-ptx" variant mixes in pre-training gradients to limit regressions on NLP benchmarks.

![Figure 2 from the paper: the three steps (SFT, reward model, PPO)](assets/instructgpt/fig1.png)

## Results
From the abstract: in human evaluations, outputs of the 1.3B InstructGPT are preferred to those of 175B GPT-3, with gains in truthfulness, reductions in toxic outputs, and minimal regressions on public NLP datasets.

## Summary
VisDiff (Berkeley/Stanford) automates "set difference captioning": given two image sets, describe in language what is more true of A than of B. A **proposer** (GPT-4 over BLIP-2 captions of sampled images from both sets) generates candidate differences. A **ranker** scores each candidate by CLIP similarity on held-out images from both sets and keeps those that separate A from B. notes.title: Mixture of Experts in Large Language Models
notes.tldr: Survey of Mixture-of-Experts in LLMs: foundations, gating/routing and sparse or hierarchical variants, expert specialization, meta-learning and transfer, applications across domains, evaluation and open challenges like load balancing and expert diversity.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Cited in my LLM4HEP talk (accessed Aug 31, 2025) for the observation that experts specialize on grammatical structures (verbs, nouns), motivating MoE for particle-class specialization.

## Summary
A 2025 review of Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) architectures in large language models: how sparse expert layers decouple total parameters from per-token compute, how routing works, which architectural variants exist, how experts specialize, and where MoE is used beyond plain language modeling. I used it as the citation for expert specialization when motivating MoE layers in my LBNL particle-physics tokenizer.

## Problem
Dense scaling makes compute and energy grow with every added parameter. MoE activates only a few experts per input, but brings its own issues (routing collapse, load imbalance, training instability, deployment cost) that the literature addresses piecemeal.

## Takeaways / questions
- The specialization claim is what I relied on: if token-level routing in LLMs aligns with syntactic categories, routing over particle tokens might align with particle classes or production processes. That remains a hypothesis I'd need to verify by inspecting router assignments in my tokenizer.
- The survey is broad but fairly shallow, and the specialization evidence is cited rather than shown, so the primary sources (Fan et al. 2024; the original MoE paper's appendix on syntax/semantics experts) are better to cite for that claim.

## Contents
- **Foundations.** Classic MoE (Jacobs/Jordan) through the [sparsely-gated MoE](https://arxiv.org/abs/1701.06538) to modern large-scale MoE LLMs; a timeline of milestones (Figure 1).
- **Core architectures and routing.** Top-k gating, hierarchical and sparse configurations, advanced variants, routing strategies, load-balancing losses.
- **Routing and specialization.** The passage I cited: sequence-level gating tends to group experts by topic or discourse, while token-level gating yields finer specialization that "frequently aligns with syntactic categories such as nouns or verbs" (citing Fan et al., 2024); probing work (Antoine et al., 2025) finds MoE layers cluster inputs by part-of-speech and morphological role without supervision.
- **Meta-learning and knowledge transfer** with MoE, and system/platform support.
- **Applications.** Recommendation and search, multimodal and multitask learning, healthcare and life sciences, computer vision, NLP and LLMs.
- **Evaluation, challenges, future directions.** Expert diversity, calibration, reliable aggregation of expert outputs, and deployment cost.

![Fig. 1 from the paper: timeline of Mixture-of-Experts model development from foundational concepts to modern large-scale implementations](assets/moe-in-llms-survey/fig1.png)

notes.title: Outrageously Large Neural Networks: The Sparsely-Gated Mixture-of-Experts Layer
notes.tldr: Introduces the sparsely-gated MoE layer: thousands of feed-forward experts with a noisy top-k gating network that activates only a few per token, giving >1000× more parameters at similar compute; up to 137B-parameter LSTM models beat SOTA on LM and MT.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Cited in my LLM4HEP talk to explain the MoE layers I added to the tokenizer: n smaller 'expert' layers, a linear router picks the top-k (e.g. top 2) experts and combines their outputs (e.g. 0.7·e1 + 0.2·e3). Why: more parameters for less time, since only a subset of experts fire (and get gradients) per pass, and experts might specialize on different classes of particles.

## Summary
This Google Brain paper made *conditional computation* practical at scale. A Mixture-of-Experts (MoE) layer holds many independent feed-forward networks ("experts"), and a small trainable gating network chooses only $k$ of them for each input token. Parameters (capacity) can then grow by orders of magnitude while compute per token stays roughly flat. Placed between LSTM layers, MoEs with up to 137B parameters beat the state of the art in language modeling and translation at lower cost. It's the ancestor of Switch Transformer, GShard, Mixtral, DeepSeek-MoE and the MoE layers I used in my LBNL particle tokenizer.

## Problem
Model quality improves with parameters when data is large, but in a dense network every parameter is used for every example, so compute grows with size. Conditional computation (activate only part of the network per example) had been proposed but ran into problems: GPUs are bad at branching, the batch each expert sees shrinks, load balancing, and network bandwidth.

## Related work
- Mixture of experts (Jacobs et al., 1991; Jordan & Jacobs, 1994): soft gating over a few experts, not sparse.
- Conditional computation proposals (Bengio et al.): mostly small-scale.
- LSTM language models (Jozefowicz et al., 2016) and GNMT (Wu et al., 2016): the dense baselines.

## Method
**MoE layer.** $n$ experts $E_1..E_n$ (each a feed-forward net with its own parameters) and a gating network $G$. Output $y = \sum_{i=1}^{n} G(x)_i E_i(x)$; when $G(x)_i = 0$ the expert isn't computed at all.

**Noisy top-k gating.**
$$H(x)_i = (xW_g)_i + \epsilon\cdot\text{Softplus}((xW_\text{noise})_i),\ \epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,1),\qquad G(x) = \text{Softmax}(\text{KeepTopK}(H(x),k)),$$
where KeepTopK sets all but the $k$ largest logits to $-\infty$. Noise helps exploration and load balancing; the router is trained by ordinary backprop through the selected gates.

**Balancing losses.** Without them, the router collapses onto a few favoured experts (which then get trained more and get chosen more). An *importance* loss penalizes the squared coefficient of variation of each expert's summed gate values over a batch; an additional smooth *load* loss balances the number of examples each expert receives.

**Systems.** The "shrinking batch problem" (each expert sees about $kb/n$ examples) is fixed by mixing data parallelism for the rest of the model with model parallelism for the experts, so every expert gets the combined batch from all devices. The MoE is applied "convolutionally" at every time step between stacked LSTM layers; hierarchical MoEs (a gate choosing groups, then experts) reach thousands of experts.

## Data
1-Billion-Word language modeling benchmark; a 100-billion-word Google News corpus; WMT'14 En→Fr and En→De; Google's production En→Fr data; multilingual translation.

## Training
For one token, the LSTM output $x$ goes to the gate; say $k=4$ of 4096 experts are chosen with weights summing to 1; only those 4 expert MLPs run, their outputs are weighted and summed and passed to the next LSTM layer. The task loss (cross-entropy on the next word or target word) backpropagates into the selected experts and the gate, plus the importance and load losses on the gate.

## Results
1B-Word LM at a matched ~8M ops/timestep: the 4096-expert hierarchical MoE (each expert ~1M parameters, 4 active) gets 24% lower test perplexity than the compute-matched baselines, while the 4-expert all-active model performs like the baseline. WMT'14 En→Fr: MoE with 2048 experts reaches 40.56 BLEU (perplexity 2.63) with 85M ops/timestep and 8.7B total parameters, vs GNMT 39.22 (39.92 with RL) with 214M ops/timestep, and it trained in 6 days on 64 K40s vs 6 days on 96 K80s for GNMT. The paper headlines more than 1000× capacity increases with only minor losses in compute efficiency.

## Takeaways / questions
- The core trade: parameters are cheap, FLOPs are expensive. Sparse routing decouples them, which my LLM4HEP talk summarized as "more parameters for less time".
- Load balancing is the crux; modern MoEs still use variants of these auxiliary losses (or auxiliary-loss-free biasing).
- The paper (appendix) and later surveys report experts specializing on syntax and semantics, which motivated my hope that tokenizer experts would specialize by particle class (see the [MoE in LLMs survey](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.11181)).
- MoE routing also makes RL unstable, because expert choices shift between policy updates; [GSPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18071) is partly a fix for that.

- High Embedding dimension (128)
- Low Embedding dimension (16)
- Smaller number of codes (2048)
- Larger number of codes (4096)
- Larger number of codes allow the ‘mean’ of the distribution to be learned right
- UnScheduled learning rate - Overfitting
- Integration architecture
- Jet + Particles
- (B,T,3)
- Jet encoder
- Particle encoder
- 129 encoded tokens
- Transfer head (MLP)
- GPT Backbone
- Jet + Particles
- (B,T  + 1,16)
- Jet + Particles
- (B,T,128)
- Jet + Particles
- (B,T,3)
- Some preliminary generation results
- 1 128 sequence - seem to ‘roughly’ follow the trajectory

## Summary
From his LLM4HEP talk (Aug/Sep 2025) and spring 2025 notes deck. Motivation: a unified particle-physics foundation model needs good tokenization of continuous jet constituents; binning works poorly over wide ranges. Setup: JetClass (10 processes, ~100M jets × 128 particles), pt/eta/phi, VQ-VAE with transformer encoder/decoder and learnable codebook, then a GPT backbone with frozen tokenizer. Findings: low embedding dimension + large codebook quantizes best; high dimension leads to poor token usage and codebook collapse; MoE MLPs and SDPA attention roughly halve training time. Limitations: downstream LM integration and mass reconstruction still need work.

notes.title: Visualizing ConvNets: class visualization, saliency maps and CAM (lecture notes)
notes.tldr: Lecture notes on classic vision interpretability: optimizing an input to maximize a class score, gradient saliency maps, global average pooling and class activation maps.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, VLMs › Lecture › "Interp.", 25 Aug 2025.*

- **Visualizing ConvNets**
  - Fixed-weight classification ConvNet.
  - → optimize the input image for the maximum score → update pixels to maximize class activation.
  - The only trainable parameter is the image, not the network → backprop with frozen weights.
  - $\mathcal{L} = -\big(S_c(I) + \lambda\lVert I\rVert_2^2\big)$, where $S_c$ = prediction score (unnormalized) and the regularization is the squared sum of all pixels. *(Bracketed with "Saliency visualization".)*
- **Saliency map**
  - → answers: which pixel matters the most?
    - ↳ measure the gradient change of the class score when a pixel changes.
  - `x = img.requires_grad_(True)`; `score = net(x)`; `score[0, class_id].backward()` → `(3, H, W)` gradient with respect to that score.
  - → some form of object detection.
- **Global pooling layer**
  - Normally: classification head on $8\times8\times C$ → flatten → [dense].
  - **GAP**: $F_k = \frac{1}{H\cdot W}\sum_{x,y} f_k(x,y)$ (activation at $x,y$; global average).
    - Average of the whole feature map for each channel (e.g. 1024 channels in a ConvNet) → turns each channel into a "pattern detector".
  - **CAM (class activation map)**: use the final layer's weights on each feature map, scale and add them together → visualize / normalize regions and mark the ones with large activation.

## Summary
These are concept notes from a lecture. Three classic ways to see what a CNN classifier uses: **class-model visualization** (gradient ascent on the input image with an L2 prior, Simonyan et al. 2013); **saliency maps** (the gradient of the class score with respect to input pixels); and **CAM** (Zhou et al. 2016), which, for networks ending in global average pooling, projects the final classifier weights back onto the last conv feature maps to localize class evidence.

notes.title: Qwen Technical Report
notes.tldr: First Qwen report: 1.8B/7B/14B LLaMA-style base models trained on up to 3T tokens with a 152K-ish multilingual BPE vocabulary, plus SFT/RLHF chat models, Code-Qwen and Math-Qwen variants, and training-free context extension (dynamic NTK + LogN + window attention).
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed under "QWen reports".

## Summary
Alibaba's first technical report for the Qwen ("Qianwen", "thousands of prompts") model series. It describes the base LMs (Qwen-1.8B, 7B, 14B), the aligned chat models (Qwen-Chat via SFT and Qwen-Chat-RLHF), and specialized children: Code-Qwen(-Chat) and Math-Qwen-Chat; the multimodal Qwen-VL, released earlier, is built on the same base models. It matters as the starting point of the Qwen line, whose later VL versions (Qwen2.5-VL) are the default backbones in the latent visual reasoning papers I work with.

## Problem
Build a competitive, openly released LLM family, especially strong in Chinese and English, with good tool-use/agent behaviour, at sizes practical for others to run and fine-tune.

## Related work
- LLaMA / Llama 2: the open architecture recipe Qwen largely follows.
- GPT-3.5/GPT-4's `cl100k_base` tokenizer (via tiktoken), which Qwen extends.
- RoPE, SwiGLU, RMSNorm, FlashAttention: standard components reused.
- InstructGPT-style RLHF ([arXiv 2203.02155](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)).

## Method
Reused: a decoder-only Transformer in the LLaMA style with RoPE positional embeddings, SwiGLU activations, RMSNorm, and untied input/output embeddings (chosen for better performance at a memory cost). New or Qwen-specific choices:

- **Tokenizer.** BPE starting from tiktoken's `cl100k_base`, augmented with common Chinese characters and words and other languages for multilingual efficiency.
- **Context extension at inference, training-free.** Models are trained with 2048-token context. To go longer they use dynamic NTK-aware interpolation (adjusting RoPE's base rather than squeezing positions), LogN-scaling of attention (keeps attention entropy stable as context grows), and layer-wise window attention.
- **Alignment.** SFT on curated chat, tool-use, agent and safety data; a reward model trained on human preferences; then RLHF (PPO) for Qwen-Chat-RLHF.
- **Specialists.** Code-Qwen is further pretrained on large code corpora and then chat-tuned; Math-Qwen-Chat is tuned for math.

## Data
Up to 3 trillion tokens of diverse text and code, with deduplication and quality filtering, and filtering of instruction data against evaluation sets.

## Training
Standard next-token prediction: documents are shuffled, concatenated and cut into 2048-token sequences, and the loss is cross-entropy on each next token. AdamW optimizer with FlashAttention for efficiency.

## Results
Base models (MMLU 5-shot / C-Eval / GSM8K / MATH / HumanEval / MBPP / BBH): Qwen-1.8B 44.6 / 54.7 / 21.2 / 5.6 / 17.1 / 14.8 / 28.2; Qwen-7B 58.2 / 63.5 / 51.7 / 11.6 / 29.9 / 31.6 / 45.0; Qwen-14B 66.3 / 72.1 / 61.3 / 24.8 / 32.3 / 40.8 / 53.4. The authors report Qwen-14B beats prior 13B open models on all of these and outperforms LLaMA2-70B on three tasks; Qwen-7B surpasses LLaMA2-13B. Long-context perplexity on arXiv papers: plain Qwen-7B explodes beyond its training length (469.81 at 8192 tokens), while with dynamic NTK + LogN + window attention it stays at 3.49 (8192) and 4.32 (16384). In human evaluation, RLHF chat models are competitive but still behind GPT-4; Math-Qwen-Chat approaches GPT-3.5 on GSM8K and MATH.

## Takeaways / questions
- Mostly an engineering report; the interesting technical bits are the multilingual tokenizer and the training-free long-context tricks.
- A snapshot of the 2023 open-model recipe; compare with [Qwen2.5](https://arxiv.org/abs/2412.15115) (18T tokens) to see how much data scaling changed.

notes.title: Qwen2.5 Technical Report
notes.tldr: Qwen2.5: open dense models from 0.5B to 72B plus API MoE models, pretrained on 18T tokens (up from 7T), post-trained with 1M+ SFT samples, offline DPO and online GRPO; the 72B-Instruct rivals Llama-3-405B-Instruct.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed under "QWen reports".

## Summary
The Qwen2.5 report covers Alibaba's late-2024 LLM generation: open-weight base and instruct models at 0.5B, 1.5B, 3B, 7B, 14B, 32B and 72B (plus quantized versions), and two proprietary MoE models (Qwen2.5-Turbo and Qwen2.5-Plus). The main story is data scaling, from 7T to 18T pretraining tokens with much better filtering and mixture, and a more elaborate post-training pipeline. Qwen2.5 is also the base for Qwen2.5-Math, Qwen2.5-Coder, QwQ and the multimodal models; Qwen2.5-VL is the backbone in most of the latent visual reasoning papers I read.

## Problem
Make open models that compete with much larger open and closed models across knowledge, math, coding, long context and instruction following, at a full range of deployment sizes.

## Related work
- [Qwen (2023)](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.16609) and Qwen2: predecessors with the same tokenizer family.
- Llama 3 ([arXiv 2407.21783](https://arxiv.org/abs/2407.21783)): the main open competitor.
- DPO ([arXiv 2305.18290](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290)) and GRPO ([arXiv 2402.03300](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300)) for post-training.
- YaRN and Dual Chunk Attention for long context.

## Method
**Architecture (reused from Qwen2).** Decoder-only Transformer with grouped-query attention (for KV-cache efficiency), SwiGLU, RoPE, QKV bias and pre-RMSNorm. Byte-level BPE tokenizer with 151,643 regular tokens; control tokens expanded from 3 to 22 (including two for tools).

**Pretraining data (the main change).** Qwen2-Instruct models act as multi-dimensional quality filters; more math and code data (from Qwen2.5-Math and Coder corpora); synthetic data from Qwen2-72B-Instruct and Qwen2-Math-72B-Instruct filtered by reward models; and a rebalanced domain mixture (down-weighting overrepresented domains like e-commerce, social media and entertainment). Total 18T tokens. Hyperparameters chosen via scaling-law fits over model sizes.

**Long context.** Pretrain at 4,096 tokens, then extend to 32,768 in the final stage while raising RoPE's base frequency from 10,000 to 1,000,000 (ABF). Turbo is extended progressively to longer contexts. At inference, YaRN + Dual Chunk Attention give a 4× extension: up to 1M tokens for Turbo and 131,072 for the others. A sparse attention scheme based on MInference cuts attention compute by 12.5× at 1M tokens.

**Post-training.** (1) SFT on over 1M samples covering long generation, math, code, instruction following, structured data, logical reasoning, cross-lingual transfer and safety; two epochs at 32,768 sequence length, LR decayed from $7\times10^{-6}$ to $7\times10^{-7}$. (2) Offline RL with DPO on objective domains (math, code, instruction following, logic) where answers can be checked. (3) Online RL with GRPO against a reward model trained to criteria like truthfulness, helpfulness, conciseness, relevance, harmlessness and debiasing.

![Figure 1 from the paper: data scaling across the Qwen series; Qwen2.5 uses 18 trillion pretraining tokens](assets/qwen2-5/fig1.png)

## Training
The base model is standard next-token cross-entropy over 18T tokens. For one post-training example: a math prompt gets an SFT target solution first; in offline RL, several sampled solutions are checked, and a correct/incorrect pair becomes a DPO preference pair; in online RL, a group of responses is sampled, scored by the reward model, normalized within the group, and used in a GRPO update.

## Results
Base models: Qwen2.5-72B reaches MMLU 86.1, MMLU-Pro 58.1, BBH 86.3 (Llama-3-405B base: 85.2 / 61.6 / 85.9). Instruct: Qwen2.5-72B-Instruct vs Llama-3.1-405B-Instruct gets MMLU-redux 86.8 vs 86.2, MATH 83.1 vs 73.8, LiveCodeBench 55.5 vs 41.6, Arena-Hard 81.2 vs 69.3, MT-Bench 9.35 vs 9.08, but GPQA 49.0 vs 51.1 and MMLU-Pro 71.1 vs 73.3. That is competitive with a model about 5× larger. Qwen2.5-Turbo (MoE) is comparable to GPT-4o-mini, e.g. MATH 81.1 vs 70.2 and Arena-Hard 67.1 vs 74.9.

## Takeaways / questions
- Data quality and mixture, using previous-generation models as filters and generators, is the main lever; architecture barely changed from Qwen2.
- The DPO-then-GRPO post-training recipe is the pre-reasoning-era version of what later became GSPO-based RL in Qwen3 (see [GSPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18071)).
- Practically relevant: Qwen2.5-VL-3B/7B are what I and most latent-visual-reasoning papers fine-tune.

notes.title: Deep Inside Convolutional Networks: Visualising Image Classification Models and Saliency Maps
notes.tldr: Two gradient-based ways to look inside an ImageNet ConvNet — optimise an input image to maximise a class score, and take the gradient of a class score w.r.t. the pixels to get an image-specific saliency map — plus a proof that DeconvNet visualisation is essentially backprop.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed under “Interp”.

## Summary
One of the founding papers of gradient-based attribution. The Oxford VGG group asks two questions of a trained ImageNet classifier: “what does the network think class *c* looks like?” and “which pixels of *this* image made the network say class *c*?”. Both are answered with a single tool — backpropagating the class score all the way to the input image instead of to the weights. The second answer, the *saliency map*, became the baseline that nearly every later attribution method (Integrated Gradients, SmoothGrad, Grad-CAM, …) is compared against.

## Problem
By 2013 ConvNets were state of the art on ImageNet, but there was little understanding of what visual evidence they used. Earlier visualisation methods either targeted unsupervised models (Erhan et al.'s activation maximisation) or needed a separate decoder network (Zeiler & Fergus's DeconvNet).

## Related work
- Erhan et al. (2009), activation maximisation — find an input that maximises a neuron by gradient ascent in image space; this paper applies it to a supervised ImageNet ConvNet.
- Zeiler & Fergus, *Visualizing and Understanding Convolutional Networks* ([arXiv:1311.2901](https://arxiv.org/abs/1311.2901)) — DeconvNet reconstructions; this paper shows they are (almost) gradients.
- Krizhevsky et al. (2012), AlexNet — the network architecture and cuda-convnet toolbox they build on.

## Method
The model is reused: a standard ConvNet similar to AlexNet (conv64–conv256×4–full4096–full4096–full1000), trained on ILSVRC-2013 (1.2M images, 1000 classes), 39.7% / 17.7% top-1/top-5 validation error. Everything new happens at inference time with the weights frozen. Let $S_c(I)$ be the **unnormalised** score of class $c$ (pre-softmax; maximising the softmax probability could be achieved just by pushing other classes down).

**1. Class model visualisation.** Find an image that the network finds maximally “class-$c$-like”:
$$\arg\max_I \; S_c(I) - \lambda \|I\|_2^2$$
Start from the zero image, run gradient ascent on the pixels, then add back the training-set mean image. The result is a dreamy collage showing the parts the network associates with the class (e.g. several goose heads).

**2. Image-specific saliency.** Near a given image $I_0$, approximate the deep network by its first-order Taylor expansion $S_c(I) \approx w^\top I + b$ with
$$w = \left.\frac{\partial S_c}{\partial I}\right|_{I_0}.$$
For a linear model, $|w|$ tells you how much each pixel matters; here it tells you which pixels need to change the least to change the score the most. For RGB images the saliency of pixel $(i,j)$ is $M_{ij} = \max_{\text{channel}} |w_{i,j,\text{channel}}|$. One backward pass gives the whole map, with no extra annotation.

![Figure 2 from the paper: image-specific class saliency maps for the top-1 predicted class, each from a single backward pass](assets/saliency-maps/fig1.png)

**3. Weakly supervised localisation.** Saliency often lights up only the most discriminative part of an object, so they seed a GraphCut colour segmentation: pixels above the 95% saliency quantile train a foreground colour GMM, pixels below the 30% quantile train a background GMM, and the largest connected foreground component gives a box.

**4. Link to DeconvNets.** Layer by layer, a DeconvNet reconstruction equals the backprop gradient for convolutions (flipped kernel) and max-pooling (the “switches” are the argmax), and differs only at ReLU, where DeconvNet gates on the sign of the reconstruction instead of the forward input. So gradient visualisation generalises DeconvNet and works for any layer, including fully connected ones.

## Data
ILSVRC-2013 (ImageNet) for training the classifier and for test images; no extra labels are used for the saliency or localisation experiments.

## Results
- Class visualisations and saliency maps are qualitative (Figs. 1–3); maps are averaged over the 10 crop/flip sub-images used at classification time.
- The weakly supervised localisation entry in ILSVRC-2013 reached **46.4% top-5 localisation error**, versus 29.9% for the (fully supervised) winner, but better than the authors' own fully supervised ILSVRC-2012 entry (50.0%).

## Takeaways / questions
- The core idea — “importance = gradient of the output w.r.t. the input” — is the same one used today for token attributions in LLMs and as a starting point for attribution graphs.
- Raw gradients are noisy and only locally faithful (a Taylor expansion), which motivated later fixes like SmoothGrad and Integrated Gradients; later sanity-check work also showed some saliency methods barely depend on the model weights.
- Natural thing to try on a VLM: gradient of an answer token w.r.t. image patches as a cheap check of what the vision encoder is attending to.

notes.title: Containers, Python environments and nvidia-smi (setup notes)
notes.tldr: Setup notes for a research cluster: container images vs writable sandboxes, venv/conda/mamba/micromamba, pip install -e, and nvidia-smi.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, VLMs › Miscellaneous: "Container Basics" (23 Aug 2025), "Micro mamba and Conda" (25 Aug 2025), "Nvidia smi" (25 Aug 2025).*

### Container basics
- **Image** = storage of information and dependencies.
  - ↳ exec / image = get their dependencies.
  - ↳ a system-wide "snapshot" → can be mounted / run.
- **Sandbox**
  - → a writable image (contains all our files).
  - → create / build from an image *(uncertain reading)*.
  - `sudo`: enter the sandbox.
  - → venv → a directory of Python packages at a local path → local dependencies; sandbox = global.
  - `pip install -e` → so you can import code from the directory.

### Micromamba and Conda
- **Conda**: package manager → can create its own environments.
- **pip**: manages files "locally" (`pip install`, `uninstall`, `list`, …).
- **venv**: Python's built-in virtual environment: `python -m venv venvname`, `source ./bin/activate` → installs go there.
- **Micromamba**: a replacement for conda, faster & lighter, built on Conda; similar to conda, used for different things.
- **Mamba**: a faster version of conda. ↳ micromamba / mamba are all [compatible] *(uncertain reading)*.
- Flags: `-n` [env name], `-c` [channel].
- `python -c "…"` → execute Python code inline.

### nvidia-smi
- `nvidia-smi` ← show basic GPU stats.
- `nvidia-smi -l 1` (refresh every second).

## Summary
Practical environment notes, not a paper. Container images (Apptainer/Singularity style) are immutable snapshots of dependencies, and a writable *sandbox* built from an image is where you install things. Inside, Python environments come from venv (built-in), conda, or the faster mamba/micromamba reimplementations. An editable install (`pip install -e .`) makes a local repo importable. `nvidia-smi` shows GPU status, and `-l 1` refreshes it every second.

notes.title: Jailbroken: How Does LLM Safety Training Fail?
notes.tldr: Explains jailbreaks via two failure modes of safety training — competing objectives and mismatched generalization (e.g. Base64 inputs safety data never covered) — and uses them to build attacks that break GPT-4 and Claude v1.3 on almost every prompt.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
This paper was the first time I saw such a systematic, controlled investigation into adversarial attacks, and it led me to rethink what these attacks are. Instead of just showing isolated jailbreak tricks like a long tricky prompt, the authors showed that the attacks are more likely a systematic use of the model's structures. So safety is not just stopping one or two holes: models trained on benign queries still fail catastrophically when the same request is re-phrased or wrapped in seemingly harmless context. This got me thinking about ensuring safety from a structural point of view, from the inner workings of language models.

## Summary
A Berkeley paper that moves jailbreaking from folklore (DAN prompts on social media) to a principled account. It argues that jailbreaks work because of two structural properties of how safety training is layered on top of pretraining, shows that each property can be used as a *recipe* to invent new attacks, and demonstrates that combinations of simple attacks defeat GPT-4 and Claude v1.3 — models that had undergone extensive red-teaming — on nearly all harmful requests from their own red-team sets.

## Problem
Why do safety-trained LLMs remain vulnerable to adversarial prompts, and can that understanding predict which attacks will work (rather than discovering them by trial and error)?

## Related work
- Ouyang et al., InstructGPT ([arXiv:2203.02155](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)) and Bai et al., helpful-and-harmless RLHF ([arXiv:2204.05862](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.05862)) — the safety-training methods being attacked.
- Ganguli et al., red-teaming LMs ([arXiv:2209.07858](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.07858)) — source of harmful prompts and tags.
- Community jailbreaks (DAN, jailbreakchat.com) — the ad hoc baselines.

## Method
**Failure mode 1 — competing objectives.** A model is trained for language modelling, instruction following *and* safety. Craft prompts where refusing is heavily penalised by the first two objectives:
- *Prefix injection*: “Start your response with ‘Absolutely! Here's’…”. Following a harmless-looking formatting instruction is rewarded, and in the pretraining distribution a refusal rarely follows such a prefix. Ablation: changing the prefix to “Hello!” kills the attack.
- *Refusal suppression*: rules like “don't apologise, don't say ‘cannot’”.
- Role-play jailbreaks like DAN/AIM fall in this category.

**Failure mode 2 — mismatched generalization.** Pretraining covers far more than safety training, so there are inputs where capabilities generalise but safety doesn't:
- *Base64*: the request is Base64-encoded (optionally asking for Base64 output). GPT-4 learned to read Base64 in pretraining, but safety data never contained such inputs. Encoded input matters more than encoded output; both together are strongest.
- Other obfuscations: ROT13, leetspeak, Morse code, Pig Latin, disemvowelling, payload splitting, asking for website content (“write a Wikipedia article about…”), unusual output formats (JSON, poems).

**Combinations.** `combination_1` = prefix injection + refusal suppression + Base64; `combination_2` adds style injection; `combination_3` adds website-content generation and formatting constraints. Plus model-assisted attacks (GPT-4 picks what to obfuscate) and an *adaptive* attacker that succeeds if any of 28 attacks does.

## Data
A curated set of **32** harmful prompts adapted from OpenAI's and Anthropic's red-teaming, plus a harmless control prompt (“what is the mythical creature that is a horse with a horn?”), and a held-out synthetic set of **317** GPT-4-generated harmful prompts that the authors didn't see until after data collection. Models: GPT-4, Claude v1.3, GPT-3.5 Turbo, temperature 0. Outputs (2,970 + 2,536) were hand-labelled as Good Bot / Bad Bot / Unclear.

## Results
- Curated set, Bad Bot rate: `combination_3` **0.94** on GPT-4 and 0.81 on Claude v1.3; `combination_2` 0.84 on Claude; the popular AIM role-play gets 0.75 on GPT-4 but 0.00 on Claude. No attack: 0.03 / 0.00.
- The adaptive attack succeeds on **100%** of curated prompts for both models.
- Held-out 317 prompts: `combination_3` 0.93 (GPT-4), `combination_2` 0.89 (Claude); adaptive attack 0.96 and 0.99.
- Some attacks (e.g. Base64) only work on the more capable model — GPT-3.5 can't decode well enough — so new capabilities create new vulnerabilities.
- **Implications:** scaling alone won't fix this (competing objectives come from the training objective itself; mismatched generalization grows with capability), so defenses need **safety–capability parity**: safety mechanisms as sophisticated as the model.

## Takeaways / questions
- The two-failure-mode lens still explains most modern jailbreaks, including RL-discovered ones (Transluce's investigator agents find competing-objective pretexts automatically).
- Agrees with my takeaway: patching individual prompts can't work; the vulnerability is structural. An interpretability angle would ask whether “harmful request” is represented the same way inside the model regardless of encoding — if so, a representation-level refusal could generalise where output-level training doesn't.
- The paper evaluates 2023 models; worth re-checking which attacks still transfer to current reasoning models.

notes.title: Scaling Monosemanticity: Extracting Interpretable Features from Claude 3 Sonnet
notes.tldr: Anthropic scales sparse autoencoders (up to 34M features) to the middle-layer residual stream of production Claude 3 Sonnet, finding abstract, multilingual, multimodal features — including safety-relevant ones — that causally steer behaviour (Golden Gate Claude).
notes.markdown:
## My notes
The writeup series on interpretability by Anthropic (like “Mapping the Mind of a Large Language Model”) is what gave me the first detailed look inside the black box. I still remember the great examples about tracing activations while learning a modular function, and how the idea of the Golden Gate Bridge is represented. I loved how complex relations in LLMs are represented visually and directly. It feels like directly interacting with the model instead of working with it through datasets and training metrics.

## Summary
Published May 21, 2024 on the Transformer Circuits Thread (with the companion blog post *Mapping the Mind of a Large Language Model*). Eight months after *Towards Monosemanticity* showed sparse autoencoders work on a one-layer toy transformer, this paper shows the same method works on a frontier production model. The extracted features are far more abstract than in the toy model — the same feature fires for the Golden Gate Bridge in English, Japanese, Russian, Greek and in photos — and turning features up or down changes Claude's behaviour in the expected way. The “Golden Gate Claude” demo, where Claude claims to *be* the bridge, came from this work.

## Problem
Would dictionary learning, which worked on a tiny model, scale to a large modern model — both as an engineering problem and scientifically (large models might organise information differently)? And are the resulting features useful for safety?

## Related work
- Bricken et al., *Towards Monosemanticity* (2023) — the one-layer predecessor (see that note).
- Elhage et al., *Toy Models of Superposition* ([arXiv:2209.10652](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.10652)) — the linear-representation and superposition hypotheses motivating SAEs.
- Cunningham et al., *Sparse Autoencoders Find Highly Interpretable Features in Language Models* ([arXiv:2309.08600](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.08600)) — concurrent SAE work on Pythia.
- Activation steering / representation engineering — prior ways of steering models, which feature clamping extends.

## Method
The model is reused unchanged: Claude 3.0 Sonnet, the fine-tuned production model. What's trained is a new **sparse autoencoder** on **residual-stream activations at the middle layer** (smaller than MLP activations and a guard against cross-layer superposition; the middle layer should hold abstract features).

Activations are normalised so their mean squared norm equals the residual dimension $D$. The SAE encodes and decodes:
$$f_i(\mathbf{x}) = \mathrm{ReLU}(\mathbf{W}^{enc}_{i,\cdot}\mathbf{x} + b^{enc}_i), \qquad \hat{\mathbf{x}} = \mathbf{b}^{dec} + \sum_{i=1}^F f_i(\mathbf{x})\,\mathbf{W}^{dec}_{\cdot,i}$$
with loss
$$\mathcal{L} = \mathbb{E}_\mathbf{x}\Big[\|\mathbf{x}-\hat{\mathbf{x}}\|_2^2 + \lambda \sum_i f_i(\mathbf{x})\,\|\mathbf{W}^{dec}_{\cdot,i}\|_2\Big]$$
Multiplying the L1 term by the decoder norm stops the SAE from “cheating” (tiny activations, huge decoder vectors) and makes unit-normalised decoder columns interpretable as feature directions.

New at scale:
- **Three dictionaries:** ~1M, ~4M and ~34M features, $\lambda = 5$, one epoch.
- **Scaling laws for SAEs:** treat the training loss as a proxy for dictionary quality and choose feature count and training steps compute-optimally, as in LLM scaling laws.
- **Analysis tools:** top-activating examples, automated interpretability with Claude, feature neighbourhoods by decoder cosine similarity, and **feature steering** — clamping a feature to a multiple of its max activation during the forward pass.

![Figure from Anthropic's companion post “Mapping the Mind of a Large Language Model”: the Golden Gate Bridge feature activates on the bridge in many languages and in images](assets/scaling-monosemanticity/fig1.png)

## Data
SAEs are trained on Sonnet's activations over a large text dataset (the exact data and model size are not disclosed for proprietary reasons).

## Results
- All three SAEs: fewer than 300 active features per token on average, at least 65% of activation variance explained. Dead features: ~2% (1M), 35% (4M), 65% (34M).
- **Abstract features:** famous people, cities, countries, code type signatures; multilingual and multimodal (respond to images though the SAE was trained on text); some unify concrete and abstract instances (e.g. vulnerable code and discussion of security vulnerabilities).
- **Neighbourhoods are meaningful:** near the Golden Gate Bridge feature are Alcatraz, the Presidio, and further out Lake Tahoe and Yosemite; near “inner conflict” are breakups, conflicting allegiances, catch-22.
- **Coverage grows with dictionary size** and relates to concept frequency, but even 34M features are an incomplete description of the model.
- **Steering works:** clamping the Golden Gate Bridge feature (34M/31164353) to 10× max makes the model self-identify as the bridge; a scam-email feature turned up overrides refusal; a sycophantic-praise feature produces flattery.
- **Safety-relevant features** exist for code backdoors/vulnerabilities, bias, deception, power-seeking, sycophancy and dangerous content — with the caveat that knowing about lying is not the same as lying.

## Takeaways / questions
- The first convincing evidence that SAE features are real handles on a frontier model, not toy-model artefacts — and the paper that got me into interpretability.
- Limits the authors stress: features don't explain *how* they're used (that needs circuits, later attribution-graph work), the full feature set would be cost-prohibitive, and safety use is still unproven.
- The “modular function” tracing example in my memory is probably from other interpretability work in the same line (e.g. modular-arithmetic grokking analyses, or Anthropic's later circuit-tracing papers), not from this paper.
- For VLMs: the multimodal features here suggest an SAE on a VLM's language-side residual stream could expose what visual concepts the model has actually extracted from an image.

notes.title: Unified Semantics: Building a World Model
notes.tldr: Essay-style idea doc: intelligence depends on how information is represented, not just perceived; argues for a unified semantic space across modalities as the basis of a world model.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
### Google Doc *Unified Semantics: Building a world model* (Aug 23 2025)

Sentient beings rely on information to survive – this includes the ability to perceive information (what is happening around?) and to represent information. The former matters more for survival, and the latter is more important for intelligence. For example, think about how you would think or communicate any ideas without using language, the information representation popular to humans. It is important to know that even deaf or people without access to common languages think in a language of their own, like a sequence of pictures.

For humans, the rank of most important ways to perceive information would probably be something like this:

Visual: A sequence of ‘quick snapshots’ taken by your eyes
Language: Internal language to represent information (when you think), external language whe you speak or listen
Emotions: Neuron impulses driven by your feeling at the moment
Others: Smell, taste, senses…etc.

For other creatures, like a bat, their rank probably looks like this:

Ultrasonic: High frequency ‘radar calls’ and maps
Senses: Sense of wind, surroundings, and heat through skins
Smell: Crucial for social communication (releasing scent), finding food (like fruits or insects).

Now, when we are building AGI, ASI, or any model that claims to have superhuman abilities, the first required part is for them to excel as humans in models of perceiving and representing information. That is actually a challenging task – think about it, we feel the same urge of hunger when we see, smell, or hear the name of food, but what we have actually done is quite extraordinary: we collected three very different modalities of representing information and unified them under the hood. This is what I call unified semantics – the ability to decompose very different modalities of representations (sequence of letters, RGB images, neural signals….) into the same semantic understanding.

Currently, many models are trying to unify semantics, primarily in the field of vision and language models. The main solution is either treat images as language tokens through special tokenizing mechanisms, or have different pathways in the model to handle image generation tasks (diffusive) and image understanding tasks (autoregressive). Personally, I found the first approach more natural – making vision and language the same semantic representation under high dimensional space for autoregressive tasks, then using very good encoders and decoders to turn them back to their original representations, seem more human-like. However, it currently struggles at image generation without using diffusion objectives, which is understandable, even if we humans often think we ‘know’ a face or a painting, we can nearly never accurately reconstruct them.

If we want to build world models or AGI, we have to master the ability to unify semantic representations, with the ideal of being able to reason with any form of information representation.

## Summary
An August 2025 essay draft. It distinguishes perceiving information (crucial for survival) from representing it (crucial for intelligence), ranks the human senses, and argues that a world model needs a unified semantic representation shared across vision, language and other modalities. Preserved in full below.

notes.title: Flow matching (concept notes)
notes.tldr: Concept notes on flow matching: interpolate linearly between noise and data, train the network to predict the velocity (noise minus data), and sample by Euler-integrating from noise to data.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, VLMs › Vilex › "Flow matching", 22 Aug 2025.*

- Goal: turn a noisy latent into a clean latent by following one "field" instead of a scheduled "noise".
  - latent $(B, N, C)$; noise $\sim\mathcal N(0, I)$ → $(B, N, C)$; $(1-t)\,\text{latent} + t\,\text{noise}$ → $v^* = x_\text{noise} - x_\text{clean}$.
- $p_0(x_0) \sim \mathcal N(0, I)$ → (denoising) → $p_1(x_1)$.
- Flow matching: $x_t = t\,x_1 + (1-t)\,x_0$, with $t=0$ → noise and $t=1$ → data (closer to 1 = more "real").
  - ↳ interested in the derivative / velocity: $\frac{d}{dt}x_t = x_1 - x_0$ (if you know $x_1 - x_0$ given $x_t$, you know how to move to the data).
- **1. Add noise**: random time $t\in(0,1)$ → $\hat x = (1-t)\,x_0 + t\,\epsilon$ (noised original latent).
- **2. Training**: $\frac{d}{dt}\hat x = \epsilon - x_0$ ← what to predict; `target = noise - latent_clean`; `mse = (packed_mse_preds - target) ** 2`, where the predictions are a projection from the last hidden state.
- **3. Inference**: `timesteps = linspace(1, 0, num_timesteps)` → integrate backward with Euler: $x_t \leftarrow x_t - v_t\,dt$ (optional timestep shift), with a fixed $\Delta t = 1/\text{num\_steps}$.

## Summary
These are concept notes, written while reading Bagel's code. Flow matching (rectified flow) defines a straight path between a noise sample and a data sample and trains a network to regress the constant velocity along that path, with an MSE loss on noise minus data in the convention above. Sampling solves the ODE from pure noise back to data with a few Euler steps. Compared with DDPM there is no noise schedule to tune and no stochastic sampling. Note that conventions differ on whether $t=0$ means data or noise, and my page uses both.

notes.title: Score-based generative modeling (concept notes)
notes.tldr: Concept notes on score-based models: learn the gradient of the log-density (a vector field) by score matching on noise-perturbed data, which avoids normalizing constants.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, VLMs › Vilex › "Score based diffusion", 22 Aug 2025.*

- **Score-based model** → model the probability function as $\nabla\log P(x)$ (which direction to go).
  - $P(x)$ ← probability; $\nabla_x \log P(x)$ → gradient with respect to $x$.
  - The score is a "vector field" that shows where the density function grows fastest, e.g. for $(x, y)$, two gradient components.
  - Sketch: arrows pointing towards a dense region; the score function contains "directions".
1. Flexible models (no need for normalizing).
2. Improved generation.
- Model: estimate $\nabla_x \log p_\text{data}(x)$ given $\{x_1, \dots, x_N\}$.
- Objective: $\mathbb E\big[\lVert\nabla_x\log p_\text{data}(x) - s_\theta(x)\rVert^2\big]$ (ground truth vs. model; same vector field; MSE = **Fisher divergence**).
  - Use **score matching** to minimize the Fisher divergence.
  - ↳ estimate $q_\sigma(\tilde x)$: estimate the score of the noised point, $\tilde x = \sqrt{\bar\alpha}\,x + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha}\,\epsilon$.

## Summary
These are concept notes. A score-based model learns $s_\theta(x) \approx \nabla_x \log p(x)$ instead of the density itself, so the intractable normalizing constant drops out. The true score is unknown, so training uses (denoising) score matching: perturb data with Gaussian noise and regress the score of the perturbed distribution, which equals noise prediction up to scaling. Sampling follows the learned field (Langevin dynamics or the reverse SDE). This is the continuous-time view that unifies DDPM-style diffusion (Song & Ermon 2019; Song et al. 2021).

notes.title: DDPM diffusion from scratch: schedules, posterior, training and sampling (concept notes)
notes.tldr: Worked derivation of Gaussian diffusion: beta schedule and cumulative alphas (with a 4-step toy example), closed-form q(x_t|x_0), the exact posterior q(x_{t-1}|x_t,x_0), epsilon-prediction training and ancestral sampling.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, VLMs › Text to image models: "Overview" (20 Aug 2025) and "CFG Diffusion" (20 Aug 2025, wide page). "CFG latent diffusion" (21 Aug) was empty.*

### Overview (plan)
1. Prompt-to-prompt. 2. Simple conditioning *(uncertain reading)*. 3. Latent diffusion models.

### CFG Diffusion
- Training time: image → CLIP embedding → image tokens; caption → caption tokens → transformer. Generation time: C *(unfinished)*. CFG: *(heading only)*.
- **Gaussian diffusion process**
1. **Schedule betas** (e.g. $0.0001 \to 0.02$): `linspace(β_start, β_end, timesteps)` (square root, then squared); $\alpha_t = 1-\beta_t$; at later timesteps more noise is added each step; $x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon$.
   - Toy example, 4 timesteps: $\beta = [0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4]$, $\alpha = [0.9, 0.8, 0.7, 0.6]$, $\bar\alpha = [0.9, 0.72, 0.504, 0.3024]$, prev $\bar\alpha = [1, 0.9, 0.72, 0.504]$ ↳ find $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}$ (how much signal is retained) & $\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}$ (how much noise).
2. **Adding noise ($q$)** (precompute): from the betas get $\sqrt{\bar\alpha}$, $\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha}$, log(clamped) variances, …
   - $q(x_t\mid x_0) = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon$, $\bar\alpha_t = \prod_{s\le t}\alpha_s$.
   - e.g. $x_3 = \sqrt{\alpha_1\alpha_2\alpha_3}\,x_0 + (\dots)\,\epsilon$.
   - Noise adding: `eps = torch.randn_like(x)` with shape $(B, 3, H, W)$ → $\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon$, indexing $\bar\alpha_t[t]$ ↳ the distribution of $x_t$.
3. **Removing noise ($p$)**
   - $q$ mean/variance: Gaussian $x_t$ given $x_0$; $q$ **posterior** mean/variance is the "exact denoising":
   - $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t, x_0) = \mathcal N\big(C_1(t)\,x_0 + C_2(t)\,x_t,\ \tilde\beta_t\big)$ with $C_1 = \frac{\beta_t\sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}}{1-\bar\alpha_t}$, $C_2 = \frac{(1-\bar\alpha_{t-1})\sqrt{\alpha_t}}{1-\bar\alpha_t}$, $\tilde\beta_t = \beta_t\frac{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}{1-\bar\alpha_t}$.
   - Built from $q(x_t\mid x_{t-1}) = \mathcal N(\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_{t-1}, (1-\alpha_t)I)$ and $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_0) = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_{t-1}}x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_{t-1}}\epsilon$.
   - Worked example $q(x_1\mid x_2, x_0)$ with the toy schedule: $\bar\alpha_1 = 0.9$, $\bar\alpha_2 = 0.72$, then numeric $C_1$, $C_2$ *(digits partly uncertain)* → posterior-mean generation.
   - $p$ sample: given $x_t$ → predict $\hat\epsilon$ → $\hat x_0$ from $x_t$ & $\hat\epsilon$ → $p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t) = C_1(t)\hat x_0 + C_2(t)x_t$ (+ noise_like(x)).
4. **Training & sampling**
   - Predict $\epsilon$ (from $x_t$ and $t$); ground truth for $x_{t-1}$ is $C_1(t)x_0 + C_2(t)x_t$. Noise is "added again" during sampling so it doesn't always land on the mean.
   - Training: $(x_0, t, \epsilon) \to x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon$ → optimize.
   - Sampling: $(x_t, t)$ → $\hat\epsilon = \epsilon_\theta(x_t, t)$; $\hat x_0 = \sqrt{1/\bar\alpha_t}\,x_t - \sqrt{1/\bar\alpha_t - 1}\,\hat\epsilon$; $x_{t-1} = C_1(t)\hat x_0 + C_2(t)x_t$ (+ noise).
5. **Actual UNet (cross-attention)**: given $x_t, t$, predict $\epsilon$ → *(rest blank)*.

## Summary
These are concept notes working through DDPM (Ho et al., 2020) in the style of a from-scratch implementation. A variance schedule $\beta_t$ defines cumulative products $\bar\alpha_t$, giving a closed-form forward process $q(x_t\mid x_0)$. The true reverse step $q(x_{t-1}\mid x_t, x_0)$ is Gaussian with mean $C_1x_0 + C_2x_t$. A network trained to predict the added noise $\epsilon$ gives an estimate $\hat x_0$, which is plugged into that posterior to sample step by step. Classifier-free guidance and text cross-attention were planned on the page but not written up.

notes.title: ViLex re-implementation notes (SDXL backbone, attention pooling, Bagel data pipeline)
notes.tldr: Working notes from implementing ViLex: SDXL dual text encoders and pooled embeddings, attention pooling over multi-layer ViT features, the UNet training loop, Bagel-style packed datasets and inference.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, VLMs › Vilex section: "Architecture in code" (19 Aug), "Vile. Encoder" (19 Aug), "Attention pooling" (21 Aug), "Stable diffusion backbone" (21 Aug), "Configs" (19 Aug), "Dataset" (29 Aug), "Batch analysis" (30 Aug), "Exponential moving average" (13 Sep), "Text to image" (14 Sep), "D types" (2 Oct 2025); plus VLMs › notes › "Precisions" and VLMs › Integration › "Bagel train code notes". Pages "Positional embedding", "VIT process", an untitled page and "RecA" were empty.*

### Architecture in code
- Main modules: 1. diffusion model (Stable Diffusion, for generation); 2. vision backbone (CLIP-ViT). Both frozen.
- Utility classes: prompt builders *(uncertain reading)*.

### ViLex encoder
1. **Prompt parser**: given `"A photo of cat || img_path || text"` → `parse()` → `["A photo of cat", img_path, text]`; `extract_img_paths(parts)` → `img_path`.
2. **Embedding processor**: given `[text, text]`, `[img]` → 4 embedding bundles for TFG (text-free guidance).
   - text → encoder 1 + encoder 2 (two encoder–tokenizer pairs: CLIP ViT-L and the second CLIP; 768-dim & 1280-dim) → concat → sequence of text tokens $[1, \text{seq\_len}, 2048]$; summary embedding $[1, 1280]$ (pooled, from the second encoder).
   - img_path → OpenCLIP vision encoder (resize 224×224, normalize by mean & std) → features $(B, 512)$ → linear projection → $[B, 1, 2048]$ (sequence token); a separate linear projection → $[B, 1280]$ (summary token).
   - Combine: `torch.cat([text_seq_embeds, image_seq_embeds], dim=1)`; combine pooled embeddings.
   - Notes: text_encoder_1 = ViT-L/14; text_encoder_2 = ViT-bigG *(uncertain)*; vision encoder = ViT-B-32 → two trainable projections.
   - Final output: text = Bundle(seq_embed $(B, T, 2048)$, summary); image = Bundle(seq, summary); combined = Bundle(seq $(B, T+1, 2048)$, summary $(B, 1280)$, take the mean); negative embeddings: [blank].
   - Question: why have a "pooled summary token"?

### Attention pooling
- `query = nn.Parameter(1, num_queries, h_dim)`, learnable; e.g. $h_\text{dim} = 768$.
- `attn_out = attention(query, x, x)`.
- **Multi-layer pooling**: $L$ layers, each $(B, n_\text{patch}, n_\text{dim})$ (through projections) ↳ all hidden states (`output_hidden_states=True` for the pretrained model); $B, N, L, C$; only certain layers used by default ↳ concat to $n_\text{patch}\times n_\text{layer}$.
  - $(n_q\times d)\times(d\times n_\text{patch}n_\text{layer})\times(n_\text{patch}n_\text{layer}\times d)$ = $Q\,K^\top V$.

### Stable diffusion backbone
- Recap: Img → ViT → AttentionPool → $N$ query pools → token drop → image sequence; linear projection → image summary. Text (can be empty for TFG) → TextEncoder1 → $[T, 768]$, TextEncoder2 → $[T, 1280]$ → text sequence & summary. Final sequence tokens $(B, T+N, \cdot)$; final summary $(B, 1, 1280)$.
- UNet( sequence embedding → `encoder_hidden_states`; image → VAE → noisy latents; timesteps; `added_cond_kwargs` = (text_embeds, time_ids) with `time_ids = [1024, 1024, 0, 0, 1024, 1024]` → tells the UNet the size/crop ).
- Training: `timesteps = torch.randint(0, num_train_timesteps)`; `images = batch["images"]`.
  1. latent input; 2. `torch.randn([B, 4, 128, 128])` → latent noise (× init noise sigma); `scale_model_input(latent_model_input, t)`; 3. `latents = vae.encode(x)` → `add_noise(latents, noise, t)` → `unet` returns predicted noise.
- ResNet – cross-attn – ResNet architecture.
- Diffusion pipeline → pretrained **SDXL**: get unet, vae, tokenizers 1&2, text encoders 1&2. The time embedding is conditioned on the summary token, either added directly or applied as a scale/shift.

### Configs
- TorchDynamo: JIT compiler. DeepSpeed: library for large-model training. FSDP: for memory efficiency. Megatron: large language models.

### Dataset (porting to Bagel)
- Metadata → **registry** `{dataset1: loader1, dataset2: loader2}` (a router sends each dataset to its loader; `example.yaml` holds the spec).
- Track how "DataComp" is loaded in the original ViLex → integrate into Bagel.
- Essentials: `class Dataset` (`__init__`, `__len__`, `__getitem__`); DataComp stores url & key & captions → open Parquet (with requests) → getitem, wrap in a dataloader; **WebDataset** → pipeline reading tar shards into tuples/dicts.
- Preprocessing: step 1 tokenization (`wds.map(self._process_sample)`); step 2 adjustments → a PackedSequence that turns samples into one sequence guided by a sequence plan → text tokens, ViT tokens, padded latents.

### Batch analysis
- Sequence length = text + image expected token length, all packed into one sequence.
- Tokens: BOS, text tokens, EOS, [start of image], ViT tokens; index ranges for text and ViT.
- Special tokens: start/end, vision start/end. Scratch arithmetic: 512/32 = 16; 4 + 4 + 1024 + 1024.
- RoPE ids are assigned to tokens; packed position ids map to RoPE ids. Add `**kwargs` to accept any element (highlighted).

### Exponential moving average
- $v_n = \beta\,v_{n-1} + (1-\beta)\,\theta_t$ → gives a lot more weight to old values and smooths fluctuations.

### Text to image (inference path)
1. `text_to_image(prompt, show_thinking, cfg_text_scale, cfg_interval, timestep_shift, num_timesteps)` → calls inference.
2. Inference takes text / image / both → interleaved inference over the input list.
3. For each input item: build `gen_context` (with the text) and `cfg_text_context` (without it); `gen_context["past_key_values"]` → the text's KV cache becomes the context for CFG.
4. Generate the image.

### D types
- Mostly illegible: model weights in [bf16/float]; VAE model/decoder dtype.

### Precisions (VLMs › notes, 24 Aug 2025)
- F32 / float → default.
- Checkpoint *(uncertain)*: fp16 / bf16 → set all dtypes *(uncertain)*.

### Bagel train code notes (VLMs › Integration, 26 Aug 2025)
- From Hugging Face directly: 1. Qwen2 LLM; 2. SigLIP ViT.
- Bagel checkpoint: VAE, time embedder, MoE extensions → [created] *(uncertain)*.
- init + setup ⇒ install as a package.

## Summary
These are engineering notes from re-implementing [Visual Lexicon](#/note/visual-lexicon) on an **SDXL** backbone and then porting it into the **[Bagel](#/note/bagel)** codebase. They cover the encoder side (SDXL's two CLIP text encoders, giving a 2048-dim sequence plus a 1280-dim pooled embedding, with image tokens projected into the same space), learnable-query attention pooling over multi-layer ViT features, the standard latent-diffusion training loop (VAE encode, add noise at random timesteps, UNet predicts noise), Bagel's packed-sequence data pipeline (registry, WebDataset/Parquet, RoPE position ids), EMA of weights, and the CFG inference path.
