notes.title: TULIP: Towards Unified Language-Image Pretraining
notes.tldr: TULIP is a drop-in CLIP/SigLIP replacement from Berkeley that adds image-image and text-text contrastive losses, generative positive/negative augmentations (GeCo) and reconstruction regularizers so the encoder keeps fine visual detail while staying language-aligned.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Second paper sent to me in the *VLM papers* doc (tulip-berkeley.github.io).

## Summary
TULIP (UC Berkeley, Darrell group, with David Chan) starts from a known weakness of CLIP-style encoders: because they are trained only to match images with captions, they emphasize high-level semantics and lose visual detail, so they do badly at counting, depth, fine-grained recognition and other "vision-centric" tasks. Vision-only self-supervised models (DINO, MAE) keep that detail but do not understand language. TULIP tries to get both in one encoder that can directly replace SigLIP. It adds contrastive learning between different views of the same image and of the same text, uses generative models to create those views (including hard negatives), and regularizes the embeddings by asking them to reconstruct the input.

## Problem
Contrastive image–text models prioritize semantics over visual understanding, which hurts tasks requiring high-fidelity perception; vision-centric models lack language grounding. The goal is a language-aligned encoder with fine-grained visual features.

## Related work
- CLIP ([2103.00020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020)), SigLIP ([2303.15343](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.15343)) and SigLIP 2 — contrastive image–text encoders; TULIP uses SigLIP's sigmoid loss and initializes from SigLIP checkpoints.
- DINO ([2104.14294](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.14294)) / DINOv2 — EMA teacher with global/local multi-crop views, adopted for the image branch.
- MAE — masked autoencoding, used as the image reconstruction regularizer.
- Generative augmentation work (e.g. ALIA) — diffusion-based data augmentation; TULIP plugs it directly into the contrastive loss.

## Method
![Figure 1 from the paper: TULIP overview, combining generative data augmentation, global-local patch-wise image contrastive learning and reconstruction-based regularization on top of image-text contrastive learning](assets/tulip/fig1.png)

All contrastive terms use the SigLIP sigmoid loss $L_{\text{SigLIP}}(\{x\},\{y\})$ between two sets of views:
- **Image–text:** $L_{\text{I-T}} = L_{\text{SigLIP}}(\{x_I\},\{x_T\})$, the standard SigLIP objective.
- **Image–image:** $L_{\text{I-I}}$ between an image and an augmented view. Following DINOv2, an EMA teacher sees only global crops while the student sees global and local crops, with patch-level objectives to encode spatial detail.
- **Text–text:** $L_{\text{T-T}}$ between a caption and its paraphrase, using SigLIP's text encoder with tied weights (no EMA teacher).
- **GeCo (Generative Contrastive view augmentation):** Llama-3.1-8B-Instruct writes positive paraphrases (same meaning) and negative ones (subtly changed meaning). An instruction-based image-editing diffusion model, adapted with learned soft-prompt embeddings, generates positive views (trained on consecutive video frames and multi-view images) and negative views (trained on InstructPix2Pix-style edits, e.g. adding a car to a picture of a bike). Pairs are weighted +1 (positive), −1 (negative) or 0 (ignore).
- **Reconstruction regularization:** an MAE-style decoder reconstructs masked image patches using the image embedding as a bottleneck, and a T5-based causal decoder reconstructs the caption from the text embedding: $L_{\text{recons}} = \lambda_i L_{\text{image}} + \lambda_t L_{\text{text}}$. This counteracts the invariances that heavy augmentation would otherwise impose.

Reused: SigLIP architectures and weights, DINOv2's teacher–student multi-crop scheme, MAE, Llama-3.1 and an image-editing diffusion model. New: combining all of these objectives in one encoder and the GeCo generative positive/negative view pipeline.

## Data
500M samples from DataComp-1B, with 20% of captions replaced by re-captioned text (50% for the text-reconstruction branch). GeCo's image editor is trained on WebVid-10M consecutive frames (within 0.2 s), MVImgNet multi-view images and InstructPix2Pix data.

## Training
For one image–caption pair: GeCo produces a positive and a negative edited image and a positive and a negative paraphrase. The image and its views pass through the ViT (student) and EMA teacher for image–image losses; the caption and paraphrases pass through the text encoder for text–text losses; image and text embeddings meet in the SigLIP image–text loss, with negatives labeled −1. The image embedding also feeds the MAE decoder, and the text embedding the T5 decoder, for reconstruction. All terms are optimized in the same step. Setup: weights initialized from SigLIP (new projection heads and decoders from scratch), Adam with LR $10^{-5}$, batch 49,152, up to 32 A100 GPUs for several days.

## Results
- New state-of-the-art zero-shot ImageNet-1K performance among comparable models, scaling to over 1B parameters, and strong text-to-image retrieval on COCO and Flickr30K.
- Up to **2×** better than SigLIP on RxRx1 linear-probe few-shot classification; linear-probe results even beat larger models like AIMv2 3B on several datasets.
- When used as a VLM's vision encoder, over **3×** higher scores than SigLIP on MMVP, plus gains on vision-centric benchmarks and Winoground.

## Takeaways / questions
- A nice synthesis: contrastive alignment for language, self-distillation for spatial detail, reconstruction to prevent over-invariance. Each piece is known; the combination is the contribution.
- Directly relevant to my group: same lab as ViLex, and both attack the "CLIP loses visual detail" problem from different sides (TULIP with more objectives, ViLex with a generative decoder as supervision).
- The cost is complexity: several extra models (LLM, image editor, decoders) in the training loop.

notes.title: GLIDE: Towards Photorealistic Image Generation and Editing with Text-Guided Diffusion Models
notes.tldr: OpenAI's GLIDE trains a 3.5B text-conditional pixel diffusion model and compares CLIP guidance vs classifier-free guidance; humans prefer classifier-free guidance, and GLIDE beats DALL-E in human evals and can be fine-tuned for text-driven inpainting.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed under “T2I – pure image generation”.

## Summary
GLIDE (Guided Language to Image Diffusion for Generation and Editing) is OpenAI's late-2021 text-to-image diffusion model and the direct predecessor of DALL-E 2's decoder. Its main contribution is an empirical comparison of two ways to steer a diffusion model toward a text prompt — CLIP guidance and classifier-free guidance — finding that classifier-free guidance wins on both photorealism and caption match. It also shows that the same model, fine-tuned with masks, becomes a strong text-driven inpainting/editing tool.

## Problem
Diffusion models had just overtaken GANs on class-conditional ImageNet using *classifier guidance* (see [diffusion-models-beat-gans](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.05233)), but free-form text is not a fixed set of labels. How should one guide a diffusion model with arbitrary captions, and can the result beat autoregressive models like DALL-E?

## Related work
- Diffusion Models Beat GANs — [2105.05233](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.05233): ADM U-Net and classifier guidance, which GLIDE extends to text.
- Classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans, 2021): guidance without a separate classifier.
- CLIP — [2103.00020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020): used here as the "classifier" for CLIP guidance.
- DALL-E — [2102.12092](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.12092): the autoregressive baseline; GLIDE trains on the same dataset.
- SDEdit (Meng et al., 2021): sketch-plus-noise editing, combined with GLIDE in the paper.

## Method
**Architecture.** A 64×64 text-conditional diffusion U-Net in the ADM style (3.5B parameters), plus a 1.5B text-conditional upsampler to 256×256. Text is tokenized into $K$ tokens and passed through a new Transformer text encoder (24 residual blocks, width 2048, ~1.2B parameters). Its final token embedding replaces the class embedding in the U-Net, and the last-layer token embeddings are projected into every attention layer so the image features can attend to the text.

**Two guidance strategies compared.**
- *CLIP guidance*: train a "noised" CLIP (a 64×64 ViT-L that sees noisy images) and, at each sampling step, nudge the mean of the denoising step along the gradient of the CLIP image–caption similarity.
- *Classifier-free guidance*: during training, captions are sometimes replaced by an empty sequence $\emptyset$, so one network learns both conditional and unconditional predictions. At sampling time
$$\hat\epsilon = \epsilon_\theta(x_t\mid\emptyset) + s\,\big(\epsilon_\theta(x_t\mid c) - \epsilon_\theta(x_t\mid\emptyset)\big),$$
with guidance scale $s>1$ extrapolating toward the caption.

**Inpainting (new fine-tuning).** Random regions of training images are erased, and the model receives the remaining pixels plus a mask channel as extra input. This turns GLIDE into an editor: users can erase a region and describe what should appear, iterate edits to build complex scenes, or combine sketches with text via SDEdit.

![Figure 1 from the paper: one of the selected GLIDE samples generated with classifier-free guidance](assets/glide/fig1.png)

**What is reused vs new.** The diffusion backbone and training recipe come from ADM/improved DDPM; CLIP's training recipe is reused for the noised CLIP. New: the text-conditioning pathway, the systematic guidance comparison, the inpainting fine-tune, and a smaller released "filtered" model.

## Data
Trained on the same image–text dataset as DALL-E. For the public release, OpenAI trained a smaller model on a filtered dataset (for example, removing training images containing people), and noted the filtered model is less capable and still shows biases.

## Training
A caption–image pair: the caption goes through the text Transformer; the image (64×64 for the base model) is noised to a random timestep; the U-Net, attending to the text tokens, predicts the noise and is trained with the denoising objective (captions dropped to $\emptyset$ some of the time so classifier-free guidance works). The upsampler is trained analogously, conditioned on the low-res image. Evaluation sampling uses 250 diffusion steps for the base model.

## Results
- Human evaluators prefer classifier-free guidance over CLIP guidance for both photorealism and caption similarity.
- Samples from the 3.5B model with classifier-free guidance are preferred over DALL-E's, even when DALL-E uses expensive CLIP reranking and GLIDE samples are blurred to match DALL-E's VAE.
- Zero-shot MS-COCO 256×256 FID of 12.24 (12.89 on a validation subset purged of images similar to the training set).
- Classifier-free guidance gives a clean FID-vs-alignment trade-off as the scale increases.

## Takeaways / questions
- GLIDE is where classifier-free guidance became the default for text-to-image; nearly every later system (Imagen, Stable Diffusion, DALL-E 2) uses it.
- Interesting that a "dumb" trick (dropping the caption) beat explicit CLIP gradients: CLIP guidance can be exploited adversarially by the sampler.
- Pixel-space generation at 3.5B parameters is costly; DALL-E 2 kept this decoder but added a CLIP-latent prior.

notes.title: Photorealistic Text-to-Image Diffusion Models with Deep Language Understanding
notes.tldr: Imagen (Google) pairs a frozen T5-XXL text encoder with a cascade of pixel-space diffusion models (64→256→1024 px); scaling the text encoder matters more than scaling the image model, giving zero-shot COCO FID 7.27.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed under “T2I – pure image generation (often heavily diffusion based)”.

*From onenote (2025-08-17):*

*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, VLMs › Vilex › "Imagen", 17 Aug 2025.*

- **Conditioning**: cross-attention / text conditioning (query = image features, key & value = text).
- **CFG**: sometimes don't condition, so the model learns denoising with and without guidance.
- Text → encoder → text tokens → UNet → image.
  - Diffusion UNet (scaling blocks + self-attention + cross-attention with the text).
- **Training**: given a noisy image, $t_i$ and text → predict the noise / denoised image.
  - $x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon$, $\epsilon\sim\mathcal N(0, I)$; as $t\to\infty$, $\bar\alpha_t\to0$, so $x_t$ becomes pure $\epsilon$.
- **Inference**: $(t_i, x_t) \to (t_{i-1}, x_{t-1})$.

## Summary
Imagen is Google Brain's 2022 text-to-image model. Its headline finding is surprisingly simple: a large language model trained only on text (T5-XXL), kept frozen, is an excellent text encoder for image generation, and making that text encoder bigger helps image quality and prompt-following more than making the image diffusion model bigger. Combined with a cascade of diffusion models and a new sampling trick (dynamic thresholding), it set a new zero-shot COCO FID of 7.27 and introduced the DrawBench prompt suite for human evaluation.

## Problem
Text-to-image models need two things: understanding the prompt (objects, counts, spatial relations, text to render) and producing photorealistic pixels. Prior systems (DALL-E, GLIDE, DALL-E 2) mostly relied on text encoders trained on image–text pairs (e.g. CLIP) or trained jointly. The question Imagen asks is whether a generic, text-only LLM is a better language backbone, and how to push guidance strength without images becoming oversaturated.

## Related work
- DDPM — [2006.11239](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11239): the denoising diffusion framework.
- Cascaded diffusion models (Ho et al., 2021): low-res model plus super-resolution diffusion models with noise conditioning augmentation.
- Classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans, 2021): trading diversity for fidelity/alignment.
- GLIDE — [2112.10741](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.10741) and DALL-E 2 — [2204.06125](https://arxiv.org/abs/2204.06125): concurrent/prior text-guided diffusion systems.
- T5 (Raffel et al.): the text-only encoder that Imagen reuses frozen.

## Method
Imagen is a pipeline of three diffusion models conditioned on text embeddings:

1. **Text encoder (reused, frozen):** T5-XXL maps the prompt to a sequence of embeddings. It is never fine-tuned. The paper compares BERT, T5 and CLIP encoders: T5-XXL and CLIP look similar on COCO, but humans prefer T5-XXL on the harder DrawBench prompts.
2. **Base model (new):** a 64×64 text-conditional diffusion U-Net (2B parameters by default). Text is injected via pooled embeddings and cross-attention over the token sequence.
3. **Two super-resolution diffusion models (new):** 64→256 (600M) and 256→1024 (400M). These use *noise conditioning augmentation*: the low-res input is corrupted with noise during training, and the model is told the noise level, which makes the cascade robust to artifacts from the previous stage. The SR models use a new **Efficient U-Net** variant that the authors describe as simpler, faster to converge and more memory efficient.

**Classifier-free guidance + dynamic thresholding.** Large guidance weights improve alignment but push predicted pixels outside $[-1,1]$, giving saturated, unnatural images. Imagen's fix: at each sampling step, take a high percentile $s$ of the absolute pixel values of the predicted clean image $\hat{x}_0^t$; if $s>1$, clip to $[-s,s]$ and divide by $s$. This pulls saturated pixels inward at every step and allows very large guidance weights with better photorealism.

## Data
About 460M image–text pairs from internal datasets plus the public LAION dataset (about 400M pairs). No COCO training data is used, so COCO results are zero-shot.

## Training
For one training example: the caption goes through frozen T5-XXL to get token embeddings; the image is resized to 64×64; a random timestep $t$ is sampled and Gaussian noise is added; the base U-Net, conditioned on the text embeddings (and dropped text some fraction of the time, enabling classifier-free guidance), predicts the noise, and the loss is the standard denoising MSE. Super-resolution models are trained the same way but additionally conditioned on a (noise-augmented) low-res version of the image. All models use batch size 2048 and 2.5M training steps.

## Results
- Zero-shot FID-30K on COCO of **7.27**, a new state of the art at the time, better even than models trained on COCO.
- Human raters find Imagen on par with the COCO reference images for image–text alignment; for photorealism it gets a 39.2% preference rate against the real images (rising to about 43% on the subset without people).
- On DrawBench, human raters prefer Imagen over VQ-GAN+CLIP, Latent Diffusion, GLIDE and DALL-E 2 in side-by-side comparisons for both quality and alignment.
- Scaling the text encoder improves fidelity and alignment much more than scaling the image U-Net.

## Takeaways / questions
- The core lesson ("language understanding is the bottleneck, and text-only LLMs already have it") foreshadows later systems that plug LLMs into image generators.
- Pixel-space cascades are expensive; latent diffusion ([stable-diffusion](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.10752)) took the opposite route of compressing first.
- Dynamic thresholding is a nice example of a tiny sampling-time fix enabling a big change in behavior (very high guidance).
- Imagen was not released publicly; DrawBench is a human-preference benchmark, so comparisons depend on rater setup.

notes.title: Emerging Properties in Unified Multimodal Pretraining
notes.tldr: BAGEL (ByteDance Seed) is an open unified model on Qwen2.5 with separate understanding and generation Transformer experts sharing attention, pretrained on trillions of interleaved text/image/video tokens; reasoning-heavy editing emerges late.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed under “T2I – pure image generation”; also recommended to me in the *VLM papers* doc (“You might also be interested in this model: bagel-ai.org”).

From my latent-visual-reasoning notes (Aug 2026): BAGEL is interesting for a related but different reason. It's a unified decoder-only multimodal model that supports both understanding and visual generation, so it potentially gives us a backbone where internal visual states are not connected only to perception but also to a generative visual pathway. That makes it interesting for grounding and observability: ideally I want a reasoning latent that affects the final answer causally, but I also want some mechanism for asking what visual information that latent contains. Again, generation ability doesn't prove causal reasoning, but it gives us a much richer experimental platform for studying that relationship.

*From onenote (2025-08-17):*

*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, VLMs › Vilex › "Bagel", 17 Aug 2025.*

- **Mixture of transformer experts**: selective activation of modality-specific parameters → a generation expert & an understanding expert.
- Image (one model) → SigLIP ViT → linear → sequence of ViT tokens; image → VAE → latent tokens. Text → `embed_tokens` → text tokens.
- Sample → **packed sample** = one long sequence (each sample has its own loss).
  - (1) $[\text{text}_1 \dots \text{text}_L]$ causal; (2) $[\text{ViT}_1 \dots \text{ViT}_M]$ bidirectional; (3) $[\text{VAE}_1 \dots \text{VAE}_N]$ bidirectional.
  - split $[T, M, S]$ → modes ["causal", "bidir", "bidir"]; attention mask $(B, \text{heads}, \text{seq}, \text{seq})$ over T1, T2, ViT1, ViT2, VAE1, VAE2 (✓/✗ matrix).
  - `ce_loss_mask` = boolean, True on text; `mse_loss_mask` = True on the VAE image tokens.
- (2) Image → patchify → tokens → ViT: $(C, H/P, W/P, P)$ → $(H/P\cdot W/P,\ P^2C)$ = (num_patch × patch_dim); linear projection → token embed + positional embed (from position ids) = input embed.
- (3) Image → VAE encode → padded latent $(B, 4, H/8, W/8)$; $H_\text{vae} = H/\text{down}$, $H^* = H_\text{vae}/p$ → $[H^*, W^*, 2, 2, 4]$ → $[H^*W^*, 2\cdot2\cdot4]$ → **flow matching** (create random noise).
- → **Qwen**( normalization → separate; self-attention → shared; MLP → separate for understanding & generation ).
- **Losses**: generation = flow-matching loss (MSE on the last hidden state); CE = `cross_entropy(ce, label_ids)`.
- **Datasets**: 1. t2i pretrain (image + captions; text causal; VAE full noise); 2. unified editing (images + instructions → ViT + text (causal) + VAE → generation loss on VAE); 3. VLM data (text interleaved with images → text + ViT tokens, no VAE → loss on assistant tokens).

## Summary
BAGEL (Scalable Generative Cognitive Model, ByteDance Seed) is an open-source model that both understands and generates images inside one decoder-only Transformer, in the spirit of proprietary systems like GPT-4o. It starts from the Qwen2.5 LLM, adds a second full copy of the Transformer as a "generation expert", and lets both experts share self-attention over one interleaved sequence of text, understanding tokens (from SigLIP2) and generation tokens (FLUX VAE latents trained with rectified flow). The paper's headline is about scale and data: as pretraining on interleaved web and video data grows, abilities appear in a sequence, first basic understanding and generation, then editing, then "intelligent" editing that needs reasoning and world knowledge.

## Problem
Open unified models lagged far behind proprietary ones. The authors argue that the bottleneck is less architecture than data: image–text pairs alone do not teach the rich, reasoning-heavy behavior seen in closed systems, so they build large interleaved datasets and an architecture with no bottleneck between understanding and generation.

## Related work
- Transfusion ([2408.11039](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.11039)) — one Transformer with next-token loss on text and diffusion loss on continuous image latents.
- Chameleon ([2405.09818](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.09818)) — early-fusion with discrete image tokens.
- Mixture-of-Transformers — modality-specific Transformer weights with shared attention, the MoT design adopted here.
- Janus / Janus-Pro and MetaQuery — other unified models used as baselines.
- SigLIP ([2303.15343](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.15343)) — SigLIP2 initializes the understanding ViT.

## Method
![Figure 2 from the paper: BAGEL's two Transformer experts (understanding and generation) with shared multimodal self-attention, and separate ViT and VAE encoders](assets/bagel/onenote-fig1.png)

**Reused pieces:** Qwen2.5 LLM (decoder-only, RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE) as initialization; SigLIP2-so400m/14 as the understanding encoder; the pretrained FLUX VAE (8× downsampling, 16 latent channels) for generation, with a 2×2 patch embedding.

**New pieces:**
- **Mixture-of-Transformer-Experts (MoT):** all Qwen2.5 parameters are duplicated into a generation expert. Hard routing: VAE tokens go through the generation expert; text and ViT tokens go through the understanding expert. Both experts share self-attention in every layer, so information flows freely between them. Total 14B parameters, 7B active per token. In a 1.5B-scale ablation MoT beat both a dense model and an MoE (FFN-only duplication) variant at identical FLOPs.
- **Objectives:** next-token prediction for text; Rectified Flow (flow matching) with an MSE loss for image latents. A timestep embedding is added directly to VAE tokens instead of AdaLN.
- **Generalized causal attention:** the sequence is split into single-modality spans; each span can attend to earlier spans, with images represented as noised VAE tokens (for the loss), clean VAE tokens and ViT tokens (as context for what comes later). Later tokens see only clean VAE and ViT tokens of earlier images, never their noised versions.

## Data
Text, image–text pairs, multimodal conversation, and two kinds of interleaved data the authors build: from **video** (inter-frame captions describing changes between consecutive frames, written by a distilled Qwen2.5-VL-7B captioner) and from **web documents** (filtered tutorials and encyclopedic pages with captions added to localize each image). Also reasoning-augmented data for text-to-image, editing and free-form manipulation. The pretraining stage alone uses 2.5T tokens.

## Training
Four stages: (1) **Alignment**, training only the MLP connector between frozen SigLIP2 and frozen Qwen2.5 on captioning; (2) **Pre-training**, adding QK-Norm and training everything except the VAE on 2.5T tokens; (3) **Continued training** at higher resolution; (4) **SFT** on curated generation and understanding sets (filtered from LLaVA-OV and Mammoth-VL). For an editing example, the source image enters as ViT and clean VAE tokens, the instruction as text, and the target image as noised VAE tokens at a random flow time; the generation expert predicts the velocity, scored with MSE, while any text in the sequence gets cross-entropy. Tokens are dropped randomly (text 0.1, ViT 0.5, clean VAE 0.1) to enable classifier-free guidance. AdamW ($\beta_1=0.9$, $\beta_2=0.95$) with constant learning rate.

## Results
- Understanding: at 7B active parameters, beats other unified models, e.g. +14.3 on MMMU and +17.1 on MM-Vet over Janus-Pro, and is better on most benchmarks than specialized VLMs like Qwen2.5-VL and InternVL2.5.
- Generation: **88%** overall on GenEval (82% without an LLM prompt rewriter), above FLUX-1-dev (82%), SD3-Medium (74%), Janus-Pro and MetaQuery-XL (80%).
- With explicit chain-of-thought before generating, WISE score goes from 0.52 to **0.70** (previous open SOTA 0.55). Competitive with Step1X-Edit on GEdit-Bench and comparable to Gemini 2.0 on their IntelligentBench.
- Emergence: the Intelligent Edit task needs about 3.61T training tokens to reach 85% of its final score, much later than basic understanding and generation.

## Takeaways / questions
- The MoT idea is a clean answer to the conflict between understanding and generation: separate weights, shared attention.
- "Thinking before generating" helping image generation is directly relevant to interleaved visual reasoning.
- I later used BAGEL as a backbone in my COVA project, and the COVA deck lists it among the latent-visual-reasoning models evaluated on CoVA data.
- Open question from my notes: does the generative pathway actually make latent visual states more inspectable, or just more expressive?

notes.title: BLIP: Bootstrapping Language-Image Pre-training for Unified Vision-Language Understanding and Generation
notes.tldr: BLIP is a single vision-language model that can act as a contrastive encoder, an image-text matcher or a captioner, and it cleans noisy web data by generating synthetic captions and filtering bad pairs (CapFilt) before re-training.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed as “BLIP 2” under “Pretrained (frozen) transformer backbone”.

## Summary
BLIP (Salesforce Research) tackles two weaknesses of vision-language pre-training at the time. On the model side, systems were good either at understanding (retrieval, VQA) or at generation (captioning), not both. On the data side, gains came from scaling up noisy web alt-text, which often does not describe the image. BLIP introduces a "multimodal mixture of encoder-decoder" (MED) that shares weights across three modes, and CapFilt, a bootstrapping loop where the model writes its own captions for web images and a filter discards mismatched pairs. The cleaned dataset then trains a better model.

## Problem
Encoder-only models do not transfer well to text generation, and encoder–decoder models do not do well on retrieval. Web image–text pairs are abundant but noisy, which is a poor supervision signal.

## Related work
- CLIP ([2103.00020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020)) — contrastive pre-training on web pairs.
- ALBEF — image–text contrastive + matching + MLM; BLIP follows its ITC loss, hard negatives and pre-training data.
- SimVLM — generative pre-training on large noisy data.
- BERT ([1810.04805](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805)) — initializes the text transformer.
- ViT ([2010.11929](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929)) — the image encoder (ViT-B/16 or ViT-L/16, ImageNet-pretrained).

## Method
![Figure 2 from the paper: BLIP's multimodal mixture of encoder-decoder and its three pre-training objectives (ITC, ITM, LM)](assets/blip/fig1.png)

**MED architecture.** A ViT image encoder plus a BERT-based text transformer that can run in three modes:
1. **Unimodal text encoder:** encodes text alone; trained with an image–text contrastive (ITC) loss against the image encoder's output.
2. **Image-grounded text encoder:** adds cross-attention to image features in each block; a `[Encode]` token output goes to a linear head for image–text matching (ITM), a binary matched/unmatched classifier using hard negatives.
3. **Image-grounded text decoder:** replaces bidirectional self-attention with causal self-attention and is trained with a language-modeling (LM) loss to generate captions.

The encoder and decoder share all parameters except the self-attention layers, since the difference between encoding and decoding is best captured there.

**CapFilt.** Both a captioner (the decoder, fine-tuned with LM on COCO) and a filter (the grounded encoder, fine-tuned with ITC/ITM on COCO) start from the pre-trained MED. The captioner writes one synthetic caption per web image; the filter removes any web or synthetic caption that its ITM head judges as unmatched. Filtered pairs plus human-annotated pairs form a new dataset to pre-train a fresh model.

Reused: ImageNet-pretrained ViT and BERT-base weights; ALBEF's ITC loss. New: the shared-parameter MED with an LM decoder, and CapFilt.

## Data
14M images: COCO and Visual Genome (human-annotated) plus Conceptual Captions, Conceptual 12M and SBU (web). Larger runs add 115M LAION images (129M total).

## Training
For one image–caption pair: the ViT encodes the image. The text encoder encodes the caption alone, and ITC pulls the matched image and text embeddings together versus others in the batch. The grounded encoder reads the caption while cross-attending to the image and predicts "match" (and "no match" for mined hard-negative captions) for ITM. The decoder reads the caption causally while cross-attending to the image and predicts each next word for LM. All three losses are computed in one step (one image forward pass, three text passes). Setup: 20 epochs, batch 2880 (ViT-B) / 2400 (ViT-L), peak LR 3e-4 / 2e-4.

An important ablation: generating synthetic captions with stochastic nucleus sampling works better than deterministic beam search, because diverse (if noisier) captions carry more new information.

## Results
From the abstract: state of the art on image–text retrieval (**+2.7%** average recall@1), image captioning (**+2.8%** CIDEr) and VQA (**+1.6%** VQA score), plus strong zero-shot transfer to video-language tasks.

## Takeaways / questions
- CapFilt is an early, clean example of a model improving its own training data; this "synthetic re-captioning" idea later became standard for training both VLMs and text-to-image models.
- The finding that diversity beats per-caption quality for synthetic data is worth remembering for dataset work like CoVA-SFT.
- **Label mismatch:** I labeled this link "BLIP 2", but 2201.12086 is BLIP (v1). BLIP-2 is [2301.12597](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.12597), which adds the Q-Former bridge between a frozen image encoder and a frozen LLM, and is the one that fits my "pretrained frozen backbone" heading.

notes.title: Chameleon: Mixed-Modal Early-Fusion Foundation Models
notes.tldr: Chameleon (Meta) turns images into discrete tokens and trains one Llama-style Transformer from scratch on interleaved text and image tokens, so it can both read and generate any mix of images and text; making this stable needed QK-Norm, norm reordering and z-loss.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed under “Full autoregressive models”.

## Summary
Chameleon (Meta FAIR) is a "fully token-based" multimodal model. Instead of bolting a vision encoder onto a language model, it converts every image into a sequence of discrete codes from a learned image tokenizer, adds those codes to the vocabulary, and trains a single decoder-only Transformer to predict the next token, whether that token is a word or a piece of an image. Because images and text share one sequence from the very first layer ("early fusion"), the same model can caption, answer questions, generate images, and write documents with images interleaved anywhere. The paper's main engineering contribution is how to keep such training stable at 7B and 34B scale.

## Problem
Most multimodal models process each modality with separate encoders or decoders ("late fusion"), which limits their ability to handle and generate arbitrary interleaved image–text documents. Training a single early-fusion model is attractive but hard: mixing modalities causes optimization instabilities that do not appear in text-only LLMs.

## Related work
- Make-A-Scene image tokenizer (Gafni et al. 2022) — basis for Chameleon's VQ image tokenizer.
- Llama 2 — the base architecture (RMSNorm, SwiGLU, RoPE) and part of the text data.
- Flamingo, IDEFICS, LLaVA-1.5 ([2304.08485](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08485) is v1) — late-fusion VLM baselines.
- Swin Transformer v2 ([2103.14030](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.14030) is v1) — source of the norm-reordering trick.
- Transfusion ([2408.11039](https://arxiv.org/abs/2408.11039)) — later work from Meta that keeps images continuous and uses diffusion instead of discrete tokens.

## Method
**Tokenization (new tokenizer, existing design).** A VQ image tokenizer encodes a 512×512 image into 1024 discrete tokens from a codebook of 8192. A BPE text tokenizer has a 65,536-token vocabulary that includes the 8192 image codes. The paper notes the tokenizer's core weakness is reconstructing images with lots of text, which caps OCR-heavy performance.

**Architecture.** A standard Llama-2-style decoder-only Transformer (7B and 34B). Images are just token spans in the sequence, marked by special start/end-of-image tokens. No separate vision encoder or image decoder head.

**Stability changes (new for this setting):**
- **QK-Norm:** layer-normalize queries and keys inside attention to control norm growth of the softmax inputs. They traced late-training divergences to the softmax's translation invariance when modalities with very different entropy are mixed, which lets norms drift upward slowly.
- **Dropout** after attention and feed-forward layers (needed for 7B).
- **Norm reordering** (Swin-v2 style, normalizing the output of each sub-block before adding to the residual) for 34B, which bounds feed-forward norm growth.
- **z-loss** on the output softmax's partition function to prevent logit drift.

## Data
- 2.9 trillion text-only tokens (Llama-2 and CodeLlama data mixes).
- 1.4 billion image–text pairs (public and licensed), resized and center-cropped to 512×512, giving 1.5 trillion tokens; half the time the image comes before the text (captioning direction).
- 400 billion tokens of interleaved web image–text documents.
- Two stages: the first 80% of training on this mix; for the last 20% the first-stage data is down-weighted by 50% and higher-quality data (including filtered instruction-tuning sets) is mixed in. 2.1 epochs, 9.2 trillion tokens seen in total.

## Training
A document like "Here is a photo of my dog: [image] What breed is it?" becomes one flat token sequence: text tokens, a begin-image token, 1024 image codes, an end-image token, more text. The Transformer predicts every next token with ordinary cross-entropy over the joint vocabulary, so image codes are learned exactly like words. At generation time, when the model emits begin-image, it samples 1024 codes that the tokenizer's decoder turns back into pixels. Optimization: AdamW ($\beta_1=0.9$, $\beta_2=0.95$), 4000 warm-up steps, weight decay 0.1; global batch about 8M tokens (7B) and 12M tokens (34B). This is followed by supervised fine-tuning and alignment.

## Results
- Image captioning and VQA: Chameleon-34B reaches state-of-the-art captioning results, outperforming models like Flamingo, IDEFICS and LLaVA-1.5; its 2-shot COCO result beats the 80B Flamingo and IDEFICS models with 32 shots.
- Text-only: outperforms Llama-2 and is competitive with Mixtral 8x7B and Gemini-Pro.
- Human evaluation on long-form mixed-modal prompts: 60.4% preference vs Gemini-Pro and 51.6% vs GPT-4V; 55.2% of Chameleon responses fully fulfil the task vs 37.6% for Gemini+ and 44.7% for GPT-4V+ (baselines augmented with generated images).

## Takeaways / questions
- The cleanest version of "everything is a token": one vocabulary, one loss, one model. Its weakness is the lossy discrete image tokenizer, which limits image quality and text-in-image fidelity.
- The stability tricks (QK-Norm, z-loss, norm placement) are useful knowledge for anyone training multimodal Transformers from scratch.
- For latent visual reasoning, early-fusion models like this one are natural candidates because the model can "think" in image tokens mid-sequence, though discrete tokens may be a coarse substrate for that.

notes.title: Learning Transferable Visual Models From Natural Language Supervision
notes.tldr: CLIP trains an image encoder and a text encoder together on 400M web image–caption pairs to pick the right caption for each image, giving image features that transfer zero-shot to new tasks by just naming the classes in text.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed under “Vision Transformers → Basic – image encoders”.

## Summary
CLIP (Contrastive Language–Image Pre-training, OpenAI) is the paper that made "learn vision from raw web captions" work at scale. Instead of training an image classifier on a fixed list of labels like ImageNet's 1000 classes, it trains two encoders, one for images and one for text, so that matching image–caption pairs land close together in a shared embedding space. At test time you can classify an image into any set of categories by writing the category names as text and picking the closest one. CLIP's encoders became the default vision backbone for most later vision-language models (LLaVA, MiniGPT-4 via EVA-CLIP, Stable Diffusion's text encoder, and so on).

## Problem
Standard vision models are trained to predict a fixed, predetermined set of categories, so recognizing any new concept needs new labeled data. Text on the internet describes a far wider range of visual concepts for free, but earlier attempts to learn from it (e.g. predicting caption words) were inefficient and reached only 11.5% zero-shot ImageNet accuracy.

## Related work
- VirTex, ICMLM, ConVIRT — learn image representations from text with captioning, masked LM or contrastive objectives, but at small scale (one to two hundred thousand images).
- Visual N-Grams (Li et al. 2017) — earlier zero-shot transfer from text n-grams (11.5% on ImageNet).
- InfoNCE / multi-class N-pair loss — the contrastive batch objective CLIP adopts.
- Vision Transformer ([2010.11929](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929)) — one of the two image-encoder families used.

## Method
![Figure 1 from the paper: CLIP's contrastive pre-training of an image and text encoder, and how the text encoder builds a zero-shot classifier at test time](assets/clip/fig1.png)

Two encoders are trained from scratch together:
- **Image encoder:** either a modified ResNet (ResNet-D tweaks, blur pooling, and attention pooling instead of global average pooling) or a Vision Transformer (ViT-B/32, ViT-B/16, ViT-L/14) with one extra layer norm.
- **Text encoder:** a GPT-2-style Transformer (base: 63M parameters, 12 layers, width 512, 8 heads, BPE vocab 49,152, max length 76). The activation at the `[EOS]` token is the text feature.

Each encoder's output goes through a single linear projection into a shared embedding space (no non-linear projection head). Nothing is reused from pretrained models; what is new is the scale and the choice of a contrastive "which caption goes with which image" task instead of predicting the caption's exact words. The authors found that this switch was 4x more efficient for zero-shot ImageNet than a bag-of-words prediction baseline, which itself was 3x faster than a Transformer captioning model.

**Zero-shot classification:** embed each class name in a prompt such as "A photo of a {label}." with the text encoder, embed the image, and pick the class with the highest cosine similarity. Ensembling several prompts helps further.

## Data
WIT (WebImageText): 400 million (image, text) pairs collected from public internet sources, built by searching for text containing one of 500,000 queries (frequent Wikipedia words, bigrams, Wikipedia article titles, WordNet synsets), with up to 20,000 pairs per query to roughly balance it.

## Training
Take a batch of $N$ image–caption pairs. Each image goes through the image encoder and each caption through the text encoder; both are projected and L2-normalized to vectors $I_i$ and $T_j$. Compute the $N \times N$ matrix of cosine similarities scaled by a learned temperature $\tau$: $s_{ij} = I_i \cdot T_j / \tau$. The diagonal entries are the true pairs. The loss is a symmetric cross-entropy: for each image, softmax over all $N$ captions and maximize the probability of its own caption; for each caption, softmax over all $N$ images likewise; average the two.

Reported details: 32 epochs, Adam with decoupled weight decay, cosine LR schedule, batch size 32,768, temperature initialized to 0.07 and clipped so logits are scaled by at most 100, random square crop as the only augmentation. The largest ResNet (RN50x64) took 18 days on 592 V100 GPUs.

## Results
- Zero-shot ImageNet top-1 goes from 11.5% (Visual N-Grams) to **76.2%**, matching the original fully supervised ResNet-50 without using any of its 1.28M labeled training images.
- Across a 27-dataset suite, zero-shot CLIP beats a fully supervised linear classifier on ResNet-50 features on 16 datasets.
- Zero-shot CLIP roughly matches 16-shot logistic regression on the best public ImageNet-21K features (BiT-M), and is much more robust to natural distribution shift than ImageNet-trained models.

## Takeaways / questions
- The core idea is tiny (a contrastive loss over a batch) but scale and data turn it into a general-purpose visual vocabulary; most later VLMs simply reuse CLIP's ViT.
- Because it only learns "which caption matches," CLIP features are global and semantic; fine detail, counting and spatial relations are weak, which later work (SigLIP, TULIP, ViLex) tries to fix.
- CLIP's image–text similarity is also the basis of the CLIPScore caption metric that I re-implemented.

notes.title: CoCa: Contrastive Captioners are Image-Text Foundation Models
notes.tldr: CoCa trains one image-text model with both a CLIP-style contrastive loss and a captioning loss by splitting its text decoder into a text-only half and an image-conditioned half, getting retrieval, classification and captioning from a single network.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed under “Basic – image encoders”.

## Summary
CoCa (Contrastive Captioner, Google) merges the two dominant ways of learning vision from text. Contrastive dual encoders like CLIP give aligned image and text embeddings (good for retrieval and zero-shot classification) but cannot generate text or fuse modalities. Encoder–decoder captioners like SimVLM can generate and fuse, but do not give a text embedding aligned with the image. CoCa gets both in one model and one forward pass, with a cheap architectural trick: the bottom half of the text decoder does not look at the image at all, so its output can serve as the text embedding for the contrastive loss, while the top half cross-attends to the image and is trained to caption.

## Problem
Vision foundation models were split across three families (single-encoder classifiers, contrastive dual encoders, generative encoder–decoders), each good at a different set of downstream tasks. The goal is one pretrained model that serves recognition, crossmodal retrieval, captioning and multimodal understanding.

## Related work
- CLIP ([2103.00020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020)) and ALIGN — contrastive dual encoders.
- SimVLM — encoder–decoder pre-training with a (prefix) language-modeling loss.
- LiT and BASIC — combine supervised image pre-training with contrastive text training in multiple stages; CoCa does it in one stage from scratch.
- ViT ([2010.11929](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.11929)) — the image encoder is a ViT (ViT-giant setup for the largest model).

## Method
![Figure 2 from the paper: CoCa architecture, with an image encoder, a unimodal text decoder trained with the contrastive loss, and a multimodal text decoder trained with the captioning loss](assets/coca/fig1.png)

- **Image encoder:** a ViT. Images at 288×288 with 18×18 patches give 256 image tokens.
- **Decoupled text decoder:** a causal Transformer split in half. The bottom $n_{\text{uni}}$ layers use only causally masked self-attention (no image), producing unimodal text representations. A learnable `[CLS]` token appended to the end of the sentence gives the text embedding. The top $n_{\text{multi}}$ layers add cross-attention to the image tokens and predict the caption autoregressively.
- **Attentional poolers:** a single multi-head attention layer with learnable queries summarizes the image tokens. The contrastive loss uses a pooler with 1 query (one global image vector); the captioning branch uses a pooler with 256 queries (finer-grained tokens).

The total loss is $\mathcal{L}_{\text{CoCa}} = \lambda_{\text{Con}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{Con}} + \lambda_{\text{Cap}}\mathcal{L}_{\text{Cap}}$. Because the decoder is causal, both losses come out of one forward pass, so the overhead over a plain captioner is small.

Nothing is reused from pretrained checkpoints: everything is trained from scratch. What is new is the split-decoder design and the attentional poolers that let one network serve both objectives. Sizes: CoCa-Base 383M, CoCa-Large 787M, and CoCa 2.1B parameters (1B in the image encoder).

## Data
JFT-3B (labelled images, where label names are turned into text like "a photo of the cat, animal") plus the ALIGN dataset of noisy web alt-text. Each batch is half JFT, half ALIGN. Near-duplicates of downstream test sets (3.6M images) were removed. Text uses a 64k SentencePiece vocabulary.

## Training
An image is split into 256 patches and encoded by the ViT. Its caption runs through the unimodal decoder layers; the `[CLS]` output and the 1-query pooled image vector go into a CLIP-style contrastive loss against the other pairs in the batch (temperature initialized at 0.07). The same text then continues through the multimodal layers, which cross-attend to the 256-query pooled image tokens and predict each next caption token (cross-entropy). The two losses are summed with $\lambda_{\text{Cap}}=2.0$, $\lambda_{\text{Con}}=1.0$.

Reported setup: batch 65,536 pairs, 500k steps (about 5 epochs of JFT and 10 of ALIGN), Adafactor, peak LR $8\times10^{-4}$, about 5 days on 2,048 Cloud TPUv4 chips, then one extra epoch at 576×576 resolution.

## Results
- ImageNet: **86.3%** zero-shot top-1, 90.6% with a frozen encoder plus learned head, and 91.0% after fine-tuning (state of the art at the time).
- Frozen encoder on video: 88.0% / 88.5% / 81.1% on Kinetics-400/600/700, 47.4% on Moments-in-Time.
- After light fine-tuning: 82.3% on VQA and 120.6 CIDEr on NoCaps; also better zero-shot retrieval on MSCOCO and Flickr30k than prior dual encoders.

## Takeaways / questions
- The split decoder is an elegant way to get "CLIP plus captioner" almost for free; captioning acts as a denser training signal than contrastive matching alone.
- The finding that a 1-token pooled vector helps recognition while many tokens help VQA is a useful design principle for vision towers in VLMs.
- Trained on private data (JFT-3B, ALIGN) with huge compute, so hard to reproduce; open re-implementations exist (e.g. in OpenCLIP), but the paper's numbers come from the private setup.

notes.title: F-VLM: Open-Vocabulary Object Detection upon Frozen Vision and Language Models
notes.tldr: F-VLM builds an open-vocabulary object detector on a completely frozen CLIP image encoder, training only a Mask R-CNN detector head and mixing its scores with CLIP's region scores at test time, beating prior LVIS results with far less compute.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed as “Frozen” under “Pretrained (frozen) transformer backbone”.

## Summary
F-VLM (Google) shows that you can turn a frozen CLIP-style vision–language model into a strong open-vocabulary object detector, one that can find categories it never saw boxes for, without fine-tuning the backbone, distilling knowledge, or special detection pre-training. The authors observe that frozen CLIP features already carry two things a detector needs: they are locality-sensitive (object boundaries show up in the feature map) and they classify cropped regions well. So they bolt a standard detector head onto the frozen backbone, train only the head, and at test time combine the head's scores with CLIP's own region classification.

## Problem
Box and mask annotation is expensive, so detection vocabularies stay around $10^3$ categories. Vision–language models know far more concepts, but prior ways of using them for detection (ViLD-style distillation, detection-tailored pretraining, weak supervision) are multi-stage and compute-heavy.

## Related work
- CLIP ([2103.00020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020)) and ALIGN — the frozen VLMs used.
- ViLD — open-vocabulary detection by distilling CLIP into a detector; the main baseline.
- Mask R-CNN, FPN, RPN — the detector head components.
- OWL-ViT, DetPro, RegionCLIP — other open-vocabulary detectors compared on LVIS.

## Method
![Figure 2(a) from the paper: F-VLM training, a detector head on a frozen VLM backbone with base-category text embeddings as the classifier](assets/f-vlm/fig1.png)

**Reused, frozen:** the CLIP image encoder's feature extractor $\mathcal{F}$ (e.g. ResNet-50 up to R50x64), its final attention-pooling layer $\mathcal{P}$, and the matching CLIP text encoder.

**New, trained:** only the detector head (RPN + FPN + Mask R-CNN heads), with class-agnostic box and mask prediction.

1. **Text-embedding classifier.** The detector's last classification layer is replaced by CLIP text embeddings of the base category names plus a "background" phrase. A region embedding $\mathbf{r}_b$ is classified by cosine similarity to these, softmaxed with a learnable temperature, giving detection scores $\mathbf{z}(\mathbf{r}_b)$.
2. **VLM region scores at test time.** For each proposed box, the frozen backbone features are cropped with ROI-Align and passed through CLIP's own pooling layer to get $\mathbf{v}_b$, then scored against text embeddings of all (base + novel) categories, giving $\mathbf{w}(\mathbf{v}_b)$.
3. **Score combination.** Geometric mean with separate weights for base and novel classes:
   $$s_i = z_i^{1-\alpha} w_i^{\alpha}\ \ (i \in C_B), \qquad s_i = z_i^{1-\beta} w_i^{\beta}\ \ (i \in C_N)$$
   The detector head is good at localization quality; CLIP is good at recognizing novel categories.

## Data
LVIS (1203 categories): frequent and common categories are "base" for training, rare categories are held out as "novel". Also COCO's open-vocabulary split (48 base / 17 novel) and transfer to Objects365.

## Training
An image (1024×1024, large-scale jittering) passes through the frozen CLIP backbone. The trainable FPN/RPN proposes boxes; ROI features go through the head to get a region embedding, which is compared with the text embeddings of base classes and "background"; the loss is softmax cross-entropy on those logits, plus standard box regression and mask losses. Proposals that do not match a base-class box count as background. Setup: 46.1k iterations, batch 256. Novel categories are only added at test time by appending their text embeddings.

## Results
- LVIS open-vocabulary: the best model (R50x64 backbone) reaches **32.8 mask AP on rare (novel) categories**, +6.5 over the best previous system (ViLD-EN-B7) and +14.2 over F-VLM's own R50 version.
- Performance scales with frozen backbone size even though trainable parameters stay fixed.
- Compared with ViLD at system level, F-VLM is 226× more compute-efficient and 57× faster in wall-clock training.
- Competitive on COCO open-vocabulary and on cross-dataset transfer to Objects365.

## Takeaways / questions
- Strong evidence that contrastive VLM feature maps retain spatial, region-level information, even though CLIP is only trained on global image–caption matching.
- Freezing the backbone both saves compute and prevents overfitting to base classes, which is what keeps the novel-class recognition intact.
- **Label mismatch:** I labeled this link "Frozen", but 2209.15639 is F-VLM (Kuo et al.), not the 2021 "Frozen" paper by Tsimpoukelli et al. ([2106.13884](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.13884)), which feeds image features into a frozen language model for few-shot captioning/VQA and fits my "pretrained frozen backbone" category better.

notes.title: FLAVA: A Foundational Language And Vision Alignment Model
notes.tldr: FLAVA is one model with an image encoder, a text encoder and a fusion encoder, pretrained on public data with contrastive, masked-modeling and matching losses so it handles vision-only, language-only and joint vision-language tasks.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed under “Masked – reasoning (no generation)”.

## Summary
FLAVA (Meta AI) argues that a real vision-and-language foundation model should be good at three things at once: pure vision tasks, pure language tasks, and tasks that need both. CLIP-style models give good separate embeddings but cannot reason over an image and text jointly; fusion models like those trained for VQA often ignore single-modality performance. FLAVA combines both designs in one Transformer stack and trains it with a mix of objectives on both paired and unpaired data, all from openly available datasets. It understands but does not generate, which is why it sits in my "masked, reasoning, no generation" bucket.

## Problem
Models were usually either cross-modal (contrastive, separate encoders) or multimodal (early fusion), not both, and typically relied on large private datasets. The paper asks whether one model trained on public data can be strong across 35 vision, language and multimodal tasks.

## Related work
- CLIP ([2103.00020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020)) and ALIGN — contrastive dual encoders on private data.
- BERT ([1810.04805](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805)) — masked language modeling.
- BEiT — masked image modeling by predicting discrete dVAE tokens for masked patches.
- DINO ([2104.14294](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.14294)) — one option tried for initializing the image encoder.
- SimVLM, VinVL, UniT — earlier vision-language pre-training approaches it compares against.

## Method
![Figure 2 from the paper: FLAVA's image encoder, text encoder and multimodal encoder, with the unimodal and multimodal pretraining losses](assets/flava/fig1.png)

Three Transformers, all with the ViT-B/16 architecture (separate weights):
- **Image encoder:** standard ViT over image patches with a `[CLS_I]` token.
- **Text encoder:** the same ViT architecture applied to word embeddings, with a `[CLS_T]` token.
- **Multimodal encoder:** the image and text hidden states are linearly projected, concatenated with a `[CLS_M]` token, and fused by self-attention across both.

Objectives:
- **Global contrastive (GC):** CLIP-style loss between projected `[CLS_I]` and `[CLS_T]`, but with gradients back-propagated through embeddings from all GPUs, not just the local one (worth +1.65% macro average in their ablation).
- **Masked multimodal modeling (MMM):** image patches are tokenized by a pretrained dVAE (the same as BEiT); block-shaped regions of the image and 15% of text tokens are masked, and the multimodal encoder predicts both.
- **Image–text matching (ITM):** a classifier on `[CLS_M]` predicts whether an image and text belong together.
- **Unimodal MIM and MLM:** on image-only and text-only data, the respective encoder reconstructs masked patches or words.

Reused: the ViT architecture, BEiT's masking scheme and dVAE tokenizer, and BERT-style MLM. New: the specific three-encoder combination and training it jointly on unimodal plus multimodal data.

## Data
PMD (Public Multimodal Datasets): 70M image–text pairs (68M unique images, average caption 12.1 words) assembled from public sources including filtered YFCC100M. Unimodal data: ImageNet-1K for images, CCNews and BookCorpus for text.

## Training
The text encoder is first pretrained with MLM on text; the image encoder is initialized from unimodal image pretraining (they tried MIM and DINO, and found DINO initialization worked well). The multimodal encoder starts from scratch. Then the full model trains with round-robin sampling across datasets: an image-only batch gets the MIM loss, a text-only batch gets MLM, and an image–text batch gets GC (on unmasked inputs) plus MMM and ITM (on masked inputs through the fusion encoder).

## Results
- The full FLAVA model has the best macro average over vision, language and multimodal tasks among all ablations across 35 tasks.
- Adding MMM and ITM to contrastive-only training improves the multimodal average by +2.86% and the NLP average by +9%.
- Compared to the released CLIP ViT-B/16 (400M pairs), FLAVA uses about 6x less data and is significantly better on language and multimodal tasks, slightly worse on some vision-only tasks. It approaches BERT on several GLUE tasks.

## Takeaways / questions
- Good blueprint of the "pre-LLM" VLM era: separate encoders plus a fusion encoder, many objectives, no generation.
- Shows that masked modeling and matching losses add language and multimodal skill that contrastive training alone does not give.
- Later VLMs largely replaced the fusion encoder with a large language model fed by a frozen vision encoder (LLaVA, BLIP-2), trading FLAVA's balanced design for generation ability.

notes.title: Masked Vision and Language Modeling for Multi-modal Representation Learning
notes.tldr: MaskVLM masks both image patches and words and reconstructs each modality with help from the other (raw pixels from text, words from the image), plus contrastive and matching losses, giving strong vision-language representations especially with little data.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed as “MaskVLM” under “Masked – reasoning (no generation)”.

## Summary
MaskVLM (AWS AI Labs) takes the "mask and reconstruct" idea that worked for text (BERT) and images (MAE, SimMIM) and makes it explicitly cross-modal. When you mask the word "dog" in a caption, the model should recover it by looking at the dog in the image; when you mask the patch with the green ball, it should recover the pixels using the words "green ball". Training on both directions forces the model to learn which words go with which image regions, without any frozen object detector or image tokenizer in the loop.

## Problem
Earlier vision-language models either masked only text (learning $p(T\mid I)$ but not $p(I\mid T)$), or masked image features produced by a frozen object detector or a frozen dVAE tokenizer. Those frozen components need extra training data and block end-to-end learning of image–text interactions.

## Related work
- BERT ([1810.04805](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805)) — masked language modeling.
- MAE and SimMIM — masked image modeling directly on raw pixel patches.
- BEiT and FLAVA ([2112.04482](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.04482)) — mask image tokens from a pretrained dVAE instead of raw pixels.
- ALBEF — image–text contrastive plus matching with hard negatives; MaskVLM follows its retrieval and negative-sampling recipe.
- CLIP ([2103.00020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020)) — contrastive alignment.

## Method
![Figure 2 from the paper: joint masked vision and language modeling, where masked images are reconstructed with text and masked text with the image](assets/maskvlm/fig1.png)

Architecture:
- **Image encoder** (12 self-attention blocks, a ViT initialized from ImageNet pretraining) and **text encoder** (12 blocks, initialized from RoBERTa). These are reused.
- **Image and text cross-modality encoders** (3 cross-attention blocks each, new): the image one attends to text features and vice versa.
- **Cross-modality decoders** (new): the image decoder (3 cross-attention blocks + a linear layer) maps back to RGB pixels; the text decoder predicts masked tokens.

Losses:
- **Joint masked V+L modeling:** reconstruct the original text from (original image, masked text) with cross-entropy on masked tokens, and reconstruct the original image from (masked image, original text) with an L1 loss on masked pixels:
  $$\mathcal{L}_{MVLM} = \mathcal{H}\big(y_T^M, \phi_{txt}^M(I, T_m)\big) + \tfrac{1}{\Omega(I^M)}\big\|I^M - \phi_{im}^M(I_m, T)\big\|_1$$
- **Image–text contrastive (ITC):** CLIP-style loss on the encoders' `[CLS]` / `[START]` features.
- **Image–text matching (ITM):** binary classifier on the cross-modality features, with hard negatives sampled by similarity.

Total loss: $\mathcal{L} = \mathcal{L}_{MVLM} + \mathcal{L}_{ITC} + \mathcal{L}_{ITM}$.

## Data
The standard "4M" pre-training set: Conceptual Captions, SBU Captions, Visual Genome and COCO Captions (4.1M unique images, 5.2M image–text pairs). Limited-data experiments use subsets with about 39%, 25% and 16% of those pairs.

## Training
Take an image–caption pair at 224×224. For image reconstruction, 60% of the image is masked using 32×32 masking blocks (bigger than the 16×16 ViT patches, so the model cannot just copy neighbors); the masked image and the full caption go through their encoders, the image cross-modality encoder attends to the text, and the decoder outputs pixels scored by L1 on the masked area. For text reconstruction, 30% of tokens are replaced by `[MASK]` (higher than BERT's 15% because the image supplies extra information); the full image and masked caption go through the encoders, the text cross-modality encoder attends to the image, and masked words are predicted with cross-entropy. ITC and ITM are added on top. Setup: batch 512 on 16 V100s, AdamW, 50 epochs on the 4M data, peak LR $3\times10^{-4}$ (lower $10^{-5}$ for the pretrained encoders).

## Results
- With common alignment losses, MaskVLM reaches state-of-the-art results among models pre-trained on millions of pairs across retrieval (COCO, Flickr30k), VQA and NLVR2 (per the abstract; I did not copy individual table numbers).
- The gain is largest with limited data: the paper reports that about 40% of the data used by state-of-the-art models is enough to match their performance.
- Ablations show that masked V+L modeling adds to ITC + ITM even on retrieval tasks.

## Takeaways / questions
- Clean demonstration that reconstructing one modality from the other implicitly learns word–region alignment.
- Reconstructing raw pixels with an L1 loss is a weak, blurry target; it works as a training signal, not as image generation.
- Like FLAVA, this is an understanding-only model from before LLM-based VLMs took over.

notes.title: MiniGPT-4: Enhancing Vision-Language Understanding with Advanced Large Language Models
notes.tldr: MiniGPT-4 reuses BLIP-2's frozen EVA-CLIP ViT and Q-Former, connects them to a frozen Vicuna LLM through one trainable linear layer, and adds a tiny curated detailed-description fine-tune to get GPT-4-like image chat cheaply.
notes.markdown: ## My notes Listed as “Mini GPT” under “Pretrained (frozen) transformer backbone”. ## Summary MiniGPT-4 (KAUST) appeared days after LLaVA with a similar bet: GPT-4's impressive multimodal demos (explaining memes, writing websites from sketches) mostly come from having a strong language model, so plugging good visual features into a strong open LLM should reproduce many of them. It keeps almost everything frozen, the vision side from BLIP-2 and the Vicuna LLM, and trains only a single linear projection between them. A key practical finding is that alignment on noisy web captions alone produces broken, repetitive text; a second, very small fine-tune on 3,500 high-quality detailed descriptions fixes this. ## Problem GPT-4's vision capabilities were impressive but undisclosed. The question is whether a strong open LLM plus a light alignment step is enough to get similar abilities, and how cheaply. ## Related work - BLIP-2 — supplies the frozen vision components (EVA-CLIP ViT-G/14 + Q-Former); BLIP-2 itself used weaker LLMs. - Vicuna (built on LLaMA) — the frozen LLM. - LLaVA ([2304.08485](https://arxiv.org/abs/2304.08485)) — concurrent work with a similar projector design but end-to-end LLM fine-tuning on GPT-4-generated instructions. - Flamingo, Kosmos-1 — earlier LLM-based multimodal models. ## Method ![Figure 1 from the paper: MiniGPT-4 architecture, a frozen ViT and Q-Former, one trainable linear projection, and a frozen Vicuna LLM](assets/minigpt-4/fig1.png) - **Reused and frozen:** BLIP-2's visual pipeline, a ViT-G/14 from EVA-CLIP followed by the Q-Former (which compresses the image into a small fixed set of query tokens), and the Vicuna LLM. - **New and trained:** only one linear projection layer that maps Q-Former outputs into Vicuna's input embedding space. The image appears in the prompt as `###Human: ###Assistant:`, where `` is the projected visual tokens. ## Data - **Stage 1:** a combined captioning set from LAION, Conceptual Captions and SBU, about 5 million image–text pairs seen. - **Stage 2:** a self-built set of 3,500 detailed image descriptions. They prompted the stage-1 model to describe 5,000 Conceptual Captions images in detail (asking it to "Continue" if the output was under 80 tokens), had ChatGPT fix repetitions and fragments, then filtered and manually checked the results. ## Training An image goes through the frozen ViT and Q-Former, the linear layer turns the query outputs into soft tokens, and Vicuna is asked to produce the caption; the loss is next-token cross-entropy on the text, with gradients only reaching the projection layer. - Stage 1: 20,000 steps, batch 256, about 10 hours on 4 A100 (80GB) GPUs. - Stage 2: the same setup on the 3,500 curated descriptions in Vicuna's conversation template; 400 steps at batch 12, about 7 minutes on one A100. ## Results - Human evaluation on 100 images over 4 tasks (meme explanation, recipes, ads, poems): MiniGPT-4 satisfies **65/100** requests vs 5/100 for BLIP-2. - COCO captions judged by ChatGPT for covering ground-truth objects and relations: 66.2% vs 27.5% for BLIP-2. - Stage-2 fine-tuning cuts the generation failure rate from 35% to 2% for detailed captions and 32% to 1% for poems. - Limitations shown in the paper: it hallucinates objects (e.g. a non-existent tablecloth) and struggles with spatial localization. ## Takeaways / questions - Confirms the LLaVA-era lesson from another angle: a strong LLM carries most of the "advanced" behavior, and a small amount of clean, well-formatted data matters a lot for output quality. - Freezing the LLM keeps training extremely cheap but limits how much the model can learn to ground language in the image; LLaVA's end-to-end fine-tuning is the contrasting choice. - The Q-Former's small fixed token budget is a bottleneck for fine detail.

notes.title: Sigmoid Loss for Language Image Pre-Training
notes.tldr: SigLIP replaces CLIP's batch-wide softmax contrastive loss with an independent sigmoid (yes/no) loss on every image–text pair, which is simpler, more memory-efficient and better at small batch sizes.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed as “SigClip” under “Basic – image encoders”.

## Summary
SigLIP (Google DeepMind) keeps the CLIP recipe, an image encoder and a text encoder trained to align matching image–caption pairs, but changes the loss. CLIP turns each row and column of the batch similarity matrix into a softmax ("which of these $N$ captions is the right one?"). SigLIP instead asks, for every single image–text pair independently, "do these two match, yes or no?" using a sigmoid. That small change removes the need to normalize over the whole batch, makes distributed training cheaper, and works better when the batch is small. SigLIP encoders later became a very common vision tower in open VLMs.

## Problem
The softmax contrastive loss couples every example in the batch: normalization needs all pairwise similarities across devices, needs an extra pass for numerical stability, and its quality depends heavily on very large batch sizes. That makes language–image pre-training expensive and hard to study.

## Related work
- CLIP ([2103.00020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020)) and ALIGN — softmax contrastive image–text pre-training at scale.
- LiT (Locked-image Tuning) — freeze a pretrained image encoder and only train the text side; SigLIP's sigmoid version is "SigLiT".
- FLIP — speeds up CLIP training by randomly dropping image patches.

## Method
For a batch of $|\mathcal{B}|$ pairs with normalized image embeddings $x_i$ and text embeddings $y_j$, the loss is

$$\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{|\mathcal{B}|}\sum_{i}\sum_{j} \log \sigma\big(z_{ij}\,(t\, x_i\cdot y_j + b)\big)$$

where $z_{ij}=1$ if image $i$ and text $j$ are a true pair and $-1$ otherwise, $t$ is a learnable temperature and $b$ a learnable bias. Each term is just binary logistic regression on one pair, so no softmax over the batch is needed. Because negatives vastly outnumber positives, the bias is initialized to $-10$ (and $t'=\log t$ to $\log 10$) so training starts near the right prior.

A "chunked" implementation makes this cheap across devices: each device computes the loss for its own images against its own texts, then passes its texts to the neighbor device and repeats, so the full $N\times N$ similarity matrix is never materialized at once.

What is reused: standard ViT image encoders and Transformer text encoders (and, for SigLiT, a frozen pretrained image backbone). What is new: only the loss, the bias term, and the efficient implementation.

## Data
SigLIP is pre-trained on WebLI image–text pairs (English only for the main experiments; mSigLIP keeps all 100 languages). SigLiT uses the LiT image–text dataset. Images at 224×224; text tokenized with a 32k SentencePiece vocabulary, max 16 tokens.

## Training
An image goes through a B/16 ViT, its caption through a B-sized text Transformer, and both are normalized. For a batch, every image–text dot product is scaled by $t$, shifted by $b$, and passed through a sigmoid. The true pair is pushed toward 1, every mismatched pair toward 0, and the losses are summed. With four TPU-v4 chips the sigmoid version fit a batch of 4096 for a Base model versus 2048 for CLIP.

## Results
- SigLiT with a frozen g/14 image model reaches **84.5%** zero-shot ImageNet accuracy in two days on four TPU-v4 chips; with a B/8 model, 79.7% in one day.
- SigLIP from scratch (B/16) reaches 73.4% zero-shot ImageNet in 5 days on 32 TPU-v4 chips, compared with roughly 5–10 days on 256 TPUv3 cores for FLIP and CLIP.
- Sigmoid beats softmax clearly below a 16k batch size; the gap closes as batch grows. SigLIP peaks at batch 32k, while softmax needed 98k and still did not beat it; very large batches (up to one million tested) give quickly diminishing returns.

## Takeaways / questions
- A good example of a one-line change with big practical impact: decoupling the loss from the batch makes training cheaper and easier to reason about.
- The finding that ~32k batch is "enough" is useful for anyone training contrastive encoders on a budget.
- Still a global-embedding contrastive model, so it shares CLIP's weaknesses on fine-grained detail.
