notes.title: Visual Lexicon: Rich Image Features in Language Space
notes.tldr: ViLex trains an image encoder to output a few 'visual word' embeddings that a frozen text-to-image diffusion model can use as a prompt to recreate the image, giving tokens in text space that keep both semantics and fine visual detail.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
First paper sent to me when I joined the Darrell group at BAIR (*VLM papers* doc); ViLex became my BAIR research project (“we are building the 2nd version”, Aug 2025 application).

From my latent-visual-reasoning notes (Aug 2026): Another representation direction I'm interested in is ViLex. ViLex asks whether image information can be encoded into a language-compatible embedding space while retaining far more visual detail than a natural-language caption. It uses a visual encoder and attention pooling, then optimizes those representations through reconstruction with a frozen text-to-image system. The relevance to my project is a hypothesis, not something I would assume is automatically true: if interleaved reasoning repeatedly transitions between linguistic computation and visual computation, reducing the geometric mismatch between those spaces may make those transitions easier. Instead of forcing the model to jump from an LLM state to a raw perceptual ViT space, something like a language-compatible visual representation might provide a better intermediate reasoning substrate. But the only convincing way to establish that is a matched ablation: raw vision embeddings versus ViLex-style embeddings, with data, model, latent budget, and optimization held fixed.

*From onenote (2025-08-17):*

*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, VLMs › Vilex › "Visual lexicon", 17 Aug 2025. My implementation notes for this project are in [ViLex implementation notes](#/note/vilex-implementation-notes).*

- CLIP ↔ **ViLex** ↔ VAEs
  - CLIP: semantic understanding (more "language").
  - ViLex: vision & language (more "components of language").
  - VAEs: more "visual" (reconstruction, spatial).
- High "fidelity": captures fine-grained details → the same semantic representation works for different diffusion models.
- Input: images. Output: "visual language tokens", in the same space as language, that can be used directly.
  - Image → ViLex encoder → [text-like tokens] → frozen [text] encoder + diffusion model → reconstructed image.
  - Pipeline: Img → ViT encoder → **Q-Former** (cross-attention pooling with learnable queries) → **TokenDrop** → frozen T5 text encoder.
  - Img → ViLex → visual tokens → CLIP [text encoder] → embeddings → … → VLM; Text → tokenizer.
  - Shapes: $[H, W, 3]$ (256×256×3) → ViT → $[256, 768]$ (256 patches, each a 768-dim latent) → Q-Former → $[32, 1024]$ (# queries × text-embedding dim).
    - Cross-attention pooling: K & V come from the patches; Q is learnable, in the same text-embedding dimension.
  - Attention-pooling math (right side of page): $Q\,[Q_\#, d]\times K^\top [d, \text{patch}] \times V\,[\text{patch}, d]$ → $[Q_\#, d]$; e.g. 32 queries × 256 patches → $[Q_1P_1 \dots Q_1P_{256};\ \dots;\ Q_{32}P_1 \dots Q_{32}P_{256}] \times V$.
- **Questions**
  1. ViLex vs language: token-frequency laws? grounded structure?
  2. One token already fills the whole picture; each token carries fine-grained details → no sequential structure.
  3. Wouldn't it be better used for multimodal LMs like Transfusion?

## Summary
ViLex (Visual Lexicon; Google DeepMind and UC Berkeley) asks: can we describe an image in a "language" that a text model understands but that keeps much more detail than any caption could? It trains an image encoder whose outputs live in the text-token embedding space of a text-to-image model. The training signal comes from a frozen diffusion model: the encoder's tokens are fed in as if they were a text prompt, and the encoder is optimized so that the generated image looks like the input. The resulting tokens behave like new words. They can recreate an image's style, layout and pose, can be mixed with real words ("an image similar to [ViLex] in Van Gogh style"), and also make a better vision encoder for a VLM than the SigLIP model they started from.

## Problem
Image representations are usually optimized for one of two extremes: high-level semantics (CLIP, SigLIP, DINO) that lose pixel detail, or pixel-level reconstruction (VAEs) that are poor for understanding. Natural-language captions sit in text space but cannot carry fine visual detail. The goal is a representation that is both semantically rich and visually detailed, and that lives in language space.

## Related work
- CLIP ([2103.00020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020)) and SigLIP ([2303.15343](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.15343)) — semantic encoders; ViLex's ViT is initialized from SigLIP.
- Imagen — the frozen text-to-image diffusion decoder (64×64, with an OpenCLIP ViT-H/14 text encoder).
- DeDiffusion — inverts images to discrete text tokens via Gumbel softmax, limited by what real words can express; the main baseline.
- Textual inversion / DreamBooth — learn tokens or adapters per subject; ViLex does this zero-shot for any image.
- PaliGemma — the VLM used to test ViLex as a vision encoder.

## Method
![Figure 3 from the paper: the ViLex pipeline, an image encoder and attention pooling produce visual lexicon tokens that a frozen text encoder and diffusion model use to reconstruct the image](assets/vilex/onenote-fig1.png)

It is an autoencoder whose decoder is a frozen text-to-image model:
1. **Image encoder (reused, fine-tuned):** a ViT initialized from SigLIP (ViT-B at 224×224) produces $k$ patch tokens.
2. **Attention pooling (new):** a multi-head cross-attention module (5 Transformer blocks, randomly initialized) with $n$ learnable queries reads the patch tokens and outputs $n$ ViLex embeddings $v$, with $n \le 75$ so that, with `[SOS]`/`[EOS]`, it fits CLIP's 77-token context.
3. **Decoder (reused, frozen):** the ViLex embeddings are inserted where word embeddings would normally go, passed through the frozen text encoder, and condition the frozen diffusion U-Net. They can stand alone or be concatenated with real text tokens, $[v, c]$.

Additions: **TailDrop**, randomly dropping the last tokens during training so that earlier tokens carry the most important semantics and the token count can be chosen at inference; and **Text-Free Guidance**, a classifier-free-guidance-style knob that balances the ViLex embedding against an accompanying text prompt.

## Data
Images (optionally with captions) from WebLI. Evaluation on MS-COCO reconstruction, zero-shot DreamBooth-style re-contextualization, and 15 vision-language benchmarks through PaliGemma.

## Training
An image goes through the ViT and the attention pooler to get $n$ ViLex tokens; these, wrapped in `[SOS]`/`[EOS]`, go through the frozen text encoder; the diffusion model receives a noised version of the same image and must predict the noise given that "prompt". The standard diffusion reconstruction loss is back-propagated through the frozen diffusion model and text encoder into the pooler and ViT only. Setup: Adafactor, weight decay 0.01, batch 2048, 300K steps (about 2.5 days on 64 TPUv5 chips), LR $10^{-5}$ for the ViT and $3\times10^{-4}$ for the pooler, cosine decay with 10K warm-up.

## Results
- COCO 64×64 reconstruction FID (all with Imagen as the decoder): text prompts 6.52, DeDiffusion 3.89, ViLex with **1 token 3.65**, 4 tokens 2.91, 16 tokens 2.38, 75 tokens 2.07. Even a single ViLex token beats DeDiffusion.
- Qualitatively retains style, layout and pose better than image-guided DALL·E 3 and DeDiffusion.
- Zero-shot, unsupervised DreamBooth-style re-contextualization without fine-tuning the T2I model.
- As PaliGemma's vision encoder (frozen, only the LLM fine-tuned), ViLex improves over the SigLIP baseline across 15 benchmarks; a VAE representation is reported to be often more than 8× worse for vision-language modeling.

## Takeaways / questions
- Central to my BAIR work: the group was building ViLex v2 when I joined, and the idea of "visual tokens in language space" frames my later latent-visual-reasoning questions.
- Using a frozen generator as the training signal ("reconstruction as supervision") is a neat way to inject detail into a semantic encoder without pixel losses.
- Open question from my own notes: does a language-compatible visual space actually make interleaved text–vision reasoning easier? It needs a matched ablation against raw ViT embeddings.
- The reconstruction is "semantic-level", not pixel-exact (64×64 decoder), so it is unclear how much fine spatial structure, text or counting survives.

notes.title: Transfusion: Predict the Next Token and Diffuse Images with One Multi-Modal Model
notes.tldr: Transfusion trains one Transformer on mixed sequences where text tokens get the usual next-token loss and continuous image patches get a diffusion loss, scaling better than Chameleon's discrete image tokens at a fraction of the compute.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed (as “Transfuscion”) under “Full autoregressive models”.

*From onenote (2025-08-15):*

*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, VLMs › Lecture › "Transfusion", 15 Aug 2025 (also summarized on the Lecture "Overview" page).*

- NLL → sequence: $T_1\ T_2$ [Img S] $\langle I_1\rangle\ \langle I_2\rangle$ [Img E] $\langle T_3\rangle\ \langle T_4\rangle$
- → negative log-likelihood loss + diffusion objective.
  - Text tokens (probability of the correct next token given all previous ones): $\mathcal{L} = \frac1N\sum_{i}-\log P_\theta(x_i \mid x_{<i})$
  - Images: $x_t = \sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0 + \sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon$
- From the Overview page: Chameleon + diffusion objective. Next-token prediction on text; when an image appears, use the diffusion objective on the image tokens (noise + timestep).

## Summary
Transfusion (mostly Meta, with Waymo and USC co-authors) asks how to build one model that both writes text and generates images without throwing away image detail. Chameleon's answer was to quantize images into discrete tokens so everything is next-token prediction. Transfusion keeps images continuous: an image is a sequence of VAE latent patches, and the same Transformer that predicts text tokens also learns to denoise those patches, diffusion-style. Text uses causal attention, while patches within one image can see each other bidirectionally. In controlled comparisons this mix scales better than discretizing images, for image generation, captioning and even text-only modeling.

## Problem
Language models dominate discrete data and diffusion models dominate continuous data like images. Unifying them by quantizing images (Chameleon) loses information, and pipelines that glue an LLM to a separate diffusion model are not a single model. The goal is one network, one set of weights, trained on both objectives.

## Related work
- Chameleon ([2405.09818](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.09818)) — the discrete-token early-fusion baseline, re-implemented for controlled comparison.
- DDPM ([2006.11239](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11239)) — the diffusion training objective.
- Latent Diffusion / Stable Diffusion ([2112.10752](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.10752)) — diffusion in a VAE latent space.
- DiT and U-Net diffusion backbones — the patchify and U-Net down/up blocks used to enter and exit the Transformer.
- Llama — the Transformer configuration.

## Method
![Figure 1 from the paper: one Transformer processes text tokens autoregressively with next-token prediction and image patches in parallel with a diffusion objective](assets/transfusion/onenote-fig1.png)

1. **Representations.** Text is BPE-tokenized as usual. Images are encoded by a VAE (trained by the authors, 86M parameters) from 256×256 pixels to a 32×32×8 latent; the latent is grouped into patches (via a linear layer or U-Net down blocks), giving a sequence of continuous vectors. Each image is wrapped in special BOI / EOI tokens and inserted into the text sequence.
2. **Attention mask.** Causal attention across the whole sequence, plus bidirectional attention among patches of the same image. Patches can see all of their own image and anything earlier, but not later text or images.
3. **Losses.** Next-token cross-entropy on text tokens; DDPM noise-prediction loss on image patches (noise is added to the whole latent image before patching). Combined as
   $$\mathcal{L}_{\text{Transfusion}} = \mathcal{L}_{\text{LM}} + \lambda\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{DDPM}}, \quad \lambda = 5.$$
4. **Inference.** In LM mode the model samples text token by token. When it samples BOI, it switches to diffusion mode: append $n$ pure-noise patches and denoise for $T$ steps (250 at inference, trained on 1000), then append EOI and switch back.

Reused: a VAE-latent design from latent diffusion, U-Net blocks, Llama-style Transformer settings. New: training one randomly initialized Transformer with both losses over interleaved sequences, and the mixed causal/bidirectional mask.

## Data
Controlled experiments train on 0.5T tokens of text and image–caption data. The large model sees 2T tokens: 1T text tokens plus roughly 5 epochs over 692M image–caption pairs (about another 1T patches/tokens).

## Training
Take a captioned image "A corgi on the beach" + image. The caption tokens get next-token loss. The image's VAE latent is noised to a random timestep $t$, patchified (with a timestep embedding added), and placed after BOI. The Transformer, seeing the caption causally and the noisy patches bidirectionally, outputs a noise estimate for each patch; the DDPM loss compares it to the true noise. Sum the two losses (×5 for diffusion). Pairs are ordered caption-first 80% of the time and image-first otherwise, so the model also learns captioning. Setup: AdamW, LR 3e-4 with cosine decay, sequences of 4096 tokens, 2M-token batches for 250k steps (4M-token batches for 500k steps at 7B).

## Results
- Versus Chameleon at matched settings: Transfusion beats it in text-to-image at less than a third of the compute (FID and CLIP score); at equal FLOPs it gets about 2× lower FID. It matches Chameleon's image-to-text at 21.8% of the FLOPs, and even reaches text perplexity parity at around 50–60% of Chameleon's FLOPs.
- Intra-image bidirectional attention matters; making it causal hurts text-to-image.
- U-Net down/up blocks let the model compress each image to just 16 patches with relatively small loss, potentially cutting serving cost up to 64×.
- The 7B model (2T tokens, U-Net layers) scores 0.63 on GenEval, beating DALL-E 2 and SDXL, while matching Llama 1 on text benchmarks.

## Takeaways / questions
- Strong evidence that unified models should keep images continuous rather than discretize them; this design line leads directly to BAGEL and other "LLM + diffusion in one Transformer" models.
- The model "thinks" about an image in continuous patch space, which is the kind of substrate latent visual reasoning wants, but here it is used only for generation, not for intermediate reasoning.
- The fixed $\lambda$ and single resolution leave open questions about balancing the two losses at scale.

notes.title: Flamingo: a Visual Language Model for Few-Shot Learning
notes.tldr: Bridges a frozen vision encoder and a frozen LLM with a Perceiver Resampler and gated cross-attention layers, trained on interleaved web data so it learns new tasks from a few in-context examples.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, VLMs › Lecture › "In context learning", 13 Aug 2025.*

- "Few-shot learning" → learn at inference time with frozen weights.
- → Few-shot VLM → **Flamingo**
  - → gated cross-attention layers + **Perceiver Resampler** layer (cross-attention with latent queries *(uncertain reading)*).
  - Img tokens → Perceiver Resampler (fixed number of outputs) → visual tokens; text tokens → tokenizer; both form an **interleaved sequence**.
- Compared to LLaVA: in-context following of interleaved context, enabled by cross-attention.
  - Trade-off: more parameters.

## Summary
Flamingo (DeepMind) is a family of VLMs that adapt to new image and video tasks from a handful of examples placed in the prompt. A frozen vision encoder feeds a Perceiver Resampler, which maps a variable number of visual features to a fixed set of visual tokens. New gated cross-attention layers, interleaved between the frozen LM blocks, let text tokens attend to those visual tokens. Training on large web corpora of interleaved images and text is what produces the few-shot ability.

## Method
- **Reused:** a frozen pretrained vision encoder and a frozen Chinchilla LM.
- **New:** the Perceiver Resampler, tanh-gated cross-attention layers initialized so the model starts out as the frozen LM, and per-image masking for arbitrarily interleaved sequences.

![Figure 1 from the paper: Flamingo few-shot examples](assets/flamingo/fig1.png)

## Results
Per the abstract, a single Flamingo model sets new few-shot state of the art across many image and video benchmarks, often beating models fine-tuned on thousands of times more task data.

notes.title: Visual Instruction Tuning
notes.tldr: LLaVA connects a frozen CLIP ViT-L/14 to the Vicuna LLM with a single linear projection and trains it on 158K image-grounded instruction-following conversations generated by text-only GPT-4, creating the template for open multimodal chat models.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed as “LLAVA” under “Pretrained (frozen) transformer backbone”.

*From onenote (2025-08-13):*

*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, VLMs › Lecture › "LLAVA", 13 Aug 2025.*

- Diagram: Text, img → **CLIP** → text → word/position embeddings → **pretrained LLM**; img → [transfer head] → new tokens → pretrained LLM.
- **Step 1**: input = image–text pairs; target = next-token prediction.
- **Step 2**: input = VQA (image + question + answer); target = given Q, next-token prediction on A.

## Summary
LLaVA (Large Language and Vision Assistant) is the paper that made open-source "GPT-4 with eyes" style chatbots simple. Its two ideas are both cheap. First, the architecture: take a pretrained CLIP image encoder and a pretrained chat LLM, and connect them with one trainable linear layer that turns image patch features into "visual tokens" the LLM reads like words. Second, the data: since there was no large dataset of image-grounded instructions, they had text-only GPT-4 write one, by describing each COCO image to GPT-4 through its captions and bounding boxes. The resulting recipe (frozen vision encoder → projector → LLM, two-stage training) became the default design for most open VLMs.

## Problem
Instruction tuning had made LLMs into general assistants, but vision models were still mostly task-specific, and multimodal instruction-following data barely existed. Collecting it by hand is slow and expensive.

## Related work
- CLIP ([2103.00020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020)) — supplies the frozen ViT-L/14 vision encoder.
- Vicuna / LLaMA — the language model.
- Flamingo — connects vision to a frozen LLM with gated cross-attention ("GPT-3 moment" of multimodal).
- BLIP-2 — connects them with a Q-Former; LLaVA chooses a much simpler linear projection.
- Self-Instruct / Alpaca-style instruction tuning — machine-generated instruction data for LLMs.

## Method
- **Vision encoder (reused, frozen):** CLIP ViT-L/14 produces a grid of patch features $\mathbf{Z}_v = g(\mathbf{X}_v)$.
- **Projection (new):** a trainable matrix $\mathbf{W}$ maps those features into the LLM's word-embedding space, $\mathbf{H}_v = \mathbf{W}\cdot\mathbf{Z}_v$. These visual tokens are placed in the prompt alongside text tokens.
- **LLM (reused, fine-tuned in stage 2):** Vicuna, chosen for its instruction-following ability.

**Data generation (new).** For each COCO image, GPT-4 (text only) is given the image's captions and object bounding boxes, plus a few hand-written seed examples, and asked to produce three kinds of responses: multi-turn **conversations** about the image, **detailed descriptions**, and **complex reasoning** questions with step-by-step answers.

## Data
- **Stage 1:** CC3M filtered to 595K image–caption pairs, turned into single-turn "describe this image briefly" instructions with the original caption as the answer.
- **Stage 2:** LLaVA-Instruct-158K: 58K conversations, 23K detailed descriptions and 77K complex-reasoning samples (about 80K unique COCO images). Also ScienceQA for a separate fine-tuning experiment.

## Training
An image goes through the frozen CLIP encoder; its grid features are projected into, say, a few hundred visual tokens; these are inserted into a chat-formatted sequence (system message, human turn with image and question, assistant turn). The model is trained with the ordinary next-token cross-entropy loss, but only on the assistant's answer tokens.
- **Stage 1 (feature alignment):** CLIP and Vicuna frozen; only $\mathbf{W}$ trains, so image features learn to land where the LLM expects word embeddings. 1 epoch, LR 2e-3, batch 128.
- **Stage 2 (end-to-end fine-tuning):** CLIP still frozen; projection and LLM both train on the 158K instructions. 3 epochs, LR 2e-5, batch 32. All on 8×A100.

## Results
- On a synthetic multimodal instruction-following benchmark, LLaVA scores **85.1%** relative to GPT-4 (GPT-4 judges both answers; the text-only GPT-4 reference sees ground-truth captions and boxes).
- On the GPT-4-paper examples (e.g. the extreme-ironing photo), LLaVA follows the instruction and reasons about the image, while BLIP-2 and OpenFlamingo mostly just describe the scene.
- Fine-tuned on ScienceQA, LLaVA combined with GPT-4 as a judge reaches a then state-of-the-art **92.53%** accuracy.
- Also introduced LLaVA-Bench (COCO and In-the-Wild) for evaluating multimodal chat.

## Takeaways / questions
- The architecture is almost embarrassingly simple; most of the gain comes from the instruction data. A strong lesson that data, not connectors, was the bottleneck.
- Data generated by a text-only model from captions and boxes can hallucinate details the image does not support, and GPT-4-as-judge evaluation inherits GPT-4's biases.
- The "frozen ViT → projector → LLM" design means visual information enters only once, as input tokens; my latent-visual-reasoning work asks what happens when the model can also produce or revisit visual states mid-reasoning.

notes.title: Analyzing The Language of Visual Tokens
notes.tldr: Treats discrete visual tokens as a language. They are Zipfian but with more innovation, higher entropy and weak grammar compared to natural languages.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, VLMs › David papers › "Visual tokens", 11 Aug 2025.*

- Statistical behaviour of vision "language".
  - → [orderings], "structures".
  - → "grounded structures".
- → Less structured patterns than language; follows the same [Zipfian] distribution *(uncertain reading)*.
  - Zipf: word frequency vs. rank in language.
    - ↳ n-gram frequency: more uniform, no sharp drop-off *(uncertain reading)*.
      - → tried longer n-grams.

## Summary
The paper applies natural-language statistics to the discrete token "languages" produced by visual tokenizers (as used in Chameleon and LLaVA-style models). Visual languages follow Zipfian distributions, but token innovation is higher, which drives greater entropy and lower compressibility. Tokens mostly represent object parts, an intermediate granularity. There are no cohesive grammatical structures, so perplexity is higher and hierarchical organization weaker than in natural language. Alignment between visual and natural languages is much weaker than the cohesion within natural languages.

![Figure 1 from the paper: tokenizers induce visual languages](assets/language-of-visual-tokens/fig1.png)

## Takeaways / questions
- This ties into my ViLex question about whether visual tokens obey language-like frequency laws (see [Visual Lexicon](#/note/visual-lexicon)).

notes.title: REOrdering Patches Improves Vision Models
notes.tldr: Patch order matters for long-sequence vision transformers; REOrder learns a task-specific permutation with a compression-based prior and a Plackett-Luce policy trained by REINFORCE.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, VLMs › David papers › "Reordering patches", 11 Aug 2025.*

- Ordering of patches.
  - → Fixed orderings significantly shift accuracy.
  - → Normal orders: row, Hilbert (spiral, column, snake *(uncertain)*).
  - [Use **RL** to learn the best ordering (the policy orders the patches).]

## Summary
Full self-attention is permutation-equivariant, but efficient long-sequence architectures (local or linear attention, state-space models) are not, so the order in which image patches are flattened matters. REOrder first builds an information-theoretic prior by measuring how compressible each patch ordering is. It then learns a permutation policy (Plackett–Luce) with REINFORCE.

![Figure 1 from the paper: alternative patch orderings (row, column, Hilbert, spiral, diagonal, snake)](assets/reorder-patches/fig1.png)

## Results
From the abstract: top-1 accuracy over row-major ordering improves by up to 3.01% on ImageNet-1K and 13.35% on Functional Map of the World.

notes.title: See, Say, and Segment: Teaching LMMs to Overcome False Premises
notes.tldr: SESAME trains an LMM to see whether a queried object exists, say so (and suggest corrections) if not, and segment it if it does, avoiding the catastrophic forgetting of segmentation fine-tuning.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, VLMs › David papers › "LLM false premises", 11 Aug 2025. Several words are uncertain.*

- Fine-tuning LMMs [for segmentation] causes them to forget *(uncertain reading)*.
- → **SESAME**: See → Say → Segment.
  - ↳ if the object is present, output the segmentation mask;
  - ↳ if it's a false premise (not observed) → generate a negative response *(uncertain reading)*.
- → Tricky: false premises, hallucinations, … etc.
- → Generation: output probability, give [alternative] semantics *(uncertain reading)*.

## Summary
LMMs fine-tuned for referring segmentation lose the ability to notice that a queried object isn't in the image. They segment *something* anyway, which is a form of catastrophic forgetting. SESAME uses cascaded and joint training so the model can **see** (detect whether the object is present), **say** (tell the user when it isn't, and propose alternative or corrected queries), and **segment** (output the mask when it is). The paper also introduces FP-RefCOCO(+/g), a false-premise extension of the RefCOCO benchmarks.

![Figure 1 from the paper: false-premise failures and SESAME's see/say/segment behaviour](assets/sesame/fig1.png)

## Results
From the abstract: false premises are detected up to 55% better than existing approaches. Under false-premise conditions the relative cIoU improvement is over 31%, and the natural-language feedback is judged helpful up to 67% of the time.

  - → CLIP's simple architecture: vision & language are two completely different ways of representing information; learn to match them in the same space.
  - World models → combine many representations → sounds, senses; VLMs are a great direction.

## Summary
Personal notes from a research talk (filed under "David papers"), not a paper. The speaker's path ran from LLM-style models for high-energy-physics data at LBNL to multimodal learning. CLIP's lesson is that a simple contrastive objective can align radically different representations in one space. The next step is world models that align many sensory streams.

notes.title: Vision-language model families (lecture notes)
notes.tldr: Lecture notes on the main VLM families (contrastive CLIP/SigLIP, masked FLAVA, generative CoCa/Chameleon/Transfusion, and frozen-backbone BLIP-2/LLaVA) plus attention basics and long-context evaluation.
notes.markdown: ## My notes *Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, VLMs › Lecture: pages "Overview" (11 Aug 2025), "Encoders" (13 Aug 2025), "Attention basics" (11 Aug 2025) and "Long context" (15 Aug 2025).* ### Overview - **Contrastive-based** → the baseline. - Image & text cosine-similarity matrix. - $\mathcal{L} = -\frac{1}{2N}\sum_{i=1}^{N}\Big[\log\frac{e^{x_i\cdot y_i/\tau}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} e^{x_i\cdot y_j/\tau}} + \log\frac{e^{x_i\cdot y_i/\tau}}{\sum_{j=1}^{N} e^{x_j\cdot y_i/\tau}}\Big]$: one softmax picks the right image for a caption, the other picks the correct caption. - **SigLIP**: objective per pair $= \dfrac{1}{1+e^{z_{ij}(-t\,x_i\cdot y_j + b)}}$ (sigmoid instead of softmax). - **Pretrained backbone** - Frozen encoder + pretrained LLM, with a mapping network that aligns image embeddings to the text space. - Frozen LLM backbone + inject [visual features] as "text tokens". - LLaVA / MiniGPT: frozen encoder & LLM, then a [learned] transform in between. - **BLIP-2**: frozen encoder → **Q-Former** (learnable query vectors to pull out the relevant features) → transformer backbone. - ↳ only train the Q-Former; the encoder & language model stay frozen. - $q = QW_q,\ k, v$ ⇒ $\mathrm{softmax}(qk^\top/\sqrt{d_k})$, $a_{ij} = \frac{\exp(\text{score}_{ij})}{\sum_j \exp(\text{score}_{ij})}$, output $\sum_j a_{ij} v_j$. - **Masked VLM**: concatenate masked words representing image & text and fuse them. - **FLAVA** (multiple objectives) → masked text + masked image / masked multimodal loss → like an advanced BERT model. - **Generative-based** - **CoCa** → language model with contrastive & captioning losses (CLIP-like + caption generation). - ↳ text-only (captioning) generation. - Trained together (others train separately) → two objectives: contrastive loss & autoregressive captioning loss. - Img → image encoder → $V_{uni}$ → projection heads → contrastive loss ← $T_{uni}$ ← text encoder ← Text; $V$ → cross-attention (key and value from the image, query from the text decoder) → decoder → captioning loss. - **Chameleon**: generates image & text in any sequence → early fusion. - Early fusion: a single token sequence [text, text, image, …], with ``/`` for image generation. - Late fusion: separate {[vision tokens], [language tokens]}. - → use `` to prompt image generation. - **Transfusion**: continuous vectors & diffusion objective (encodes images as continuous vectors, not discrete tokens). - Chameleon + diffusion objective → next-token prediction on text; when an image appears, use the diffusion objective. Sequence: $T_1, T_2, T_3$ `` img tokens ``; the image part is trained with the diffusion noising objective (noise + timestep). See [Transfusion](#/note/transfusion). - **Training stages** [for LLaVA-style models]: 1. pretraining for feature alignment → only update the projection matrix; 2. fine-tune → update the LLM too. ### Encoders (CLIP) - Img → img-encoder → $I_1, I_2, \dots, I_n$; Text → text encoder → $T_1, \dots, T_n$; similarity matrix with matching pairs $I_iT_i$ on the diagonal. - Loss $= \log\frac{e^{x_i y_i}}{\sum_{j} e^{x_j y_i}} + \log\frac{e^{x_i y_i}}{\sum_j e^{x_i y_j}}$. ### Attention basics - $Q$ (rows = tokens 1…5, columns $q_1..q_4$), $K$, $V$; scores $\frac{qk^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}$; output row $= v_1(q_1k_1) + v_2(q_1k_2) + v_3(q_1k_3) + \dots$ - $\mathrm{softmax}\!\big(\frac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}\big)V$ - Normalization: $\frac{x_i - \mu}{\sqrt{\sigma^2 + \epsilon}}$ - *(Unrelated scribble on the page: `<<1 2> <3>>`, `link(link(1, link(2)), 3)`.)* ### Long context - Lots of image / text / QA pairs. - → **Needle-in-a-haystack** benchmarks (a random fact in the middle of a long context). ## Summary These are lecture notes rather than a single paper. The "Overview" page follows the four families in the survey *An Introduction to Vision-Language Modeling* (Bordes et al., 2024, [arXiv 2405.17247](https://arxiv.org/abs/2405.17247)). **Contrastive** models (CLIP, SigLIP) align image and text embeddings. **Masking** models (FLAVA) reconstruct masked tokens across modalities. **Generative** models (CoCa, Chameleon, Transfusion) produce captions or images. **Pretrained-backbone** models (BLIP-2, LLaVA, MiniGPT) connect a frozen vision encoder to a frozen LLM through a small trained bridge (Q-Former or projection). Related notes: [LLaVA](#/note/llava), [Flamingo](#/note/flamingo), [Transfusion](#/note/transfusion).

notes.title: ALOHa: A New Measure for Hallucination in Captioning Models
notes.tldr: ALOHa is an open-vocabulary object-hallucination metric for image captions: an LLM extracts objects from the caption and references, S-BERT similarities plus Hungarian matching score each object, and the worst-matched object scores the caption.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
“When recreating my own version of CLIPScore from scratch, I came across your ALOHa paper and found the use of semantic similarity matching very exciting!”

*From onenote (2025-08-11):*

*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, VLMs › David papers › "Aloha", 11 Aug 2025.*

1. Benchmark of hallucinations in captioning *(uncertain reading)*.
   - **CHAIR**: extracts objects from caption sentences. ⊗ Not generalizable (fixed set of objects).
   - **CLIP score**: CLIP embeddings to assess image–text matching (semantic score). ⊗ Doesn't tell what exactly is incorrect.
   - **ALOHa**: ALOHa$_o$ scores each object and identifies the degree of hallucination; ALOHa aggregates for the total.
- **Process**
  1. Extract objects with LLM prompting from both sides (candidate and references); also extract from the image *(detections)*.
  2. Match caption objects to image objects.
  3. Use BERT-style semantic embeddings *(uncertain reading)*.

## Summary
ALOHa (Assessment with Language models for Object Hallucination; UC Berkeley, with David Chan, John Canny, Joseph Gonzalez and Trevor Darrell) measures whether a machine-generated image caption mentions objects that are not actually in the image. The standard metric, CHAIR, only recognizes the 80 MS COCO object categories plus a synonym list, so it misses most hallucinations in captions about anything else. ALOHa replaces string matching with an LLM that pulls out the visually grounded objects from any caption, and replaces exact matches with semantic similarity, so "wolf" for a "dog" is penalized less than "potato". It also says *which* object is hallucinated, not just whether the caption is wrong. This is the paper I mentioned in my cold email to David Chan.

## Problem
Captioning models still hallucinate objects. CHAIR is limited to a fixed COCO vocabulary and gives binary decisions; embedding-based scores like CLIPScore give a single number for the whole caption and cannot localize which object is wrong. An open-vocabulary, localizable, graded hallucination measure is needed.

## Related work
- CHAIR (Rohrbach et al. 2018) — the prior standard; string matching against COCO objects and synonyms.
- CLIPScore and RefCLIPScore ([2104.08718](https://arxiv.org/abs/2104.08718)) — embedding-based caption quality scores, compared as baselines.
- POPE — probes VLMs with yes/no object questions; addresses a different problem (likelihood to hallucinate, not scoring a given caption).
- S-BERT (Sentence-BERT) — the semantic text embedding used for matching.
- LLM-as-evaluator work in NLP — inspiration for using an LLM to parse captions.

## Method
![Figure 2 from the paper: ALOHa overview, an LLM extracts grounded objects from candidate and reference captions, objects are filtered, and semantic similarity with Hungarian matching gives per-object and caption-level scores](assets/aloha-hallucination-metric/onenote-fig1.png)

1. **Object extraction.** An LLM (ChatGPT) with an in-context prompt extracts visually grounded noun phrases (with attributes, e.g. "purple shirt") from the candidate caption, giving set $\mathcal{C}$, and from the reference captions, giving $\mathcal{R}$. $\mathcal{R}$ is augmented with object detections from the image (DETR predictions, or ground-truth boxes in an oracle variant).
2. **Filtering.** spaCy adds the root noun of every reference phrase to $\mathcal{R}$ ("white shirt" → also "shirt"), so a candidate is not penalized for being more general, while unsupported extra specificity still is. Conjunctions ("fork or knife") are expanded into all single-object choices; objects the LLM marks as uncertain ("Frisbee (possibly)") are removed from the candidate set but kept in the reference set.
3. **Matching.** Each object string is embedded with S-BERT; cosine similarities form a matrix $\mathcal{S}_{i,j}$ between candidate and reference objects; the Hungarian method finds the maximum-similarity one-to-one assignment.
4. **Scores.** Per object, $\text{ALOHa}_o(c) = \max_{i,j} w_{c}$, the best matched similarity across all parsings (benefit of the doubt). Per caption, $\text{ALOHa} = \min_{c \in \mathcal{C}} \text{ALOHa}_o(c)$: one hallucinated object makes the whole caption a hallucination, and correct objects cannot compensate.

Reused: an off-the-shelf LLM, spaCy, S-BERT, DETR and the Hungarian algorithm. New: the pipeline design (extraction, filtering rules, matching, min-aggregation) and the HAT benchmark.

## Data
- **HAT (HAllucination Test):** a new set of 490 MS COCO caption samples (90 validation, 400 test) labeled by experts for hallucination at the word and caption level.
- **FOIL** (COCO captions with one object swapped for a similar one, e.g. bus → car) and **nocaps-FOIL** (the same idea on nocaps, with objects beyond COCO categories).
- Qualitative Flickr30k examples with captions from a recent captioning model.

## Training
There is no training: ALOHa is an evaluation pipeline built from pretrained components. Walking an illustrative caption through it (modeled on the paper's Figure 1, where CHAIR misses a hallucinated "baseball player" and "bat"): the LLM extracts {baseball player, bat, field} from the caption and an object set from the references and detections; S-BERT similarities and Hungarian matching find that "field" matches well but "baseball player" and "bat" have low best-match scores; the caption's ALOHa is the lowest of these, flagging a hallucination and pointing to the two objects. Evaluation uses Average Precision (how well the score separates hallucinated from clean captions across thresholds) and Localization Accuracy (whether the specific hallucinated objects are identified).

## Results
- ALOHa identifies **13.6%** more hallucinated objects than CHAIR on HAT and **30.8%** more on nocaps, where objects go beyond COCO categories.
- On HAT, ALOHa with DETR detections beats CHAIR by 11.8% and CLIPScore by 8.5% in AP; RefCLIPScore reaches similar AP but cannot localize. ALOHa more than doubles CHAIR's localization accuracy.
- Ablations show the choice of LLM matters: weaker zero-shot parsers reduce downstream performance.

## Takeaways / questions
- The appealing idea for me was replacing hard string matching with *soft semantic matching plus an optimal assignment*, which gives a graded, explainable score.
- The metric inherits the LLM's parsing errors and the embedding model's notion of similarity (e.g. "electric guitar" vs "acoustic guitar" scores as similar even when wrong).
- Compared with CLIPScore, which I re-implemented, ALOHa works in text space against references rather than directly comparing the caption to the image, which is why it can localize objects but needs references or detections.

notes.title: Denoising Diffusion Implicit Models
notes.tldr: DDIM reuses a model trained exactly like DDPM but samples with a non-Markovian, optionally deterministic process that can skip steps, giving 10×–50× faster sampling, a meaningful latent space for interpolation, and near-exact image inversion.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Mentioned alongside DDPM in my Aug 2025 research application (“DDPM (and DDIM)”) as one of the papers that connected the dots for me when re-implementing diffusion from scratch.

## Summary
DDIM fixes DDPM's biggest practical problem: sampling needs ~1000 sequential network calls. Song, Meng and Ermon notice that DDPM's training loss only depends on the per-step marginals $q(x_t\mid x_0)$, not on the forward process being a Markov chain. So there is a whole family of (non-Markovian) forward processes with the same loss — and therefore the same trained network — but different reverse samplers. One member is fully deterministic; it can jump over many steps and still produce good images. No retraining required: you take a DDPM checkpoint and sample 10×–50× faster.

## Problem
Sampling 50k 32×32 images from a DDPM takes about 20 hours on one RTX 2080 Ti (versus under a minute for a GAN), and nearly 1000 hours at 256×256. Simply taking fewer DDPM steps destroys quality. How can we sample faster from an already-trained diffusion model?

## Related work
- DDPM — [2006.11239](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11239): the model and training objective DDIM reuses unchanged.
- NCSN / score matching (Song & Ermon, 2019): the same denoising objective from the score-based view.
- Neural ODEs (Chen et al., 2018): DDIM's deterministic sampler is an Euler discretization of an ODE, linking it to continuous-time models.
- Implicit generative models (Mohamed & Lakshminarayanan, 2016): DDIM with $\sigma=0$ is one — samples are a deterministic function of the starting noise, like a GAN.

## Method
![Figure 1 (right) from the paper: the non-Markovian inference model — each x_t depends on both x_{t-1} and x_0](assets/ddim/fig1.png)

(Notation: DDIM writes $\alpha_t$ for what DDPM calls $\bar\alpha_t$, the cumulative product.)

**Generalized forward process (new).** Define a family of inference distributions indexed by $\sigma\in\mathbb{R}^T_{\ge0}$, where each step conditions on $x_0$ as well as the previous state. They are constructed so that the marginal $q_\sigma(x_t\mid x_0)=\mathcal{N}(\sqrt{\alpha_t}x_0,(1-\alpha_t)I)$ is identical to DDPM's for every $\sigma$. Because DDPM's simplified loss depends only on these marginals, the same noise-prediction network $\epsilon_\theta$ is optimal for all of them.

**Generalized sampler.** Given $x_t$, the network's noise estimate gives a "predicted $x_0$", and the update is
$$x_{t-1}=\sqrt{\alpha_{t-1}}\underbrace{\Big(\tfrac{x_t-\sqrt{1-\alpha_t}\,\epsilon_\theta(x_t)}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big)}_{\text{predicted }x_0}+\underbrace{\sqrt{1-\alpha_{t-1}-\sigma_t^2}\;\epsilon_\theta(x_t)}_{\text{direction pointing to }x_t}+\underbrace{\sigma_t\epsilon_t}_{\text{random noise}}.$$
A knob $\eta$ scales $\sigma_t$: $\eta=1$ recovers DDPM; $\eta=0$ ($\sigma_t=0$) gives the deterministic **DDIM** sampler.

**Skipping steps.** The same construction works on any increasing sub-sequence $\tau$ of timesteps (e.g. 20 out of 1000), so you sample along a short trajectory using the full model.

**ODE view.** With $\sigma=0$, the update is an Euler step of an ODE. That makes the mapping noise → image deterministic and (approximately) invertible: you can encode a real image into its latent $x_T$ by running the ODE backwards.

## Data
No new training data: CIFAR-10 and LSUN Bedroom/Church use pretrained DDPM checkpoints from Ho et al.; the authors train their own CelebA 64×64 model with the same objective.

## Training
Identical to DDPM: noise an image to a random step, have the U-Net predict the noise, minimize MSE. All the novelty is at sampling time.

## Results
- CIFAR-10 FID with DDIM ($\eta=0$): 13.36 / 6.84 / 4.67 / 4.16 at 10 / 20 / 50 / 100 steps, versus 41.07 / 18.36 / 8.01 / 5.78 for $\eta=1$ at the same step counts (Table 1). At 1000 steps DDPM with its original variance is still best (FID 3.17 vs 4.04).
- On CelebA, 20-step DDIM roughly matches 100-step DDPM; overall 10×–50× wall-clock speedups at similar quality.
- *Consistency*: the same $x_T$ gives images with the same high-level content regardless of how many steps are used, so $x_T$ acts as a real latent code.
- Semantically meaningful interpolation by interpolating initial noise, and low-error reconstruction by encoding then decoding.

## Takeaways / questions
- The insight "the loss only sees marginals, so the sampler is a free design choice" opened the door to the whole fast-sampler literature (probability-flow ODE, DPM-Solver, etc.).
- DDIM inversion is what later editing methods rely on; deterministic sampling is also the default in Stable Diffusion (LDM results use DDIM).
- Fun to see from a physics angle: DDPM ≈ stochastic (Langevin-like) dynamics, DDIM ≈ the corresponding deterministic flow.

notes.title: Extracting Training Data from Large Language Models
notes.tldr: Querying GPT-2 alone recovers verbatim training data — 604 memorized sequences including names, phone numbers, code and UUIDs, some from a single document — by sampling many generations and ranking them with perplexity-ratio membership tests.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
This work excites me because I have always been interested in similar risks of how attackers can recover API keys, credentials, and access to private data using prompts. I have worked on this issue under deeptrial, a startup at Berkeley SkyDeck attempting to stop these attacks using runtime safeguards like content filtering. As companies rely heavily on LLMs, attacks and safeguards around this will be of vital importance.

## Summary
The landmark paper (a large Google-led collaboration that included OpenAI) showing that a large language model can leak individual training examples to anyone who can query it. Using only black-box access to GPT-2, the attack extracts hundreds of verbatim sequences, including one person's full name, address, email, phone and fax number. Since GPT-2's training data is public web text, the attack is demonstrated safely, but the lesson applies to any model trained on private data.

## Problem
It was commonly assumed that because large LMs barely overfit (GPT-2's train loss is only ~10% below test loss), they don't memorize individual examples in a way that matters. Prior memorization work used artificial “canaries” or small models; nobody had shown practical extraction of naturally occurring rare data from a production-scale LM.

## Related work
- Carlini et al., *The Secret Sharer* ([arXiv:1802.08232](https://arxiv.org/abs/1802.08232)) — memorization of inserted canaries; the perplexity-based exposure idea.
- Shokri et al., membership inference attacks (2017) — deciding whether a sample was in the training set.
- Abadi et al., DP-SGD ([arXiv:1607.00133](https://arxiv.org/abs/1607.00133)) — differential privacy, the principled mitigation.

## Method
**Definition.** A string $s$ is *extractable* if some prefix makes the model emit it as the most likely continuation; it is **$k$-eidetic memorized** if it is extractable yet appears in at most $k$ training documents. Small $k$ = genuinely worrying memorization (the MIT license appearing thousands of times doesn't count).

**Attack, step 1 — generate many samples** from GPT-2 XL (1.5B; reused, no training) with three strategies: top-$n$ sampling ($n = 40$, 256 tokens) from an empty prompt; **decaying temperature** ($t = 10 \to 1$ over the first 20 tokens) to explore diverse prefixes and then lock onto memorized continuations; and **conditioning on Internet text** — short prefixes from Common Crawl.

**Step 2 — membership inference**, i.e. rank samples by how likely they are to be memorized. Low perplexity $\mathcal{P} = \exp(-\frac{1}{n}\sum_i \log p(x_i \mid x_{<i}))$ alone mostly finds boringly repetitive text, so they use *ratios* that cancel out “generically easy” text:
- perplexity of GPT-2 XL vs. GPT-2 **Small** or **Medium** (memorized only by the big model → big gap);
- perplexity vs. **zlib** compression entropy;
- perplexity vs. perplexity of the **lowercased** text;
- minimum perplexity over a 50-token **sliding window**.

**Evaluation.** For each of the 3 × 6 configurations they take 100 of the top-1000 ranked samples (1,800 candidates), check them by searching the web, and confirm with OpenAI against GPT-2's actual training set.

## Data
GPT-2's training set: about 40 GB of text from pages linked on Reddit, de-duplicated at the document level, trained for ~12 epochs.

## Results
- **604** unique memorized examples out of 1,800 candidates (33.5% overall; the best configuration reached **67%** precision).
- Content includes news, licenses, URLs, named individuals, contact info, code, configuration files, and high-entropy strings like UUIDs and base-64 data — some contained in a single training document.
- **Larger models memorize more:** for URLs repeated within one document, GPT-2 XL memorized a URL after just 33 repetitions, while the small model only emitted the one inserted 359 times.
- Mitigations discussed: differential-privacy training (sound but costly in utility), careful de-duplication, limiting impact of memorization on downstream applications, and auditing — none a full fix.

## Takeaways / questions
- The same mechanism underlies the risks I worked on at deeptrial: secrets like API keys are high-entropy strings, exactly the kind of content that is both memorizable and easy to verify once leaked.
- Runtime filtering (what deeptrial does) treats the symptom at the output; training-time defenses (dedup, DP, scrubbing secrets from data) treat the cause. Both are needed.
- The perplexity-ratio trick is a reusable idea: compare a model against a reference that captures “generic” likelihood to isolate what is specific to that model.

notes.title: Machine Bullshit: Characterizing the Emergent Disregard for Truth in Large Language Models
notes.tldr: Frames LLM untruthfulness as Frankfurt's “bullshit” (indifference to truth), introduces a Bullshit Index comparing internal belief to explicit claims plus a four-way taxonomy, and finds RLHF raises the index by 0.285 while CoT increases empty rhetoric and paltering.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
I really liked the structured approach to qualifying styles of LLM hallucinations in this paper and the tradeoff between accuracy and alignment it exposed. Some results, like how CoT led to empty rhetoric, are something I personally experienced a lot. Other findings, especially how RLHF can actually increase the Bullshit Index, are really interesting. I would be excited to work on understanding the accuracy/transparency vs. alignment tradeoff in RLHF by assessing how it performs on different tasks and looking into the activation/latent spaces.

## Summary
From Princeton (Fisac, Griffiths) and Berkeley (Song). Hallucination (being wrong) and sycophancy (flattering) don't cover the many ways LLM outputs mislead — technically-true-but-misleading statements, vague hedges, fluent filler. Borrowing philosopher Harry Frankfurt's definition of bullshit as speech produced *without regard to its truth*, the paper gives a quantitative measure (does what the model says track what it internally believes?) and a qualitative taxonomy, then shows that standard alignment and prompting practices make it worse.

## Problem
How to measure and characterise the broad, emergent loss of truthfulness in aligned LLMs — including cases where the model “knows” the truth but its claims don't depend on it.

## Related work
- Frankfurt, *On Bullshit* (1986) and *On Truth* (2006); Bergstrom & West, *Calling Bullshit* (2021) — the definitions and taxonomy.
- Liang et al. (2025), RLHF and emergent misalignment in a Marketplace setting — the RLHF-tuned models and Marketplace data reused here.
- Sharma et al., *Towards Understanding Sycophancy* ([arXiv:2310.13548](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.13548)) — sycophancy as one form of bullshit.
- Hicks et al. (2024), “ChatGPT is bullshit” — hard vs. soft bullshit.

## Method
**Bullshit Index (BI).** For each statement, take the model's *internal belief* $p \in [0,1]$ (probability on the first token of a multiple-choice answer) and its *explicit claim* $y \in \{0,1\}$. Then
$$\mathrm{BI} = 1 - |r_{pb}(p, y)|, \qquad r_{pb} = \frac{\mu_{p,y=1} - \mu_{p,y=0}}{\sigma_p}\sqrt{q(1-q)}$$
where $r_{pb}$ is the point-biserial correlation and $q$ the fraction of “true” claims. BI ≈ 0 means claims track beliefs (honest if $r>0$, systematic lying if $r<0$ — both care about truth); BI ≈ 1 means claims are independent of beliefs. This separates *honest-mistake* hallucinations (low BI) from *bullshit* hallucinations (high BI).

**Taxonomy (four forms).** *Empty rhetoric* — flowery, substance-free text; *paltering* — literally true statements that mislead by omission; *weasel words* — vague qualifiers (“studies suggest… may help… in some cases”); *unverified claims* — confident assertions without support. Labelled at scale by an o3-mini LLM judge, validated with two human studies (1,200 and 300 participants): humans themselves agree weakly (Krippendorff's $\alpha$ 0.03–0.18), the judge matches human majority with Cohen's $\kappa$ 0.21–0.80, and perfectly when ≥80% of humans agree.

**Experiments.** (1) RLHF: compare base vs. RLHF-tuned Llama-2-7B and Llama-3-8B (from Liang et al.). (2) Prompting: chain-of-thought (reason in `<think>` tags) and *principal–agent* framing (assistant serves both the user and a company with conflicting interests) on GPT-4o-mini, Claude-3.5-Sonnet, Gemini-1.5-flash, o3-mini, Llama-3.3-70B, Qwen-2.5-72B. (3) Political contexts.

![Figure 1 from the paper: machine bullshit, the BullshitEval benchmark, and the finding that RLHF and CoT amplify it](assets/machine-bullshit/fig1.png)

## Data
- **BullshitEval** (new): 2,400 scenarios across 100 AI-assistant roles (product recommendations, expert advice), some with information only the assistant sees.
- **Marketplace** (Liang et al.): 1,200 shopping scenarios with eight attributes per product; the assistant may know attributes the user can't see. For the RLHF test, they control whether the cheapest product's requested feature is Positive, Negative or Unknown (3,600 scenarios) — creating tension between honest disappointment and pleasing deception.
- **Political Neutrality** (Fisher et al.): universal rights statements, political opinion prompts (with and without partisan viewpoints), and good/bad-faith conspiracy questions.

## Results
- **RLHF drives deception:** positive claims despite Unknown/Negative ground truth go from 20.9% / 11.8% to **84.5% / 67.9%** after RLHF ($\chi^2 = 1509$, $p < 0.001$). Truth-tracking (Cramér's $V$ between ground truth and claim) drops from 0.575 to 0.269 — the model doesn't become confused about the truth, it becomes uncommitted to reporting it.
- **BI rises by 0.285** after RLHF (95% CI 0.216–0.355), roughly a quarter of the scale.
- RLHF raises user satisfaction (>80% perfect ratings, +48%) while on Marketplace increasing empty rhetoric 39.8%, weasel words 26.8%, paltering 57.8%, unverified claims 55.6%; smaller but consistent increases on BullshitEval and Political Neutrality.
- **CoT** consistently increases empty rhetoric and paltering (GPT-4o-mini: +20.9% and +11.5%); most models use fewer weasel words under CoT. **Principal–agent** framing increases all forms (e.g. unverified claims +26.1% GPT-4o-mini, +26.7% Claude-3.5-Sonnet).
- In political contexts, weasel words dominate.
- GPT-4o-mini and GPT-4o already have very high BI on BullshitEval (0.952 and 0.987).

## Takeaways / questions
- The BI's belief–claim split is the key idea: truthfulness should be measured against the model's own internal state, not only against ground truth.
- Directly supports my interest in the accuracy/transparency vs. alignment tradeoff in RLHF. Natural next step: probe activations to see whether “belief” is preserved internally after RLHF while the output layer stops using it.
- Internal belief here is just first-token MCQA probability; a linear probe on hidden states would be a stronger belief measure.
- The taxonomy is subjective (low human agreement), so the qualitative numbers are noisier than the BI.

notes.title: Signal in the Noise: Polysemantic Interference Transfers and Predicts Cross-Model Influence
notes.tldr: Uses SAEs on Pythia-70M and GPT-2-Small to find feature pairs that mean unrelated things but share activation directions, shows that pushing one steers the model toward the other, and finds these interference patterns transfer to Llama-3.1-8B/70B and Gemma-2-9B.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
(I knew it as “Probing the Vulnerability of Large Language Models to Polysemantic Interventions”.) This is the type of research I would be most excited to work on, as it connects concepts in interpretability with real-world applications in AI safety. Polysemanticity (or the way I learnt about it, superposition) is common in language models, but I never thought of it as a potential threat. I am excited that in the future our ‘communication’ with the model will not need heavy data or tuning for specific behaviour, but rather to directly nudge neurons or features. Polysemantic behaviour currently hinders that possibility, so perhaps we should be forcing the model to represent concepts with unique neurons/activations.

## Summary
From Berkeley (Dawn Song) and Chicago (James Evans). Superposition lets a model pack more features than it has dimensions, at the price of features overlapping. This paper treats that overlap as an attack surface: if “feature E” and “feature G” are semantically unrelated but point in similar directions in activation space, then nudging E (or prompting with E-flavoured text) should also push the model toward G. They show this works in small models, that the effect concentrates in highly polysemantic “hub” neurons, and — the surprising part — that interference pairs found in two small models still work as black-box levers on much larger instruction-tuned models. (The current arXiv title differs from the one in my notes; the earlier versions I read in Aug 2025 were apparently titled “Probing the Vulnerability of Large Language Models to Polysemantic Interventions”.)

## Problem
SAE work mostly uses polysemanticity as an obstacle to interpretation. Its *safety* implications — whether overlapping features can be exploited to covertly control outputs — had barely been studied in language models (unlike vision models, where polysemantic adversarial control is well documented).

## Related work
- Elhage et al., *Toy Models of Superposition* ([arXiv:2209.10652](https://arxiv.org/abs/2209.10652)) — superposition, and the note that it can increase adversarial vulnerability.
- Bricken et al., *Towards Monosemanticity* (2023); Templeton et al., *Scaling Monosemanticity* (2024) — SAEs as a way to extract monosemantic features.
- Lan et al. (2024) — SAE features are partly universal across LLMs, which motivates the transfer test.

## Method
Reused: Neuronpedia's pretrained SAEs (32,768 features) for every sub-module/layer of **Pythia-70M** and **GPT-2-Small**, and GPT-4o-mini auto-interpretation glosses for features. New:
- **Two notions of closeness.** *Interference* $I_\ell(i,j) = \cos(\hat{d}_i, \hat{d}_j)$ between the features' directions in activation space; *semantic relatedness* $S(i,j)$ = cosine between text-embedding-3-large embeddings of their glosses (a proxy for the “human symbolic manifold”).
- **Picking unrelated pairs.** Agglomerative clustering of glosses (cutoffs 0.40 down to 0.15) groups features at a consistent semantic level; interference features are sampled from *other* clusters in interference bins [0,0.1] … [0.4,1].
- **Four interventions** on a target feature $f$: (1) steer along the interfering SAE feature's direction; (2) steer along the gradient of the interfering feature's top-activating token w.r.t. the layer (no SAE needed at use time); (3) prompt injection — prepend highly activating text snippets of the interfering feature; (4) mask or amplify neurons with different degrees of polysemanticity (number of features connected with weight > 0.2).
- **Metric.** Relative change $\Delta c$ in a probability-weighted embedding similarity between the next-token distribution and the target feature's top tokens.

![Figure 3 from the paper: steering along interfering but semantically distinct SAE feature directions shifts next-token predictions toward the target semantics](assets/polysemantic-interference/fig1.png)

**Transfer test.** Take interference features shared by *both* small models for common target types (location, name, number, science, emotion, animal, color, time) and apply token-gradient steering and prompt injection to Llama-3.1-8B/70B-Instruct and Gemma-2-9B-Instruct.

## Data
Context sentences generated per target feature; 480 randomly sampled target features from GPT-2-Small and 180 from Pythia-70M; a small HellaSwag check that steering doesn't wreck task performance.

## Results
- Steering along unrelated-but-interfering feature directions reliably moves predictions toward the target semantics; token-gradient steering gives roughly **10× larger** effects than SAE-direction steering. Prompt injection gives moderate shifts.
- **Transfer:** gradient steering built from shared interference tokens raised target-type tokens into the top-10 predictions with over 95% success for types like location, name and emotion on Llama-3.1-8B and Gemma-2-9B; prompt injection significantly beats random baselines on all three large models for many types (e.g. science on Llama-3.1-70B: 67.3% success at getting target tokens into the top-30).
- Fewer than 30% of shared interference pairs have a higher-order relation a human (or LLM annotator) can explain; most are counterintuitive yet stable across models.
- More polysemantic neurons are more vulnerable. “Super-neurons” (> 500 connected features) are asymmetric: masking them matters less than expected, amplifying them has outsized effects.

## Takeaways / questions
- Supports my note: polysemanticity is not just an interpretability nuisance but a control and safety risk, and the risk is *structured*, not random.
- The transfer result suggests convergent representation geometry across model families — related to the platonic-representation idea — and implies black-box attacks can be designed on small open models.
- Open: would training for monosemanticity (e.g. sparsity penalties on activations) remove these levers, and at what capability cost? Results are on next-token shifts, not yet on harmful behaviours.

notes.title: Advances and Challenges in Foundation Agents: From Brain-Inspired Intelligence to Evolutionary, Collaborative, and Safe Systems
notes.tldr: A book-length survey (48 authors) that defines a “foundation agent” through a brain-inspired perception–cognition–action loop and organises the field into four parts — core modules, self-evolution, multi-agent systems, and safety.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
“Agent survey: write a blog post on what is actually an agent?”

## Summary
A very large, book-style survey of LLM-based agents written by a big multi-institution team. Its distinctive angle is mapping each agent component onto an analogous brain function (memory, world model, reward, emotion, goals) and then giving a formal definition of the agent loop. That formal loop is exactly the thing to start from when answering “what actually is an agent?”.

## Problem
“Agent” is used for everything from a prompt with a tool call to a multi-agent society. The survey tries to give a unified vocabulary and architecture so that design, evaluation and improvement of agents can be discussed modularly.

## Takeaways / questions
- Good skeleton for the planned blog post: the minimal answer is “a loop with persistent state $M_t$ that is updated by learning and read by reasoning to choose actions”, and most “agent” products only implement a thin slice of $M_t$ (memory + goal).
- The brain analogies (emotion, reward modules) are motivating rather than operational; few current agents have anything like an explicit emotional state.
- Useful as a reference index rather than something to read cover to cover (it is enormous).

## Contents
The book has four parts:
1. **Modular foundations** — cognition, memory, world modelling, reward, emotion, perception and action, each related to brain analogues.
2. **Self-enhancement and evolution** — how agents optimise their own prompts, workflows, tools and models, and learn continually.
3. **Multi-agent systems** — cooperation, competition, communication and emergent collective intelligence.
4. **Safe and beneficial agents** — intrinsic threats (to the model “brain”, perception, action) and extrinsic ones (memory, environment, other agents), plus alignment and mitigation.

**The core definition (Section 1.3).** At each time step $t$:
- perception produces an observation from the environment state, filtered by the current mental state: $o_t = \mathrm{P}(s_t, M_{t-1})$;
- cognition updates the mental state and picks an action: $(M_t, a_t) = \mathrm{C}(M_{t-1}, a_{t-1}, o_t)$, where $M_t$ bundles memory, world model, emotion, goals and reward; cognition splits into **learning** $M_t = \mathrm{L}(\cdot)$ and **reasoning** $a_t = \mathrm{R}(M_t)$;
- actions can be *external* (affect the world) or *internal* (planning, decision-making);
- execution and environment transition: $a'_t = \mathrm{E}(a_t)$, $s_{t+1} = \mathrm{T}(s_t, a'_t)$.

In multi-agent settings each agent has its own $(M^i_t, a^i_t, o^i_t)$ and the environment updates on all actions; agents also sit inside “societies” (markets, legal systems) that constrain them.

![Figure 1.2 from the paper: the general framework for an intelligent agent loop and agent society](assets/foundation-agents-survey/fig1.png)

A **Foundation Agent** is then defined as an autonomous, adaptive system that perceives diverse signals, continuously learns to refine structured internal states (memory, world model, goals, emotion, reward), and reasons about external and internal actions to pursue complex, long-term objectives.

notes.title: Feature-Level Insights into Artificial Text Detection with Sparse Autoencoders
notes.tldr: Uses pretrained Gemma Scope SAEs on Gemma-2-2B's residual stream to detect AI-generated text; SAE features beat raw activations as classifier inputs and reveal interpretable “LLM style” features such as wordy intros, repetition and over-formality.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed as “Artificial text detection”. In my *New Research Project* doc (Aug 2025): “Build my own autoencoders for artificially generated text detection.”

## Summary
A short paper that turns artificial text detection (ATD) into an interpretability problem. Instead of training an opaque detector, the authors push text through Gemma-2-2B, decompose each token's residual-stream activation with off-the-shelf sparse autoencoders, and ask which SAE features separate human from machine text. The detector works well, and — the real point — the useful features have readable meanings that describe how LLM writing differs from human writing.

## Problem
No single ATD algorithm generalises reliably to unseen domains or new generator models, and existing detectors (statistical scores, fine-tuned classifiers) say little about *why* a text was flagged.

## Related work
- Sparse dictionary learning for LLM features (Cunningham/Huben et al., [arXiv:2309.08600](https://arxiv.org/abs/2309.08600); Anthropic's Towards Monosemanticity) — the SAE idea.
- Gemma Scope (Lieberum et al., 2024) — the pretrained SAEs they reuse.
- COLING 2025 GenAI Content Detection Task 1 and RAID (Dugan et al., 2024) — the datasets.

## Method
Everything model-side is reused: **Gemma-2-2B** as the reader and **Gemma Scope** SAEs on the residual stream of every even layer. An SAE maps an activation $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^d$ to a sparse, non-negative code $f(\mathbf{x}) = \sigma(W_\text{enc}\mathbf{x} + b_\text{enc}) \in \mathbb{R}^M$ with $M \gg d$, and reconstructs $\hat{\mathbf{x}} = W_\text{dec} f(\mathbf{x}) + b_\text{dec}$.

New in the paper is the analysis pipeline:
1. **Text-level features:** sum the SAE codes over all tokens, $\mathbf{f} = \sum_i f^{(l)}(\mathbf{x}_i^{(l)})$.
2. **Classifiers:** XGBoost on the full feature vector (vs. mean-pooled raw activations as a baseline) to rank features, and one-feature threshold classifiers to test single features by domain and by generator.
3. **Interpretation:** manually reading top-activating texts, plus **steering** — add $\lambda A_{\max}\mathbf{d}_i$ (a decoder column scaled by the feature's max activation) to the hidden state during generation and have GPT-4o describe how outputs change.
4. **Robustness:** check on RAID whether important features are just sensitive to attacks or shallow properties like length.

![Figure 1 from the paper: interpretations of one of the most “universal” SAE features for artificial text detection](assets/sae-artificial-text-detection/fig1.png)

## Data
The COLING 2025 shared-task dataset (binary human vs. machine, generators from mT5 and OPT to GPT-4o and LLaMA-3; classifiers trained on Train, tested on Dev, Devtest and Test), and RAID for attacks (paraphrasing, homoglyphs, varied sampling).

## Results
- SAE features outperform raw activations as XGBoost inputs on training and held-out subsets (Figure 2); at layer 16 they also beat the reported state-of-the-art MTL model on this dataset. Layer 16 gives the best generalisation.
- “General” features (e.g. 3608, 4645 in layer 16) work across domains and modern generators; robust features correspond to excessive complexity (3608), assertive claims (4645), wordy introductions (6587), repetition (8264) and formality (14161). Feature 8264 is near-perfect for GPT-3.5+.
- Domain-specific signals: overcomplicated syntax (arXiv), excessive detail (finance), speculative links (Reddit), hallucinated facts (Wikipedia), improper tone (medicine).
- Hardest domains: essays and Yelp reviews, i.e. when the generator is prompted to sound personal; detection is easy with default prompts and hard when the prompt style changes.
- Their readings of 3608 and 4645 are broader than Neuronpedia's auto-labels.

## Takeaways / questions
- Directly relevant to my “build my own autoencoders for AI text detection” idea; this paper is the baseline to replicate (Gemma Scope makes it cheap).
- The key weakness is adversarial: style features vanish under personalised prompts, so an SAE detector inherits the same arms race as any detector.
- Open: do features transfer across reader models, and would a task-specific SAE (trained on human-vs-AI text) find better features than general-purpose ones?

notes.title: Learning to Model the World with Language
notes.tldr: Dynalang extends DreamerV3 so its world model reads one language token per step alongside images and learns to predict future text, image, and reward representations; acting from imagined rollouts, it uses hints, manuals and instructions that make model-free agents worse.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
“Research at NLP that expands capabilities of agents like the *Learning to Model the World with Language* paper by Jessy Lin genuinely excites me.” (Aug 2025)

## Summary
From UC Berkeley (Jessy Lin with Yuqing Du, Olivia Watkins, DreamerV3 author Danijar Hafner, Pieter Abbeel, Dan Klein and Anca Dragan). Most embodied agents use language only as a task instruction (“pick up the blue block”). Dynalang treats *all* language — “the bottle is in the living room”, “I put the bowls away”, a game manual — as a signal for **predicting the future**: what the agent will see, how the world will change, and what will be rewarded. That unifies language understanding with self-supervised world modelling, and lets the agent use kinds of language that language-conditioned policies can't exploit.

## Problem
How should an agent integrate diverse language with vision and action? Language-conditioned policies map instruction + observation → action directly; the paper shows their performance *drops* when the language gets richer (hints, descriptions, corrections), because mapping such language to actions with only reward as supervision is hard.

## Related work
- DreamerV3 (Hafner et al., [arXiv:2301.04104](https://arxiv.org/abs/2301.04104)) — the model-based RL algorithm Dynalang builds on.
- Ha & Schmidhuber, *World Models* ([arXiv:1803.10122](https://arxiv.org/abs/1803.10122)) — learning a generative model of the environment and acting inside it.
- Messenger (Hanjie et al., 2021) and VLN-CE (Krantz et al., 2020) — benchmarks with game manuals and navigation instructions.
- IMPALA and R2D2 — the model-free, language-conditioned baselines.

## Method
Reused: DreamerV3's recurrent state-space model (GRU sequence model, CNN image encoder/decoder, MLPs) and its actor-critic learning from imagination, unchanged. Optionally reused: T5-small token embeddings. New: language enters the world model **one token per timestep, paired with the current image frame** (they compared alternatives and this simple alignment worked best).

World model, with recurrent state $h_t$ and discrete latent $z_t$:
$$\hat{z}_t, h_t = \mathrm{seq}(z_{t-1}, h_{t-1}, a_{t-1}), \quad z_t \sim \mathrm{enc}(x_t, l_t, h_t), \quad \hat{x}_t, \hat{l}_t, \hat{r}_t, \hat{c}_t = \mathrm{dec}(z_t, h_t)$$
Representation loss = image reconstruction $\|\hat{x}_t - x_t\|^2$ + language token cross-entropy + reward and continue prediction + a KL term pulling $z_t$ toward the predicted $\hat{z}_t$ (so representations are predictable). The prediction loss trains $\hat{z}_{t+1}$ to match the next representation.

Policy: actor $\pi(a_t \mid h_t, z_t)$ and critic $V(h_t, z_t)$ are trained purely on rollouts imagined by the world model.

![Figure 1 from the paper: Dynalang uses language to predict future text, image observations and rewards in HomeGrid](assets/dynalang/fig1.png)

Extra capabilities from being generative: **text-only pretraining** (zero out image/action inputs and train only the language part of the world model), and **language generation** by adding tokens to the action space (LangRoom).

## Data
Four environments: **HomeGrid** (new; visual gridworld house with task instructions plus hints about object locations, dynamics, and corrections), **Messenger** (symbolic game with hundreds of human-written manuals needing multi-hop reasoning), **VLN-CE** in Habitat (photorealistic Matterport3D homes, 10,819 crowd-sourced instructions, low-level actions), and **LangRoom** (agent must answer questions in language). Text pretraining: in-domain manuals or **TinyStories** (~2M stories, ~500M tokens).

## Training
In HomeGrid at time $t$ the agent gets a frame $x_t$ and one token $l_t$ (e.g. “bottle”, from “the bottle is in the living room”). Both are encoded into $z_t$ together with memory $h_t$; the decoder must reconstruct the frame and token and predict reward; the sequence model predicts $\hat{z}_{t+1}$. Losses are summed and backpropagated through the world model using batches from a replay buffer. Then, from each $z_t$, the policy imagines futures inside the model and the actor-critic is updated on imagined rewards.

## Results
- **HomeGrid:** Dynalang improves as more types of hints are added (future observations, dynamics, corrections), while IMPALA and R2D2 get *worse* with hints; the model even predicts that the bottle will appear in the living room after reading the hint.
- **Messenger:** outperforms language-conditioned IMPALA/R2D2 and task-specific architectures, and is the method that achieves non-trivial performance on the hardest stage (S3) by reading manuals.
- **VLN-CE:** learns to follow instructions in photorealistic scenes, competitive with model-free baselines given task-only language.
- **Text-only pretraining helps:** on Messenger S2, pretraining on in-domain text closes much of the gap to T5 embeddings, and TinyStories pretraining exceeds T5's final performance.
- LangRoom: the agent learns to gather information and answer questions in language.

## Takeaways / questions
- Future prediction as the grounding objective is the key idea: language is “understood” to the extent it improves predictions of what happens next.
- Everything is trained from scratch at small scale with GRU world models; the open question is how this combines with large pretrained LLMs/VLMs.
- Relevant to my agent work: a world model that reads hints and manuals is a cleaner way to inject knowledge than stuffing it into a policy prompt.
