notes.title: Group Sequence Policy Optimization
notes.tldr: Qwen's GSPO replaces GRPO's per-token importance ratios with a length-normalized sequence-level ratio and clips whole responses, which stabilizes large-scale RL (especially MoE) and was used to train Qwen3.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed under "Advanced Language Models". Also listed twice in my *Blogs to write* doc as a candidate blog-post topic.

## Summary
GSPO is the Qwen team's RL algorithm for LLMs and a direct fix to GRPO. The argument is that GRPO misuses importance sampling: it applies an importance weight per token, based on a single sample from each next-token distribution, which adds noise that grows with response length and can cause irreversible collapse in big models. GSPO instead computes one importance ratio per response from the whole sequence likelihood, normalized by length, and clips at the response level. It matches "the unit of reward" (a whole response) with "the unit of optimization". It removes the need for tricks like Routing Replay in MoE RL and was used for Qwen3.

## Problem
Scaling RL needs stable training, but GRPO training of very large and MoE models on long responses often collapses, and the authors found that collapse is often unrecoverable even by rolling back checkpoints and retuning. In MoE models a gradient step changes which experts fire for the same tokens (about 10% of activated experts change per update in the 48-layer Qwen3-30B-A3B), making per-token ratios swing wildly.

## Related work
- PPO ([arXiv 1707.06347](https://arxiv.org/abs/1707.06347)): clipped importance-weighted objective with a learned value model.
- GRPO ([DeepSeekMath, arXiv 2402.03300](https://arxiv.org/abs/2402.03300)): drops the value model, uses group-normalized rewards as advantages, but keeps token-level ratios.
- DeepSeek-R1 ([arXiv 2501.12948](https://arxiv.org/abs/2501.12948)): large-scale RL for reasoning that popularized GRPO.

## Method
Reused from GRPO: sample $G$ responses per query, group-normalized advantage $\hat A_i = \frac{r(x,y_i)-\text{mean}}{\text{std}}$, PPO-style clipping, no value model. New: the sequence-level ratio.

GRPO uses a per-token ratio $w_{i,t} = \pi_\theta(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t}) / \pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(y_{i,t}\mid x,y_{i,<t})$. GSPO uses
$$s_i(\theta) = \left(\frac{\pi_\theta(y_i\mid x)}{\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(y_i\mid x)}\right)^{1/|y_i|} = \exp\Big(\tfrac{1}{|y_i|}\sum_t \log \tfrac{\pi_\theta(y_{i,t}\mid\cdot)}{\pi_{\theta_\text{old}}(y_{i,t}\mid\cdot)}\Big),$$
$$\mathcal{J}_\text{GSPO} = \mathbb{E}\Big[\tfrac{1}{G}\sum_i \min\big(s_i\hat A_i,\ \text{clip}(s_i, 1-\varepsilon, 1+\varepsilon)\hat A_i\big)\Big].$$
The length normalization (geometric mean) keeps $s_i$ in a common numerical range across lengths; without it a few tokens would swing the ratio enormously.

**Gradient view.** GSPO weights every token's $\nabla\log\pi$ in a response equally (by $s_i\hat A_i/|y_i|$), while GRPO weights each token by its own ratio, and those uneven weights accumulate. **GSPO-token** is a variant with $s_{i,t} = \text{sg}[s_i]\cdot \pi_\theta(y_{i,t})/\text{sg}[\pi_\theta(y_{i,t})]$, numerically identical to GSPO when advantages are shared, but allowing per-token advantages (e.g. for multi-turn RL).

## Training
One step: for a math query, sample $G$ answers from the old policy, score them with a verifier ($r\in[0,1]$), normalize within the group to get $\hat A_i$. For each answer compute the average per-token log-ratio between the current and old policy, exponentiate to get $s_i$, and if $s_i$ falls outside $[1-\varepsilon, 1+\varepsilon]$ (in the direction that matters) the whole response is dropped from the gradient. Otherwise all its tokens get the same push in direction $\hat A_i$. Settings in the experiments: cold-start model from Qwen3-30B-A3B-Base, each rollout batch split into 4 mini-batches; GSPO clip ranges 3e-4 (left) and 4e-4 (right), vs GRPO's carefully tuned 0.2 / 0.27. The ranges differ by orders of magnitude because the ratios are defined differently.

## Results
Results are reported as curves (no headline table): GSPO trains stably and keeps improving with more compute, refreshed queries and longer generation, and reaches higher training reward and better AIME'24, LiveCodeBench and CodeForces scores than GRPO at the same compute. GRPO needs Routing Replay (caching the old policy's expert routing) to converge on MoE at all; GSPO doesn't. Counter-intuitively, GSPO clips about two orders of magnitude more tokens than GRPO yet learns more efficiently, which the authors read as evidence that GRPO's token-level gradient estimates are noisy. Because sequence likelihoods tolerate precision mismatch, GSPO may let you use inference-engine (vLLM/SGLang) likelihoods directly without recomputing them in the training engine.

## Takeaways / questions
- A clean conceptual point: importance weights only correct a distribution mismatch when averaged over many samples, and one token sample per position doesn't do that.
- The comparison is shown on one model family with curves rather than tables, and GRPO is run with Routing Replay, so the size of the gains is hard to quantify.
- Relevant to latent-reasoning RL (Monet's VLPO, LVR's GRPO_latent), which inherits GRPO's token-level ratios. A sequence-level ratio over text and latent steps is an interesting alternative.

notes.title: Hierarchical Reasoning Model
notes.tldr: A 27M-parameter recurrent model with a slow high-level and a fast low-level module that reasons in latent space; trained from scratch on ~1000 examples, it nearly solves Sudoku-Extreme and 30x30 mazes and scores 40.3% on ARC-AGI-1.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed as “HRM”. In my Aug 2025 research application I mentioned re-implementing it from scratch: “To get a strong foundation, I particularly liked to implement important model architectures from scratch – from the family of auto encoders, to TinyLlama, DDPM, and more recent models like Hierarchical Reasoning Models.”

## Summary
HRM (Sapient Intelligence, with Tsinghua) argues that the bottleneck for reasoning is *effective computational depth*, not parameter count or chain-of-thought text. It builds a small recurrent network out of two coupled Transformer modules running at different speeds — a slow “planner” and a fast “worker” — and lets it iterate many times in latent space before answering. With no pretraining and no CoT data, a randomly initialised 27M-parameter model trained on about 1000 examples per task solves puzzles where frontier CoT models score 0%. It became one of the most-discussed “latent reasoning” papers of 2025.

## Problem
A standard Transformer has fixed depth, so a single forward pass is a bounded amount of computation; the paper shows that on hard Sudoku, making a Transformer wider doesn't help and making it deeper saturates. CoT works around this by writing intermediate steps as tokens, but that is data-hungry, slow and brittle. Plain RNNs could iterate, but they converge to a fixed point too early (later steps do nothing) and training them with backprop-through-time (BPTT) costs $O(T)$ memory.

## Related work
- Chain-of-thought prompting ([arXiv:2201.11903](https://arxiv.org/abs/2201.11903)) — the token-level reasoning HRM wants to replace.
- Deep Equilibrium Models (Bai, Kolter, Koltun, NeurIPS 2019) — fixed-point view and implicit-function gradients that justify HRM's one-step gradient.
- Adaptive Computation Time / PonderNet-style halting — HRM learns when to stop with a Q-learning head instead.
- Universal / recurrent Transformers — the recurrent baselines HRM compares against.

## Method
HRM has four learnable parts: an input embedding $f_I$, a low-level module $f_L$, a high-level module $f_H$, and an output head $f_O$. Both $f_L$ and $f_H$ are ordinary encoder-only Transformer blocks with Llama-style tweaks (RoPE, gated linear units, RMSNorm, no biases, Post-Norm) — reused components. What's new is how they are wired in time.

**Two timescales.** One forward pass runs $N$ high-level cycles of $T$ low-level steps. Inputs are combined by simple element-wise addition:
$$z_L^i = f_L(z_L^{i-1}, z_H^{i-1}, \tilde{x}), \qquad z_H^i = \begin{cases} f_H(z_H^{i-1}, z_L^i) & i \equiv 0 \pmod T \\ z_H^{i-1} & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
and the answer is read out as $\hat{y} = f_O(z_H^{NT})$.

**Hierarchical convergence.** Within a cycle, L settles toward a local equilibrium that depends on the fixed H state. Then H updates using L's result, which gives L a fresh context and restarts its convergence. So instead of an RNN that goes quiet after a few steps, HRM performs $N$ nested, stable sub-computations, for an effective depth of $NT$ steps.

**One-step gradient (no BPTT).** All but the last L and H updates run under `no_grad`; gradients flow only through output head → final H state → final L state → input embedding. This is $O(1)$ memory. The justification is the DEQ implicit-function-theorem gradient $\partial z^\star/\partial\theta = (I-J_\mathcal{F})^{-1}\partial\mathcal{F}/\partial\theta$, truncating the Neumann series $(I-J)^{-1} = I + J + J^2 + \dots$ to its first term $I$.

**Deep supervision.** A training example is processed in several *segments* (forward passes). After each segment the loss is computed, an optimizer step is taken, and the hidden state is *detached* before being fed to the next segment.

**Adaptive computation time.** A Q-head reads $z_H$ and predicts values for “halt” and “continue”; halting gives reward 1 if the answer is right. This lets the model “think fast or slow” per example, and at inference you can raise the segment limit $M_{\max}$ for extra accuracy without retraining.

## Data
Each task has roughly 1000 training examples, framed as sequence-to-sequence on flattened grids: **ARC-AGI-1/2** (with translation/rotation/flip/colour augmentations and a learned per-puzzle token; at test time 1000 augmented variants are solved and the two most common answers kept), **Sudoku-Extreme** (a new, much harder Sudoku set built by counting solver backtracks; augmented by band/digit permutations), and **Maze-Hard** (30×30 mazes with shortest path length > 110; 1000 train / 1000 test).

## Training
For one Sudoku example: the 81 cells are tokens, embedded by $f_I$; the model runs $N \times T$ L/H updates (only the last pair with gradients), the head predicts a digit per cell, and the loss is token-averaged cross-entropy (stablemax instead of softmax in small-sample runs) plus the Q-head's binary loss for halting. The detached state is carried into the next segment and the process repeats until the Q-head halts. Optimizer: Adam-atan2 with constant learning rate and warm-up.

## Results
- **ARC-AGI-1: 40.3%**, ahead of o3-mini-high (34.5%) and Claude 3.7 8K (21.2%), with 27M parameters and a 900-token context.
- Near-perfect accuracy on Sudoku-Extreme and optimal paths on Maze-Hard, where the CoT models evaluated score 0% (exact numbers are in the paper's Figure 1).
- Inference-time scaling: raising $M_{\max}$ helps a lot on Sudoku, little on ARC.
- After training, the high-level state has much higher effective dimensionality (participation ratio 89.95) than the low-level one (30.22), whereas an untrained HRM shows no such gap — the authors compare this to the mouse cortex hierarchy.

## Takeaways / questions
- A clean, small architecture to re-implement from scratch (as I did): the `no_grad` loop + one-step gradient + detach-between-segments is the whole trick.
- It is task-specific: each model is trained per benchmark on ~1000 examples, so “beats o3 on ARC” is not a like-for-like comparison with general LLMs.
- Follow-up analyses (e.g. the ARC Prize team's ablations and the Tiny Recursive Model paper) suggested much of the gain comes from the outer deep-supervision refinement loop rather than the two-level hierarchy; worth checking against my own re-implementation.
- Conceptually close to the latent-reasoning line I care about (Coconut, Mirage-style latent visual thinking): compute in hidden state, not in decoded tokens.

notes.title: Large Language Models Meet NLP: A Survey
notes.tldr: Survey of how LLMs are applied to classic NLP tasks, organized by a two-way taxonomy: parameter-frozen (zero-/few-shot prompting) vs parameter-tuning (full and parameter-efficient fine-tuning), task by task, plus open frontiers.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed as "Application in NLP".

## Summary
A task-by-task survey of LLMs for natural language processing, accepted at Frontiers of Computer Science. It frames everything around one question: for each traditional NLP task, how are LLMs used today, and have they "solved" it? Its organizing idea is a simple taxonomy of *how much you touch the weights*, which is a handy mental map for choosing between prompting and fine-tuning. A companion GitHub list (Awesome-LLM-for-NLP) collects papers and resources.

## Problem
LLMs turned many separate NLP tasks into one generative interface, and in some cases zero-shot LLMs beat supervised task-specific models. The literature grew so fast that there was no systematic, per-task view of where LLMs stand and what remains open.

## Takeaways / questions
- The frozen-vs-tuned axis is the useful bit: it is the first decision when applying an LLM to a task, and PEFT (e.g. [LoRA](https://arxiv.org/abs/2106.09685)) sits in between.
- I didn't find a crisp, quantified answer to its own question 2 ("have traditional NLP tasks been solved?") in what I read; it's more a map of methods than a verdict.
- As a 2024 survey, it predates most of the reasoning-RL era (o1/R1-style training), though a long-CoT section was added.

## Contents
**Taxonomy.**
- *Parameter-frozen paradigm*: zero-shot learning (an instruction prompt only) and few-shot learning (instruction + in-context demonstrations).
- *Parameter-tuning paradigm*: full-parameter fine-tuning and parameter-efficient tuning (adapters, LoRA, prompt/prefix tuning and similar).

**Natural language understanding**: sentiment analysis, information extraction, dialogue understanding, table understanding.

**Natural language generation**: summarization, code generation, machine translation, mathematical reasoning.

**Frontiers and challenges**: multilingual LLMs, multimodal LLMs, tool use, "X-of-thought" prompting (chain/tree/graph of thought), hallucination, safety, and long chain-of-thought.

notes.title: A Survey of State of the Art Large Vision Language Models: Alignment, Benchmark, Evaluations and Challenges
notes.tldr: A survey of large vision-language models covering how architectures evolved (two-tower, LLM-plus-projector, native multimodal, unified input/output), how benchmarks and metrics work, post-training/alignment, applications, and open problems like hallucination and safety.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed as “VLM survey”.

## Summary
A broad, selective survey of large vision-language models (VLMs). It organizes the field into architectural "eras", reviews the building blocks shared by nearly all VLMs, walks through how benchmarks are built and scored, and closes with applications and challenges. It is a good map of the field rather than a deep technical source. Note that the survey is a living document: the arXiv version I fetched for this note (v7) has been updated through 2026, so it covers models released after I first read it in August 2025.

## Problem
VLM research moves so fast that it is hard to see the overall structure: which design choices recur, how evaluation has changed, and what is still unsolved.

## Takeaways / questions
- Useful as an index for finding the canonical paper behind each design choice; the era framing (where fusion happens, and whether outputs stay text-only) is a clean mental model.
- Being intentionally selective and frequently revised, specific model lists and numbers should be checked against the original papers.
- The shift toward unified and world-action models lines up with the backbones I care about for latent visual reasoning (e.g. BAGEL).

## Contents
- **Architectural eras.** (1) Contrastive or bridged two-tower models (CLIP-style); (2) projector-based LLM backbones, where a vision encoder feeds an LLM through a projector, resampler or cross-attention bridge (LLaVA, Qwen2-VL, DeepSeek-VL2, Pixtral); (3a) native multimodal-input models that pretrain one trunk on all modalities but output text; (3b) unified input/output models that also generate images or other modalities (Emu3, Janus-Pro); (4) emerging "world-action" models that treat actions as another modality.
- **Building blocks.** A visual encoder or tokenizer, a language tokenizer/decoder, alignment modules or shared token spaces, and post-training. It separates training from scratch from using a pretrained LLM as backbone.
- **Alignment / post-training.** SFT defines formats and tool use; DPO and PPO-style preference optimization improve quality and safety; the strongest recent trend is GRPO-style rule-based RL for visual and spatial reasoning.
- **Benchmarks and evaluation.** How benchmark data is collected, and the observation that common metrics mostly check whether a short-form answer matches the reference, with evaluation moving toward long-video, spatial, embodied, reward-model-judged and domain-specific tests.
- **Applications.** Computer-use/GUI/web agents, document intelligence and accessibility, generative media, robotics and autonomous driving, high-stakes domain assistants.
- **Challenges.** Hallucination, safety, fairness, alignment, training efficiency and data scarcity.

notes.title: Multi-turn Reinforcement Learning from Preference Human Feedback
notes.tldr: Extends RLHF to whole conversations: preferences compare two full multi-turn dialogues, and MTPO (mirror descent + self-play) provably reaches a Nash equilibrium and beats single-turn RLHF on a new Education Dialogue task.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed as "Multiturn RL".

## Summary
Standard RLHF (and DPO-style methods) judges one response at a time. This Google Research / DeepMind paper argues that for dialogue, tool use and other multi-step interactions, what matters is the whole conversation, and a turn that looks bad locally (a seller asking a high price) can be good as part of a strategy. They formalize multi-turn RL with a single preference comparison between two complete conversations at the end, derive an algorithm (MTPO) with convergence guarantees in the tabular case, turn it into a deep policy-gradient method, and show on T5 models that conversation-level feedback beats turn-level feedback.

## Problem
How do you do RL from preferences when the agent interacts with a stochastic environment (a user) over many turns, and feedback only compares entire trajectories? Single-turn reward or preference models struggle to assign credit for a decision whose effect only shows later, and single-turn methods only compare "local" alternatives sharing the same conversation prefix.

## Related work
- RLHF ([Christiano et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03741), [InstructGPT](https://arxiv.org/abs/2203.02155)): Bradley–Terry reward model + RL.
- DPO ([arXiv 2305.18290](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.18290)) and IPO: direct preference optimization, single-turn.
- Nash-MD ([Munos et al., arXiv 2312.00886](https://arxiv.org/abs/2312.00886)): treats preference learning as a game and finds a Nash equilibrium; MTPO extends this to multi-turn.
- LMRL-Gym (Car Dealer environment).

## Method
Setting: a contextual MDP where states are conversation prefixes, the agent writes its turn, the environment (simulated user) replies, and at the end a preference model says how much conversation A is preferred to conversation B.

- **MTPO (Multi-turn Preference Optimization).** Mirror-descent policy updates plus self-play. The key object is a new *preference-based Q-function*: the expected preference of continuing from a state with a given action under the current policy, against conversations sampled from (a version of) the same policy. It captures long-term consequences of individual turns. In the tabular case it provably converges to a Nash equilibrium, a policy preferred to any other.
- **MTPO-τ.** Same, but the opponent is a geometric mixture of the current policy and a fixed reference policy (rate τ), as in Nash-MD.
- **Multi-turn RLHF.** Learn a Bradley–Terry reward on whole conversations and optimize it with a multi-turn Q-function; converges to the optimal policy for the learned reward.
- **Deep version.** Policy-gradient variants of these, applied to T5 encoder–decoder models (T5-Large 770M, T5-XL 3B).

## Data
**Education Dialogue**, a new released environment: a teacher agent tutors a student (simulated by prompted Gemini) on a random topic, and conversation-level preferences come from Gemini Ultra following a "constitution" of effective teaching. So the "human" preferences are actually LLM preferences. **Car Dealer** from LMRL-Gym, which has an explicit reward (sale price), is used to compare preference-based learning to reward-based RL.

## Training
One training example: start from a topic and the SFT teacher policy. Roll out two full conversations (teacher turns from the policy, student turns from the simulated student), ask the preference model which conversation was better, and use that single end-of-conversation signal to update the teacher's per-turn action probabilities through the preference-based Q-function, with self-play supplying the comparison trajectories.

## Results
Education Dialogue, side-by-side win rates judged by Gemini Ultra: for T5-XL, MTPO-τ is preferred over SFT 0.959, over single-turn RLHF 0.951, and over multi-turn RLHF 0.861; for T5-Large the corresponding numbers are 0.914, 0.723 and 0.712. All multi-turn methods beat all single-turn baselines, and MTPO-τ beats MTPO (the authors attribute this to more diverse self-play samples from the mixture policy). Car Dealer, sale price: RL with the true reward gets 58.4 and MTPO with an online preference oracle 57.1; when learning from preference data, MTPO gets 58.6 vs multi-turn RLHF 53.2, so MTPO matches reward-based RL using only preferences.

## Takeaways / questions
- The main conceptual point carries over to agents: credit assignment across turns needs trajectory-level feedback, not per-response grading.
- Experiments are small (T5 models) and the preferences come from an LLM judge, so it's a proof of concept rather than evidence at modern LLM scale.
- Relevant to RL for multi-turn agents and tool use, where GRPO-style outcome rewards are the trajectory-level analogue with explicit rewards.

notes.title: Scaling Laws for Precision
notes.tldr: Precision-aware scaling laws: low-precision training shrinks the effective parameter count, and post-training quantization hurts more the longer a model is pretrained.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
*From the OneNote page "Low precision" (Deep learning › Bagel section, 31 Jul 2025). The page starts with a pasted photo of a printed page of this paper showing its unified scaling-law form $L(N, D, P_\text{train}, P_\text{post})$, with my annotations. Below it is a long handwritten section that seems to be about a different topic (working with AI systems / production); I only partly read it and it is kept in the raw file with [unsure] marks.*

- Photo annotation: $N$ = number of parameters, $D$ = amount of data *(uncertain reading)*.
- "Lower precision → more params, less data" *(uncertain reading)*.

## Summary
Kumar et al. add precision to Chinchilla-style scaling laws. Training in lower precision acts like reducing the model's **effective parameter count**, which predicts the extra loss from low-precision training. For inference, the damage from **post-training quantization grows with the amount of pretraining data**, so beyond some point more pretraining data actively hurts a model that will be quantized. Combining both effects gives one functional form for loss as a function of $N$, $D$, training precision and post-training precision. It suggests that training larger models in lower precision can be compute-optimal.

![Figure 6 from the paper: scaling-law predictions vs empirical loss across precisions](assets/precision-scaling-laws/fig1.png)

## Results
From the abstract: the laws are fitted on more than 465 pretraining runs and validated on models up to 1.7B parameters.

notes.title: Sparse Autoencoders for Hypothesis Generation
notes.tldr: HypotheSAEs trains a top-k sparse autoencoder on text embeddings, picks the SAE neurons that predict a target with Lasso, and has an LLM label them — turning interpretable features into testable natural-language hypotheses (45/60 significant on three real datasets).
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed right after “Learn sparse autoencoder and replicate”.

## Summary
A Cornell paper that uses sparse autoencoders as a tool for *science* rather than for understanding a model. Given a text dataset with a label (headlines and click-rates, speeches and party, reviews and stars), it asks “what about the text predicts the label?” and answers in plain English. The trick is to do the statistics on SAE neurons — cheap, numeric, and interpretable — and only use an LLM at the end to name the few neurons that matter. It is also a compact, well-documented SAE pipeline (with a pip package), which makes it a good thing to replicate when learning SAEs.

## Problem
LLM-based hypothesis generators either prompt an LLM with a handful of positive/negative examples (doesn't scale past the context window) or interpret neurons of a supervised model (neurons are polysemantic and hard to read). Classical tools like topic models output word lists that still need a domain expert.

## Related work
- Bricken et al., *Towards Monosemanticity* (Anthropic, 2023) and Templeton et al., *Scaling Monosemanticity* (2024) — SAEs produce interpretable features.
- Gao et al., *Scaling and evaluating sparse autoencoders* ([arXiv:2406.04093](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.04093)) — the top-k SAE and dead-latent auxiliary loss they adopt.
- Bills et al. (2023), automated neuron explanations — the autointerpretability approach behind step 3.
- BERTopic, HypoGeniC, NLParam — the baselines.

## Method
A theory result first: a “triangle inequality” (Proposition 3.1) says that if a neuron predicts the target, then a high-enough-fidelity description of that neuron also predicts it. That justifies a three-step recipe:

1. **Feature generation (unsupervised).** Embed each text with a reused off-the-shelf model, OpenAI's text-embedding-3-small ($D = 1536$). Train a new $k$-sparse autoencoder on the embeddings:
$$z_i = \mathrm{ReLU}(\mathrm{TopK}(W_\text{enc}(e_i - b_\text{pre}) + b_\text{enc})), \qquad \hat{e}_i = W_\text{dec} z_i + b_\text{dec}$$
with reconstruction loss $\|e_i - \hat{e}_i\|_2^2$ plus an auxiliary loss against dead latents. $M$ is the total number of concepts, $k$ the number active per text.
2. **Feature selection (supervised).** Fit an $L_1$-regularised linear/logistic regression from the $N \times M$ activation matrix to the target, binary-searching $\lambda$ until exactly $H$ neurons have non-zero weight.
3. **Feature interpretation (the only LLM step).** For each selected neuron, show GPT-4o 10 high-activating and 10 *low-but-nonzero* activating texts (hard negatives) and ask for a concept present in the first group and absent in the second. Score each candidate label's *fidelity* as the F1 of GPT-4o-mini annotations against the neuron on 100 positive and 100 negative samples; keep the best. Each label is a hypothesis, then tested on held-out data.

## Data
Synthetic: Wiki (11,979 articles) and Bills (21,149) with human topic labels; the target is “belongs to one of the top-5 (or top-15) topics”, so the reference hypotheses are known. Real: Upworthy Headlines (which of two headlines got more clicks; 8.8K train / 4.4K held-out), Yelp (200K reviews for training, predict 1–5 stars), Congress (109th Congress speeches, predict party).

## Results
- Synthetic: beats baselines on 8 of 9 dataset–metric pairs, at least +0.06 F1 in recovering reference hypotheses; much better than NLParam (+0.36 mean F1) and HypoGeniC (+0.40).
- Real: **45 of 60** hypotheses are significant in a held-out multivariate regression, vs. at most 24 for any baseline (about twice as many).
- More than 10× faster/cheaper than LLM baselines, similar cost to BERTopic.
- Example findings: headlines that mention being surprised or shocked get more clicks, ones that ask the reader a question get fewer; Republicans discuss illegal immigration, Democrats criticise tax breaks for the wealthy; Yelp reviews mentioning plans to return go with higher ratings.
- Higher-fidelity labels give more predictive hypotheses (17 of the top 20 Yelp neurons).

## Takeaways / questions
- A good replication target for “learn SAEs”: small (an SAE on 1536-d embeddings), cheap, with open code (`pip install hypothesaes`).
- Hypotheses are correlational; they tell you what to test, not what causes clicks.
- The same pipeline could run on image embeddings (the authors suggest it), which would be a natural way to find what visual features predict a VLM's errors.

*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, Reinforcement Learning notebook: Theory › "Policy gradients" (20 Jul 2025), Practise › "Policy gradients" (9 Jul 2025) and Practise › "Gym cart pole" (27 Apr 2025).     evaluate: ∇_θ J(θ): take the summed log of π_θ & the summed reward

```text
  2. how to train? -> use action-sample distribution to select action based on [prob.]

Compare to maximum likelihood (highlighted)
  imitation learning: learn action given state by looking at good actions (simply increase good ones [unsure])
  policy gradient: increase / decrease trajectories based on likelihood × reward
  one trick: π_θ(a_t|s_t) -> just have a normal & let a network learn the mean
     -> want to give the right "mean" -> increase [probability] that gives good rewards
  -> problems of policy gradient:
     1. high variance: very high/low rewards tweak the policy distribution too much
     2. randomness: because [of] each episode's random behaviour/trajectories; can get bad rewards on good actions
Reducing variance (highlighted)
  assume policy at t won't affect reward at earlier time steps:
  (1/N) sum_{i=1}^{N} sum_{t=1}^{T} ∇ log π_θ(a_{i,t}|s_{i,t}) [ sum_{t'=t}^{T} r(s_{i,t'}, a_{i,t'}) ]  ↳ only consider future rewards
  1. cut off past rewards' influence on r(s_{i,t'}, a_{i,t'}) (causality)
  2. introduce baseline (highlighted): ∇J(θ) = (1/N) sum_i ∇ log p_θ(τ_i) [ r(τ_i) - b ]  (average baseline from rewards, to reduce fluctuations)
```

### Reinforcement Learning / Practise / Gym cart pole — 2025-04-27 (Sun) 01:07
```text
Policy -> your neural network -> action (sampled from softmax)
  ↑ obs. space: take current obs  <- [env] produces next [obs]
Loss:
  -> compute from discounted return -> 1·r_0 + 0.99 r_1 + 0.99^2 r_2 ...
  for each epoch: -> collect [states], [actions], [rewards] -> act/sample from each individual step until terminate
     pass back to loss function
  -> logits = policy(stack(states))  (collection in that epoch)
     log(softmax(logits)) = action log-probs
     -> action_log_probs = the log of the action actually taken
     loss: negative log-likelihood of the selected probs * returns
       ↳ closer to 1, the better; if big reward, big emphasis on the selected prob -> contributes more to loss (better/larger [gradient])
       ↳ if big reward, there will be large positive gradient (negative log-likelihood = negative loss [as written])
     -> if negative reward, there will be negative gradient -> positive loss, push model parameters away
Key (highlighted): design reward & policy (your model) ↳ input = current observation
  ↳ negative log-likelihood: log prob × reward of action (taken) ↳ results in big negative loss = large positive gradient ↳ push closer to that action
```

## Summary
These are concept notes. Policy-gradient methods optimize $J(\theta) = \mathbb E_{\tau\sim p_\theta}[r(\tau)]$ directly. The log-derivative trick gives $\nabla_\theta J = \mathbb E[\sum_t \nabla_\theta\log\pi_\theta(a_t\mid s_t)\, r(\tau)]$, and the environment dynamics drop out. **REINFORCE** estimates this from sampled episodes; in code that means minimizing $-\log\pi(a_t\mid s_t)\cdot G_t$, as in the CartPole exercise. Variance is reduced with causality (reward-to-go) and a baseline. For LLMs, **PPO** adds a value head for advantages and a clipped importance ratio against the old policy. **GRPO** drops the learned value function and reward model, sampling a group of responses and normalizing their (often rule-based) rewards, $A = (R - \text{mean})/\text{std}$.

notes.title: ImageNet Classification with Deep Convolutional Neural Networks
notes.tldr: AlexNet, an 8-layer CNN trained on two GPUs with ReLUs, dropout, max pooling and heavy data augmentation, won ImageNet 2012 by a huge margin and started the deep learning era in computer vision.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
“ALEXNET – classic CNN, downsampling, max pooling… etc.” Also #9 on the classics reading schedule in my *Learning* doc.

## Summary
AlexNet is the network that convinced the computer vision community to switch to deep learning. In the 2012 ImageNet challenge (ILSVRC-2012) it reached a top-5 error of 15.3%, while the runner-up, built on hand-engineered features, got 26.2%. The ingredients were not individually new (convolutional networks date back to LeCun's LeNet), but AlexNet combined a much larger and deeper CNN, GPU training, ReLU activations, dropout and data augmentation, and showed that with enough labeled data (1.2M images) end-to-end learned features beat everything hand-designed. This note is written from well-established facts about the paper; I did not re-read the full text for it.

## Problem
Classify natural images into 1000 ImageNet categories. Earlier methods used hand-crafted features (SIFT, HOG, Fisher vectors) with shallow classifiers, and neural networks had been too slow and too prone to overfitting to train at this scale.

## Related work
- LeNet (LeCun et al.) — the original convolutional network for digit recognition.
- ImageNet / ILSVRC (Deng et al.) — the large labeled dataset that made training such a model possible.
- Dropout (Hinton et al.) — regularization adopted in the fully connected layers.

## Method
- **Architecture:** 8 learned layers, 5 convolutional followed by 3 fully connected, ending in a 1000-way softmax; about 60 million parameters. The first conv layer uses 96 kernels of size 11×11 with stride 4 on a 224×224 RGB crop, so the spatial resolution drops quickly (the "downsampling" in my note).
- **ReLU** $f(x)=\max(0,x)$ instead of tanh or sigmoid, which trained several times faster.
- **Overlapping max pooling** (3×3 windows with stride 2) after some conv layers, to downsample while keeping the strongest responses.
- **Local response normalization** after the first two conv layers (a lateral-inhibition-style normalization later abandoned by most architectures).
- **Two-GPU training:** the network was split across two GTX 580 GPUs with 3GB each, with some layers only connecting within one GPU.
- **Regularization:** dropout (p = 0.5) in the first two fully connected layers, plus data augmentation (random 224×224 crops and horizontal flips from 256×256 images, and PCA-based color jittering).

## Data
ImageNet ILSVRC: about 1.2 million training images in 1000 classes, with 50,000 validation and 150,000 test images.

## Training
A training image is resized to 256×256, a random 224×224 patch is cut out and possibly flipped, colors are perturbed, and it passes through the five conv layers (with ReLU, normalization and pooling) and three fully connected layers to a 1000-way softmax; the loss is cross-entropy against the label. Optimization used SGD with momentum 0.9, batch size 128, weight decay 0.0005, and a learning rate starting at 0.01 that was divided by 10 when validation error plateaued. Training took roughly five to six days on the two GPUs. At test time predictions are averaged over ten crops (corners, center and their flips).

## Results
- ILSVRC-2010 test set: 37.5% top-1 and 17.0% top-5 error.
- ILSVRC-2012: **15.3% top-5 error** (with an ensemble), versus 26.2% for the second-best entry.
- The learned first-layer filters show oriented edges and color blobs, and last-layer features retrieve semantically similar images.

## Takeaways / questions
- The turning point for deep learning in vision: scale (data and compute) plus a few simple tricks beat decades of feature engineering, a pattern that repeats in ViT and CLIP.
- Many details (LRN, the two-GPU split, huge 11×11 first-layer filters) were dropped by later networks such as VGG, GoogLeNet and ResNet; ReLU, dropout, augmentation and GPU training stayed.
- Worth comparing with ViT: AlexNet hard-codes locality and translation equivariance through convolutions, whereas ViT learns them from data.

notes.title: Going Deeper with Convolutions
notes.tldr: GoogLeNet introduced the Inception module, parallel 1×1, 3×3 and 5×5 convolutions plus pooling with cheap 1×1 dimension reductions, to build a 22-layer network that won ILSVRC 2014 (6.67% top-5 error) with 12× fewer parameters than AlexNet.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed as “Going deeper with convolutions”.

## Summary
This is the GoogLeNet / Inception paper from Google. Its goal was to make a CNN much deeper and wider without blowing up computation. The key building block, the Inception module, looks at the same input at several scales in parallel (1×1, 3×3 and 5×5 convolutions and a pooling branch) and concatenates the results, using 1×1 convolutions first to shrink the number of channels so the large filters stay affordable. Stacking these modules gave a 22-layer network that won the ILSVRC 2014 classification challenge with 6.67% top-5 error, while using 12× fewer parameters than AlexNet. The 1×1 "bottleneck" idea became standard (ResNet's bottleneck blocks reuse it).

## Problem
Making networks bigger (deeper and wider) is the obvious way to improve accuracy, but it increases parameters (overfitting risk) and compute dramatically. The authors want a design that grows depth and width while keeping the inference budget fixed (about 1.5 billion multiply-adds), so the model is practical, including on limited devices.

## Related work
- AlexNet (Krizhevsky et al. 2012) — ILSVRC-2012 winner; GoogLeNet uses 12× fewer parameters while being more accurate.
- Network in Network (Lin et al.) — introduced 1×1 convolutions and global average pooling; source of the "Inception" name together with the "we need to go deeper" meme.
- Arora et al. — theory on building networks layer by layer from correlation statistics, motivating approximating sparse structure with dense blocks.
- R-CNN — the detection framework GoogLeNet's detection entry builds on.

## Method
**Inception module.** Each module takes the previous layer's feature map and runs four branches in parallel:
- a 1×1 convolution,
- a 1×1 reduction followed by a 3×3 convolution,
- a 1×1 reduction followed by a 5×5 convolution,
- 3×3 max pooling followed by a 1×1 projection.

Their outputs are concatenated along the channel dimension. The motivation is "multi-scale processing": some features are best captured locally (1×1), others over larger areas (5×5), and the next layer can combine them. The naive version (without the 1×1 reductions) would make the 5×5 and pooling branches explode the channel count; the 1×1 convolutions compress channels first, acting as cheap "embeddings", and add extra ReLU non-linearity.

**GoogLeNet.** 22 layers with parameters (27 counting pooling), with traditional convolutions in the lower layers and stacked Inception modules above, occasional stride-2 max pooling to halve resolution, and global average pooling plus one linear layer before the softmax instead of large fully connected layers. Dropout (40%) before the classifier.

**Auxiliary classifiers.** Because the network is deep, small side classifiers are attached to intermediate modules (4a and 4d): average pooling, a 1×1 conv, an FC layer, dropout and a softmax. Their losses are added to the total with a weight of 0.3 during training to strengthen gradients and regularize; they are discarded at inference.

Reused: convolution, ReLU, max pooling, dropout, and Network-in-Network's 1×1 convs and average pooling. New: the Inception module design and its systematic use under a fixed compute budget.

## Data
ILSVRC 2014 classification: about 1.2 million training images, 50,000 validation and 100,000 test images in 1000 classes; no external data. Detection: the ILSVRC 200-class detection task.

## Training
An image crop passes through the stem convolutions and the stacked Inception modules; at the end, average pooling, dropout, a linear layer and softmax give class probabilities, scored by cross-entropy. The two auxiliary heads produce their own cross-entropy losses from intermediate features, added with weight 0.3. Training used asynchronous SGD with momentum 0.9 on Google's DistBelief system (CPU-based), with the learning rate reduced 4% every 8 epochs and Polyak averaging for the final model. A crop-sampling recipe verified afterwards: random patches covering 8%–100% of the image area with aspect ratio between 3/4 and 4/3 (later known as "Inception-style" random resized crops).

## Results
- ILSVRC 2014 classification: **6.67% top-5 error**, first place, using an ensemble of 7 models and aggressive multi-crop testing (144 crops per image). This is a 56.5% relative reduction compared with the 2012 winner (AlexNet/SuperVision).
- ILSVRC 2014 detection: 43.9% mAP with an R-CNN-style pipeline using Inception as the region classifier, first place; detection accuracy almost doubled compared with the 2013 winner.

## Takeaways / questions
- The 1×1 bottleneck is the lasting idea: reduce channels cheaply before expensive operations. ResNet's bottleneck blocks and many efficient mobile networks build on it.
- Auxiliary classifiers were later found to matter less than expected, and residual connections (ResNet) solved deep-network training more cleanly.
- The "random resized crop" augmentation introduced here is still the default in image pre-training pipelines today, including for ViTs.

notes.title: You Only Look Once: Unified, Real-Time Object Detection
notes.tldr: YOLO treats object detection as a single regression: one CNN looks at the whole image once and directly outputs bounding boxes and class probabilities on a 7×7 grid, running in real time (45 fps) at competitive accuracy.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed as “YOLO Object detection”. (Fall 2025 *Fall Learning* doc also has a poker project idea built on YOLO + bounding boxes.)

## Summary
YOLO ("You Only Look Once") reframed object detection. Earlier detectors like R-CNN were pipelines: propose thousands of candidate regions, run a classifier on each, then clean up boxes. YOLO instead runs a single convolutional network once over the whole image and directly regresses all boxes and class scores in one shot. That made it dramatically faster (real-time video) and, because it sees the full image, less likely to mistake background for objects. The price was weaker localization, especially for small, clustered objects. The YOLO family went on to become the default practical detector.

## Problem
Detection systems repurposed classifiers through multi-stage pipelines (sliding windows in DPM, region proposals plus per-region CNNs in R-CNN) that are slow and hard to optimize as a whole, since each stage is trained separately.

## Related work
- R-CNN, Fast R-CNN, Faster R-CNN — region-proposal-based detectors; Fast R-CNN is the main accuracy baseline.
- DPM (Deformable Parts Models) — sliding-window detector.
- GoogLeNet ([1409.4842](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.4842)) — inspiration for the backbone (1×1 reduction layers followed by 3×3 convs instead of inception modules).
- OverFeat, MultiBox — earlier single-network localization/detection work.

## Method
![Figure 2 from the paper: YOLO divides the image into an S×S grid; each cell predicts B boxes with confidences and C class probabilities, encoded as an S×S×(B·5+C) tensor](assets/yolo/fig1.png)

1. **Grid.** The input image (448×448) is divided into an $S\times S$ grid. The cell containing an object's center is responsible for detecting it.
2. **Per-cell predictions.** Each cell predicts $B$ boxes, each with $(x, y, w, h)$ and a confidence $= \Pr(\text{Object}) \cdot \text{IOU}^{\text{truth}}_{\text{pred}}$, plus $C$ conditional class probabilities $\Pr(\text{Class}_i \mid \text{Object})$. For Pascal VOC, $S=7$, $B=2$, $C=20$, so the output is a $7\times7\times30$ tensor. $(x,y)$ are offsets within the cell; $w,h$ are relative to the image size.
3. **Test-time scores.** Multiplying class probabilities by box confidence gives class-specific scores $\Pr(\text{Class}_i)\cdot\text{IOU}$ for each of the 98 boxes, followed by non-maximum suppression.
4. **Network.** 24 convolutional layers plus 2 fully connected layers, leaky ReLU activations, linear final layer. Fast YOLO uses 9 conv layers.

Reused: ImageNet pre-training of the conv layers and the general GoogLeNet-style design. New: casting detection as one regression problem over a grid, trained end-to-end.

## Data
ImageNet 1000-class data for pre-training the first 20 conv layers; Pascal VOC 2007 and 2012 (20 classes) for detection. Generalization tests on artwork datasets (Picasso, People-Art).

## Training
The first 20 conv layers are pre-trained on ImageNet at 224×224 (about a week, 88% top-5); four conv and two FC layers are added and the input raised to 448×448 for detection. For one training image, the network outputs the 7×7×30 tensor. For each ground-truth object, the cell containing its center and, within it, the predicted box with the highest IOU is made "responsible". The loss is a sum of squared errors on: box centers and on $\sqrt{w}, \sqrt{h}$ (square roots so errors in small boxes count more), weighted by $\lambda_{\text{coord}}=5$; confidence for responsible boxes; confidence for boxes with no object, down-weighted by $\lambda_{\text{noobj}}=0.5$ so the many empty cells do not overwhelm training; and class probabilities for cells containing objects. Setup: about 135 epochs on VOC 2007+2012, batch 64, momentum 0.9, weight decay 0.0005, LR warmed from $10^{-3}$ to $10^{-2}$ then stepped down; dropout 0.5 and augmentation by random scaling/translation (up to 20%) and HSV exposure/saturation jitter.

## Results
- Pascal VOC 2007: YOLO gets **63.4% mAP at 45 fps**; Fast YOLO 52.7% mAP at 155 fps, more than twice as accurate as previous real-time detectors.
- Error analysis vs Fast R-CNN: YOLO makes more localization errors but far fewer background false positives (Fast R-CNN: 13.6% of top detections are background).
- Combining the two: Fast R-CNN's 71.8% mAP rises to 75.0% when rescored with YOLO.
- Generalizes better than DPM and R-CNN from natural images to artwork.
- Limitation: each cell predicts only two boxes and one class, so groups of small objects (e.g. flocks of birds) are hard.

## Takeaways / questions
- The "one pass, dense grid of predictions" idea is the ancestor of most fast detectors and of many dense prediction heads.
- For my poker project idea (cards on a table, with bounding boxes), modern YOLO versions would be the natural off-the-shelf choice; the original's trouble with small clustered objects is exactly the case of many overlapping cards.
- Contrast with F-VLM: YOLO is closed-vocabulary (fixed $C$ classes), while VLM-based detectors can name new categories from text.

notes.tldr: unCLIP (DALL-E 2) generates images in two stages: a prior maps a caption to a CLIP image embedding, and a GLIDE-style diffusion decoder turns that embedding into an image, improving diversity and enabling image variations and CLIP-space edits.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed as “CLIP diffusion”.

## Summary
This is the DALL-E 2 paper, which the authors call **unCLIP** because it generates images by inverting CLIP's image encoder. Instead of going straight from text to pixels, it first predicts *what CLIP would see* in the target image (a CLIP image embedding), then uses a diffusion decoder to paint an image with that embedding. Making the intermediate representation explicit improves diversity at little cost in realism, and because CLIP embeddings capture semantics and style, the model can make variations of a given image, blend two images, and apply text-described edits in CLIP space.

## Problem
Text-to-image diffusion models such as GLIDE produce photorealistic images, but strong guidance collapses diversity. Meanwhile CLIP had learned a very robust joint image–text space. Can CLIP's image representation be used as the bridge between captions and pixels, and what does that buy?

## Related work
- CLIP — [2103.00020](https://arxiv.org/abs/2103.00020): the frozen contrastive image/text encoders whose embedding space unCLIP generates in.
- GLIDE — [2112.10741](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.10741): the 3.5B diffusion decoder architecture reused here.
- DALL-E — [2102.12092](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.12092): the earlier autoregressive text-to-image model and dataset.
- Classifier-free guidance (Ho & Salimans, 2021) and cascaded diffusion upsamplers (Ho et al.; Saharia et al.).

## Method
![Figure 2 from the paper: unCLIP overview — above the line, CLIP training; below, a prior maps the CLIP text embedding to an image embedding, which a diffusion decoder turns into an image](assets/dalle-2/fig1.png)

Let $x$ be an image, $y$ its caption, and $z_i, z_t$ the CLIP image and text embeddings. The generative model factorizes as
$$P(x\mid y)=P(x\mid z_i,y)\,P(z_i\mid y),$$
which is valid because $z_i$ is a deterministic function of $x$.

**CLIP (reused, frozen).** A trained CLIP model provides $z_t$ for the caption and, during training, the target $z_i$ for each image.

**Prior $P(z_i\mid y)$ (new).** Two options are compared:
- *Autoregressive prior*: reduce $z_i$ with PCA, quantize, and predict the sequence of discrete codes with a Transformer.
- *Diffusion prior*: a decoder-only Transformer with a causal mask over the sequence [encoded text, CLIP text embedding, timestep embedding, noised CLIP image embedding, a final query token]; the final output predicts the *unnoised* $z_i$ directly (not $\epsilon$). At sampling, two candidates are drawn and the one with higher dot product with $z_t$ is kept. The diffusion prior is more compute-efficient and gives better samples.

**Decoder $P(x\mid z_i,y)$ (adapted from GLIDE).** The 3.5B GLIDE diffusion model, modified so the CLIP image embedding is projected and added to the timestep embedding and also projected into four extra context tokens appended to the text encoder's outputs. For classifier-free guidance, the CLIP embedding is zeroed 10% of the time and the caption dropped 50% of the time. Two diffusion upsamplers go 64→256→1024, trained with slightly corrupted conditioning images (Gaussian blur for the first stage) for robustness.

**What CLIP space enables.** *Variations*: encode an image to $z_i$ and decode with different noise — semantics and style stay, details change. *Interpolations*: slerp between two images' $z_i$. *Text diffs*: move $z_i$ along the normalized difference between two caption embeddings to apply an edit described in words.

## Data
CLIP's encoder is trained on the CLIP and DALL-E datasets (about 650M images). The prior, decoder and upsamplers are trained only on the DALL-E dataset (about 250M images); adding the noisier CLIP data hurt sample quality.

## Training
For one image–caption pair: compute $z_i$ and $z_t$ with frozen CLIP. The prior gets the caption tokens and $z_t$, a noised $z_i$ at a random timestep, and is trained with MSE to output the clean $z_i$. Separately, the decoder gets the 64×64 image noised to a random step, conditioned on $z_i$ (and sometimes the caption), and is trained with the diffusion objective (learned variances, as in GLIDE). Upsamplers are trained on low-res/high-res pairs. At generation time: caption → $z_t$ → prior samples $z_i$ → decoder → upsamplers.

## Results
- MS-COCO 256×256 zero-shot FID 10.39 with the diffusion prior (10.63 AR prior), vs 12.24 for GLIDE and 11.84 for Make-A-Scene.
- In human evals against GLIDE, samples are comparable in photorealism and caption similarity but more diverse. In a smaller-scale ablation against a decoder conditioned directly on CLIP *text* embeddings (no prior), the unCLIP stack gets better FID (7.99 vs 9.16) and humans prefer it 57.0% of the time for photorealism and 53.1% for caption similarity.
- Strong zero-shot image variations, interpolations and text-guided edits.

## Takeaways / questions
- Limitations the authors call out: worse attribute binding than GLIDE (e.g. mixing up which object is which color), poor rendering of text (CLIP embeddings may not encode spelling, made worse by BPE), and low detail in complex scenes. Imagen's argument for a large text-only encoder is partly a response to this.
- The "generate a semantic embedding first, then decode" design is a clean example of using a frozen representation as an intermediate target — relevant to my interest in latent visual reasoning: what does a compressed visual embedding keep and drop?
- PCA reconstructions of CLIP latents (Figure 7) are a nice probe of what CLIP actually encodes.

notes.title: Denoising Diffusion Probabilistic Models
notes.tldr: DDPM shows diffusion models can generate high-quality images: gradually noise data with a fixed Gaussian process, train a U-Net to predict the added noise with a simple MSE loss, and sample by iterative denoising (CIFAR-10 FID 3.17).
notes.markdown:
## My notes
“DDPM – original. Read.” (*Research* doc, “Diffusion/Vision models”.)

From my Aug 2025 research application: “DDPM (and DDIM) – I think reading and trying to reimplement the UNet of DDPM is what ‘connected the dots’ for me. The connection of this idea to the particle motions in physics really surprised and excited me. Beside the ‘unconventional’ yet amazing architecture of the diffusion model, building it from scratch gave me great practice in combining what I learned about vision models, attention layers, and training objectives.”

## Summary
DDPM is the paper that made diffusion models work. The idea (from Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015, inspired by non-equilibrium thermodynamics) is to destroy data by adding a little Gaussian noise at each of many steps until only noise remains, then learn to reverse that process one step at a time. Ho, Jain and Abbeel showed that with the right parameterization — predict the noise that was added — and a simplified loss, this produces images rivaling GANs, and they connected it to denoising score matching and Langevin dynamics. Essentially every modern image and video generator descends from this recipe.

## Problem
In 2020, the best image generators were GANs (hard to train, mode-dropping) and likelihood models like autoregressive models, VAEs and flows (worse sample quality). Diffusion probabilistic models existed but had not produced high-quality samples. Could they?

## Related work
- Sohl-Dickstein et al., 2015 — [1503.03585](https://arxiv.org/abs/1503.03585): the original diffusion probabilistic model.
- NCSN / score matching with Langevin dynamics (Song & Ermon, 2019) — [1907.05600](https://arxiv.org/abs/1907.05600): the score-based view DDPM connects to.
- PixelCNN++ (Salimans et al., 2017): the U-Net/Wide-ResNet backbone DDPM borrows.
- GANs — [1406.2661](https://arxiv.org/abs/1406.2661) and VAEs — [1312.6114](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6114): the competing generative families.

## Method
![Figure 2 from the paper: the directed graphical model — a forward noising chain q and a learned reverse denoising chain p_θ](assets/ddpm/fig1.png)

**Forward process (fixed, no learning).** Starting from a data image $x_0$, add Gaussian noise over $T=1000$ steps with a variance schedule $\beta_t$ (linear from $10^{-4}$ to $0.02$):
$$q(x_t\mid x_{t-1})=\mathcal{N}\big(x_t;\sqrt{1-\beta_t}\,x_{t-1},\,\beta_t I\big).$$
A key convenience: with $\alpha_t=1-\beta_t$ and $\bar\alpha_t=\prod_{s\le t}\alpha_s$, you can jump straight to any step:
$x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}\,x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\,\epsilon$, $\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$. This is the "particle diffusing in a fluid" picture: each step is a small random kick.

**Reverse process (learned).** $p_\theta(x_{t-1}\mid x_t)=\mathcal{N}(x_{t-1};\mu_\theta(x_t,t),\sigma_t^2 I)$ with fixed variances. Instead of predicting the mean directly, the network $\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)$ predicts the noise $\epsilon$, and the mean is
$$\mu_\theta(x_t,t)=\frac{1}{\sqrt{\alpha_t}}\Big(x_t-\frac{\beta_t}{\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}}\,\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\Big).$$
With this choice, sampling looks like Langevin dynamics: repeatedly step along a learned gradient (score) and add a bit of noise.

**Network.** A U-Net similar to an unmasked PixelCNN++ (Wide-ResNet blocks), with group normalization, self-attention at the 16×16 resolution, and the timestep $t$ injected into every residual block via the Transformer sinusoidal embedding. One set of weights is shared across all timesteps. (This is the U-Net I re-implemented.)

**What is new vs reused.** The diffusion framework is from Sohl-Dickstein et al. and the backbone from PixelCNN++; new are the $\epsilon$-prediction parameterization, the simplified loss, and the explicit link to denoising score matching.

## Data
Unconditional image datasets: CIFAR-10 (32×32), CelebA-HQ 256×256, and LSUN Bedroom/Church/Cat 256×256. Pixels are scaled linearly from $\{0,\dots,255\}$ to $[-1,1]$.

## Training
For one training image $x_0$: pick a random timestep $t\in\{1,\dots,T\}$, sample noise $\epsilon$, form $x_t=\sqrt{\bar\alpha_t}x_0+\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}\epsilon$, run the U-Net on $(x_t,t)$, and minimize
$$L_{\text{simple}}=\mathbb{E}_{t,x_0,\epsilon}\big[\lVert\epsilon-\epsilon_\theta(x_t,t)\rVert^2\big].$$
This drops the per-timestep weights of the true variational bound; it gives worse log-likelihoods but the best samples, because it down-weights the easy small-noise steps. Sampling starts from $x_T\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ and applies the reverse step 1000 times. Adam with learning rate $2\times10^{-4}$ ($2\times10^{-5}$ for 256×256); the CIFAR model trains at batch size 128 for 800k steps (about 10.6 hours on a TPU v3-8).

## Results
- Unconditional CIFAR-10: Inception score 9.46 and FID **3.17**, state of the art at the time; NLL ≤ 3.75 bits/dim (worse than the best likelihood models).
- LSUN 256×256: sample quality similar to ProgressiveGAN (FID 7.89 on Church, 4.90 on Bedroom).
- Predicting $\epsilon$ with $L_{\text{simple}}$ beats predicting the mean $\tilde\mu$ on sample quality.
- Progressive generation: large-scale features appear first, fine details last; the sampler can be read as progressive lossy decompression.

## Takeaways / questions
- The whole method fits in two short algorithms: noise-and-regress for training, iterate-and-denoise for sampling. That simplicity is why it took over generative modeling.
- Main weakness: 1000 sequential network calls per sample. DDIM ([2010.02502](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.02502)) and later samplers attack this directly.
- Physics link I found exciting: the forward process is literally Brownian-like diffusion, and the reverse sampler is Langevin dynamics on a learned score.

notes.title: Diffusion Models Beat GANs on Image Synthesis
notes.tldr: OpenAI's ADM improves the diffusion U-Net through ablations and introduces classifier guidance (steering sampling with a noisy-image classifier's gradients), beating BigGAN on ImageNet with FID 2.97 (128²), 4.59 (256²) and 3.85 (512² with upsampling).
notes.markdown:
## My notes
“Diffusion Models Beat GANs on Image Synthesis by OpenAI – score based diffusion, different approach to same problem.”

## Summary
This paper is the moment diffusion models overtook GANs on the hardest standard benchmark, class-conditional ImageNet. It does two things. First, a careful architecture search over the DDPM-style U-Net produces a much stronger backbone, usually called **ADM** (ablated diffusion model). Second, it introduces **classifier guidance**: train a classifier on noisy images and add its gradient to every sampling step, which pushes samples toward the requested class and trades diversity for fidelity — the same knob GANs get from truncation. The results set new state-of-the-art FIDs at 128, 256 and 512 resolution.

## Problem
After DDPM, diffusion models were competitive on small datasets (CIFAR-10, LSUN) but still behind GANs like BigGAN-deep on ImageNet. The authors hypothesize two reasons: GAN architectures had been explored far more, and GANs can trade diversity for fidelity, which diffusion models lacked.

## Related work
- DDPM — [2006.11239](https://arxiv.org/abs/2006.11239): the base model and U-Net.
- Improved DDPM (Nichol & Dhariwal, 2021) — [2102.09672](https://arxiv.org/abs/2102.09672): learned variances, cosine schedule, AdaGN; ADM builds directly on it.
- Score-based generative modeling / SDEs (Song et al.) — [2011.13456](https://arxiv.org/abs/2011.13456): conditioning a diffusion model with classifier gradients.
- DDIM — [2010.02502](https://arxiv.org/abs/2010.02502): fast deterministic sampler; the paper derives a guided version of it.
- BigGAN (Brock et al., 2018): the GAN state of the art being compared against.

## Method
**Architecture improvements (ablations).** Starting from the DDPM/Improved-DDPM U-Net, they measure FID versus wall-clock time for many changes (depth vs width, attention heads, attention resolutions, BigGAN-style up/downsampling blocks, rescaled residuals); everything except rescaling residual connections helps. The final model uses 2 residual blocks per resolution, multiple heads with 64 channels per head, attention at 32, 16 and 8 resolutions (not just 16), BigGAN residual blocks for up/downsampling, and **adaptive group normalization (AdaGN)**: after GroupNorm, each residual block's activations are scaled and shifted by values computed from the timestep and class embeddings, $\text{AdaGN}(h,y)=y_s\,\text{GroupNorm}(h)+y_b$. Replacing AdaGN with DDPM's "add then normalize" worsens FID (13.06 → 15.08 in their ablation).

**Classifier guidance (new).** Train a classifier $p_\phi(y\mid x_t,t)$ on *noisy* images at all timesteps (its architecture is the U-Net's downsampling trunk with an attention pool at 8×8). During ancestral sampling, shift the mean of each reverse step:
$$x_{t-1}\sim\mathcal{N}\big(\mu+s\,\Sigma\,\nabla_{x_t}\log p_\phi(y\mid x_t),\ \Sigma\big),$$
where $s$ is the guidance scale. With $s=1$ samples were only loosely on-class, so they use $s>1$; larger $s$ concentrates on high-classifier-confidence modes (higher precision, lower recall). For deterministic DDIM sampling they use the score view instead: since $\epsilon_\theta$ gives the score, $\nabla\log p(x_t)=-\epsilon_\theta(x_t)/\sqrt{1-\bar\alpha_t}$, one can add the classifier's score to it and form a modified $\hat\epsilon$. This is where the "score-based" flavor in my note comes from.

**Upsampling stack.** Guidance also combines with a cascade: a low-res guided model followed by an upsampling diffusion model.

![Figure 1 from the paper: selected samples from the best ImageNet 512×512 model (FID 3.85)](assets/diffusion-models-beat-gans/fig1.png)

## Data
ImageNet at 64, 128, 256 and 512 resolution (class-conditional), and LSUN bedroom/horse/cat 256 (unconditional) for the architecture comparison.

## Training
The diffusion model is trained like Improved DDPM: noise an image to a random step, predict the noise (and learned variances), with the class label injected via AdaGN. The classifier is trained separately on noised images with cross-entropy against the label. At sampling time the two are combined through the gradient term above; the diffusion model itself is never retrained for guidance.

## Results
- FID 2.97 on ImageNet 128×128, 4.59 on 256×256, 7.72 on 512×512 — better than BigGAN-deep, while keeping better recall (distribution coverage).
- Matches BigGAN-deep with as few as 25 forward passes per sample (using the DDIM-style sampler).
- Guided low-res + upsampling diffusion: FID 3.94 at 256×256 and 3.85 at 512×512.
- Guidance cleanly trades recall for precision as the scale grows.

## Takeaways / questions
- Small correction to my note: ADM is a DDPM-family model (noise prediction, U-Net); the score-matching view mainly appears in how guidance is derived for DDIM. Same problem as DDPM, mostly a better architecture plus a guidance trick.
- Classifier guidance needs an extra noise-aware classifier; classifier-free guidance (used in [GLIDE](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.10741)) removed that and became standard, but the diversity-for-fidelity knob idea originates here.
- The ADM U-Net became the default diffusion backbone (GLIDE, DALL-E 2's decoder, and the U-Net in latent diffusion all inherit from it).

notes.title: NeRF: Representing Scenes as Neural Radiance Fields for View Synthesis
notes.tldr: NeRF represents a 3D scene as an MLP mapping a 5D coordinate (x, y, z, viewing direction) to color and density, trained from posed photos through differentiable volume rendering; it set the state of the art for novel-view synthesis.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
“3D rendering.” (Listed under my “AI Safety” heading, but it is the NeRF paper.) Also noted in a 2025 brainstorm doc on 3D model generation: “NeRF – continuous 5D coordinate (spatial location (x,y,z) and viewing direction (θ,ϕ))”.

## Summary
NeRF (Neural Radiance Fields) showed that a plain fully-connected network can store an entire 3D scene. You give it a point in space and a viewing direction; it tells you how dense the scene is there and what color light leaves that point in that direction. Rendering an image means shooting a ray through each pixel, querying the network at many points along the ray, and compositing the results with classic volume rendering. Because every step is differentiable, the network can be fit to a scene from nothing more than a set of photos with known camera poses. NeRF's novel views were far sharper than prior methods and kicked off a huge line of neural-rendering work.

## Problem
*View synthesis*: given a sparse set of photos of a scene, render it from new viewpoints. Earlier approaches either predicted discretized voxel grids (memory-hungry, limited resolution, e.g. LLFF's per-image grids exceed 15 GB for one synthetic scene) or used neural representations (SRN, Neural Volumes) that produced oversmoothed results on complex geometry and view-dependent materials.

## Related work
- Scene Representation Networks (SRN, Sitzmann et al., 2019): MLP scene representation with a learned ray-marcher; a main baseline.
- Neural Volumes (NV, Lombardi et al., 2019): voxel-grid volume rendering with learned networks.
- Local Light Field Fusion (LLFF, Mildenhall et al., 2019): multiplane-image method for forward-facing captures.
- Transformer positional encoding (Vaswani et al.) — [1706.03762](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762): the sinusoidal mapping NeRF repurposes for continuous coordinates.

## Method
![Figure 2 from the paper: NeRF overview — sample 5D coordinates along camera rays, feed them to an MLP to get color and density, and composite them into an image with volume rendering](assets/nerf/fig1.png)

**The scene function (new).** An MLP $F_\Theta:(\mathbf{x},\mathbf{d})\mapsto(\mathbf{c},\sigma)$, where $\mathbf{x}=(x,y,z)$, $\mathbf{d}$ is the viewing direction (θ, φ, in practice a 3D unit vector), $\mathbf{c}$ is RGB color and $\sigma$ is volume density. To keep geometry consistent across views, density depends only on position: the encoded $\mathbf{x}$ passes through 8 fully-connected ReLU layers of 256 channels, which output $\sigma$ and a feature vector; that feature plus the encoded direction goes through one more layer to produce view-dependent color (this is what captures shiny, non-Lambertian highlights).

**Volume rendering (classic, reused).** For a camera ray $\mathbf{r}(t)=\mathbf{o}+t\mathbf{d}$, the expected color is
$$C(\mathbf{r})=\int_{t_n}^{t_f}T(t)\,\sigma(\mathbf{r}(t))\,\mathbf{c}(\mathbf{r}(t),\mathbf{d})\,dt,\qquad T(t)=\exp\!\Big(-\!\int_{t_n}^{t}\sigma(\mathbf{r}(s))ds\Big),$$
where $T$ is the probability the ray travels that far unblocked. It is approximated by summing over sampled points along the ray (stratified sampling so the network sees continuous positions).

**Positional encoding (key trick).** MLPs are biased toward smooth functions, so raw coordinates give blurry scenes. Each coordinate $p$ is mapped to $\gamma(p)=(\sin(2^0\pi p),\cos(2^0\pi p),\dots,\sin(2^{L-1}\pi p),\cos(2^{L-1}\pi p))$, with $L=10$ for position and $L=4$ for direction. This lets the network represent high-frequency detail.

**Hierarchical sampling.** Two networks are trained: a "coarse" one evaluated at $N_c=64$ stratified points per ray, whose compositing weights define a distribution along the ray, and a "fine" one evaluated at those 64 plus $N_f=128$ extra points sampled where the coarse network found content. This spends samples on surfaces instead of empty space.

## Data
Per scene, a set of RGB images with camera poses (poses for real scenes estimated with COLMAP). Benchmarks: DeepVoxels' Diffuse Synthetic 360° (4 simple Lambertian objects, 479 input views each), the authors' new Realistic Synthetic 360° (8 path-traced objects with complex geometry and materials), and Real Forward-Facing (8 handheld cellphone scenes with 20–62 images each).

## Training
There is no dataset-level training: one network is optimized per scene. Each iteration samples a batch of 4096 rays (pixels) from all training images; both coarse and fine networks render each ray, and the loss is the squared error between rendered and true pixel colors, summed over the coarse and fine renderings:
$$\mathcal{L}=\sum_{\mathbf{r}}\Big[\lVert\hat C_c(\mathbf{r})-C(\mathbf{r})\rVert_2^2+\lVert\hat C_f(\mathbf{r})-C(\mathbf{r})\rVert_2^2\Big].$$
Optimization takes about 100–300k iterations, roughly 1–2 days on one V100.

## Results
- Best PSNR/SSIM on all three benchmarks (Table 1): e.g. 40.15 dB on Diffuse Synthetic, 31.01 dB on Realistic Synthetic (vs 26.05 for NV, 24.88 LLFF, 22.26 SRN), 26.50 dB on Real Forward-Facing (LLFF has slightly better LPIPS there).
- Network weights are only 5 MB per scene, about 3000× smaller than LLFF's voxel grids.
- Ablations: positional encoding and view dependence give the largest gains, then hierarchical sampling; with only 25 input images NeRF still beats baselines given 100.

## Takeaways / questions
- The big idea — a scene is a continuous function stored in network weights, trained through a differentiable renderer — reshaped 3D vision and is the foundation for later 3D generation work (relevant to my 2025 3D-generation brainstorm).
- Limitations: per-scene optimization is slow (days), rendering needs hundreds of network queries per pixel, and it needs accurate poses. Later work (Instant-NGP, 3D Gaussian Splatting) attacks speed.
- Positional encoding as a fix for spectral bias is a reusable trick beyond NeRF.

notes.title: Chain-of-Thought Prompting Elicits Reasoning in Large Language Models
notes.tldr: Putting a few worked examples with step-by-step reasoning into the prompt makes large LMs write their own reasoning before answering; this lifts PaLM 540B on GSM8K from 17.9% to 56.9% and only helps at roughly 100B+ parameters.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Listed under “Chain of thought prompting”.

## Summary
The Google Brain paper that introduced chain-of-thought (CoT) prompting. Instead of few-shot examples that map question → answer, each example shows question → *natural-language reasoning steps* → answer. The model imitates the format and reasons step by step on the new question. No training, no new architecture — just a different prompt — yet it set a new state of the art on grade-school math and became the foundation of today's “reasoning model” era.

## Problem
Scaling LMs improved many tasks but left multi-step reasoning (arithmetic word problems, commonsense multi-hop, symbolic manipulation) relatively flat. Prior fixes either trained models to produce rationales (costly, needs annotated data) or used plain few-shot prompting (which doesn't help much on reasoning).

## Related work
- GPT-3 few-shot prompting (Brown et al., [arXiv:2005.14165](https://arxiv.org/abs/2005.14165)) — the in-context learning setup CoT modifies.
- Cobbe et al., GSM8K and verifiers ([arXiv:2110.14168](https://arxiv.org/abs/2110.14168)) — the benchmark and the fine-tuned GPT-3 + verifier baseline CoT surpasses.
- Nye et al., scratchpads ([arXiv:2112.00114](https://arxiv.org/abs/2112.00114)) — training models to emit intermediate computation.

## Method
Nothing is trained. The models are reused as-is: GPT-3 (InstructGPT variants up to text-davinci-002), LaMDA (up to 137B), PaLM (up to 540B), UL2 20B and Codex. What's new is the prompt: eight hand-written exemplars of the form

> Q: Roger has 5 tennis balls. He buys 2 more cans of 3 tennis balls each. How many does he have now?
> A: Roger started with 5 balls. 2 cans of 3 tennis balls each is 6 tennis balls. 5 + 6 = 11. The answer is 11.

followed by the test question. The model then generates its own chain of thought and an answer, which is parsed from the end. The same eight exemplars are used for all math benchmarks (AQuA gets four multiple-choice ones); commonsense and symbolic tasks get their own short sets.

![Figure 1 from the paper: chain-of-thought prompting versus standard prompting, with the reasoning highlighted](assets/chain-of-thought/fig1.png)

Why it helps is probed with ablations: (1) *equation only* — output just the math equation before the answer; (2) *variable compute only* — output dots of the same length as the reasoning, to test whether extra tokens alone help; (3) *reasoning after answer* — answer first, then explain, to test whether the reasoning is actually used.

## Data
Arithmetic: GSM8K, SVAMP, ASDiv, AQuA, MAWPS. Commonsense: CSQA, StrategyQA, BIG-bench Date and Sports Understanding, SayCan. Symbolic: last-letter concatenation (“Amy Brown” → “yn”) and coin-flip tracking, with out-of-distribution tests using more words/flips than the exemplars.

## Results
- **GSM8K, PaLM 540B:** 17.9% → **56.9%** with CoT (58.6% with an external calculator), beating the prior best of fine-tuned GPT-3 175B with a verifier (55%). Codex: 19.7% → 63.1%.
- **Emergence with scale:** CoT gives no gains for small models (they write fluent but illogical chains) and only helps at around 100B parameters; gains are largest on harder, multi-step problems.
- **Ablations:** on GSM8K, equation-only, variable-compute-only and reasoning-after-answer all fall well short of full CoT, suggesting the content and the ordering of the natural-language reasoning matter, not just extra tokens.
- **Robustness:** different annotators' chains, a concise style, and exemplars taken from GSM8K all still beat standard prompting by large margins (variance exists, but CoT wins consistently).
- Symbolic tasks: CoT enables length generalisation to longer inputs than shown in the exemplars.

## Takeaways / questions
- The paper is explicit that it doesn't prove the model is “actually reasoning”; whether written chains are faithful to the underlying computation is still an open interpretability question.
- CoT is the explicit, token-level baseline that latent-reasoning work (Coconut, HRM, Mirage-style latent visual thoughts) tries to move beyond.
- Today the behaviour is trained in with RL (reasoning models) rather than prompted, but the basic insight — spend tokens on intermediate steps — is the same.
