notes.title: An Image is Worth 16x16 Words: Transformers for Image Recognition at Scale
notes.tldr: ViT cuts an image into 16×16 patches, linearly embeds each one like a word token, and runs a plain Transformer encoder over the sequence; with enough pre-training data it matches or beats the best CNNs at lower pre-training cost.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
“An image is worth 16x16 words” – slicing with Conv2d: a smart representation of an image as a sequence.

## Summary
The Vision Transformer (ViT, Google Brain) showed that you do not need convolutions to do state-of-the-art image recognition. It treats an image like a sentence: chop it into a grid of fixed-size patches, flatten each patch and project it to a vector (a "visual word"), add position embeddings, and feed the sequence into a standard Transformer encoder, the same one used for BERT. Trained on small datasets ViT underperforms ResNets, because it lacks their built-in assumptions about images, but with large pre-training sets (ImageNet-21k, JFT-300M) "large scale training trumps inductive bias". ViT became the standard image encoder for almost everything that followed, including CLIP and nearly every VLM.

## Problem
Transformers had become the default in NLP, but vision still relied on CNNs, with attention used only alongside or inside convolutional architectures. Could a pure Transformer, with minimal changes, work directly on images?

## Related work
- Transformer ([1706.03762](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762)) — the unchanged encoder architecture.
- BERT ([1810.04805](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805)) — source of the learnable `[class]` token idea.
- ResNet / BiT ([1512.03385](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385)) — CNN baselines; BiT is a large-scale-pretrained ResNet.
- Noisy Student EfficientNet — previous ImageNet state of the art.
- Local self-attention and axial attention for images — earlier attempts that needed specialized attention patterns.

## Method
![Figure 1 from the paper: ViT splits an image into fixed-size patches, linearly embeds them, adds position embeddings and a class token, and feeds them to a standard Transformer encoder](assets/vit/fig1.png)

1. **Patchify.** An image $\mathbf{x}\in\mathbb{R}^{H\times W\times C}$ is reshaped into $N = HW/P^2$ flattened patches of size $P\times P$ (e.g. $P=16$, so a 224×224 image gives 196 patches).
2. **Patch embedding.** A trainable linear projection $\mathbf{E}$ maps each flattened patch to a $D$-dimensional vector. (In practice this is implemented as a Conv2d with kernel size and stride equal to $P$, which is the "slicing with Conv2d" trick in my note.)
3. **Class token and positions.** A learnable `[class]` embedding is prepended, and learnable 1D position embeddings are added:
   $$\mathbf{z}_0 = [\mathbf{x}_{\text{class}};\ \mathbf{x}_p^1\mathbf{E};\ \dots;\ \mathbf{x}_p^N\mathbf{E}] + \mathbf{E}_{pos}$$
   2D-aware position embeddings gave no significant gain.
4. **Transformer encoder.** $L$ layers of pre-LayerNorm multi-head self-attention and GELU MLP blocks with residual connections.
5. **Head.** The final state of the `[class]` token goes to an MLP head (pre-training) or a single linear layer (fine-tuning).

The only image-specific assumptions are the patch cutting and the 2D interpolation of position embeddings when fine-tuning at a higher resolution. A "hybrid" variant feeds CNN feature-map patches instead of raw pixels. Model sizes follow BERT: ViT-Base (86M), Large (307M), Huge (632M); "ViT-L/16" means Large with 16×16 patches.

What is reused: the exact NLP Transformer encoder. What is new: the patch-embedding front end and the demonstration that this works at scale.

## Data
Pre-training on ImageNet-1k (1.3M images), ImageNet-21k (14M images, 21k classes) or Google's internal JFT-300M (303M images). Transfer to ImageNet, ImageNet-ReaL, CIFAR-10/100, Oxford Pets, Flowers and the 19-task VTAB suite.

## Training
An image is cut into patches, embedded, prefixed with the class token and processed by the encoder; the class token's output passes through the head to predict the image's label, and the loss is ordinary cross-entropy over classes. After pre-training, the head is replaced by a zero-initialized linear layer for the downstream classes and the model is fine-tuned, often at higher resolution (e.g. 512 for ViT-L/16, 518 for ViT-H/14), keeping the patch size fixed so the sequence gets longer.

## Results
- Best model (ViT-H/14 pre-trained on JFT-300M): **88.55%** ImageNet top-1, 90.72% on ImageNet-ReaL, 94.55% on CIFAR-100 and 77.63% on VTAB.
- ViT-L/16 on JFT-300M beats BiT-L (same data) on all tasks while needing substantially less pre-training compute.
- With small pre-training data, ResNets do better; ViT overtakes them as the pre-training set grows, and keeps improving where ResNets plateau.

## Takeaways / questions
- The key conceptual move is representing an image as a sequence of tokens; once that is done, everything built for language (scaling, pre-training, multimodal sequences) applies to images.
- The patch-token representation is exactly what later lets VLMs drop image tokens into an LLM's input, and what image tokenizers like ViLex compress further.
- Weakness: quadratic attention cost in the number of patches, and no built-in multi-scale features, which Swin Transformer addresses.

notes.title: Generative Adversarial Networks
notes.tldr: GANs train a generator and a discriminator against each other in a minimax game; at the optimum the generator reproduces the data distribution, and the whole system trains with backpropagation alone, with no Markov chains or approximate inference.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
On the classics reading schedule in my *Learning* doc (“Paper schedule: read a list of papers, understand a list of models”).

## Summary
The original GAN paper (published as "Generative Adversarial Nets" at NIPS 2014). It proposes training a generative model by pitting it against a classifier: the generator $G$ turns random noise into fake samples, and the discriminator $D$ tries to tell real data from fakes. $G$ improves by fooling $D$. The paper proves that, with enough capacity, this game has a unique equilibrium where $G$ exactly matches the data distribution and $D$ outputs 1/2 everywhere. GANs went on to dominate image generation for about seven years, until diffusion models overtook them.

## Problem
Deep discriminative models (classifiers) were thriving thanks to backprop, dropout and ReLUs, but deep generative models lagged because maximum-likelihood training needs intractable probability computations (partition functions, posterior inference), typically approximated with Markov chains (Boltzmann machines) or variational bounds. Can we train a generative model that only needs to *sample*, using only backprop?

## Related work
- Restricted/Deep Boltzmann machines and deep belief networks: undirected models needing MCMC.
- Variational autoencoders — [1312.6114](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6114): concurrent approach with an encoder and a variational bound.
- Generative stochastic networks (Bengio et al.): train a Markov chain's transition operator; GANs remove the chain.
- Noise-contrastive estimation: also uses a discriminative criterion, but with a fixed noise distribution.

## Method
**Players.** A generator $G(z;\theta_g)$ (an MLP) maps noise $z\sim p_z$ to data space, defining an implicit distribution $p_g$. A discriminator $D(x;\theta_d)$ (an MLP) outputs the probability that $x$ came from the data rather than from $G$.

**Objective.** A two-player minimax game:
$$\min_G\max_D V(D,G)=\mathbb{E}_{x\sim p_{\text{data}}}[\log D(x)]+\mathbb{E}_{z\sim p_z}[\log(1-D(G(z)))].$$

**Theory.** For fixed $G$, the optimal discriminator is $D^*_G(x)=\frac{p_{\text{data}}(x)}{p_{\text{data}}(x)+p_g(x)}$. Plugging it in, the generator's objective becomes
$$C(G)=-\log 4+2\cdot\mathrm{JSD}(p_{\text{data}}\,\|\,p_g),$$
minimized only when $p_g=p_{\text{data}}$ (Jensen–Shannon divergence is zero). They also show convergence if $D$ is allowed to reach its optimum at each step and $p_g$ is updated in function space.

**Practical trick.** Early in training $D$ easily rejects fakes and $\log(1-D(G(z)))$ saturates, giving $G$ tiny gradients; so $G$ is trained to *maximize* $\log D(G(z))$ instead (same fixed point, stronger gradients) — the "non-saturating" loss used ever since.

![Figure 2 from the paper: random (not cherry-picked) samples from the trained models; the rightmost column shows the nearest training example to demonstrate the model has not memorized the training set](assets/gan/fig1.png)

## Data
MNIST, the Toronto Face Database (TFD) and CIFAR-10.

## Training
Alternate minibatch SGD (Algorithm 1): for $k$ steps (they use $k=1$), sample a minibatch of noise and of real data and take a gradient *ascent* step on $D$'s objective; then sample fresh noise and take a step on $G$ to fool $D$. Concretely for one real image $x$ and one noise vector $z$: $D$ is pushed to output 1 on $x$ and 0 on $G(z)$ (binary cross-entropy); then gradients flow through $D$ into $G$ to make $D(G(z))$ larger. Generators used ReLU and sigmoid units; discriminators used maxout with dropout; noise enters only at the generator's bottom layer.

## Results
- Because GANs have no tractable likelihood, the paper estimates log-likelihood with a Gaussian Parzen window fit to samples: 225 ± 2 on MNIST (best in their table) and 2057 ± 26 on TFD (vs 2110 for stacked CAE). The authors note this estimator has high variance and works poorly in high dimensions.
- Qualitatively, samples are fair random draws, not cherry-picked, and are not copies of training examples; linear interpolation in $z$ gives smooth transitions between digits.

## Takeaways / questions
- Big idea: replace an intractable likelihood with a learned critic. That idea reappears everywhere — VQGAN's adversarial loss, the patch discriminator in latent diffusion's autoencoder, and adversarial distillation of diffusion models.
- The paper already names the core weakness: $D$ and $G$ must stay synchronized, or $G$ collapses many $z$ to the same output (the "Helvetica scenario", i.e. mode collapse). Instability and evaluation difficulty are why diffusion models later won ([diffusion-models-beat-gans](https://arxiv.org/abs/2105.05233)).
- Evaluation was a weak point from day one (Parzen estimates), which motivated later metrics like Inception Score and FID.

notes.title: Neural Machine Translation by Jointly Learning to Align and Translate
notes.tldr: Introduces attention for seq2seq: instead of squeezing the source sentence into one fixed vector, the decoder computes a soft weighted average of all encoder states at every output step, learning alignment jointly with translation.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
On the classics reading schedule in my *Learning* doc ("Paper schedule: read a list of papers, understand a list of models").

## Summary
This is the paper that introduced (additive, "Bahdanau") attention. RNN encoder–decoders compressed a whole source sentence into a single fixed-length vector, which broke down on long sentences. Here the decoder, at each output word, looks back over all encoder hidden states and takes a learned weighted average of them, so it can "search" the source for the relevant words. The learned weights turn out to be soft word alignments. This idea, generalized, became the core of the Transformer.

## Problem
In the encoder–decoder of Cho et al. / Sutskever et al., the encoder must cram all information into one vector, so performance drops sharply as sentence length grows.

## Related work
- RNN encoder–decoder (Cho et al., 2014) and [seq2seq](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215): fixed-vector bottleneck.
- Gated recurrent units (Cho et al., 2014): the hidden units used here.
- Phrase-based SMT (Moses): the conventional baseline.

## Method
**Encoder.** A bidirectional RNN (GRU-style gated units) reads the source; each word's *annotation* $h_j$ concatenates forward and backward states, so it summarizes the words around position $j$.

**Decoder with attention.** At output step $i$, with previous decoder state $s_{i-1}$:
$$e_{ij} = a(s_{i-1}, h_j) = v_a^\top \tanh(W_a s_{i-1} + U_a h_j),\quad \alpha_{ij} = \frac{\exp e_{ij}}{\sum_k \exp e_{ik}},\quad c_i = \sum_j \alpha_{ij} h_j.$$
The context $c_i$ is recomputed for every target word and fed, with $y_{i-1}$ and $s_{i-1}$, into the decoder to produce $s_i$ and the distribution over $y_i$. The alignment model $a$ is a small feed-forward net trained jointly with everything else by backpropagation; alignment is "soft", not a latent discrete variable.

![Figure 3 from the paper: four sample alignments found by RNNsearch-50; each pixel is the attention weight of a source (English) word for a generated target (French) word](assets/bahdanau-attention/fig1.png)

## Data
WMT'14 English→French parallel corpora (850M words reduced by data selection to 348M), 30,000-word shortlists per language (others mapped to UNK), test on news-test-2014 (3003 sentences). Models trained on sentences up to 30 or 50 words.

## Training
For one sentence pair, the encoder computes annotations, then the decoder, fed the true previous French word (teacher forcing), computes attention weights, the context vector and the next-word softmax; the loss is the negative log-likelihood of the reference translation. Both the baseline (RNNencdec) and RNNsearch use 1000 hidden units; beam search at test time.

## Results
Test BLEU (all sentences / sentences with no unknown words): RNNencdec-50 17.82 / 26.71, RNNsearch-50 26.75 / 34.16, and a longer-trained RNNsearch-50* 28.45 / 36.15, vs phrase-based Moses 33.30 / 35.63. So on sentences without unknown words the attention model matches conventional SMT. Crucially, RNNsearch's quality doesn't degrade with sentence length the way the fixed-vector model does, and the attention maps show sensible (including non-monotonic) alignments, e.g. reordering adjective–noun pairs between English and French.

## Takeaways / questions
- The key move is replacing a fixed bottleneck with *content-based retrieval* over all positions, which is exactly what self-attention does in the [Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762), minus the recurrence.
- The additive score $v^\top\tanh(Ws+Uh)$ was later largely replaced by the cheaper dot-product score (see [Luong attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/1508.04025)).
- Attention maps as interpretable alignments is an early example of "look at the weights", though later work warned attention is not always explanation.

notes.title: Playing Atari with Deep Reinforcement Learning
notes.tldr: DQN: a CNN trained with Q-learning and experience replay learns to play Atari games directly from pixels with one architecture and hyperparameter set; it beat prior RL methods on 6 of 7 games and an expert human on 3.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
On the classics reading schedule in my *Learning* doc ("Paper schedule: read a list of papers, understand a list of models").

## Summary
DeepMind's original Deep Q-Network paper was the first to learn control policies end to end from raw high-dimensional sensory input (game frames) with deep RL. A convolutional network predicts the value of each joystick action from the last few frames, and is trained with Q-learning on transitions sampled from a replay memory. With the same network and settings for every game, it learned to play several Atari 2600 games well. It kicked off the deep RL era that later led to AlphaGo and, indirectly, to RL for LLMs.

## Problem
RL from pixels was considered unstable with neural nets: consecutive samples are highly correlated, the data distribution shifts as the policy changes, and rewards are sparse, noisy and delayed. Earlier successes relied on hand-crafted features.

## Related work
- Q-learning (Watkins) and TD-Gammon (Tesauro): earlier RL with function approximation.
- Neural fitted Q-iteration: batch Q-learning with neural nets.
- Arcade Learning Environment (Bellemare et al.): the benchmark.
- Experience replay (Lin, 1993).

## Method
**Q-learning target.** The optimal action-value function satisfies the Bellman equation $Q^*(s,a) = \mathbb{E}\big[r + \gamma\max_{a'} Q^*(s',a')\big]$. Train a network $Q(s,a;\theta)$ by minimizing
$$L(\theta) = \mathbb{E}_{(s,a,r,s')}\Big[\big(r + \gamma \max_{a'} Q(s',a';\theta_{\text{prev}}) - Q(s,a;\theta)\big)^2\Big],$$
where the target uses the parameters from the previous iteration. (This 2013 version has no separate, periodically updated target network; that came in the 2015 Nature paper.)

**Experience replay.** Store transitions $(s_t, a_t, r_t, s_{t+1})$ in a memory of the last 1M frames and train on random minibatches from it. This breaks correlations between consecutive samples, reuses data, and averages over many past behaviours.

**Network.** Input: the last 4 frames, grayscale, downsampled and cropped to 84×84. Conv 16 filters 8×8 stride 4 → conv 32 filters 4×4 stride 2 → fully connected 256 ReLU units → linear output with one Q-value per action, so all actions are scored in one forward pass.

**Behaviour.** $\epsilon$-greedy, with $\epsilon$ annealed from 1 to 0.1 over the first million frames; frame skipping (act every $k$-th frame).

## Data
Seven Atari 2600 games in the ALE: Beam Rider, Breakout, Enduro, Pong, Q*bert, Seaquest, Space Invaders. The agent sees only pixels, rewards, terminal signals and the action set.

## Training
One step: the agent picks an action $\epsilon$-greedily from $Q$, the emulator returns the next frame and reward (clipped to −1, 0 or +1 so one learning rate works across games), and the transition goes into replay. A random minibatch of 32 transitions is drawn, targets $r + \gamma\max_{a'}Q(s',a')$ are computed, and RMSProp updates the network on the squared error. 10M frames per game.

## Results
Average scores (DQN vs best prior RL method vs human): Breakout 168 vs 6 (Contingency) vs 31; Pong 20 vs 19 (HNeat Best) vs −3; Enduro 470 vs 159 vs 368; Beam Rider 4092 vs 3616 vs 7456; Seaquest 1705 vs 920 vs 28010; Space Invaders 581 vs 1720 (HNeat Best) vs 3690. DQN beats all previous RL algorithms on 6 of 7 games and an expert human on Breakout, Enduro and Pong; it remains far from humans on Q*bert, Seaquest and Space Invaders, which need longer-horizon strategy.

## Takeaways / questions
- The two ingredients that made deep RL work, decorrelated replay data and a fixed-ish bootstrapped target, are stability tricks; stability is still the main issue in RL for LLMs (compare [GSPO](https://arxiv.org/abs/2507.18071)).
- Value-based methods like DQN need a discrete action space with a max over actions; LLM RL instead uses policy-gradient methods (PPO/GRPO) because the "action space" is a huge vocabulary over long sequences.
- Reward clipping is a simple example of reward shaping trading fidelity for stability.

notes.title: Dropout: A Simple Way to Prevent Neural Networks from Overfitting
notes.tldr: Dropout randomly zeroes hidden units during training so units can't co-adapt, implicitly training an exponential ensemble of thinned networks; at test time the full network with scaled weights approximates the ensemble average. Big gains across vision, speech and text.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
On the classics reading schedule in my *Learning* doc ("Paper schedule: read a list of papers, understand a list of models").

## Summary
Dropout is the regularizer that made large neural nets practical before huge datasets were common. During training, each unit is kept with probability $p$ (e.g. 0.5 for hidden units, 0.8 for inputs) and otherwise set to zero, independently for every example. Each minibatch therefore trains a different random "thinned" sub-network, all sharing weights. At test time nothing is dropped and weights are scaled by $p$, which approximates averaging the predictions of all $2^n$ thinned networks. This JMLR paper is the full journal write-up of the idea, which Hinton et al. had introduced in a 2012 preprint and which AlexNet used (this note is based on the JMLR PDF text).

## Problem
Large networks overfit small datasets, and the usual remedy of averaging many separately trained big models is too expensive to train and to run. Hidden units also learn fragile *co-adaptations*, features that only work in combination with specific other features.

## Method
For layer $l$ with activations $y^{(l)}$:
$$r_j^{(l)} \sim \text{Bernoulli}(p),\qquad \tilde y^{(l)} = r^{(l)} \odot y^{(l)},\qquad z^{(l+1)} = W^{(l+1)}\tilde y^{(l)} + b^{(l+1)}.$$
Backprop only goes through the retained units for that example. At test time use all units with outgoing weights multiplied by $p$, so expected inputs match training. (Modern frameworks use "inverted dropout", scaling by $1/p$ during training instead, which is equivalent.)

Useful companions from the paper: **max-norm** regularization (constrain each unit's incoming weight vector to $\lVert w\rVert_2 \le c$), large decaying learning rates and high momentum, which work well together with dropout because the noise prevents blow-ups. The paper also motivates dropout via sexual reproduction (genes must work with random partners), relates it to Bayesian model averaging, analyzes it for linear regression (where it is equivalent to a form of ridge regression), and introduces dropout RBMs and Gaussian (multiplicative) noise variants.

## Data
MNIST, TIMIT (speech), CIFAR-10/100, SVHN, ImageNet (ILSVRC-2012), Reuters-RCV1 (text), and an alternative-splicing genetics dataset.

## Results
Dropout improved generalization on every dataset tried. MNIST test error: a standard net gets 1.60%; dropout with ReLUs 1.25%; dropout + max-norm 0.95% (2 layers × 8192 units); DBM-pretrained dropout nets 0.79%. ImageNet: conv nets with dropout won ILSVRC-2012 with 16.4% top-5 test error (an average of 5 nets) vs 26.2% for the best non-neural entry. All dropout nets use $p=0.5$ for hidden units and $p=0.8$ for inputs. Analyses show dropout yields sparser activations and features that are individually meaningful. The cost: training typically takes 2–3× longer because gradients are noisy.

## Takeaways / questions
- "Train an ensemble for the price of one" is a strong intuition; the weight-scaling trick is a cheap approximation to the geometric mean of the ensemble.
- Still standard in Transformers (the original Transformer used residual dropout 0.1), though large LLM pretraining often uses little or no dropout because there's so much data that overfitting isn't the bottleneck.
- Inspired related ideas: DropConnect, stochastic depth, attention dropout, and MC-dropout for uncertainty.

notes.title: GloVe: Global Vectors for Word Representation
notes.tldr: GloVe learns word vectors by fitting dot products to the log of global word–word co-occurrence counts with a weighted least-squares loss, combining count-based matrix factorization with word2vec-style linear structure (e.g. king − man + woman ≈ queen).
notes.markdown:
## My notes
On the classics reading schedule in my *Learning* doc ("Paper schedule: read a list of papers, understand a list of models").

## Summary
GloVe ("Global Vectors") is one of the two classic static word-embedding methods, alongside word2vec. Instead of predicting words in a sliding window, it first counts how often every pair of words co-occurs across the whole corpus, then learns vectors whose dot products reproduce the log of those counts. The resulting embeddings have the famous linear analogy structure. Note: I couldn't fetch the paper PDF in this import, so this note is written from well-established facts about GloVe and kept short.

## Problem
Two families of word vectors existed: global count/matrix-factorization methods (LSA), which use corpus statistics efficiently but do poorly on analogies, and local context-window prediction methods (word2vec skip-gram/CBOW), which capture analogies but don't directly use global counts. GloVe asks what model would give linear meaning directions directly from co-occurrence statistics.

## Method
Let $X_{ij}$ be how often word $j$ appears in the context of word $i$. The key observation is that *ratios* of co-occurrence probabilities carry meaning: $P(\text{solid}\mid\text{ice})/P(\text{solid}\mid\text{steam})$ is large, while for "water" or "fashion" it is near 1. Requiring vector differences to encode such ratios leads to $w_i^\top \tilde w_j + b_i + \tilde b_j \approx \log X_{ij}$, fitted with a weighted least-squares objective:
$$J = \sum_{i,j} f(X_{ij})\,\big(w_i^\top \tilde w_j + b_i + \tilde b_j - \log X_{ij}\big)^2,\qquad f(x) = \begin{cases}(x/x_\text{max})^{\alpha} & x < x_\text{max}\\ 1 & \text{otherwise}\end{cases}$$
The weighting $f$ ignores zero counts, down-weights rare noisy pairs and caps very frequent ones (the paper uses $x_\text{max}=100$, $\alpha=3/4$). Each word gets a word vector $w$ and a context vector $\tilde w$; the final embedding is their sum. Training only iterates over the nonzero entries of $X$.

## Data
Large unlabeled corpora such as Wikipedia + Gigaword and Common Crawl; pretrained GloVe vectors (50–300 dimensions) were released and became a standard resource.

## Results
The abstract reports 75% accuracy on the word analogy task, a new state of the art at the time, and strong results on word similarity and named entity recognition, outperforming related models at comparable corpus sizes. I did not verify the detailed tables for this note.

## Takeaways / questions
- A neat bridge: word2vec's skip-gram with negative sampling was later shown to implicitly factorize a shifted PMI matrix, so the two families are closer than they look.
- Static embeddings give one vector per word regardless of context, which contextual models (ELMo, [BERT](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805)) fixed. In Transformers the input embedding table plays this role, but meaning is built in context.

notes.title: Long Short-Term Memory
notes.tldr: LSTM fixes vanishing/exploding gradients in RNNs with a memory cell whose self-connection keeps error flow constant (the constant error carousel), guarded by multiplicative input and output gates; it can bridge time lags of over 1000 steps.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
On the classics reading schedule in my *Learning* doc ("Paper schedule: read a list of papers, understand a list of models").

## Summary
The LSTM paper introduced the gated recurrent unit design that dominated sequence modeling for two decades (speech recognition, translation via [seq2seq](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215), language models) until Transformers. Its core idea is a memory cell with a self-loop of weight 1, so information and gradients can flow across many time steps without shrinking or exploding, plus learned gates that decide when to write to and read from the cell. Note: I couldn't fetch the PDF in this import, so this note is written from well-established facts about the paper and kept short.

## Problem
Training RNNs with backpropagation through time (or real-time recurrent learning) fails on long time lags: the error signal is multiplied by the recurrent weights and activation derivatives at every step, so it decays exponentially (vanishing) or blows up (exploding). Hochreiter had analyzed this in his 1991 thesis. Plain RNNs could not learn dependencies spanning more than about 10 steps.

## Method
- **Constant error carousel (CEC).** A linear memory cell $c_t$ with a self-connection of weight 1, so its error signal neither decays nor grows as it flows back in time.
- **Multiplicative gates.** An *input gate* controls what gets written into the cell (protecting stored contents from irrelevant inputs), and an *output gate* controls when the cell's content affects the rest of the network. In the original formulation, roughly:
$$c_t = c_{t-1} + i_t \odot g(\text{input}_t),\qquad h_t = o_t \odot h(c_t),$$
with gates $i_t, o_t$ computed by sigmoids from the current input and previous outputs.
- **Memory blocks** group cells that share gates; training uses a truncated gradient, so errors flow back only through the cells, keeping cost $O(1)$ per time step and weight.
- The **forget gate**, $c_t = f_t\odot c_{t-1} + i_t\odot g_t$, which lets the cell reset itself, was added later (Gers, Schmidhuber & Cummins, 2000) and is part of the "standard" LSTM used today.

## Results
On synthetic tasks designed to need long memory (e.g. remembering a symbol over long noisy delays, adding and multiplication problems, temporal order), LSTM learned to bridge time lags in excess of 1000 discrete steps, where earlier recurrent methods (BPTT, RTRL, recurrent cascade-correlation, Elman nets and others) failed or were much slower. I did not verify the specific tables for this note.

## Takeaways / questions
- The CEC is the same principle as a residual connection: an identity path through which signal and gradient pass unchanged ([ResNet](https://arxiv.org/abs/1512.03385), and the Transformer's residual stream). The GRU later simplified the gating.
- LSTMs are sequential in time, which limits parallel training; the [Transformer](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762) removed recurrence for this reason. Recent recurrent/state-space models (Mamba, xLSTM) revisit gated recurrence with parallel training.

notes.title: Effective Approaches to Attention-based Neural Machine Translation
notes.tldr: Systematizes attention for NMT: global attention over all source words vs local attention over a predicted window, simple score functions (dot, general, concat), and input feeding; +5.0 BLEU over non-attentional baselines and SOTA on WMT'15 En→De.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
On the classics reading schedule in my *Learning* doc ("Paper schedule: read a list of papers, understand a list of models").

## Summary
Luong, Pham and Manning took Bahdanau's attention idea and made it simpler and more systematic. They compare *global* attention (look at every source word) with *local* attention (look at a small window around a predicted position), introduce the multiplicative "dot" and "general" scoring functions that are now standard, and feed past attention decisions back into the decoder ("input feeding"). The dot-product score is the direct ancestor of the Transformer's scaled dot-product attention.

## Problem
Attention had just been proposed, but it wasn't clear which design choices mattered, and attending over every source word for every target word is costly for long inputs.

## Related work
- [Bahdanau et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473): additive attention with a bidirectional encoder.
- [Seq2seq](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.3215): stacked LSTM encoder–decoder with input reversal.
- Soft vs hard attention in image captioning (Xu et al., 2015): inspiration for local attention.

## Method
Base model: a stacked (4-layer) LSTM encoder–decoder. At each target step $t$, with top-layer decoder state $h_t$, compute a context vector $c_t$ from source states $\bar h_s$, then an attentional state and prediction:
$$\tilde h_t = \tanh(W_c[c_t; h_t]),\qquad p(y_t\mid y_{<t},x) = \text{softmax}(W_s \tilde h_t).$$

**Global attention.** $a_t(s) = \text{softmax}_s\big(\text{score}(h_t, \bar h_s)\big)$, $c_t = \sum_s a_t(s)\bar h_s$, with
$$\text{score}(h_t,\bar h_s) = \begin{cases} h_t^\top \bar h_s & \text{dot} \\ h_t^\top W_a \bar h_s & \text{general} \\ v_a^\top \tanh(W_a[h_t;\bar h_s]) & \text{concat} \end{cases}$$
plus a "location" variant that scores from $h_t$ alone. Unlike Bahdanau, it uses the *current* top-layer state $h_t$, a simpler computation path.

**Local attention.** Predict an aligned source position $p_t = S\cdot\sigma(v_p^\top\tanh(W_p h_t))$ (local-p), or simply $p_t = t$ (local-m), and attend only to a window $[p_t-D, p_t+D]$, with weights multiplied by a Gaussian centered at $p_t$. A cheaper, differentiable blend of soft and hard attention.

**Input feeding.** Concatenate $\tilde h_{t-1}$ with the next input embedding so the model knows its previous alignment decisions (like coverage in SMT).

![Figure 2 from the paper: global attention, where an alignment weight vector over all source states produces a context vector combined with the current target state](assets/luong-attention/fig1.png)

## Data
WMT'14 English–German training data, 4.5M sentence pairs (116M English, 110M German words), 50K vocabularies; tested on newstest2014 and newstest2015, both translation directions.

## Training
Same teacher-forced cross-entropy setup as seq2seq: the reversed source goes through the encoder, the decoder predicts each German word from previous ones plus the attention context, and the loss is the negative log-likelihood. Dropout and unknown-word replacement (copying source words via alignments) are added on top.

## Results
WMT'14 En→De BLEU builds up step by step: base 11.3 → +reverse 12.6 → +dropout 14.0 → … → local-p attention (general score) + input feeding 19.0 → +unk replace 20.9 → ensemble of 8 models 23.0, vs 20.7 for the winning WMT'14 phrase-based system. Local attention gives a 5.0 BLEU gain over non-attentional systems that already use dropout. On WMT'15 En→De the ensemble reaches 25.9 BLEU, +1.0 over the previous best NMT + n-gram reranker system. They also report better alignment quality and better handling of long sentences.

## Takeaways / questions
- "dot" and "general" scores won out because they are just matrix multiplies, which is what makes attention cheap at scale; the Transformer adds the $1/\sqrt{d_k}$ scaling and multiple heads.
- Local attention is an early answer to the quadratic-cost problem, foreshadowing windowed/sliding-window attention in modern LLMs.

notes.title: Sequence to Sequence Learning with Neural Networks
notes.tldr: A deep LSTM encodes the source sentence into a fixed vector and a second LSTM decodes the translation from it; with input reversal and beam search, an ensemble reaches 34.81 BLEU on WMT'14 En→Fr, beating a phrase-based SMT baseline.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
On the classics reading schedule in my *Learning* doc ("Paper schedule: read a list of papers, understand a list of models").

## Summary
The seq2seq paper showed that one general neural recipe can map an input sequence to an output sequence of different length: read the input with an LSTM into a vector, then generate the output token by token with another LSTM conditioned on that vector. Applied to English→French translation, plain end-to-end networks beat a strong statistical MT system for the first time. It defined the encoder–decoder framing that attention and the Transformer then improved.

## Problem
Standard deep nets need fixed-size inputs and outputs, but translation, speech recognition and QA map variable-length sequences to variable-length sequences with unknown alignment.

## Related work
- LSTM ([Hochreiter & Schmidhuber, 1997](https://www.bioinf.jku.at/publications/older/2604.pdf)): the recurrent unit that handles long dependencies.
- RNN encoder–decoder (Cho et al., 2014) and neural LMs for MT rescoring.
- [Bahdanau attention](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473): concurrent work that removes the fixed-vector bottleneck.

## Method
Model the conditional probability of output $y_1..y_{T'}$ given input $x_1..x_T$:
$$p(y_1,\dots,y_{T'}\mid x_1,\dots,x_T) = \prod_{t=1}^{T'} p(y_t \mid v, y_1,\dots,y_{t-1}),$$
where $v$ is the encoder LSTM's final hidden state. Two separate LSTMs (encoder and decoder), each 4 layers deep with 1000 cells per layer and 1000-dim word embeddings (384M parameters, so an 8000-number sentence representation). Output is generated until an end-of-sentence token, with a simple left-to-right beam search.

**Input reversal.** Feed the source sentence backwards (c b a → α β γ). This puts the first source words close to the first target words, creating many short-term dependencies that make optimization much easier.

![Figure 1 from the paper: the model reads the input sentence "ABC" and produces "WXYZ", stopping after the end-of-sentence token](assets/seq2seq/fig1.png)

## Data
WMT'14 English→French, a 12M-sentence subset (348M French words, 304M English words). Vocabularies: 160,000 source words and 80,000 target words; others become UNK.

## Training
For a pair (English sentence, French sentence), the reversed English is fed to the encoder; the decoder starts from its final state and is trained to maximize the log-probability of each correct French word given the previous correct ones. SGD without momentum at a fixed learning rate of 0.7 (halved every half epoch after 5 epochs, 7.5 epochs total), batches of 128, uniform init in [-0.08, 0.08], and a hard constraint on the gradient norm to prevent exploding gradients. Deep LSTMs significantly beat shallow ones.

## Results
An ensemble of 5 reversed deep LSTMs with beam search gets 34.81 BLEU, vs 33.30 for the phrase-based SMT baseline, despite the 80K-word output vocabulary penalizing every out-of-vocabulary reference word. Using the LSTM to rerank the SMT system's 1000-best lists gives 36.5, close to the best published result then. Reversing inputs markedly improves BLEU and long-sentence performance; the LSTM did not struggle on long sentences. PCA of the sentence vectors shows they are sensitive to word order but fairly invariant to active vs passive voice.

## Takeaways / questions
- Introduced the encoder–decoder + autoregressive decoding + beam search template still used today (now with Transformers).
- The reversal trick is a hack around the fixed-vector bottleneck; attention solved the underlying problem.
- Note the contrast with [Bahdanau et al.](https://arxiv.org/abs/1409.0473), whose non-attention baseline degraded badly on long sentences; Sutskever et al.'s deeper LSTMs and reversal made the bottleneck less severe.

notes.title: U-Net: Convolutional Networks for Biomedical Image Segmentation
notes.tldr: U-Net is a U-shaped fully convolutional network: a contracting path captures context, a symmetric expanding path restores resolution, and skip connections copy fine detail across, letting it segment biomedical images precisely from very few labeled examples.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
On the classics reading schedule in my *Learning* doc (“Paper schedule: read a list of papers, understand a list of models”). (U-Net later became the standard diffusion backbone.)

## Summary
U-Net (University of Freiburg) is a network for image segmentation, labeling every pixel, designed for biomedical images where only a handful of annotated examples exist. Its shape gives it the name: the left side of the "U" repeatedly convolves and downsamples to understand what is in the image (context), the right side upsamples back to full resolution to say exactly where (localization), and skip connections pass high-resolution features from each level on the left directly to the matching level on the right. Combined with heavy elastic-deformation augmentation, it won biomedical segmentation challenges by large margins. The same encoder–decoder-with-skips shape later became the default denoising network in diffusion models (DDPM, Stable Diffusion).

## Problem
Biomedical segmentation needs a class label per pixel, and annotated training images are scarce (tens, not thousands). The previous best approach (Ciresan et al.) classified each pixel by running a CNN on a patch around it, which is slow (one network run per patch, lots of redundancy) and forces a trade-off between context (big patches) and localization accuracy.

## Related work
- Fully convolutional networks (Long, Shelhamer, Darrell) — replace FC layers with convolutions and upsample to produce dense predictions; U-Net modifies and extends this design.
- Ciresan et al. — sliding-window pixel classifier, the previous winner of the ISBI EM segmentation challenge.
- AlexNet-era CNN classifiers — the contracting path follows their typical conv-ReLU-pool structure.

## Method
- **Contracting path (encoder):** repeated blocks of two unpadded 3×3 convolutions with ReLU, then 2×2 max pooling with stride 2. Each downsampling step doubles the number of feature channels.
- **Expanding path (decoder):** each step upsamples the feature map with a 2×2 "up-convolution" that halves the channels, concatenates the correspondingly cropped feature map from the contracting path (the skip connection), and applies two 3×3 convolutions with ReLU. Unlike earlier FCNs, the upsampling side also has many channels, so context information propagates to high-resolution layers, making the network roughly symmetric.
- **Output:** a 1×1 convolution maps each 64-channel feature vector to class scores. 23 convolutional layers in total.
- **Overlap-tile strategy:** because convolutions are unpadded, the output is smaller than the input; large images are segmented tile by tile, with missing context at image borders filled by mirroring.

What is reused: the fully convolutional idea from FCN. What is new: the symmetric U shape with rich skip connections and the training strategy for tiny datasets.

## Data
- ISBI 2012 EM segmentation challenge: 30 training images (512×512) of a Drosophila larva nerve cord, labeled cells vs membranes.
- ISBI 2015 cell tracking challenge: "PhC-U373" (35 partially annotated phase-contrast images, provided by a UC Berkeley bioengineering lab) and "DIC-HeLa" (20 partially annotated DIC microscopy images).

## Training
An input tile (larger than the output because of unpadded convolutions) goes down the contracting path and back up the expanding path to a per-pixel score map. A pixel-wise softmax over classes is combined with a **weighted cross-entropy** loss:
$$E = \sum_{\mathbf{x}} w(\mathbf{x}) \log p_{\ell(\mathbf{x})}(\mathbf{x}), \qquad w(\mathbf{x}) = w_c(\mathbf{x}) + w_0 \exp\!\Big(-\frac{(d_1(\mathbf{x})+d_2(\mathbf{x}))^2}{2\sigma^2}\Big)$$
where $w_c$ balances class frequencies and the second term strongly up-weights pixels in the thin gaps between touching cells ($d_1, d_2$ are distances to the nearest and second-nearest cell; $w_0 = 10$, $\sigma \approx 5$ pixels), forcing the network to learn to separate them. Batch size is one large tile, so SGD uses a high momentum of 0.99. Augmentation is essential: shifts, rotations, gray-value changes, and especially **random elastic deformations** (displacements on a coarse 3×3 grid, Gaussian with 10-pixel standard deviation, interpolated bicubically). Dropout sits at the end of the contracting path.

## Results
- ISBI EM segmentation: warping error **0.0003529** (new best) and rand error 0.0382, better than Ciresan et al. (0.000420 / 0.0504).
- ISBI 2015 cell tracking: average IOU **92%** on PhC-U373 (second best 83%) and **77.5%** on DIC-HeLa (second best 46%).
- Segmenting a 512×512 image takes under a second on a GPU.

## Takeaways / questions
- Skip connections between encoder and decoder at matching resolutions are the key idea: the decoder gets both "what" (deep context) and "where" (shallow detail).
- That property is exactly why U-Nets became the denoiser in diffusion models, which must output a full-resolution noise estimate that depends on global context.
- Shows how much careful augmentation and loss weighting can substitute for data, a useful lesson for any small-data domain.

notes.title: Large Language Models Are Human-Level Prompt Engineers
notes.tldr: Automatic Prompt Engineer (APE) treats an instruction as a program — an LLM proposes candidate instructions from input/output examples, another LLM scores them, and the best (optionally resampled) wins; it matches or beats human prompts on 24/24 Instruction Induction tasks.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Linked under my project ideas: “LLM Prompt generator/optimizer”.

## Summary
APE, from the University of Toronto / Vector Institute, is one of the first papers to show that LLMs can do prompt engineering themselves. You give a few input/output examples of a task; an LLM guesses what instruction would produce them; each guessed instruction is tested by actually running it on a target LLM; the best one is kept, and new variants can be generated around it. It is essentially search over natural-language programs, and it is the ancestor of later prompt optimisers (OPRO, DSPy optimisers, etc.) — exactly the “prompt generator/optimizer” project idea.

## Problem
LLM performance depends heavily on the wording of the prompt, and good prompts are found by human trial and error. The space of possible instructions is infinite and humans have little insight into which wording a particular model responds to.

## Related work
- Honovich et al., *Instruction Induction* ([arXiv:2205.10782](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.10782)) — the task suite and the “forward” proposal prompt; APE's “Greedy” baseline.
- Kojima et al., *Large Language Models are Zero-Shot Reasoners* ([arXiv:2205.11916](https://arxiv.org/abs/2205.11916)) — “Let's think step by step”, which APE improves on.
- TruthfulQA (Lin et al., [arXiv:2109.07958](https://arxiv.org/abs/2109.07958)) — used to steer truthfulness/informativeness.

## Method
Formally: given demonstrations $\mathcal{D}_\text{train} = \{(Q, A)\}$ and a target model $\mathcal{M}$, find an instruction $\rho$ that maximises an expected score when $\mathcal{M}$ is prompted with $[\rho; Q]$:
$$\rho^\star = \arg\max_\rho \; \mathbb{E}_{(Q,A)}\big[f(\rho, Q, A)\big]$$
The LLMs are reused off the shelf (InstructGPT text-davinci-002 is the main target); the new part is the search loop:

1. **Propose.** Ask an LLM to infer the instruction from a few examples. *Forward mode*: “I gave a friend an instruction and these inputs/outputs… The instruction was ___” (left-to-right completion). *Reverse mode*: use an infilling model (e.g. InsertGPT/T5/GLM) to fill an instruction blank anywhere in a template.
2. **Score.** *Execution accuracy* $f = \mathbb{1}[\mathcal{M}([\rho; Q]) = A]$, or the softer *log probability* $\log P(A \mid [\rho; Q])$. To save compute, candidates are first scored on a small subset, and only those above a threshold get evaluated on more data (multi-stage filtering).
3. **Resample (iterative APE).** Keep the top $k\%$ and ask the LLM for semantically similar variants of them (a Monte Carlo local search), then repeat.
4. Return the highest-scoring instruction.

## Data
24 Instruction Induction tasks (five input/output pairs sampled per task to induce the instruction), 21 curated BIG-Bench tasks, the 12 zero-shot reasoning tasks from Kojima et al., and TruthfulQA. Experiments repeated over five seeds.

## Results
- Instruction Induction: equal or better than human-written instructions on **24/24** tasks; interquartile mean 0.810 vs. 0.749 for humans; beats the Greedy baseline on every task.
- BIG-Bench: better or comparable to human instructions on 17/21 tasks.
- Zero-shot CoT: APE found “Let's work this out in a step by step way to be sure we have the right answer.”, raising InstructGPT from 78.7 to **82.0** on MultiArith and 40.7 to 43.0 on GSM8K over “Let's think step by step.”
- Prepending APE instructions to few-shot prompts also improves in-context learning, and APE can steer TruthfulQA answers toward truthfulness and/or informativeness.

## Takeaways / questions
- The core loop (propose → execute → score → resample) is simple enough to build as a weekend project, which is why I flagged it.
- The score needs labelled examples; for open-ended tasks you need an LLM judge, which brings its own biases.
- Instructions found for one model don't necessarily transfer to another (the paper tests this in the appendix), so the optimiser should be model-aware.

## My notes
*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, Reinforcement Learning notebook: Theory › "History" (7 May 2025), "Markov Decision Process" (21 May), "Model free prediction" (7 May), "Q Learning" (8 Jul), "Value Function approximation" (14 Jul); Lectures › "Algorithms" (4 Jul); Practise › "Algorithms" (7 May 2025). ### Reinforcement Learning / Theory / History — 2025-05-07 (Wed) 12:26
```text
Previous sequence of action, observation & state = long history -> map to next action
  ↳ use "state" as a discrete state that captures all history as a single point (state -> obs -> action -> next state)
  ↳ definition of what saves all historical info -> give rise to next observation
Definitions of state:
  1. Environment state: the environment representation that produces next observation, normally not visible to agent (highlighted)
     [margin: environment state (highlighted); observation = environment state = agent state (fully observable)]
  2. Agent state: everything that represents the agent -> comes from previous observation -> predict reward
     [margin: partial observability (highlighted) -> build agent state -> from observation history, or build "beliefs" [unsure]; or the agent state is f(·) -> recurrent neural networks to update agent state]
  3. Information state: Markov state that contains all useful info from history (only depends on present)
     P[S_{t+1} | S_t] = P[S_{t+1} | S_1, ..., S_t]
     ↳ only depends on immediate present -> future is independent of the past given the present
RL Agents (highlighted)
  1. Policy: "output" -> behaviour, action; state -> action -> stochastic (prob. sampling) or deterministic
  2. Value: expected reward in situation -> predict future rewards
  3. Model: how agent perceives environment works
```

### Reinforcement Learning / Theory / Markov Decision Process — 2025-05-21 (Wed) 22:50
```text
[Long page; small handwriting — transcription condensed where words were too small, marked [unsure]]
Formal description (highlighted) for the process of the environment for reinforcement learning
  -> P[S_{t+1} | S_t] = P[S_{t+1} | S_1, ..., S_t]
    -> future is independent of the past given the present
    -> state describes everything
  - State transition matrix [P_11 ... P_1n; ...; P_n1 ... P_nn] -> transition probability from all previous states to all successor states; rows sum to 1 (P_11 + P_12 + ... + P_1n = 1)
  Markov process (highlighted): sequence of random states, defined by <S (states), P (transition probability)>
    - terminal state = self loop
    - sampling (possible sequences -> random states [unsure])
Markov reward process (highlighted)
  - Markov chain with values in each node (states, transition prob., action [unsure], reward)
    -> sequence = sum each node
  G_t (total reward) = sum_{k=0}^{∞} γ^k R_{t+k+1}
    ↳ random total reward from random sample; ↳ discount factor (discount future rewards) -> γ closer to 1 = more far-sighted
  Discounts allow infinite sequences to have finite reward (but the sample chain will be finite length)
Bellman equation (value function) (highlighted)
  Value function -> v(s) = E[G_t | S_t = s] (expected return)
  v(s) = immediate reward (R_{t+1}) + discounted value of successor state (G_{t+1} = γ R_{t+2} + γ^2 R_{t+3} ...) (decay factor)
    ↳ also apply weights based on probability
  e.g. [diagram: state 2 -> 0.8 -> state (-1), 0.2 -> state 3, γ = 0.9]: v(s) = 2 + 0.9 (0.8·(-1) + 0.2·3) [unsure]
  Matrix form of Bellman equation: [v(1) ... v(n)]^T = [R_1 ... R_n]^T + γ [P_11 ... P_1n; ...; P_n1 ... P_nn] [v(1) ... v(n)]^T
    e.g. v_1 = R_1 + γ P_11 v_1 + γ P_12 v_2 + ...  (transition to each state)
  v = R + γ P v -> v = (I - γ P)^{-1} R -> O(n^3) for inverting
Markov decision process (highlighted)
  MRP + action / policy (additional probability matrix) -> different probability matrix for each action (action defines [transitions])
  Policy (stochastic) -> distribution over actions given states: π(a|s) = P[A_t = a | S_t = s] -> basically defines probability matrix
    ↳ only depends on current state -> return action (or distribution of actions) given state
  State value function (highlighted): v_π(s) -> expected return in state s following policy π
    ↳ prob. of state transition is now defined by policy (given state & action)
  -> weighted average = every possible choice (probability) of different actions
  MDP = MRP + action/policy -> get reward of each action, expected [unsure]; get q_π = expected value of action (after action taken, policy);
    -> v_π = q* of next state [unsure];  Q(s, a) = R(s, a, s') + γ Q_max(s')  (cost / reward of action + future optimal reward)
Optimizing Bellman's value function (highlighted)
  Optimal value function -> max_π v_π(s) -> maximum reward from state & policy
                         -> max_π q_π(s, a) -> maximum reward from state & action
     know q*(s, a) -> get v*(s);  v*(s) = max_a q*(s, a)
  - incl. cost from each action, backtracking [unsure]: [diagram 8 -> 10 with cost]
Optimal policy (highlighted)
  Achieve the optimal value function (must exist [unsure]) (optimal action for every state & every future step)
  Optimal policy: π*(a|s) = 1 if a = argmax_a q*(s, a), 0 otherwise -> choose the action that delivers maximum reward from that state (calculated cost of action + future)
  -> thus, can form optimal policy if given optimal state-action value (look at the [unsure] cost & optimal after [it])
  Q*(s, a) = R(s, a, s') + γ max Q*(s')
  optimal action-value function = cost of action + optimal value of next state
   ↳ the max q*(s, a) at s is the correct action for the given state
```

### Reinforcement Learning / Theory / Model free prediction — 2025-05-07 (Wed) 12:02
```text
[Condensed transcription; some small words unsure]
-> Goal: estimate value function based on experience
   Monte Carlo: estimate value based on all experience
   Temporal difference: only look one step ahead
   estimate value function from rewards
Monte Carlo RL (highlighted)
  - learns complete episodes (value = mean return)
    ↳ need to terminate & break into episodes
  S_1, A_1, R_2, ..., S_k ~ π
  Monte Carlo uses expected mean return (mean of all returns, equal to mean of future [returns])
    ↳ just use the law of large numbers & run many episodes -> use average return after first visit as estimate
  1. First-visit Monte Carlo (highlighted) -> just look at first time visit state and update value
  Example: blackjack -> +1, 0, -1 for win / draw / lose; policy: stick at sum ≥ 20, otherwise twist
    [3D value plot sketch: usable ace, dealer card, player sum]
  Incremental mean (running mean + new): μ_k = μ_{k-1} + (1/k)(x_k - μ_{k-1})  (new mean = old mean + (1/count)(new element - old mean))
  Monte Carlo updates: N(S_t) <- N(S_t) + 1 (update count); V(S_t) <- V(S_t) + (1/N(S_t)) (G_t - V(S_t))  (gradient "error")
Temporal difference RL (highlighted)
  learns with bootstrapping, update a guess towards a guess
  Monte Carlo: α(G_t - V(S_t)) + V(S_t) -> V_new(S_t)   (error term)
  TD(0): V(S_t) + α(R_{t+1} + γ V(S_{t+1}) - V(S_t)) -> V_new(S_t)
     replace G_t (actual return of the episode) with estimated return: immediate reward + estimated reward; "new return" gets updated
  e.g. A -> B -> T (r = 0, then 1): V(S_A) = V(S_A) + α(0 + [γ V(S_B)] - [V(S_A)])
  TD: V(s) + α(r + γV(s') - V(s)) -> V(s);  MC: V(s) + α(G_t - V(s)) -> V(s) (G_t = R_{t+1} + γ R_{t+2} + ...)
    -> while both bound -> same [unsure] [0, 1]
  TD-based replaces G_t with R_{t+1} + γ V(S_{t+1}) (current estimate) (reward to the next one)
Comparison (highlighted)
  Monte Carlo: update everything after final outcome comes out (terminating sequences)
  TD: update guess every step (after guess) -> incomplete, non-terminating sequences
  Variance: TD much lower variance [than MC]
    TD: V(S_t) = V(S_t) + (1/N)(R_{t+1} + γV(S_{t+1}) - V(S_t))  (only one random reward (the return not [whole]))
    MC: V(S_t) = V(S_t) + (1/N)(G_t - V(S_t))  ↳ γR_{t+2} + γ^2 R_{t+3} ...
  TD is usually more efficient & more sensitive (highlighted) ↳ uses Markov property (Markov environments)
TD(λ) = TD with decaying weights: λ G_t^{(1)} + λ^2 G_t^{(2)} ...
  λ -> 0: pure TD (one step); λ -> 1: pure MC (all steps)
```

### Reinforcement Learning / Theory / Q Learning — 2025-07-08 (Tue) 19:47
```text
[Condensed transcription; wide page, some words unsure]
Policy gradient approach (highlighted)
  prob. of trajectory: P(τ) = prod_{t=1}^{T} π_θ(a_t|s_t) P(s_{t+1}|a_t, s_t)
  total maximized goal: J(θ) = (1/N) sum_{i=1}^{N} sum_{t=1}^{T} r(s_t, a_t)
  J(θ) = ∫ p(τ) r(τ) dτ [unsure: "τ = trajectory"]
  ∇J(θ) ≈ E_{τ~p(τ)} [ sum_t ∇ log π_θ(a_t|s_t) · r(s_t, a_t) ]  (log prob of action at state from policy network; reward)
Q learning (highlighted)
  Monte Carlo:
   -> estimate & optimize value function with unknown MDP
   -> alternate between policy evaluation & improvement for better convergence
   Table: policy evaluation | policy improvement | notes
     MC | greedy policy (only 1 step look-ahead; argmax value function) | limited exploration; don't know transition prob.
     MC | ε-greedy policy | explore (learn Q-function better)
     MC | GLIE (greedy in the limit with infinite exploration) | don't want to always explore -> start with more exploration, slowly reduce
     TD | GLIE | SARSA - online update
  use Q(s, a), not V(s), because V(s) doesn't tell you about action, so you need to know model R(s,a) & P(s_{t+1}|s, a)
   -> Q(s, a) directly includes action & tells you which action to take
   -> greedy policy = just follow best Q(s, a); the change: keep exploring (highlighted)
  GLIE (highlighted)
   1. N count each: N(S_t, A_t) -> N(S_t, A_t) + 1
   2. update Q(S_t, A_t): Q(S_t, A_t) + (1/N)(G - Q(S_t, A_t))   (G is got from Monte Carlo; update if same [state-action] in new episodes)
   3. change ε: ε_k = 1/k (k-th episode) [unsure], ε -> 0  ↳ reach time scale; keep exploring & slowly decrease (highlighted)
   Q(s, a) -> optimal Q*(s, a)
   Example: old = 10, N = ...: 10 + (1/3)(...), 12 + (1/2)(...)  [worked arithmetic, partly cut off]
  ε-greedy exploration
   - (1-ε) prob. to choose best action, ε random -> also explore, guarantee explore all;  value function & improve policy (learn Q(s, a) better)
  Temporal difference
   1. update Q at every single time step
   2. at every step, use current Q(s, a) for policy; update it to Q(s, a) + α(R + γQ(s', a') - Q(s, a))  (reward; Q of next state & next action)
   3. ε prob. random action, otherwise go to greedy max Q(s, a)
   4. update ε to be 1/k [unsure]
```

### Reinforcement Learning / Theory / Value Function approximation — Monday, July 14, 2025 15:29
```text
[Condensed transcription]
Real MDP: Q-function for each state is harder (too many states)
  -> directly learn a value function (highlighted)
Value function (highlighted)
  v̂(s, w) ≈ v_π(s) or q̂(s, a, w) ≈ q_π(s, a)
   { given any state (any parameters), output the approximate V(s), the value function of that state
     -> works across unseen states (highlighted) (same with action-value function)
     -> approximate given data & input [unsure] for that given state }
Incremental methods (highlighted)
  Gradient descent: Δw = -(1/2) α ∇_w J(w)   (learning rate; gradient direction)
  -> use to minimize MSE between approximate v̂(s, w) & true value v_π(s)
  Input (highlighted): represent state as a feature vector of numbers
    -> linear combination of all features based on weights as output
    -> ...
  Loss (highlighted): Δw = α (G_t - v̂(S_t, w)) ∇_w v̂(S_t, w)   (move estimate v̂(w) closer to G_t; gradient relative to the feature)
     MSE is the difference between G_t (the return actually [observed]) & v̂ (the estimated [value] by value function / neural network)
     L(w) = (1/2) (G_t - v̂(S_t, w))^2
  for TD: Δw = (1/2) α (R_{t+1} + γ v̂(S_{t+1}, w) - v̂(S_t, w)) ∇_w v̂(S_t, w)
     use the network for future -> use R (immediate) only + γ v̂(S_{t+1}) for next-state value function
  Δw = α · δ · x(S)   (step size; TD error (MSE); gradient for weights)
Forward / backward view of TD(λ) (highlighted)
  Forward view: R_{t+1} + γR_{t+2} + ... + γ^{n-1} R_{t+n} (need to wait n steps to then allow update)
   ↳ backward = [eligibility traces] [unsure] - n steps
  e.g. G(R_t) = (γR_{t+1} + γ^2 R_{t+2} + γ^3 R_{t+3}) + V(R_{t+3}) - V(R_t)   (3 actual returns; after that, use estimated value function)
```

### Reinforcement Learning / Lectures / Algorithms — 2025-07-04 (Fri) 01:02
```text
All algorithms consist of (highlighted)
  1. generate samples (test-run policy)
  2. fit model, get return
  3. improve policy  <- θ <- θ + α ∇_θ J(θ) -> backpropagate gradient
Policy gradient algorithm: sum up rewards in samples
  e.g. J(θ) = E_π [ sum_t r_t ]
  hard: learn f_θ through deep neural networks
Value functions (highlighted)
  objective: E_{τ ~ p_θ(τ)} [ sum_{t=1}^{T} r(s_t, a_t) ]   (sum of rewards given every state & action in trajectory)
    τ = (s_1, a_1, s_2, a_2, ...) trajectories of states & actions
    p_θ(τ) = prob. distribution over trajectories: π_θ(a_t | s_t)
    ↳ expand into
  Expected total reward: E_{s_1 ~ p(s_1)} [ E_{a_1 ~ π(a_1|s_1)} [ r(s_1, a_1) + ... ] ]
     (expectation over all starting [states] & pick action based on policy from state)
   every possible first state & every possible action ...
   want to know Q(s_1, a_1) = sum of all possible [future rewards]
     -> so can just argmax Q!
```

### Reinforcement Learning / Practise / Algorithms — 2025-05-07 (Wed) 12:02
```text
Q-learning / DQN (value function methods)
  - focus on learning the Q-function (Q(s, a) = expected total reward from [state, action])
Policy gradient methods
  - directly learn a policy => output probability of policy
A-C algorithms (actor-critic algorithms)
  - actor learns policy & critic tells how good [the] action [is] [unsure]
Model-based RL algorithm
```

## Summary
These are concept notes following David Silver's RL lectures. A **Markov** state summarizes history: $P[S_{t+1}\mid S_t] = P[S_{t+1}\mid S_1..S_t]$. An MRP adds rewards and discounting ($G_t = \sum_k \gamma^k R_{t+k+1}$), and the **Bellman equation** $v = R + \gamma P v$ has the closed form $v = (I-\gamma P)^{-1}R$ at $O(n^3)$ cost. An MDP adds actions and policies; optimal values satisfy $q^*(s,a) = R + \gamma\,\mathbb E\max_{a'}q^*(s',a')$, and acting greedily on $q^*$ is optimal. Without a model, **Monte Carlo** averages full returns (unbiased, high variance), while **TD(0)** bootstraps from $R + \gamma V(S')$ (biased, low variance, uses the Markov property), and **TD($\lambda$)** interpolates between them. Control uses $Q$ rather than $V$, with ε-greedy/GLIE exploration (MC control, SARSA, Q-learning). Large state spaces need function approximation, $\Delta w = \alpha\,\delta\,\nabla_w\hat v(S,w)$.

notes.title: Evaluating generative models in high energy physics
notes.tldr: A systematic study of metrics for comparing ML jet simulators to real simulations, framed as two-sample goodness-of-fit tests; proposes the Fréchet and kernel physics distances (FPD, KPD) on physics features and recommends FPD + KPD + per-feature Wasserstein distances.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Shared at the Apr 25, 2025 LLM-for-HEP group meeting I attended.

## Summary
ML generative models (GANs, flows, diffusion) are being built as fast replacements for slow Monte Carlo simulation in particle physics, but there was no agreed way to tell how good they are. This paper (UCSD/CERN) reviews candidate metrics as two-sample goodness-of-fit tests, stress-tests them on toy Gaussians and on simulated jets with deliberately injected distortions, and proposes two physics-flavored metrics borrowed from computer vision: the **Fréchet physics distance (FPD)** and **kernel physics distance (KPD)**. It also introduces a fast attention-based jet generator (GAPT) as a demonstration. The metrics are implemented in the open-source JetNet library.

## Problem
The traditional check — comparing 1D histograms of physical features — misses correlations and does not scale to many dimensions. Computer-vision metrics like FID rely on features from an ImageNet classifier that has nothing to do with physics, and classifier-based tests (train a network to separate real from generated) are black boxes without a well-defined null distribution. HEP needs metrics that are sensitive to typical failure modes, multivariate, interpretable, reproducible, efficient and standardizable across datasets.

## Related work
- FID (Heusel et al., 2017): Fréchet distance between Gaussian fits of feature activations; FPD is its physics analogue, using an effectively unbiased infinite-sample extrapolation ($\text{FGD}_\infty$).
- Maximum mean discrepancy (Gretton et al.) and KID: kernel two-sample tests; KPD is MMD on physics features.
- Energy flow polynomials (Komiske, Metodiev, Thaler) — [1712.07124](https://arxiv.org/abs/1712.07124): a complete basis of IRC-safe jet observables, used as features.
- MPGAN (Kansal et al., 2021): the message-passing GAN jet generator used as the state-of-the-art comparison.

## Method
**Framework.** Treat evaluation as testing whether samples from $p_{\text{real}}$ and $p_{\text{gen}}$ come from the same distribution. Metrics considered: Wasserstein-1 between 1D marginals, Fréchet distance, MMD, precision/recall and density/coverage, and binary-classifier AUCs.

**Features.** Each metric is computed on (i) 36 energy flow polynomials (all EFPs of degree < 5), which are interpretable physics observables, and (ii) penultimate-layer activations of a pretrained ParticleNet classifier (the "FID-style" option).

**Tests.** First on 2D Gaussian mixtures with controlled shifts, tails and mode changes; then on ~1 TeV gluon jets from the JetNet dataset (particle features $\eta^{\text{rel}},\phi^{\text{rel}},p_T^{\text{rel}}$), with distribution-level distortions (smearing, shifting, removing tails) and particle-level ones. A metric is good if it separates each distorted sample from the truth with high significance, converges with feasible sample sizes, and is cheap.

## Results
- FPD on EFPs was the most sensitive metric to every alternative jet distribution tested; it is also efficient and interpretable because the evaluator chooses the features.
- KPD and per-feature $W_1$ distances cover failure modes FPD might miss (e.g. mismatches in individual feature distributions), so the recommended suite is FPD + KPD + $W_1$ on individual features.
- Diversity/coverage scale as $O(n^2)$ and converge slowly; classifier-based metrics lack a null distribution and are hard to interpret.
- Applied to GAPT vs MPGAN, the metrics can discern differences between two state-of-the-art jet generators; GAPT is significantly faster.

## Takeaways / questions
- Directly relevant to my tokenizer work: comparing reconstructed vs original jets (mass, $p_T$ distributions) is itself a two-sample test, and FPD/KPD on EFPs would give a more principled score than eyeballing histograms or reporting means and standard deviations.
- The FID → FPD move (swap ImageNet features for physics features) is a nice general lesson: evaluation features should come from the domain.

## Summary
These are concept notes from an RL course in the style of CS 285. Imitation learning treats control as supervised learning: fit $\pi_\theta(a_t\mid o_t)$ to expert (observation, action) pairs by maximum likelihood. Errors compound because the learner visits states the expert never did (distributional shift), giving $O(\epsilon T^2)$ expected mistakes over a horizon $T$. Remedies include data augmentation (e.g. side cameras labelled with corrective actions), more expressive policies (history via sequence models, at the risk of causal confusion; latent-variable or mixture models for multimodal behaviour), and **DAgger**, which runs the learner's policy, has the expert relabel the visited states, and aggregates the data.

notes.title: Auto-Encoding Variational Bayes
notes.tldr: Kingma & Welling introduce the variational autoencoder: an encoder (recognition model) and decoder trained jointly by maximizing the ELBO, made differentiable with the reparameterization trick z = μ + σ·ε so it can be optimized with plain SGD.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Cited in my LLM4HEP notes deck (spring 2025) as background for the VQ-VAE tokenizer, alongside Kingma & Welling's “An Introduction to Variational Autoencoders” and Rezende et al. (1401.4082).

## Summary
This is the VAE paper. It asks how to learn a probabilistic model with continuous hidden variables when the true posterior over those variables is intractable and the dataset is large. The answer has two parts: (1) the **reparameterization trick**, which rewrites sampling $z\sim q(z\mid x)$ as a deterministic function of $x$ plus independent noise, so a Monte Carlo estimate of the variational lower bound (ELBO) can be differentiated and optimized with SGD; and (2) **amortized inference** — a neural network encoder that predicts the approximate posterior for any input in one forward pass. Encoder plus decoder trained this way is the variational autoencoder, the ancestor of VQ-VAE, the autoencoders in latent diffusion, and video VAEs like Wan's.

## Problem
For a directed latent-variable model $p_\theta(x,z)=p_\theta(z)p_\theta(x\mid z)$ with a neural-network likelihood, the marginal likelihood $p_\theta(x)$ and posterior $p_\theta(z\mid x)$ are intractable. Mean-field variational Bayes needs analytic expectations that do not exist here, and sampling approaches like Monte Carlo EM need an expensive sampling loop per datapoint, which does not scale to large datasets with minibatch training.

## Related work
- Wake-sleep algorithm (Hinton et al., 1995): the only prior online method for this model class, also using a recognition model, but optimizing two different objectives; the main baseline.
- Monte Carlo EM: sampling-based baseline for marginal likelihood.
- Stochastic variational inference (Hoffman et al., 2013) and score-function/REINFORCE gradient estimators: higher-variance alternatives.
- Rezende, Mohamed & Wierstra — [1401.4082](https://arxiv.org/abs/1401.4082): concurrent, independent derivation (stochastic backpropagation).

## Method
**ELBO.** For each datapoint, $\log p_\theta(x)=D_{KL}(q_\phi(z\mid x)\,\|\,p_\theta(z\mid x))+\mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;x)$, and since the KL is non-negative, $\mathcal{L}$ is a lower bound:
$$\mathcal{L}(\theta,\phi;x)=-D_{KL}(q_\phi(z\mid x)\,\|\,p_\theta(z))+\mathbb{E}_{q_\phi(z\mid x)}[\log p_\theta(x\mid z)].$$
The first term keeps the approximate posterior close to the prior (a regularizer); the second is a negative reconstruction error.

**Reparameterization trick (new).** Write $z=g_\phi(\epsilon,x)$ with $\epsilon\sim p(\epsilon)$. For a Gaussian posterior, $z=\mu+\sigma\odot\epsilon$, $\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$. The randomness now lives in $\epsilon$, so gradients flow through $\mu$ and $\sigma$ back into the encoder. This gives the SGVB (Stochastic Gradient Variational Bayes) estimator of the ELBO, which is differentiable and low-variance.

**Auto-Encoding VB (AEVB) / the VAE.** Choose prior $p(z)=\mathcal{N}(0,I)$; encoder $q_\phi(z\mid x)=\mathcal{N}(\mu(x),\sigma^2(x)I)$ given by an MLP; decoder $p_\theta(x\mid z)$ a Bernoulli or Gaussian MLP. With Gaussians, the KL term is analytic:
$$-D_{KL}=\tfrac12\sum_{j=1}^{J}\big(1+\log\sigma_j^2-\mu_j^2-\sigma_j^2\big).$$

## Data
MNIST and the Frey Face dataset (small grayscale images).

## Training
For one image $x$: the encoder MLP outputs $\mu$ and $\log\sigma^2$; sample $\epsilon\sim\mathcal{N}(0,I)$ and set $z=\mu+\sigma\epsilon$; the decoder outputs the parameters of $p(x\mid z)$; the loss is $-\big[\log p(x\mid z)-D_{KL}(q(z\mid x)\|p(z))\big]$, backpropagated through both networks. The paper uses minibatches of $M=100$ with a single sample per datapoint ($L=1$), optimized with SGD/Adagrad (Algorithm 1).

## Results
- AEVB converges considerably faster and reaches a better variational lower bound than wake-sleep on both datasets, across latent dimensionalities; more latent dimensions did not cause overfitting thanks to the KL regularizer.
- For low-dimensional latents where the marginal likelihood can be estimated, AEVB compares favorably to wake-sleep and Monte Carlo EM, especially as the training set grows.
- With a 2D latent space, the learned decoders produce smooth "manifolds" of faces and digits.

## Takeaways / questions
- The reparameterization trick is one of the most reused ideas in deep learning (VAEs, diffusion's closed-form $q(x_t\mid x_0)$ sampling, policy gradients with pathwise estimators).
- The VAE's continuous Gaussian latent is exactly what VQ-VAE replaces with a codebook lookup — the step from this paper to my tokenizer work.
- Known limitation, visible from the objective: MSE/Gaussian likelihoods give blurry samples, and strong decoders can ignore $z$ (posterior collapse), which motivated VQ-VAE and adversarial/perceptual losses.

notes.title: Neural Discrete Representation Learning
notes.tldr: VQ-VAE replaces a VAE's continuous latent with a nearest-neighbor lookup into a learned codebook, trained with a straight-through gradient plus codebook and commitment losses; with an autoregressive prior over the codes it generates images, video and speech.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Core of my LBNL tokenizer: “VQ-VAE: Variational Autoencoder + VQ layer with codebook (nearest neighbor) = discrete, categorical distributions.” I first built a VQVAE-MLP “following the original paper”, then a transformer (NormFormer) encoder/decoder version. Lesson from applying it directly to jets: with only 4 features per jet, each code ended up representing one jet – very discrete, sparse results; whole-dataset normalization (not per-batch) was needed for the loss to come down.

## Summary
VQ-VAE (Vector Quantised Variational AutoEncoder, DeepMind) is the paper that made learned *discrete* representations practical. An encoder produces vectors; each vector is snapped to its nearest entry in a learnable codebook; the decoder reconstructs the input from those codebook entries. The result is that any image, audio clip or video becomes a grid or sequence of integer codes — tokens — which a separate autoregressive model (PixelCNN, WaveNet, later transformers) can learn to generate. This "tokenize, then model the tokens" recipe underlies DALL-E, VQGAN, latent diffusion's VQ variant, most image tokenizers, and the particle tokenizers in OmniJet-α and my own LBNL work.

## Problem
VAEs learn continuous latents, but many modalities are naturally discrete (words, phonemes, object categories), and discrete codes pair well with powerful autoregressive priors. Discrete latents were hard to train (high-variance gradient estimators), and VAEs with strong autoregressive decoders suffer *posterior collapse*: the decoder ignores the latent entirely.

## Related work
- VAE — [1312.6114](https://arxiv.org/abs/1312.6114): the framework VQ-VAE modifies.
- PixelCNN (van den Oord et al., 2016) and WaveNet: autoregressive priors over the discrete codes.
- Straight-through estimator (Bengio et al., 2013): the gradient trick for the non-differentiable lookup.
- VIMCO and Gumbel-softmax/concrete relaxations: other ways to train discrete latents, compared against.

## Method
![Figure 1 from the paper: left, the VQ-VAE — encoder output z_e(x) is replaced by its nearest codebook vector e_k and passed to the decoder, with gradients copied straight through; right, the embedding space](assets/vq-vae/fig1.png)

**Components.**
- Encoder (CNN for images) outputs $z_e(x)$, a grid of $D$-dimensional vectors.
- Codebook $e\in\mathbb{R}^{K\times D}$: $K$ learnable embedding vectors.
- Quantization: each encoder vector is replaced by its nearest codebook vector,
$$z_q(x)=e_k,\quad k=\arg\min_j\lVert z_e(x)-e_j\rVert_2 .$$
Equivalently the posterior $q(z=k\mid x)$ is one-hot.
- Decoder reconstructs $x$ from $z_q(x)$.

**Gradients through argmin (straight-through).** The lookup has no gradient, so during backprop the gradient at the decoder input $z_q$ is simply copied to the encoder output $z_e$.

**Loss.**
$$L=\log p(x\mid z_q(x))+\lVert\text{sg}[z_e(x)]-e\rVert_2^2+\beta\lVert z_e(x)-\text{sg}[e]\rVert_2^2,$$
where sg is stop-gradient. Term 1 (reconstruction) trains decoder and encoder; term 2 (codebook loss) moves codebook vectors toward the encoder outputs assigned to them; term 3 (commitment loss) keeps the encoder from drifting or growing away from the codebook. $\beta=0.25$ (results were robust from 0.1 to 2.0). An appendix gives an alternative exponential-moving-average codebook update. With a uniform prior the ELBO's KL term is a constant $\log K$, so it drops out.

**Prior (separate stage).** After training, fit an autoregressive model over the code indices (PixelCNN for images, WaveNet for audio) and generate by sampling codes, then decoding.

**Why no posterior collapse.** The decoder must use the codes because the latent is the only information path and the codes are deterministic and discrete.

## Data
CIFAR-10, ImageNet 128×128, DeepMind Lab frames (images/video), and VCTK speech.

## Training
For one 128×128×3 ImageNet image: the CNN encoder produces a 32×32 grid of vectors; each is snapped to one of $K=512$ codes (a 32×32 map of integers, ~42.6× fewer bits than the pixels); the decoder reconstructs the image; the loss sums reconstruction MSE, codebook and commitment terms, with straight-through gradients into the encoder. Afterwards a PixelCNN is trained on the 32×32 code maps.

## Results
- CIFAR-10 likelihood (lower bound): VQ-VAE 4.67 bits/dim vs continuous VAE 4.51 and VIMCO 5.14 — the first discrete-latent model close to continuous VAEs.
- ImageNet: reconstructions from the 32×32×1 code map are only slightly blurrier than originals; PixelCNN-prior samples show recognizable classes.
- Speech: codes capture content independent of speaker, enabling speaker conversion; mapping codes to phonemes gives 49.3% accuracy on a 41-way task vs 7.2% for a random latent space, fully unsupervised.
- Video: action-conditioned generation in DeepMind Lab.

## Takeaways / questions
- My jet lesson fits the paper's logic: VQ-VAE works when the encoder compresses *redundant, structured* inputs (pixels, audio). With only four jet-level features there is nothing to compress, so codes degenerate into a lookup table of individual jets — which is why OmniJet-α tokenizes per particle, conditioned on the rest of the jet.
- Codebook collapse (few codes used) is the classic failure; I saw it worsen at higher embedding dimension. Later fixes: EMA updates, dead-code replacement (used in OmniJet-α), low-dimensional or factorized codes, and lookup-free schemes in modern image tokenizers ([WeTok](https://arxiv.org/abs/2508.05599), [TiTok](https://arxiv.org/abs/2406.07550)).
- Normalization matters for MSE-based reconstruction when features have very different scales — consistent with my finding that whole-dataset standardization was needed.

```

-> Training autoencoders: [reconstruction] loss (e.g. MSE) ... ↳ reconstruction quality ~ latent space quality (capturing important features)

```

## Summary
These are concept notes written while building a VQ-VAE tokenizer for particle-physics data. An **autoencoder** learns a compressed representation by reconstructing its input through a bottleneck; it is a non-linear generalization of PCA. Sparse (L1) and denoising variants force more useful features. A **VAE** makes the latent space probabilistic: the encoder outputs $\mu, \sigma$, sampling uses the reparameterization $z = \mu + \sigma\odot\epsilon$, and the loss is reconstruction plus $\mathrm{KL}(q(z\mid x)\,\|\,\mathcal N(0,I))$, so new samples can be generated from the prior. A **VQ-VAE** (van den Oord et al., 2017) discretizes the latent by snapping each encoder output to its nearest codebook vector. It trains with reconstruction + codebook ($\lVert sg[z_e]-e\rVert^2$) + β·commitment ($\lVert z_e - sg[e]\rVert^2$) losses, with gradients passed straight through. The discrete codes become tokens for a transformer, the approach used by [OmniJet-α](#/note/omnijet-alpha) for jets. My particle-level variant quantizes each particle's 4-feature vector separately.
