notes.markdown:
## My notes
Looked into while reading OmniJet-α “to learn more about the process” (Feb 2025).

## Summary
A TU Munich (Heinrich group) paper arguing that particle-physics analyses already look like foundation-model workflows and should be trained like them. In a standard LHC analysis, reconstruction algorithms (e.g. a jet tagger) are optimized first and then frozen, and the physics analysis is built on their fixed outputs. The authors treat the tagger as a pretrained *backbone* and the analysis as a *head*, and show that letting gradients flow from the analysis objective back into the jet backbone (fine-tuning) gives much better signal/background separation and data efficiency.

## Problem
Sequential optimization (reconstruction first, analysis second) is modular and easy to calibrate, but the reconstruction outputs are lossy summaries tuned for a generic pretext task rather than the final analysis. How much performance is left on the table, and does the ML pretrain/fine-tune toolkit recover it?

## Related work
- Particle Transformer / JetClass — [2202.03772](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03772): the jet backbone (ParT) and the source of pretrained weights for domain adaptation.
- Masked particle modelling (Heinrich, Golling et al.) — [2401.13537](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.13537): self-supervised backbones for HEP.
- Deep Sets (Zaheer et al.): the permutation-invariant analysis-level network.
- Simulation-based inference: framing analyses as learning optimal summary statistics.

## Method
![Figure 2 from the paper: the analogy between modern ML and HEP analysis — reconstruction acts as a backbone/foundation model producing general representations, and the physics analysis is a task-specific head](assets/finetuning-foundation-models-joint-analysis/fig1.png)

**Use case.** Search for a heavy graviton $G\to HH\to b\bar b b\bar b$ against multijet background. Reconstruction-level task ("pretext"): an $Xbb$ tagger classifying whether a large-radius jet came from $H\to b\bar b$. Analysis-level task ("downstream"): classify whole events as signal or background.

**Architecture.** Each jet's constituents go through a ParT backbone (reused architecture, without its softmax); the per-jet representations feed a Deep Sets event classifier. Three variants with decreasing hand-engineered structure:
- **S+HLF**: five high-level jet features ($p_T,\eta,\phi$, jet mass, soft-drop mass) plus one learned scalar from the backbone — the traditional setup where the scalar would be the tagger score.
- **V+HLF**: the high-level features plus the backbone's full latent vector.
- **V-Only**: just the latent vector.

**Training strategies.** *Frozen* (pretrain the tagger, freeze it, train only the analysis network — today's standard), *finetuned* (initialize from the pretrained tagger and train everything on the event-level loss), and *from-scratch* (train everything end-to-end with random init). A further variant initializes the backbone from published JetClass ParT weights (domain adaptation).

## Data
CMS Open Data simulation: 10M events of QCD background and $G\to HH$ signal (graviton masses 600–4500 GeV), used as 22M jets for $Xbb$ pretraining and as full events for end-to-end training; JetClass is used only through its pretrained ParT weights. Splits 45% / 5% / 50% train/val/test.

## Results
- Fine-tuning beats the frozen backbone for every architecture: up to about a factor of two higher background rejection at fixed sample size, and 10–100× better data efficiency to reach a given performance.
- Pretraining clearly beats from-scratch training, though with very large datasets from-scratch can overtake a frozen backbone.
- JetClass-initialized fine-tuning is consistently the best configuration.
- In from-scratch S+HLF, the learned scalar becomes a non-trivial $Xbb$ tagger without ever seeing jet labels; during fine-tuning it trades $Xbb$ performance for downstream performance (it gets "overloaded" with other useful information).

## Takeaways / questions
- Directly relevant to my OmniJet question about whether pretraining "just saves compute": here pretraining plus fine-tuning improves both final performance and data efficiency.
- Open issues the authors flag: calibration — a shared frozen backbone can be corrected against real data once, whereas analysis-specific fine-tuning would need in-situ calibration; and the interplay between detector design and end-to-end optimization.

## Summary
OmniJet-α (Hamburg) is a step towards foundation models for particle physics. Jets, as sets of constituent particles with kinematics $(p_T, \eta, \phi)$, are tokenized with a VQ-VAE; the paper introduces evaluation measures for tokenization quality that motivate a higher-fidelity tokenizer than earlier work. A GPT-style decoder-only transformer is pre-trained to generate jets token by token (next-token prediction), then fine-tuned for jet tagging. The JetClass dataset's Higgs and top decay classes are what my "Plot" page lists.

![Figure 1 from the paper: tokenization, generation and classification in OmniJet-α](assets/omnijet-alpha/onenote-fig1.png)

## Problem
Foundation models could save compute and labeled data in particle physics, but physics data are continuous point clouds, not words. The most pressing problem is how to turn particles into tokens without losing physics (e.g. jet mass), and whether a single backbone can serve both generation and classification. Prior transfer results were within one task class (classification→classification).

## Related work
- Particle Transformer / JetClass — [2202.03772](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03772): the 100M-jet dataset used here.
- VQ-VAE — [1711.00937](https://arxiv.org/abs/1711.00937): the discrete tokenizer.
- Finetuning foundation models for joint analysis optimization — [2401.13536](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.13536): related pretraining/fine-tuning work in HEP.
- Learning the language of QCD jets with transformers (Finke et al.) — [2303.07364](https://arxiv.org/abs/2303.07364): binning-based tokenization.
- Jet Diffusion versus JetGPT (Butter et al.) — [2305.10475](https://arxiv.org/abs/2305.10475): Gaussian-mixture tokenization.
- Masked particle modeling on sets (Heinrich, Golling et al.) — [2401.13537](https://arxiv.org/abs/2401.13537): conditional VQ-VAE tokens with codebook 512, which OmniJet-α extends to 8192.
- NormFormer (Shleifer et al.): the transformer block used in the tokenizer.

## Method
![Figure 1 from the paper: the steps of OmniJet-α — tokenization, generation and classification](assets/omnijet-alpha/onenote-fig1.png)

**1. Tokenization (adapted).** Each jet constituent has three features: $p_T$, $\eta^{\text{rel}}$, $\phi^{\text{rel}}$ (momentum and angular position relative to the jet axis). Three strategies are compared:
- *Binned*: a regular grid (e.g. 21×21×21 = 9261 cells), one token per cell.
- *Unconditional VQ-VAE*: each particle is encoded independently by an MLP.
- *Conditional VQ-VAE*: encoder and decoder are transformers (4 NormFormer blocks, embedding dim 128, 8 heads), so each particle is encoded and decoded *conditioned on the other particles in the jet*. The same token can therefore decode to slightly different values depending on context. Codebook vectors are 4-dimensional, codebook size up to 8192 (up from 512 in prior work); dead codes are replaced every 10 iterations. Loss: $\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\text{task}}+\alpha\,\mathcal{L}_{\text{commit}}$ with MSE reconstruction as task loss and $\alpha=10$.
Token quality is judged by reconstruction of jet-level observables (jet mass, $\tau_{32}$) and by classifier tests distinguishing original from tokenized-then-reconstructed jets. Conditional tokens with the 8192 codebook win.

**2. Generative backbone (new for HEP).** A jet with $n$ particles (ordered by $p_T$) becomes the sequence $(\texttt{start}, x_1,\dots,x_n,\texttt{stop})$. An embedding layer feeds a stack of GPT blocks (causal multi-head attention, residuals, layer norm, ReLU MLP); no positional encoding is used because jets are sets. The model is trained with next-token prediction; generation starts from the start token and samples until stop (or 128 particles), then the VQ-VAE decoder maps tokens back to physical features.

**3. Transfer to classification.** The generative backbone is reused with a new classification head for top-quark ($t\to bqq'$) vs quark/gluon jets, compared three ways: from scratch, fine-tuning everything, and fine-tuning with the backbone frozen.

## Data
JetClass: ten jet classes (q/g, top decays, W/Z/H decays), 100M training jets, 5M validation, 20M test, up to 128 particles per jet; only per-particle kinematics are used. Generation is trained on all ten classes combined.

## Training
For one jet: its constituents' ($p_T,\eta^{\text{rel}},\phi^{\text{rel}}$) go through the frozen VQ-VAE encoder → nearest codebook index per particle → token sequence with start/stop tokens → GPT backbone predicts each next token, cross-entropy against the true next token. For classification fine-tuning, the backbone output feeds a head trained with AdamW (lr $10^{-4}$, weight decay 0.01) on labeled jets.

## Results
- Conditional tokenization with codebook 8192 reproduces jet mass and substructure much better than binning or unconditional tokens.
- Generated jets match reconstructed JetClass tokens well; a classifier test separating generated from real (tokenized) jets gives AUC 0.54 (close to 0.5 = indistinguishable).
- Transfer: up to 17 percentage points higher accuracy than from-scratch with few training jets; e.g. ~90% vs ~75% accuracy with 1000 training jets, ~85% with only 100 jets (from scratch needs >10,000 jets for that), and still a few points ahead at 2M jets. Freezing the backbone is only slightly worse than full fine-tuning.

## Takeaways / questions
- This is the paper my LBNL tokenizer work replicated and extended; my talk's findings (low embedding dim + large codebook best; higher dims → codebook collapse; MoE + SDPA ~1 h → 35 min per 10 epochs on 10M jets) build directly on its conditional VQ-VAE.
- On my question 2: the paper's Figure 7 shows the gap does shrink with more data but never fully closes (a few points at 2M jets), so pretraining helps both data efficiency and final accuracy, not just compute.
- Open questions it raises: tokenizer resolution limits physics precision (mass reconstruction), and transfer was shown only for one classification task.

notes.title: Particle Transformer for Jet Tagging
notes.tldr: Introduces JetClass, a 100M-jet, 10-class simulated jet-tagging dataset, and Particle Transformer (ParT), a transformer that adds pairwise particle-interaction features as an attention bias, beating ParticleNet and transferring well via fine-tuning.
notes.markdown:
## My notes
Read to understand the JetClass dataset while working through OmniJet-α (Feb 2025); JetClass was the dataset for my tokenizer experiments.

## Summary
This ICML 2022 paper makes two contributions to *jet tagging* — classifying which particle produced a jet at the LHC. First, **JetClass**: a public dataset of 100M simulated jets across 10 classes, about two orders of magnitude larger than previous public jet datasets. Second, **Particle Transformer (ParT)**: a transformer over the set of particles in a jet that injects physics-motivated pairwise features (angular distance, relative momentum, invariant mass) directly into the attention scores. ParT clearly beats the previous state of the art (ParticleNet), and models pretrained on JetClass fine-tune to new records on two standard benchmarks. JetClass later became the pretraining set for jet foundation models such as OmniJet-α.

## Problem
When a top quark or a W/Z/Higgs boson decays at high energy, its products land in the detector as one collimated "jet" of particles, just like ordinary quark/gluon jets. Telling them apart is critical for LHC physics. Deep learning had improved tagging, but public datasets were small (~2M jets, two classes), limiting larger models and covering few decay modes.

## Related work
- ParticleNet (Qu & Gouskos, 2020): graph network on particle clouds; the previous state of the art and same first author.
- Particle Flow Networks / Energy Flow Networks (Komiske et al., 2019): Deep Sets for jets.
- Top-tagging (Butter/Kasieczka et al., 2019) and quark–gluon (Komiske et al., 2019) datasets: the two existing benchmarks used for fine-tuning.
- CaiT (Touvron et al., 2021): class-attention design used for ParT's classification stage.
- Transformer — [1706.03762](https://arxiv.org/abs/1706.03762).

## Method
![Figure 1 from the paper: jet tagging at the LHC — collisions produce unstable particles that decay into collimated sprays of particles, reconstructed as jets and classified by a tagger](assets/particle-transformer/fig1.png)

**Input as a particle cloud.** A jet is an unordered, variable-size set of particles (typically 10–100, average 30–50). Each particle gets a feature vector (17 features on JetClass: kinematics, particle ID, track displacement), embedded to $d=128$ by a 3-layer MLP. No positional encoding, so the model is permutation invariant.

**Pairwise interaction features (new).** For every particle pair $(a,b)$ the model computes four physics quantities — angular distance $\Delta=\sqrt{(y_a-y_b)^2+(\phi_a-\phi_b)^2}$ (rapidity $y$, azimuth $\phi$), $k_T=\min(p_{T,a},p_{T,b})\Delta$, momentum fraction $z=\min(p_{T,a},p_{T,b})/(p_{T,a}+p_{T,b})$, and invariant mass squared $m^2$ — taking logarithms because they are long-tailed. A small pointwise conv net turns these into an interaction matrix $\mathbf{U}$ with one channel per attention head.

**Particle attention blocks.** $L=8$ blocks of "P-MHA": standard multi-head attention with $\mathbf{U}$ added as a bias to the pre-softmax scores,
$$\text{P-MHA}(Q,K,V)=\text{softmax}\!\left(\tfrac{QK^\top}{\sqrt{d_k}}+\mathbf{U}\right)V,$$
plus LayerNorms and an MLP. This lets physics relations steer which particles attend to each other.

**Class attention.** Two class-attention blocks where a learned class token attends to all particles; an MLP + softmax gives class scores. ParT has about 2.14M parameters.

## Data
JetClass, simulated with MadGraph5_aMC@NLO (hard process), Pythia (showering/hadronization) and Delphes with a CMS-like detector; jets clustered with anti-$k_T$, $R=0.8$, $p_T$ 500–1000 GeV, $|\eta|<2$. Ten classes: $q/g$ background, $H\to b\bar b$, $H\to c\bar c$, $H\to gg$, $H\to 4q$, $H\to \ell\nu qq'$, $t\to bqq'$, $t\to b\ell\nu$, $W\to qq'$, $Z\to q\bar q$. 100M jets for training (plus validation and test splits), balanced across classes.

## Training
For one jet: per-particle features → MLP embedding; pairwise features → interaction matrix $\mathbf{U}$; 8 P-MHA blocks; class token attends to particles; 10-way softmax; cross-entropy with the true class. Trained for 1M iterations (~5 epochs over JetClass) with learning rate 0.001, constant for 70% of training then decaying. For fine-tuning on the 2M-jet top-tagging and quark–gluon datasets, the final MLP is replaced and everything is fine-tuned with a small LR (0.0001) for pretrained weights and a larger LR for the new head.

## Results
- JetClass (Table 1): ParT accuracy 0.861, AUC 0.9877 vs ParticleNet 0.844 / 0.9849 and a plain transformer without interaction bias 0.849 / 0.9859; large gains in background rejection on hard classes (e.g. $H\to 4q$, top decays).
- More training data keeps helping (Table 3), justifying a 100M-jet dataset.
- Fine-tuned ParT sets new results on top tagging (accuracy 0.944, AUC 0.9877, background rejection 2766 ± 130 at 30% signal efficiency vs 1771 for fine-tuned ParticleNet and 2195 for LorentzNet) and on quark–gluon tagging.

## Takeaways / questions
- For my work, JetClass is the key piece: 10 classes, 100M jets, up to 128 particles per jet (as used in my tokenizer experiments with $p_T,\eta,\phi$).
- Injecting domain structure as an attention bias is a cheap, general trick (cf. relative position biases in NLP); the plain transformer's gap shows the physics features matter.
- Pretrain-on-JetClass-then-fine-tune is an early "foundation model" signal in HEP, which OmniJet-α later pushes across task types.

On my Spring 2025 LBNL research reading list (with TrackingBERT and OmniJet-α).

## Summary
A short Phys. Rev. D letter from LBNL (Mikuni and Nachman) showing that a jet foundation model is useful for real problems, not just proofs of principle. The model, **OmniLearn**, is described in a companion paper; here it is adapted to three tasks where current methods are limited by data or compute: building taggers on expensive full detector simulation, unfolding (correcting measurements for detector effects), and model-agnostic anomaly detection. In all three it beats training from scratch, and in anomaly detection it finds signals at lower significance than before. (Note: this note's id is "omnilearn", but this arXiv entry is the applications paper that uses OmniLearn, not the method paper itself.)

## Problem
Modern ML architectures in HEP are data hungry, but full detector simulation is slow and experiments cannot simply collect more data. Methods like OmniFold need thousands of retrainings for uncertainties, and anomaly detection trained directly on data is limited by small signal regions. Can a pretrained foundation model cut these costs?

## Related work
- Particle Transformer / JetClass — [2202.03772](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03772): OmniLearn is pretrained on JetClass's 100M jets.
- OmniFold (Andreassen et al.): iterative classifier-based unfolding.
- CATHODE (Hallin et al.): resonant anomaly detection via a sideband-trained generative model; the high-dimensional version (Buhmann et al., [2310.06897](https://arxiv.org/abs/2310.06897)) is the main comparison.
- OmniJet-α — [2403.05618](https://arxiv.org/abs/2403.05618): a contemporaneous, generative-pretraining approach to jet foundation models.

## Method
**OmniLearn (reused from the companion paper).** The backbone is a Point-Edge Transformer (PET), combining attention (global) with dynamic graph convolutions (local structure among particles). A shared PET body feeds two task heads: classification and particle generation. It is pretrained with supervised representation learning on JetClass and has fewer than 2M parameters, so it fits on one GPU. Irrelevant heads are dropped during adaptation.

**Three adaptations (new).**
1. *Expensive simulation*: fine-tune on the ATLAS top-tagging dataset (full detector simulation with pileup, 40M jets), using all data or only 10% (4M).
2. *Unfolding*: use OmniLearn as the classifier inside OmniFold on a Z+jets dataset (Pythia "simulation" vs Herwig "data", Delphes detector), unfolding all particle momenta.
3. *Anomaly detection*: in a CATHODE-style setup on the LHC Olympics R&D dataset, OmniLearn is used twice — its generative head produces a background reference in the signal region, and its classifier distinguishes that reference from data; a Deep Sets layer combines the two leading jets into an event model.

## Results
- ATLAS top tagging: OmniLearn trained on all 40M jets reaches AUC 0.965 and background rejection 207.3 at 50% signal efficiency, beating all previously reported models; with only 4M jets it matches the previous best (ParticleNet, AUC 0.961; rejection 172.1 vs 153.7).
- Unfolding: converges about twice as fast with lower validation loss than training from scratch, and improves physics metrics (e.g. triangular discriminator on $\tau_{21}$ of 0.05 vs 0.13 for the from-scratch PET and 0.53 for DeepSets OmniFold).
- Anomaly detection: non-trivial sensitivity for signal injections above 600 events (initial $S/\sqrt{B}\sim2$), versus above 1400 events ($S/\sqrt{B}\sim4$) in previous full-phase-space work; training from scratch does worse because the signal region has only ~100k events.

## Takeaways / questions
- A useful counterpoint to OmniJet-α: OmniLearn uses *supervised* pretraining on JetClass and stays tiny (<2M parameters), whereas OmniJet-α uses generative next-token pretraining over learned tokens. Which pretraining signal generalizes better is still open.
- Strongest practical argument for HEP foundation models so far: saving full-simulation data and retraining compute, not just leaderboard gains.

notes.markdown:
## My notes
The LBNL group's paper (Andris Huang, Yash Melkani, Xiangyang Ju et al.) that I joined after; I cited it in applications as “the last ML project I am involved with”. It is the first item (“Bert Paper”) on my Spring 2025 research reading list.

*From onenote (2025-02-21):*

*Transcribed from handwritten OneNote ink, "LLM for HEP" notebook › Side research › "Research Paper" (21 Feb 2025).*

### LLM for HEP / Side research / Research Paper — 2025-02-21 (Fri) 10:49
```text
BERT tracking paper (highlighted)
TrackingBERT model -> generalized model to integrate existing HEP [tasks] for particle tracking
  BERT: bidirectional (context from both directions (extra-dimensional context!))
  GPT: autoregressive approach (next word based on words before it)
   ↳ models work well on sequential data (learns data easily, works across different [unsure] tasks, [unsure] data structure)
     ↓
   NLP analogies to particle detector
   -> employed tokenization
   BERT: attention, Adam optimizer
    ↳ future step: more [unsure]
Omni-learning (highlighted): general / foundation model
[empty bracket sketch]
```

## Summary
A short workshop paper from the LBNL "LLM for HEP" group (Xiangyang Ju's group) proposing that particle-detector data can be modeled like language. Every detector module is a word, the set of all modules is the vocabulary, a particle's track (its sequence of hits) is a sentence, and a collision event is a paragraph. With this tokenization, they train a BERT-style model, **TrackingBERT**, using self-supervised objectives on simulated tracks. It learns to predict masked hits almost perfectly and yields learned embeddings of detector modules that could be reused by other tracking tasks.

## Problem
Deep learning is everywhere in LHC tracking, but each model is designed and trained with supervision for a single task, generalizing poorly. LLMs show that self-supervised pretraining on one representation can serve many downstream tasks. What is the "token" for a particle detector, and can a language model learn useful detector representations from tracks?

## Related work
- BERT — [1810.04805](https://arxiv.org/abs/1810.04805): the masked-language-model recipe adapted here.
- Particle Transformer — [2202.03772](https://arxiv.org/abs/2202.03772): evidence that large-scale pretraining and fine-tuning help in HEP.
- Scaling laws (Kaplan et al., 2020) — [2001.08361](https://arxiv.org/abs/2001.08361): motivation that more data and parameters help.
- TrackML challenge data and the Exa.TrkX GNN tracking pipeline: the dataset and a target downstream use.

## Method
**Tokenization (the main idea).** Each detector module gets a unique identifier, and that ID is the token. A track becomes a sequence of module tokens. (Contrast: Llama 2 has a 32k vocabulary, while a real detector has billions of sensors — how to tokenize at full scale is left open.)

**Model.** A BERT encoder with 8 attention heads, embedding dimension 64 and MLP size 512, about 1M parameters. Each input contains two tracks sampled from the training data.

**Two self-supervised tasks** (mirroring BERT's masked-LM and next-sentence prediction):
- *Masked detector modules (MDM)*: some modules in a track are masked and a classification layer predicts which module is missing; the mask rate is increased from 15% to 30% to 50% over training.
- *NTP*: a second classification layer predicts whether track B has higher momentum than track A.

![Figure 1(a) from the paper: layout of the TrackML detector (pixel, long-strip and short-strip subdetectors)](assets/trackingbert/onenote-fig1.png)

## Data
TrackML simulation: $t\bar t$ events with on average 200 pileup interactions overlaid (about 10,000 particles per event), simulated with Pythia. They use only the pixel subdetector volumes 7, 8 and 9 and keep tracks with 4–8 hits, giving about 4 million tracks.

## Training
For one example: two tracks are turned into sequences of module-ID tokens; some tokens are replaced by a mask; the encoder produces contextual embeddings; the MDM head is trained with cross-entropy to recover the masked module IDs and the NTP head with a binary loss on which track has higher momentum. Optimized with Adam plus weight decay for 200 epochs.

## Results
- Masking one module per track on 5000 test tracks, TrackingBERT predicts the exact missing module in 99.8% of cases, and 100% of predictions fall within 20 mm of the true module.
- No significant dependence on track length or on which position in the track is masked.
- Performance improves with larger datasets and models, consistent with scaling laws.

## Takeaways / questions
- This is the group's starting point that my LBNL work grew out of; my tokenizer project shifts from *discrete detector IDs* (natural tokens) to *continuous particle features*, where tokens must be learned (VQ-VAE, as in OmniJet-α).
- Limits stated by the authors: simplified dataset (pixel-only, short tracks); next steps are the OpenData Detector, strip detectors, and testing the learned module embeddings in metric-learning graph construction for Exa.TrkX.
- Open question: vocabulary scaling — billions of sensors cannot each be a token, so some hierarchical or learned tokenization will be needed.
